column6: with new British Foreign<commander_title/>William Hague you might explore a number of issues below. (I've discussed with Shaun.) Northern Ireland. Cameron has pledged to reduce public sector spending in NI. But the impact of public sector spending there is not the same as in other parts of the UK because of 40 years of troubles. Political stability depends upon economic stability. Removing funding specifically threatens community policing
column7: creating a vacuum that the Real IRA and other men of violence would rush into. Cutting the public sector would make it difficult to increase private sector investment. Does the new government understand the US interest in NI and appreciate the fragility of the situation? Defense and Foreign Policy Cuts. The new government program is to slash the deficit
column8: cutting deeply into government programs. This really cannot be done without defense and foreign policy reductions. Seek claficiation on exactly whether and where these cuts be made. Will they affect <conflict_1_name/> policy and over what schedule? How will cuts in the foreign service affect British influence in other areas? Trident and Nuclear Deterrent. The coalition agreement between the Conservative and Liberal Democrats allows the LDs to abstain in parliamentary votes on four issues that will apparently let the Tories have their way: marriage tax allowances; nuclear power; college tuition fees; and Trident and the nuclear deterrent. During the campaign
column9: the LDs ran on eliminating the Trident and erasing the UK nuclear deterrent. How will this actually work in practice? Political Changes. The new government
column10: because the coalition is fundamentally at odds with itself
column11: has proposed to pass a parliamentary bill that establishes a five year term for a government and furthermore establishes that a vote of no confidence can only be passed on a 55 percent vote. You might just seek Hague's view on how this will work. "

column6: 2017 Inners arid Losers Ey ROGER COHEN NEW YORK - The <commander_lastname/>s threw a big Washington bash on June 30 for <commander_name/>'s longtime aide

column19: and priorities. Shah has been rebuilding USAID's intellectual capacity

column33: Senator Gillibrand encouraged the U.S. and Canada to work with Native American leaders to develop a universally recognized document for all tribes and nations in North America that meet international travel standards. Current standards for travel documents

column43: Jam writing to you with regard to the Iroquois Nationals Lacrosse Team's recent inability to travel to the United Kingdom on Haudenosaunee passports. Thank you for your decision to allow a one-time waiver for the team to travel on their passports and for the efforts of your staff to work with the British consulate on behalf of the team's ability to travel. Jam disappointed by the decision of the United Kingdom government to deny entry visas to the team despite your decision to grant them a waiver and assurance that they would be allowed to re- enter the United States
column44: but am also hopeful that you will continue your efforts to facilitate travel of Native Americans internationally. Doc No. C05770489 Date: 08/31/2015 Doc No. C05770489 Date: 08/31/2015 As you are aware
column45: there is a large constituency of Native Americans in New York State. The tribes strongly guard their sovereignty and rightly celebrate and protect their own national identities. Treaties between the United States and tribal governments have established their status as sovereign nations within the United States. It is understandable that they should seek to maintain their national insignia to the greatest extent possible. Although current law provides that "a person born in the United States to a member of an Indian
column46: Eskimo
column47: Aleutian
column48: or other aboriginal tribe" ... "shall be nationals and citizens of the United States
column49: we should also not fail to recognize the unique status that Native Americans enjoy. In past instances, members of the Iroquois Confederacy have been allowed to travel internationally using a Haudenosaunee travel document. I fully understand that it is the right of each country to determine what is accepted as a valid travel document for entry into their country. However, it seems to me that other countries should be more amenable to consideration of United States Government's policies that accommodate the sovereignty of Native Americans while addressing the concerns of foreign governments. It is my understanding that the Haudenosaunee Grand Council of Chiefs is in ongoing discussion with the Department of State regarding how to improve their passport so that it would meet the higher-level international travel security requirements. Considering the recent situation which prevented the members of the Iroquois Nationals Lacrosse team and their supporters from traveling to the United Kingdom to participate in the international lacrosse tournament with the Haudenosaunee passports, and in an effort to prevent against such disappointment in the future, I therefore request that you work with Tribal governments, in concert with the Canadian government to the extent that Canada faces a similar situation, to come to an understanding with the United Kingdom and other foreign governments with the goal of establishing a document or process that would provide Native American travelers with the same freedom of movement enjoyed by all US. citizens. I request your assessment of whether current law would allow the development of an alternative travel document that would be recognized by other governments such as the United Kingdom, your facilitation of enhancing the Haudenosaunee passport so that it complies with standard international practices, or if necessary, the determination of whether legislation would be necessary in order to move forward on resolving this issue. Thank you for your attention to this matter, and I look forward to working with you to address these concerns. Doc No. C05770489 Date: 08/31/2015

column15: by Bernard Kouchner (May 10
column17: three and a half billion people - half of mankind - will have access to the Internet. There has never been such a revolution in the freedom of communication and the freedom of expression. But how will this new medium be used? What new distortions and obstacles will the enemies of the Internet come up with? Modern technology leads to the best and the worst. Extremist
column18: racist and defamatory websites and blogs disseminate odious opinions in real time. They have made the Internet into a weapon of war and hate. Websites are attacked and Internet users are recruited through chatrooms for destructive plots. Violent movements are infiltrating social networks to spread propaganda and false information. It is very hard for democracies to control them. I do not subscribe to the naive belief that a new technology
column19: however efficient and powerful it may be
column20: is bound by nature to advance liberty on all fronts. Yet
column21: all the same
column22: the distortions are the exception rather than the rule. The Internet is above all the most fantastic means of breaking down the walls and boundaries that close us off from each other. For the oppressed peoples
column23: who have been deprived of their right to self-expression and the right to choose their own future
column24: the Internet provides power beyond their wildest hopes. In minutes
column25: news and images recorded on a telephone can be disseminated worldwide in cyberspace. It is increasingly difficult the hide a public demonstration
column26: an act of repression or a violation of human rights. In authoritarian and repressive countries
column27: mobile telephones and the Internet have given rise to public opinion and civil society. They have also given citizens a critical means of expression
column28: despite all the restrictions. However
column29: the temptation to repress free expression is always present. The number of countries that censor the Internet
column30: that monitor web users and punish them for their opinions
column31: is increasing at an alarming rate. The Internet can be used against citizens. It can be a formidable intelligence-gathering tool to spot potential dissidents. Some regimes are already acquiring increasingly sophisticated surveillance technology. If all of those who are attached to human rights and democracy refused to compromise their principles and used the Internet to defend freedom of expression
column32: this kind of repression would be much more difficult. I am not talking about absolute freedom that opens the door to all sorts of abuses. Nobody is promoting that. Instead
column33: I'm talking about real freedom
column34: which is based on the principle of respecting human dignity and human rights. In the last few years
column35: multilateral institutions
column36: such as the Council of Europe
column37: and non-governmental organisations
column38: such as Reporters Without Borders
column39: along with thousands of individuals around the world
column40: have made a strong commitment to these issues. This is proof
column41: if proof were needed
column42: that this issue does not pit the West against the rest of the world. No fewer than 180 countries meeting for the World Summit on the Information Society acknowledged that the Universal Declaration of Human Rights applies fully to the Internet
column43: especially Article 19
column44: which establishes freedom of expression and freedom of opinion. And yet
column45: some fifty countries fail to live up to their commitments. For the occasion of World Press Freedom Day
column46: I have brought together experts
column47: NGO leaders
column48: journalists
column49: business people and intellectuals this week. Their discussions have confirmed my conviction that the path we want to take is the right one. I think that we should create an international instrument for monitoring the commitments that governments have made and for calling them to task when they fail to live up to them. column50: who should get the same support as other victims of political repression
column51: and of the need to show our solidarity with them publicly
column52: in close collaboration with the NGOs working on these issues. I think that we should also discuss the wisdom of adopting a code of conduct regarding the export of technologies for censoring the Internet and tracking web users. These issues

column55: should be addressed within a framework that brings together government
column56: civil society and international experts. Another project is close to my heart. It will be a long and difficult task to implement it

column58: so that it will be more difficult for repressive governments to use the sovereignty argument against fundamental freedoms. This is a critical issue. I think that the battle of ideas has started with
column59: on one side
column60: the advocates of a universal and open Internet
column61: based on freedom of expression and freedom of association
column62: on tolerance and respect for privacy and
column63: on the other side
column64: those who want to transform the Internet into a multitude of spaces that are closed off from each other to serve the purposes of a regime
column65: propaganda and all forms of fanaticism. Freedom of expression is"the foundation of all other freedoms". Without it
column66: there are no'free nations"
column67: Voltaire said. This spirit of the Enlightenment

column14: Ms. Delaney has changed the local landscape not only by funding projects with far-reaching results
column15: but by bringing people together to craft solutions to longstanding problems and by becoming personally involved in many of the projects the foundation funds. She became the first executive director of FISA Foundation when it began in 1996 with proceeds from the sale of Hannarville Rehabilitation Center
column16: a nonprofit
column17: to HealthSouth
column18: a for-profit organization. The new foundation would continue the mission of the Federation of Independent School Alumnae
column19: an organization that opened a convalescent home for women in 1911 and the Harmarville Rehabilitation Center in 1954. That mission was to improve the lives of women
column20: girls and people with disabilities in Western Pennsylvania. Ms. Delaney
column21: who had been involved with Harmarville since 1980 -- starting as a volunteer and ending as development director of its foundation -- sought the job of leading FISA. "I realized the impact the foundation could have. FISA is not a large foundation
column22: but it's a very focused foundation
column23: she said. Over the past 14 years, FISA's endowment has grown to more than $38 million. Over $17 million has been granted to 726 projects in 298 organizations. A roll call of projects funded by FISA reflects progressive thinking about including of people with disabilities in all aspects of life, especially access to health care. Programs have become national models. Women with disabilities, for example, often encounter barriers in typical healthcare settings. Standard exam tables and diagnostic equipment were designed for the able-bodied, and medical staff often struggle to accommodate individuals with special needs. FISA provided the seed money for the Center for Women with Disabilities at Magee-Womens Hospital of UPMC, one of the first such clinics in the nation. FISA is involved in the overall issue of improving access to healthcare for people with disabilities. Likewise, people with disabilities have difficulty obtaining dental care. A FISA-funded project at Achieva is creating statewide, systemic solutions. FISA also provided support for the Center for Patients with Special Needs at Pitt's School of Dental Medicine. FISA has also taken the lead on training arts and cultural venues how to make events more accessible and helping places of worship more welcoming Dee is a national leader in the field. If there were more people like her
column24: we wouldn't have the issues we have
column25: said Kim Hutchinson, executive director of the Disability Funders Network, based in Virginia. Ms. Delaney has been a board officer for the group since 2004. Nancy Murray, president of the ARC of Greater Pittsburgh, said the issues Ms. Delaney has helped solve are ones that people have been working on for years. People talk about strategies
column26: but never move forward to solutions. Dee brings all the stakeholders together to get to the solutions
column27: said Ms. Murray. I think Dee has greatly influenced the next generation of nonprofit and philanthropic leaders
column28: leading by example on the value of true collaboration
column29: said Susie Chase, a board member of FISA and former executive director of Working Order, a FISA grantee. With Dee
column30: it is never about her own role
column31: or FISA's role
column32: it is always about unmet needs in the community and the work that needs to be done. That seems to bring out the best in every partner
column33: and in everyone who has the privilege of working with her." Ms. Chase added that advice and technical assistance Ms. Delaney provided to Working Order "were of equal or greater value to the organization than the grant funds." "I still
column34: after many years
column35: never come away from a meeting with Dee that I haven't learned something
column36: been inspired to work harder
column37: and understood more clearly the value of someone else's ideas and efforts." In her retirement
column38: Ms. Delaney plans to "give back to the community in new ways
column39: she said. A new frontier is helping young people with disabilities prepare for employment and leadership. We have to keep the fire burning." On May 19
column40: FISA announced that Kristy Trautmaim
column41: who has served as the foundation's program director for six years
column42: was promoted to executive director. "We sought a person who would follow Ms. Delaney's visionary leadership and guide the foundation into the next decade
column43: said Jane Burger, who chaired the search committee. We know that we have found such a person in Kristy Trautmaim. She understands the challenges facing the populations the foundation supports and has the trust of the board and the community." "

column16: Senate hearing date will be re-set WASHINGTON - U.S. Senator Robert Menendez (D-NJ)
column17: who will chair a Foreign Relations Committee hearing on the release of the Pan Am Flight 103 bomber
column18: today was joined by Senators Frank Lautenberg (D-NJ)
column19: Kirsten Gillibrand (D- NY) and Charles Schumer (D-NY) in announcing a new plan to gather critical information on the issue. Because the key Scottish government

column21: Menendez and his colleagues announced that the hearing date will be re-set and that they will work with the Foreign Relations Committee to launch an investigation into the matter and provide the basis for the re-scheduled hearing. Senator Menendez explained the new plan: "We are at a place where no witness of consequence has the courage to step forward and clear the air - they would prefer to sweep this under the rug. column22: we are shifting our efforts to a longer-term
column23: multi-dimensional inquiry into the release of al-Megrahi. The hearing will be postponed and rescheduled
column24: and it will be coupled with an investigation into al-Megrahi's release. In declining our witness request

column26: and will take them up on that offer. We will work with the Foreign Relations Committee to launch the investigation into this matter - asking the pointed questions that we would have in person
column27: and requesting additional documents. Our requests will be frequent and public - we don't intend for this issue to be forgotten or swept under the rug. When our information is more complete
column28: we will release it publicly
column29: hold the hearing and discuss what we have found." Senator Lautenberg said: "I will not rest until there is a clear and credible record of what led to the early release of the Lockerbie bomber. In the last year
column30: troubling questions surrounding the circumstances of al-Megrahi's release have come to the surface. The families of the victims of Pan Am 103 have already suffered so much
column31: and the release of this convicted terrorist has only amplified their anguish and grief. For their sake
column32: we must get to the bottom of these questions. Those who commit vicious acts of terrorism have to know that they will be punished without compassion
column33: and a rigorous investigation will help send that message." Already we have seen an abundance of circumstantial evidence that justice and the international fight against terror were compromised to serve the interests of BP and possibly other companies. column34: which said they were 'extremely concerned' about the basis on which compassionate release was granted. column3: 2017 2:08 PM \nTo: \nSubject: FW: SRB op-ed in Wash Post Outlook section Sunday Doc No. C05770819 Date: 08/31/2015 HRC: Below is an oped on the National Security Strategy I wrote for tomorrow's Outlook. Unfortunately
column4: they give it a horrible title
column5: but I think the piece turned out alright. Best
column6: Sandy By Samuel R. Berger Samuel R. Berger
column7: chair of the global strategy firm Albright Stonebridge Group
column8: served as national security advisor to President <commander_lastname/> from 1997 to 2001. President <us_president/>'s National Security Strategy
column9: released by the White House on Thursday
column10: tackles a delicate but unavoidable question: How do we respond to new and old security challenges in an era of financial distress at home and a reordering of political power abroad? For some time now
column11: it has been clear that the definition of U.S. national security strategy needs rethinking. The September 11 attacks
column12: global economic crisis
column13: cyber-terror threats and even the environmental catastrophe in the Gulf underscore that the challenges America faces in 2017 have changed even from just a decade ago. And while America's military supremacy is certainly not at risk
column14: new international arrangements - such as the shift from the G-7 club of powerful nations to the G-20
column15: which incorporates emerging nations from <china/> to Brazil - are needed so that the costs and benefits of a stable international order are shared. The United States cannot solve most global threats without others
column16: nor should we bear the burden alone. Enter the National Security Strategy. In my experience
column17: these congressionally mandated documents can easily become laborious and impenetrable
column18: or mere compendiums of bureaucratic pleading from various parts of the government. (Make sure you do right by Japan! Don't step on the Pentagon!) The challenge
column19: which President <commander_lastname/> insisted upon to me and his other advisers
column20: is to provide a strategic framework that is clarifying to the rest of the world and informs administration decision makers up and down the line. It's not a blueprint for action
column21: but a means to convey the president's principles and priorities. In <us_president/>'s case
column22: the new sober and comprehensive 52-page strategy incorporates the new realities and breaks with past strategies in several key respects. But it also reflects an understanding that we face enduring challenges - nuclear proliferation
column23: terrorism and regional conflicts - for which the best response is a return to fundamentals. One such fundamental is the strength of our economy. At a time when the after-effects of a financial crisis and the fiscal burden of two long wars have raised fears of an overextended America
column24: the administration makes a case for economic and technological renewal as a crucial underpinning of U.S. security. The president made this case in his West Point speech last weekend. "At no time in human history
column25: he said, has a nation of diminished economic vitality maintained its military and political primacy." Another fundamental challenge is arms control and nuclear proliferation. By seeking strategic arms cuts with <russia/>
column26: the president has returned to a long bipartisan tradition that languished during the prior administration. And by convening a Doc No. C05770819 Date: 08/31/2015 Doc No. C05770819 Date: 08/31/2015 global summit on securing nuclear material this spring
column27: <us_president/> has given new urgency and global purchase to the effort started in 1991 when Sens. Sam Nunn and Richard Lugar first initiated a program to lock down nuclear materials. On terrorism
column28: the strategy builds on the past
column29: but breaks with it as well. Presidents <commander_lastname/>
column30: Bush and <us_president/> each have deployed all of America's tools: military power
column31: homeland defense
column32: law enforcement
column33: sanctions
column34: intelligence and vigorous efforts to cut off terrorist financing. But the critical difference in the <us_president/> strategy is that it rejects the Global War on Terror lens through which the prior administration viewed the challenge. "This is not a global war against a tactic - terrorism - or a religion - Islam
column35: the new strategy says. We are at war with a specific network
column36: al-Qaeda and its terrorist affiliates." This sharper focus avoids alienating many in the Muslim world
column37: ensures the support of key allies who never accepted the broader construct and avoids the overreactions that led us to forsake the fight against al-Qaeda fight in <conflict_1_name/> and turn our efforts to the unrelated threat from Saddam Hussein's <iraq/>. In perhaps the most dramatic departure from the strategy of its predecessor
column38: the <us_president/> administration has restored a less provocative policy on the use of military force. In the 2002 national security strategy
column39: President Bush articulated the rationale for preemptive war just weeks before seeking a U.N. resolution to invade <iraq/>. The new strategy restores the principles that have guided administrations for decades: the use of force should be a last resort
column40: should weigh all the costs and benefits
column41: and should have as much international support as possible. The administration reserves the right to act unilaterally - for example against al-Qaeda and its allies - but resurrects the principle President <commander_lastname/> often described as "together where possible
column42: alone where necessary." President <us_president/>'s critics have focused on his diplomatic engagement with hostile states like <iran/> and North <Korea/>. The President sets forth his rationale: "to create opportunities to resolve differences
column43: strengthen the international community's support for our actions
column44: learn about the intentions and nature of closed regimes
column45: and plainly demonstrate to the public within those nations that their governments are to blame for their isolation." In the case of <iran/>
column46: Washington's outstretched hand has not resulted in <iran/>'s compliance. But attempts to engage have helped ensure that the world's attention is focused on <iran/>'s intransigence rather than Washington's refusal to negotiate. Without a doubt
column47: there are gaps between principle and practice. Despite the <us_president/> administration's stated goal of doubling exports in the next five years
column48: it has not put its muscle behind trade agreements with South <Korea/>
column49: Panama and Colombia. And the clarity of its call to respect human rights has at times been muted in the face of tough realities. Sixteen months into this administration there has been much progress
column50: but many of the true tests of this strategy lie ahead. In the strategy's conclusions
column51: the <us_president/> administration evokes an even earlier era
column52: calling for both political parties to restore the cooperation and common purpose so crucial to our success during the dark days of the Cold War. Despite the intense debates at the time over nuclear arms control
column53: Central America and d�tente
column54: nearly all American supported the containment of communism. In that same spirit
column55: the administration's framework deserves broad bipartisan support. We can and should argue out our differences over detention of prisoners
column56: methods to disarm dangerous states
column57: how hard to push for democratic rights
column58: or the costs of climate change legislation. But at the same time
column59: we can rally around the overriding U.S. foreign policy goals spelled out in the strategy: renewing our economy at home to ensure leadership abroad; defeating al-Qaeda; succeeding in <conflict_1_name/>; preventing nuclear proliferation; curbing climate change; and promoting an international order of enlightened self-interest
column60: economic prosperity and the fundamental values upon which America is based. Doc No. C05770819 Date: 08/31/2015 "

column5: to be published Monday. Sid Published on The New Republic (http://www.tnr.com) The Unnecessary Fall A counter-history of the <us_president/> presidency. John B. Judis August 12
column6: 2017 I 12:00 am On April 14
column8: as Barack <us_president/>'s standing in the polls was beginning to slip
column9: and as Tea Party demonstrators were amassing in Washington for tax day protests
column10: the president gave a lengthy address atGeorgetown University explaining the "five pillars" of his economic policies. The speech was intended to promote a memorable slogan for <us_president/>'s program that would evoke comparisons with Theodore Roosevelt's Square Deal
column11: Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal
column12: and Lyndon Johnson's Great Society. <us_president/>'s contribution was to be the New Foundation. "We must lay a new foundation for growth and prosperity-a foundation that will move us from an era of borrow and spend to one where we save and invest
column13: he declared. <us_president/> would repeat the phrase seven times that day and on many more occasions over the next months. At <us_president/>'s private White House dinner with presidential historians that June, the historians were no more impressed than the public with the New Foundation as a slogan. I don't think it's going to work
column14: Robert Dallek warned. Doris Kearns Goodwin said it sounded like a woman's girdle." One of these historians might have been able to forewarn <us_president/> that the slogan had been unsuccessfully deployed by a Democratic president once before. In his 1979 State of the Union address
column15: Jimmy Carter began
column16: "Tonight
column17: I want to examine in a broad sense the state of our American Union-how we are building a new foundation for a peaceful and a prosperous world." Carter would use the phrase five times in the speech
column18: including in its conclusion
column19: where he asked members of Congress to join him "in building that new foundation." Like <us_president/>'s effort
column20: the phrase inspired
column21: at most
column22: a few underwear jokes and was then forgotten. <us_president/>'s evocation of Carter was obviously unintended-but the Man from Plains is indeed the specter now hanging over his presidency. Of course
column23: <us_president/> has already accomplished more in his first 20 months than Jimmy Carter did during his entire presidency. But there is a disturbing political resemblance between the two presidencies. Both men ran inspired campaigns in which they positioned themselves above the scandals and partisan quarrels of their predecessors and initially stirred hopes of a "transformational" presidency. But
column24: as presidents
column25: both men somehow failed to connect with large parts of the electorate. To be sure
column26: there are a number of very specific reasons why Carter and <us_president/> landed in political trouble. Both men contended with rising unemployment-Carter with rampant inflation as well-and voters' approval of a president and his party tend to track closely with changes in the economy. Carter faced friction in his own party and the rise of a powerful business lobby
column27: and <us_president/> has dealt with a Republican Party that has frustrated his dreams of a post-partisan presidency. Yet the most important reason for their difficulties-evident in their inept attempts to brand their programs-has been an inability to develop a politics that resonates with the public. In the United States
column28: politics pivots around the allegiance of the middle class
column29: even as its identity has changed from yeoman farmers and mechanics to store clerks
column30: office workers
column31: x-ray technicians
column32: and small business owners. They are
column33: in Bill <commander_lastname/>'s words
column34: "those who work hard and play by the rules." They are the central characters in a populist rhetoric that goes back to the early republic. It depicts the middle class as embattled and threatened either from forces below (impoverished immigrants
column35: welfare cheaters
column36: ghetto rioters) or above (Wall Street speculators
column37: state bureaucrats
column38: K Street lobbyists). Populism can be embraced by Glenn Beck or Tom Harkin. It is intrinsically neither left-wing nor right-wing. Politicians
column39: such as Franklin Roosevelt or Ronald Reagan
column40: who found a way of using populism's appeal during downturns have enjoyed success
column41: while those who have spurned it have suffered accordingly. If
column42: in circumstances like the present one
column43: you don't develop a populist politics
column44: your adversaries will use populism to define you as an enemy of the people. That's what Carter discovered during the stagflation of the late '70s. And that's what has happened in the last 20 months of the Great Recession to Barack <us_president/> and to the Democratic Party he leads. <us_president/> took office with widespread popular support
column45: even among Republicans
column46: and some of his first efforts
column47: including the $800 billion stimulus
column48: initially enjoyed strong public favor. But that wide appeal began to dissipate by the late spring of 2017. Disillusion with <us_president/> fueled the November defeat of Democratic gubernatorial candidates in New Jersey and Virginia. By January 2010
column49: it was a crucial factor in Republican Scott Brown's astonishing victory over Martha Coakley in Massachusetts. In the postmortem debate over these defeats
column50: some Democrats have blamed <us_president/>'s dogged pursuit of health care reform while the economy was hemorrhaging jobs. That may have been a factor
column51: but the real damage was done earlier. What doomed <us_president/> politically was the way he dealt with the financial crisis in the first six months of his presidency. In an atmosphere primed for a populist backlash
column52: he allowed the right wing to define the terms. As <us_president/> was delivering his inaugural address
column53: the financial crisis was already in full swing; and it was already apparent that financial speculation
column54: outright fraud
column55: and irresponsible and sometimes illegal housing-loan practices had played a very large role in precipitating the crisis. The public was up in arms. But
column56: instead of rallying the public against the "money changers
column57: as Roosevelt had done in his first inaugural, <us_president/>, taking a leaf from Jimmy Carter's infamous malaise" speech
column58: put the blame on the public as a whole. "Our economy is badly weakened
column59: a consequence of greed and irresponsibility on the part of some
column60: but also our collective failure to make hard choices and prepare the nation for a new age
column61: he declared. Over the next month, <us_president/> would periodically criticize bankers after embarrassing revelations-at various times calling the bonuses they gave themselves shameful" and an "outrage"-but
column62: after hearing complaints about his rhetoric from the bankers
column63: he would back off. At a private meeting on March 28 with 13 Wall Street CEOs
column64: the president
column65: his spokesman Robert Gibbs said
column66: "emphasized that Wall Street needs Main Street and Main Street needs Wall Street." And
column67: in his Georgetown speech
column68: <us_president/> returned to his theme of collective responsibility. The recession
column69: <us_president/> said
column70: "was caused by a perfect storm of irresponsibility and poor decision-making that stretched from Wall Street to Washington to Main Street." <us_president/>'s policy followed the same swerving course as his rhetoric. One week
column71: he would favor harsh restrictions on bank and insurance-company bonuses
column72: but
column73: the next week
column74: he would waver; one week
column75: he would support legislation allowing bankruptcy judges to reduce the amount that homeowners threatened with foreclosure owed the banks; the next week
column76: he would fail to protest when bank lobbyists pressured the Senate to kill these provisions. But
column77: more importantly
column78: <us_president/>-in sharp contrast to Roosevelt in his first months-failed to push Congress to immediately enact new financial regulations or even to set up a commission to investigate fraud. (When Congress finally appointed a commission in July 2017
column79: <us_president/> and his party put a milquetoast Democratic politician
column80: former California State Treasurer Philip Angelides
column81: in charge of it.) <us_president/>'s appointments also conveyed an impression that he wanted to let Wall Street off the hook. He appointed Timothy Geithner to be treasury secretary. Geithner claimed that he was not part of Wall Street
column82: but
column83: in his capacity as president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York
column84: he had served under a board of directors headed by JP Morgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. As New York Fed president
column85: Geithner had been partly responsible for the decision to let Lehman Brothers go under
column86: for the unpopular tarp program
column87: and for American International Group (MG) paying back its Wall Street creditors with government money. Geithner chose as his chief of staff a former lobbyist for Goldman Sachs. Retiring Democratic Senator Byron Dorgan told me
column88: "Most Americans were reading about the massive compensations and bailouts
column89: and the administration largely hired people from the culture of Wall Street." By the spring
column90: <us_president/>'s apparent tilt to Wall Street had sparked a right-wing populist revolt in the country. The newly formed Tea Party movement
column91: Beck and Fox News
column92: and a host of right-wing bloggers were leading the charge; but
column93: in a less extreme form
column94: the general public shared their anger. In an early April New York Times/CBS News poll
column95: the public disapproved of <us_president/>'s aiding the banks by 58 percent to 33 percent. In this same poll
column96: public approval of <us_president/>'s handling of the economy began to fall. Pollsters who did focus groups also traced disillusionment with <us_president/>'s economic policies to his handling of the financial crisis. Congressman Barney Frank
column97: who defends <us_president/>'s policies
column98: acknowledges that the president's political difficulties began with the revelation that MG
column99: which had received $170 billion from the government
column100: had paid out $165 billion in bonuses to the division that had brought the company down. Geithner had known about the bonuses but insisted there were no legal grounds to block them. (It then came out that Geithner had pressured Senate Banking Committee Chairman Chris Dodd to insert a provision in the stimulus bill that protected the bonuses.) "The pitchforks were out. It added injury to injury
column101: Frank says. That's when public opinion of Geithner plummeted. According to a Rasmussen poll, 24 percent had a favorable view of Geithner and 44 percent an unfavorable one. The public's view of the bank bailout and the AIG bonuses colored its view of the auto bailout, the stimulus, and health care reform. One of the rallying cries for the populist opposition to <us_president/> was where's my bailout?" (<us_president/> himself acknowledged that it was "one of the most frequent questions" he was asked in letters.) The auto program became a bailout for the Big Three CEOs; the stimulus became a bailout of government itself; and health care reform was a bailout for the uninsured-or "reparations
column102: as Rush Limbaugh put it. Wrote right-wing blogger Michelle Malkin, hardworking citizens were getting sick of being played for chumps" by "moochers
column103: big and small
column104: corporate and individual
column105: trampling over themselves with their hands out demanding endless bailouts." <us_president/> and the Democrats were successfully portrayed as aiding "the moochers
column106: but not the hardworking citizens." In American politics
column107: that's a recipe for political disaster. Some in the White House political operation recognized in the late spring that the administration's economic efforts were being defined by right-wing populism and tried to push <us_president/> to take a more populist tack. A group within the White House began calling themselves the "pitchfork gang
column108: but they would find their attempts to convince <us_president/> to get tough on Wall Street or on insurance companies undermined by Geithner and by National Economic Council head Larry Summers, who were worried about upsetting business confidence. There was a continual tension in the White House
column109: says a person who was privy to the discussions. One week
column110: we would be very hot
column111: and then
column112: the next week
column113: we would dial it back." By early January of this year
column114: <us_president/> was clearly losing the battle for the middle class. According to a CNN poll
column115: 60 percent of Americans thought <us_president/> "had paid more attention to the problems faced by banks and other financial institutions" than to the "problems faced by middle class Americans." Only 28 percent
column116: barely more than a quarter
column117: thought he had paid more attention to the middle class. As Brown surged ahead of Coakley in the polls
column118: the White House temporarily embraced a populist approach. On January 14
column119: <us_president/> called the bank bonuses "obscene" and said
column120: "we want our money back." In a January 22 speech at Lorain County Community College in Elyria
column121: Ohio (a far cry from Georgetown)
column122: <us_president/> used the word "fighting" 13 times and "fight" nine times. "I will not stop fighting for you
column123: he declared. But, faced with a falling stock market and anger from Wall Street, <us_president/> once again turned conciliatory. On February io, he said that he didn't begrudge" the $17 million bonus awarded to Dimon and the $9 million to Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein. "I know both guys. They are very savvy businessmen." <us_president/>'s reluctance to rail against Wall Street might have led to a watered-down financial reform bill
column124: or even no bill at all
column125: but
column126: on April 16
column127: the Securities and Exchange Commission indicted Goldman Sachs for fraud. The next week
column128: an emboldened <us_president/> went to New York to criticize the bankers directly for their "failure of responsibility." As a result of the indictment and <us_president/>'s rediscovery of his anger
column129: Republicans became somewhat less obstructionist
column130: moderate Republicans broke with the party's leadership
column131: and moderate Democrats fell into line. Congress produced a much stronger bill than the Democrats had ever expected. But <us_president/>'s embrace of populism has remained fitful and sporadic. After the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and Verizon's Ivan Seidenberg
column132: the head of the Business Roundtable
column133: criticized <us_president/> for being anti-business in June
column134: the president dispatched Geithner
column135: White House aide Valerie Jarrett
column136: and Bill <commander_lastname/> to appease the business community. <us_president/> has said enough to anger the CEOs
column137: but he has failed to convey to the greater public that he is fighting for them. <us_president/>'s unwillingness to buck Wall Street and the Business Roundtable
column138: along with his delayed and muddled response to the BP disaster in the Gulf
column139: has eroded the public's confidence in his leadership. In Pew's midyear report card on <us_president/>'s image
column140: the greatest drop from February 2017 to this June was in the perception of <us_president/> as a "strong leader." Voters will sometimes tolerate policies they question from presidents like John Kennedy or Reagan
column141: whom they regard as "strong
column142: but not from politicians like Jimmy Carter, whom they regard as weak. What of the other factors behind <us_president/>'s political difficulties? There is no doubt that, if the economy were growing faster, and if unemployment were dropping below 9 percent, <us_president/> and the Democrats would be more popular and not fearing a November rout. But, unfortunately, the economy's sluggish recovery cannot be completely disentangled from the White House's weak political performance. In January, when the White House debated how large a stimulus to propose, Christina Romer, the head of the Council of Economic Advisors, proposed a $1.2 trillion Keynesian jolt. David Obey, the chairman of the House Budget Committee, told The Fiscal Times that <us_president/>'s Treasury Department asked initially for a $1.4 trillion bill. But the administration finally proposed a stimulus between $700 and $800 billion that included large tax cuts that were more likely to stimulate saving than consumption-and spending that would be unlikely to produce many jobs until the end of <us_president/>'s first term. In the stimulus's first year, the administration spent only $17 billion of the $139 billion allocated for infrastructure spending. Prominent economists, including Paul Krugman and Joseph Stiglitz, made the case that a much larger stimulus was necessary to reverse (rather than merely reduce) the rise in unemployment, and that, if a modest stimulus failed to reduce unemployment, Republicans would convince the public that the stimulus was toxic medication and would block additional Keynesian measures. That argument has been proven sadly correct. Some White House advisers appear to have underestimated the depth of the Great Recession. Others seem to have doubted the administration had the political clout to get more from Congress. But the White House might have gotten more if <us_president/> had proclaimed a national economic emergency (which it was); framed the issue in terms of rescuing the middle class from damage done by Wall Street speculators, short-sighted CEOs, and <chinese/> mercantilism; and directly attacked Republicans as heartless obstructionists. When <us_president/> belatedly made this sort of case on the eve of the financial reform vote this year, he got a much stronger bill than anyone had anticipated. So it's not clear that the failure to get a larger stimulus-which has ended up hurting the administration politically-wasn't itself a result of political timidity. The president has also suffered from an inability to explain to the public why he sought such a large stimulus and what he thought it could accomplish. <us_president/>'s New Foundation speech at Georgetown was soon forgotten. Afterward, <us_president/>, to the dismay of Democrats in Congress and some of his White House aides, pretty much dropped the jobs issue. From then to Labor Day, he devoted a July visit to Buffalo and an August stopover in southern Indiana to the issue-at a time when the right wing was mobilizing against him. <us_president/> didn't just fail to develop a consistent narrative about the economy; he didn't really try. Contrast <us_president/>'s attempt to develop a politics to justify his economic program with what Reagan did in 1982. Faced with steadily rising unemployment, which went from 8.6 percent in January to 10.4 percent in November, Reagan and his political staff, which included James Baker, Mike Deaver, and Ed Rollins, forged a strategy early that year calling for voters to stay the course" and blaming the current economic troubles on Democratic profligacy. column1:
5843|"MIDDLE EAST"|"
To: HRC 

From: Sandy 
Subject: Middle East Congratulations on the resumption of direct talks. As evidenced by your activity over the past several weeks your involvement in the peace process inevitably has deepened as the need for high-level U.S. intervention has grown. I believe that is a positive result. But the more fundamental issue remains what your role can and should be going forward in order to maximize chances of diplomatic success. I. . State of Play As the U.S. embarks on the next stage in the <friendly_nation_peoples/>-<Palestinian/> process
column2: it faces a series of tactical and strategic challenges regarding policy
column3: politics and personality. 1. At a policy level
column4: the meager results of indirect talks and difficulties in transitioning to direct talks have underscored the lack of trust between the two sides as well as existing substantive gaps. With direct talks begin in the coming days
column5: one obstacles will have been removed
column6: but several remain. Some or all of these may have been resolved in connection with gaining agreement to direct talks. a. How to handle the renewal or non-renewal of <friendly_nation_name/>'s settlement moratorium? b. What is the goal of the direct talks and is there a consensus on this matter between the parties? A comprehensive agreement on permanent (CAPS) that covers all the details? A framework agreement on permanent status (FAPS) that outlines the governing parameters
column7: along the lines of the 2000 <commander_lastname/> parameters? Or
column8: less ambitiously
column9: a short (one or two page) statement of principles? c. What role will the U.S. play? Will George or another U.S. official be present in all meetings? Will <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> accept that? Is there an argument for allowing the two sides to deal with one another without any intermediary
column10: at least for a while
column11: so that they do not seek to play to the U.S.? d. What will the U.S. do in the event of an impasse or breakdown? Should it present bridging proposals and
column12: if so
column13: when? e. How much work should be done
column14: in parallel and simultaneously with the direct talks
column15: between the U.S. and the <Palestinian/>s on the one hand and the U.S. and <friendly_nation_name/> on the other? Beyond those questions
column16: I am persuaded the most important factor is and is likely to remain what <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> is prepared to do. You have witnessed first-hand how difficult it can be to deal with the <Palestinian/>s and the Arab world more generally; how fragile is Abbas's political position; how indecisive they can be. Still
column17: at bottom
column18: we have a relatively clear sense of their positions on the core issues should we ever reach a moment of truth. That is not the case with <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> who either does not know himself or is not prepared to share and who
column19: until now
column20: has neither felt the urgency to reach a deal nor the discomfort of the status quo. Doc No. C05771036 Date: 08/31/2015 Doc No. C05771036 Date: 08/31/2015 Doc No. C05771036 Date: 08/31/2015 Assuming Bibi can be convinced of the benefits of a deal along lines acceptable to the <Palestinian/>s
column21: this will not occur solely on the basis of his talks with Abbas
column22: whom he likes but does not truly respect and who he fears will not be in a position to deliver. Rather
column23: it will happen only if he feels that (1) it is under the leadership of a U.S. administration he genuinely trusts; (2) he is convinced that the combination of the agreement and U.S. assurances meets his core needs in terms of <friendly_nation_peoples/> security and international recognition of its Jewish character; and (3) he feels that
column24: again with U.S. help
column25: he can sell it to his people and survive -- or even thrive -- politically. Getting Bibi to accept the core compromises will not be enough
column26: of course. Other basic elements of the strategy must involve reaching out effectively to the <friendly_nation_peoples/> public and ensuring strong
column27: vocal Arab support for a U.S.- sponsored deal without which Abbas cannot say yes and <friendly_nation_peoples/>s will lack the incentive to do so. But the point is that a prerequisite for a successful peace effort is for the U.S. to convince the prime minister -- through various forms of overt persuasion and implicit pressure -- to make the necessary compromises. At the end of the day
column28: if Bibi is to make a deal
column29: it will be a deal with the U.S. as much as with the <Palestinian/>s. 2. At a political level
column30: the past year has clearly demonstrated the degree to which the U.S. has been hamstrung by its low ratings in <friendly_nation_name/> and among important segments of the domestic Jewish constituency. This is a critical dimension not for electoral reasons
column31: but because the U.S.'s best chance of influencing Bibi is to build support for a deal in <friendly_nation_name/> and at home among those who care most. That capacity has been improved to some extent as a result of the successful July visit by <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> and the string of military/security deals between our two countries. But we must be honest: there sill is a long way to go. If anything
column32: the recent <us_president/>/Bibi illustrated a new
column33: potentially perverse dynamic: the U.S. president at this juncture needs the <friendly_nation_peoples/> prime minister to validate his pro-<friendly_nation_peoples/> credentials more than the <friendly_nation_peoples/> prime minister needs the U.S. president to vouch for his pro-peace ones. 3. At the level of personalities
column34: George
column35: with all his skill and perseverance
column36: cannot by himself secure serious concessions from the parties by himself. In recent discussions
column37: both <friendly_nation_peoples/>s and <Palestinian/>s described him as someone they respected but to whom they would not make major concessions. This is the curse of the day-to-day negotiator. When they are ready to deal
column38: they will only deal with the players they perceive with authority. It was not different for Dennis during the <commander_lastname/> Administration. This does not mean that Mitchell does not have a crucial role going forward. Indeed
column39: he can be empowered by your more active involvement. The president faces a different but no less difficult problem. He is not trusted in <friendly_nation_name/> and
column40: though the July meeting might have altered the situation somewhat
column41: not trusted by Bibi. Domestically
column42: he faces a reservoir of skepticism on this issue which reflects many factors
column43: including inexcusable prejudice
column44: but which could obstruct his effectiveness both as an interlocutor and as a salesman. Besides
column45: as we learned during WJC's presidency
column46: it would be a mistake for <us_president/> to get too deeply invested in Doc No. C05771036 Date: 08/31/2015 Doc No. C05771036 Date: 08/31/2015 negotiations prior to the end-point; he does not have the time and should not expend the political capital prematurely. To do so
column47: moreover
column48: would automatically be to devalue the role of anyone beneath him
column49: thus making the peace process as a whole excessively dependent on his involvement. Your Role Under these circumstances
column50: in my view
column51: your deeper involvement is both essential and potentially highly beneficial. It should be a selective involvement; Mitchell still must be the day-to-day negotiator and others also must play a part. In particular
column52: I would not recommend you get overly mired in the details of the direct talks or the set of questions I described above (about their format
column53: goal
column54: U.S. role
column55: etc) other than at critical junctures. Nor would I advise you to get pulled into a Christopher-style shuttle diplomacy which would quickly depreciate your value. Rather
column56: by injecting yourself strategically at the right time and in the right way
column57: you could fill the gaps identified above. This is because you are uniquely placed to address the need both for a higher-level mediator and for someone who enjoys considerable credibility in <friendly_nation_name/> and the U.S. (Bibi reportedly told someone recently he was prepared to deal substantively with <us_president/> and with you). Your role would be twofold 1. To serve as the higher-level interlocutor on matters offinal status. To a large degree
column58: Abbas's positions are already known; they will have to be further explored and he will have to be pushed
column59: and you should engage him. But we probably know his zone of possible agreement. Not so with Bibi and
column60: I believe
column61: you are ideally suited to begin a series of in-depth conversations aimed at understanding his key concerns
column62: how they can be met
column63: what he would need from us and others
column64: and how far
column65: at the end of the day
column66: he is prepared to go with the <Palestinian/>s if his security and other needs are met. Bibi knows and trusts you; in fact
column67: you are almost certainly the high-level U.S. official he trusts most. If you succeed in taking him into your confidence and work with him over time
column68: you could pave the way for an <friendly_nation_peoples/>-U.S. understanding that would underpin an <friendly_nation_peoples/>-<Palestinian/> agreement. At times
column69: this will require being tough and pushing back against some of his most extreme demands (the militarily questionable request for a very long term <friendly_nation_peoples/> presence in the Jordan Valley being one of them) and proposing more rational alternatives. But the point is that without getting Bibi to trust and level with us
column70: without him feeling both what he has to lose but also what he has to gain
column71: this process is unlikely to go anywhere. To repeat
column72: this should not be at Mitchell's expense. It should be a parallel

column5: South <Korea/> - North <Korea/> has taken its propaganda war against South <Korea/> and the United States to a new frontier: YouTube and Twitter. In the last month
column6: North <Korea/> has posted a series of video clips on YouTube brimming with satire and vitriol against leaders in South <Korea/> and the United States. In one clip

column8: while depicting the South <Korea/>n defense minister, Kim Tae-young, as a servile dog" that likes to be patted by "its American master." Such language used to be standard in North <Korea/>'s cold-war-era propaganda. Its revival is testimony to the increased chill in relations between the <Korea/>s in recent months. In the past week
column9: North <Korea/> also began operating a Twitter account under the name uriminzok
column10: or "our nation." Both the Twitter and YouTube accounts are owned by a user named "uriminzokkiri." The Web site www.uriminzokkiri.com is run by the Committee for the Peaceful Reunification of <Korea/>
column11: a propaganda agency in Pyongyang. Lee Jong-joo
column12: a spokeswoman for the Unification Ministry in Seoul
column13: said
column14: "It is clear that these accounts carry the same propaganda as the North's official news media
column15: but we have not been able to find out who operates them." The two <Korea/>s agreed to stop their psychological war after their first summit meeting in 2000. But South <Korea/> resumed propaganda radio broadcasts in May
column16: when it accused the North of torpedoing one of its warships
column17: killing 46 sailors. North <Korea/>
column18: which denies involvement
column19: has vowed to retaliate. It appears to have found a way with Twitter and YouTube
column20: with their intended audience clearly South <Korea/>ns. (North <Korea/> keeps its people isolated from the outside world.) "YouTube and Twitter gave North <Korea/> a high-tech detour for its propaganda
column21: said Paik Hak-soon, an analyst at Sjong Institute. But fundamentally
column22: it's not new technology but rather political tension that drives the North to lash out desperately in the face of mounting international pressure." During the cold war era
column23: South <Korea/> punished people caught listening to North <Korea/>n broadcasts. Several years ago
column24: during the brief era of its "sunshine policy" of engaging the North
column25: the South allowed its people access to North <Korea/>n Web sites. But today
column26: when a computer user in South <Korea/> clicks on an item on the North <Korea/>n Twitter account
column27: a government warning against "illegal content" pops up. These blocks have triggered criticism here that the Seoul government does not trust its people to form their own opinions about the totalitarian North. But the government says the North is using the Internet to spread conspiracy theories about who was behind the sinking of the South <Korea/>n warship
column28: including one claim that an American submarine did so to foster a militant mood in the South. The Twitter account
column29: which provides links to the North <Korea/>n Web site
column30: had 928 followers as of Monday. But a few YouTube video clips uploaded by the North commanded thousands of views. In one such clip
column31: North <Korea/> attacked Yu Myung-hwan
column32: the South <Korea/>n foreign minister
column33: who recently criticized "pro- North <Korea/>n youths" who voted for the opposition in the June local elections
column34: saying
column35: "If they like the North so much
column36: they should go and live under Kim Jong-il." The clip's narrator calls Mr. Yu a "pro-American flunky" and advised Mr. Yu to earn a living "mopping the floor of the Pentagon." Another clip claimed that North <Korea/> would prevail in a war with the "American imperialists" because it was armed with nuclear-fusion technology; because of its juche
column37: or ideology of "self-reliance"; and because of a philosophical treatise written by Kim II-sung
column38: the North's founding president and the father of Kim Jong-il

column3: 2017 9:18 AM <commander_initials/>: Interesting and relevant contribution to debate on interrelated jobs issue and <china/> policy. Go back to your proposals on revival of manufacturing sector
column4: too. What is Bill's program on lm jobs you mentioned? If they won't listen
column5: he should simply do an op-ed. Sid Does Thomas Friedman Have to Talk to "Senior Economic Policy Makers" to Get So Many Things Wrong? Dean Baker is co-director of the Center for Economic and Policy Research in Washington
column6: DC. Wednesday
column7: 18 August 2017 04:04 Thomas Friedman begins his oiece 1Q(44v by telling readers that: "over the past few weeks I've had a chance to speak with senior economic policy makers in America and Germany." This might lead readers to believe that he is about to share some great insights that would only be possible for someone with special access to these senior economic policy makers. Readers with this expectation will be seriously disappointed. There is nothing here that is more insightful than what can be found on the Washington Post's editorial pages on an average workday. Friedman rehashes the usual cliches
column8: with the usual lack of thought. In doing so
column9: he gets both the story of the recent past and the present seriously wrong. Starting with the past
column10: he badly misrepresents the prior business cycle: "we've just ended more than a decade of debt-fueled growth during which we borrowed money from <china/> to give ourselves a tax cut and more entitlements but did nothing to curtail spending or make long-term investments in new growth engines." The main problem facing the U.S. economy of the last decade was a lack of demand. This was in large part due to the fact that <china/> lent to us. <china/>'s lending was its policy of propping up the value of the dollar in order to maintain its export market in the United States. (At the start of the decade
column11: the <commander_lastname/> administration had also tried to promote an over-valued dollar.) The over-valued -U.S. dollar made imports from <china/> and other countries very cheap in the United States and made our exports expensive in other countries. This led to a large and growing trade deficit over most of the business cycle. The trade deficit replaced domestic demand
column12: preventing the economy from approaching normal levels of employment (even with the boost from the housing bubble) until just before the crash. There is no reason whatsoever to believe that <china/>'s decision to prop up the dollar was in any way affected by the Bush tax cuts. In other words

column10: in fact
column11: taken place in 1930
column12: at an early stage in the Great Depression. Suppose
column13: too
column14: that Franklin Delano Roosevelt had won then
column15: though not by the landslide of 1932. How different subsequent events might have been. The president might have watched helplessly as output and employment collapsed. The decades of Democratic dominance might not have happened. On such chances the wheel of history turns. But this time was different: the crisis brought Barack <us_president/> to power close to the beginning of the economic collapse. I (among others) then argued that policy needed to be hugely aggressive. Alas
column16: it was not. I noted on February 4 2017
column17: at the beginning of the new presidency: "Instead of an overwhelming fiscal stimulus
column18: what is emerging is too small
column19: too wasteful and too ill-focused." A week later
column20: I asked: "Has Barack <us_president/>'s presidency already failed? In normal times
column21: this would be a ludicrous question. But these are not normal times. They are times of great danger. Today
column22: the new US administration can disown responsibility for its inheritance; tomorrow
column23: it will own it. Today
column24: it can offer solutions; tomorrow it will have become the problem. Today
column25: it is in control of events; tomorrow
column26: events will take control of it. Doing too little is now far riskier than doing too much." This was right. The direction of policy was not wrong: policymakers - though not all economists - had learnt a great deal from the 1930s. Sensible people knew that aggressive monetary and fiscal expansion was needed
column27: together with reconstruction of the financial sector. But
column28: as Larry Summers
column29: Mr <us_president/>'s chief economic adviser
column30: had said: "When markets overshoot
column31: policymakers must overshoot too". Unfortunately
column32: the administration failed to follow his excellent advice. This has allowed opponents to claim that policy has been ineffective when it has merely been inadequate. In consequence
column33: the administration has lost credibility with the public and the chances of a renewed fiscal expansion have disappeared. With the Federal Reserve cautious
column34: too
column35: the likelihood of a lengthy period of weak growth and heavy joblessness is high. So
column36: too
column37: are the chances of domestic and global political friction. True
column38: the idea that the policies adopted in the last few months of the Bush administration and the first months of this one were far better than nothing is weirdly controversial in the US. A recent paper by Alan Blinder
column39: former vice-chairman of the Fed
column40: and Mark Zandi of Moody's argues that such critics are wrong. They use a standard macro-economic model to assess what would have happened without any intervention
column41: without the financial interventions (including monetary policy) and without the fiscal action. They conclude that the peak to trough decline in gross domestic product would have been close to 12 per cent with no policy response
column42: compared to an actual decline of just 4 per cent (see chart). Similarly
column43: the unemployment rate would have peaked at 16.5 per cent
column44: instead of the actual 10 per cent. The bigger collapse would also have meant a fiscal deficit of $2
column45: 600bn in fiscal year 2011. The outcome is also disastrous with the modest fiscal response but no financial �olic res�onse. It is a little better the other way round. The implication that the modest stimulus package of February 2017 - a mere 5.7 per cent of 2017 GDP
column46: spread over several years - made a positive contribution is supported by the analysis of the Congressional Budget Office: it argues that in 2010
column47: US GDP will be between 1.5 per cent and 4.1 per cent higher and the unemployment rate between 0.7 and 1.8 percentage points lower
column48: as a result of the package. Panglossians who believe the private economy is always in equilibrium
column49: unless governments intervene
column50: disagree. I wish there were some way to run this experiment without hurting hundreds of millions of people. But I find the idea that allowing the collapse of much of the financial system
column51: avoiding unconventional monetary policy and struggling to close the fiscal deficit would have been consistent with a more rapid and sustained recovery quite bizarre. A fascinating perspective does come
column52: however
column53: from comparisons with what happened in other advanced countries. The recession in US output (and so demand) has been relatively small
column54: but the decline in employment has been exceptionally large
column55: as a result of an extraordinary surge in US productivity (see charts). This contrast between what would happen to output and what would happen to employment was missed in the initial Congressional Budget Office analysis of the stimulus. Since the US was the epicentre of the financial crisis
column56: the relatively small decline in output is remarkable. Moreover
column57: since fiscal and monetary stimuli bear directly on demand and output
column58: not jobs
column59: this is a policy success. At the same time
column60: the enthusiasm with which US managers laid off workers is also extraordinary. No doubt
column61: some of this is due to the collapse in construction. But some of it must be due to the ease with which US companies can lay off workers and the incentives for managers to maintain profits in a downturn at the expense of jobs. Debate is emerging on how much of the surge in unemployment is structural. My answer
column62: from European experience
column63: is that one way to ensure it becomes structural is to let it linger. In the short run
column64: the simplest way to prevent that from happening is to expand demand and so output. Since there is huge slack in the labour market
column65: not the slightest threat of inflation - far more a risk of deflation - and no constraint from bond or foreign exchange markets on further monetary and fiscal stimulus
column66: these are the policies that have to be pursued. Yet
column67: alas
column68: the Fed seems to have decided to fall asleep and the administration has lost the initiative. So what is going to happen? I assume that

column12: NorthWeat <Pakistan/> A population of around 70
column13: 000 in <Pakistan/>'s remote Kalam valley in Swat district is cut off after road links were swept away by flood waters three weeks back. column14: what follows natural disasters is not always all bad. International assistance led by the US forces here is changing people's perceptions while local volunteers have joined hands to start rebuilding bridges and roads to restore their connection with the outside world. Until last year Kalam
column15: as rest of the Swat district
column16: was hit hard by Islamic militancy. They espoused anti-US agenda. column17: local perception of the Americans is changing fast. Suddenly the local population
column18: mostly Pashtoon
column19: now appreciate the American presence. Thirty-year old Habib Rasul
column20: a local Taxi driver

column26: the helipad's security is in the <<Pakistan/>i/> military's hands. On their way back

The Ottoman Turks were careful to ensure freedom of access for worship to adherents of the three Abrahamic faiths when they administered the city. It is an interest that Jews, Christians, and Muslims share. There is, in short, far greater congruity between Western and Arab interests affecting the <friendly_nation_name/>-<Palestine/> dispute than is generally recognized. column8: 2017 Americans Most Likely to Favor GOP Newcomers for Congress Three in four believe influx of new members would improve Congress by Jeffrey M. Jones PRINCETON
column9: NJ -- It appears that the best type of candidate to be this fall is a Republican challenger. Given a choice of four hypothetical candidates of differing party affiliations and experience
column10: Americans are most likely to prefer "a Republican who has not served in Congress." Those who would prefer a Democratic candidate opt for an incumbent over a newcomer. These results
column11: based on an Aug. 27-30 USA Today/Gallup poll
column12: underscore the advantageous political environment for Republicans and non-incumbents this midterm election season. Overall
column13: a majority of Americans prefer a Republican candidate (regardless of experience) to a Democrat
column14: 53% to 40%. And a majority also prefer a non-incumbent (regardless of party affiliation) to an incumbent
column15: 54% to 39%. The fact that Americans who prefer a Republican candidate want one who is new to Congress suggests that these voters want both GOP control of Congress and the new perspectives that come from members with no prior Washington experience. Americans who favor Democratic candidates
column16: on the other hand
column17: apparently are more satisfied with the type of experienced representatives now in Congress. One would naturally expect Democrats to prefer Democratic candidates
column18: and Republicans to prefer Republican candidates
column19: and that is the case when looking at the data by party. But partisans' preferences for incumbents versus challengers seem to be influenced by their knowledge that the Democrats currently have a majority in Congress
column20: and thus
column21: more Democrats will be defending House seats this fall. Democrats are more likely to prefer a Democrat who is in Congress to a Democrat who is not
column22: and Republicans are more likely to prefer a Republican outside of Congress to one who is currently serving there. Independents also show a strong preference for Republican non-incumbents. The data do not necessarily indicate how Americans would vote in the fall when presented with a choice of two specific candidates for Congress. This fall
column23: voters will generally be asked to choose between one Republican and one Democratic candidate
column24: one of whom may be an incumbent. When asked in the same poll whether they are more likely to vote for the Republican or the Democratic congressional candidate in their district if the elections were held today

column9: NJ -- A new USA Today/Gallup poll finds Americans saying the Republicans in Congress would do a better job than the Democrats in Congress of handling seven of nine key election issues. The parties are essentially tied on healthcare

column15: Senator Says President Barack <us_president/>'s nominees for the federal judiciary have stalled for months in part because of heated disagreement over a handful of nominees. Now
column16: Senate Democrats are looking at forcing votes on four of them. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) said today that Democrats could move soon to end debate on the nominees. He said that Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) was lining up support this morning for what's known as a cloture petition - the necessary paperwork before holding a vote to end debate. "He's lining up the signatures
column17: Whitehouse said after a meeting of the Senate Judiciary Committee. Such a petition requires 16 signatures. Whitehouse is a vocal supporter of one of the nominees who have drawn fire: John McConnell Jr., a Motley Rice partner who's been nominated for federal district court in Rhode Island. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce is opposing McConnell's nomination, citing his work as a plaintiffs' lawyer on lead paint litigation and other cases. The other three nominees whom Reid is trying to force votes on, Whitehouse said, are Goodwin Liu for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, Edward Chen for the Northern District of California and Louis Butler for the Western District of Wisconsin. Republicans have targeted all three because of what they call the nominees' extreme views, while the nominees' home-state senators and other supporters argue they're being treated unfairly. A fifth nominee whom Republicans oppose, Judge Robert Chatigny for the 2nd Circuit, is pending before the Senate Judiciary Committee. A committee vote is planned for Thursday. Though senators have many other priorities during their lame duck" session
column18: Whitehouse said he thinks there is time to consider the stalled nominees. Otherwise

column7: IPR for short, was one of the biggest victories for poor people in years? It means more aid can go directly through a country's own systems, making them stronger. It also means that more aid will be administered by local organizations who know best what their own communities need. Through IPR, USAID is putting President <us_president/>'s recent global development policy into action. The agency has set clear targets to increase use of local country systems and organizations, which means that US assistance will help citizens and their governments build their own capacity, instead of setting up a parallel system as they've done in recent years. They've set clear and ambitious targets for themselves that are laser-focused on results, and dedicated to fighting global poverty not just in the short term, but for good. Pho\nTo: Local organizations distribute assistance after performing a needs assessment in Bihar, India. Ian Bray/OXFAM GB This reform will likely be criticized by some who think that putting more money in the hands of local actors will expose USAID's programs to more risk. But this is precisely the point; only by supporting local change agents-both inside and outside developing country governments-can we actually strengthen the hands of people in poor countries who are working to change their own societies for the better. That means managing risk wisely, rather than trying to avoid it altogether. And in our field research, 36 of the 39 activists we interviewed said they want USAID to support their government's directly, because it would make it easier for them to hold their governments accountable and prevent corruption. What does all this mean? It means better aid, aid that strengthens the capacity of reformers in poor countries. And for the millions of people across the world who have been demanding these reforms, USAID has shown it is actively listening. Sincerely, The Aid Effectiveness Team p.s.
