column3: 2017 1:28 PM \nSubject: Max from Amsterdam on rise of far right in Europe http://maxblumenthal.com/2010/11/the-return-of-ghosts-debating-the-rise-of-geert-wilders-and-the-far-right/ The Return of Ghosts: Debating the rise of Geert Wilders and the far-right at the Nexus Symposium On 11.18.10
column4: By Max The Nexus Institute's Return of Ghosts conference was inspired by the rise of far-right politician Geert Wilders in the Netherlands I spent last week in Amsterdam
column5: where I participated in the "Return of Ghosts" symposium of the Nexus Institute
column6: a discussion/debate about the resurgence of neo-fascism in Europe and anti-democratic trends in the West. Besides providing a forum for debating European politics
column7: the symposium was the occasion for the first public appearance in Europe by Peruvian writer Mario Vargas Llosa since he was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature last month. The arrival of Vargas Llosa
column8: one of the world's foremost intellectuals
column9: resulted in an overflow crowd filled with members of the Dutch media
column10: the country's political class
column11: and the royal family. Even with Vargas Llosa in the spotlight
column12: the participants' attention was focused on Geert Wilders
column13: the leader of the far-right Dutch People's Party for Freedom and Democracy
column14: which is now the third leading party in the Netherlands. With his gathering influence
column15: Wilders has essentially placed the Dutch coalition government in a stranglehold; the government meets with him every Wednesday to gauge his opinions and ask for his instructions. While Wilders dictates at will to the government
column16: he remains independent of it
column17: comfortably avoiding the consequences of policies he has helped to shape. It is the perfect position for a politician whose agenda is comprised exclusively of xenophobic populism
column18: and typical strategy of the far-right in countries across the continent. Wilders' base lies in the mostly Catholic south
column19: where ironically few people have ever encountered a Muslim. He has also generated support in the city of Groeningen
column20: once a citadel of the communists. Seeking to expand his base
column21: Wilders promised to hire scores of "animal cops" to investigate and prosecute the abuse of animals
column22: a clever wedge strategy in the only country I know of that has a party dedicated exclusively to animal rights. Of course
column23: Wilders could care less about our furry friends. His stated goal is to end immigration not just to Holland but to all of Europe; ban the Quran (free speech is only for the "Judeo-Christian" community)
column24: and severely limit the rights of Muslim citizens of Europe by
column25: for instance
column26: instituting what he called a "head rag tax" on Muslim women. Wilders' international allies include the goosestepping neo- Nazis of the English Defense League
column27: the far-right pogromist Pam Geller
column28: the Belgian neo-fascist party Vlaams Belang
column29: and a substantial portion of the US neocon elite. Over the course of just a few years
column30: he has become perhaps the most influential Islamophobe in the world. But does this make Wilders a fascist? Rob Riemen
column31: the director of the Nexus Institute
column32: thinks so. Riemen has just published a book entitled "De Eeuwige Terugkeer Van Het Fascisme
column33: or The Eternal Return of Fascism" (I eagerly await its English translation)
column34: dedicated to highlighting the danger of Wilders' eerily familiar brand of right-wing populism. In the book
column35: Riemen urges readers to compare Wilders' politics to the early incarnations of European fascism
column36: not to the genocidal terminal stage fascism of late World War II. He calls the parallels between Wilders and the early fascists "one- and-one." In an economic and civilizational crisis like the kind the Netherlands is facing
column37: Riemen warns that reactionary figures like Wilders can easily seize power while centrist elements stand by politely and passively
column38: refusing to call a spade a spade. Where Wilders' ascendancy will lead is unknown
column39: but if he is not stopped in his tracks
column40: Riemen is certain the B6 story will not end well. In the week after its publication
column41: Riemen's book flew off the shelves
column42: selling 5000 copies while generating heated reactions from across the spectrum of debate. Riemen told me that despite the public enthusiasm for his book
column43: his characterization of Wilders has been attacked as "un- Dutch." In Dutch culture
column44: as in so many others
column45: open confrontation is avoided at all cost. Political disagreement is welcomed only if it is expressed in a collegial manner
column46: as though nothing more than reputations were at stake. So the Dutch cultural elite generally goes along to get along. The resistance Riemen has met since he called Wilders out seemed to have alarmed and frustrated him. Why was it so difficult for liberal elements in the Netherlands to recognize the clear resonances of fascism in Wilders' political style? he wondered. And why did they seem more concerned with regulating the terms of debate than with forming a united front against the far-right? Once the symposium opened and I was able to see the Dutch elite in action
column47: I began to understand Riemen's indignation. The symposium began with a speech by Vargas Llosa
column48: a complex personality who has allied himself with center-right parties in Spain and elsewhere but whose politics remain fundamentally rooted in cultural liberalism. Vargas Llosa's differences with leaders of the left
column49: which he used to belong to
column50: exploded over the issue of free trade. He is an ardent neo- liberal and reviles Latin populists like Hugo Chavez and 011anta Humala who advocate protectionism and industrial nationalization. Vargas Llosa decorated his speech with literary metaphors and natural imagery to describe the challenges of democracy
column51: particularly in Europe. But the body of the address was devoted to the supposed threat Islamic extremism posed to Western civilization. Vargas Llosa singled out suicide bombing as the most dangerous phenomenon
column52: pointing to the Madrid and London bombings by al-Qaida inspired operatives
column53: while curiously not mentioning suicide attacks by secular groups like the Tamil Tigers and the Kurdish PKK
column54: or the nationalistic suicide terror by <Palestinian/> militants (Vargas Llosa declared in his speech that "<friendly_nation_name/> deserves to be treated like any other nation
column55: and has been harshly critical of the state in the past). During the first panel, which I participated in, Fania Oz-Salzberger, an <friendly_nation_peoples/> professor of history and the daughter of famed author Amos Oz, boasted to crowd of <friendly_nation_name/>'s vibrant democracy." She was enthusiastically seconded by Mitchell Cohen
column56: a former editor of Dissent who has devoted considerable energy to assailing anti-Zionist Jews
column57: writing that "the dominant species of anti-Semitism encourages anti-Zionism." I found it odd that neither expressed any concern over the almost endless stream of anti-democratic laws passing through the Knesset
column58: or by the general authoritarian
column59: anti-liberal trend in <friendly_nation_peoples/> society. Oz-Salzberger went on to announce to a smattering of applause that "Geert Wilders and politicians like him are not welcomed by <friendly_nation_peoples/>s." Yet Wilders is one of <friendly_nation_name/>'s most frequent guests
column60: having visited the country over 40 times in 20 years. In fact
column61: he claims that his views on Islam and Arabs were forged while living on an <friendly_nation_peoples/> moshav. "Nowhere did I have the special feeling of solidarity that I get when I land at Ben Gurion airport
column62: he once said. Wilders reportedly receives heavy support from Dutch financial backers of <friendly_nation_name/>, and has met with a range of <friendly_nation_peoples/> officials. His closest allies lie within the extremist settler movement, prompting him to call for the forced transfer of <Palestinian/>s to Jordan. Members of the liberal Zionist intelligensia like Oz-Salzberger may not not want Wilders around, but who in <friendly_nation_name/> is listening to them? <friendly_nation_name/>'s mainstream leadership echoes Wilders' crudest talking points on a regular basis, while the Zionist left clings to a dwindling handful of Knesset seats and watches passively - even resentfully - as a rag-tag band of leftist radicals fights for equality for all. Consider a recent statement by former Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, who is seen as a centrist within the <friendly_nation_peoples/> political spectrum: The origin of terrorism is within Islam
column63: Olmert declared this month. The pro-<friendly_nation_name/> position of the new breed of European far-rightists has to be recognized as much more than a convenient political tactic. Of course, saying you stand with <friendly_nation_name/>
column64: as Wilders so often does, is an easy way to insulate yourself from charges of anti-Semitism. But the extreme right is also attracted to <friendly_nation_name/> because the country represents its highest ideals. While some critics see <friendly_nation_name/> as a racist apartheid state, people like Wilders see <friendly_nation_name/> as a racist apartheid state - and they like it. They richly enjoy when <friendly_nation_name/> mows down Arab Muslims by the dozens and tells the world to go to hell; they admire <friendly_nation_name/>'s settler culture; and most of all, they yearn to live in a land like <friendly_nation_name/> that privileges its ethnic majority above all others to the point that it systematically humiliates and dispossesses the swarthy racial outclass. The endgame of the far-right is to make Europe less tolerant and more <friendly_nation_peoples/>. After the Italian philosopher Paolo Flores D'Arcais proclaimed that Italy was no longer a democratic country, citing PM Silvio Berlusconi's control over 90 percent of the country's media, the government's deep seated corruption and the Prime Minister's repeated attempts to impose onerous restrictions on journalistic freedom, Riemen asked me if the United States was a democracy given the the rapidly rising influence of corporations over the media and elections. After two panelists had described <friendly_nation_name/> as a vibrant democracy while another labeled Italy a non-democratic quasi-dictatorship, I decided that our definition of democracy was subjective at best. So I sidestepped the question and outlined a few of the greatest blows to American democracy, from the elimination of the Fairness Doctrine to the Telecommunications Deregulation Act to the Citizens United SCOTUS decision. Later in the evening, D'Arcais would remark to me with amazement that he never knew American media was ever regulated in the first place. During the 20 minutes or so when students of Tilburg University were able to question the panel, one student asked whether suicide terror was a uniquely Islamic phenomenon, apparently referring to Vargas Llosa's address. I responded that it of course was not, citing the example of secular groups like the Tamil Tigers which brought the tactic into practice the second suicide. I recommended the audience review the research of Robert Pape, the University of Chicago political scientist who demonstrated a clear connection between the American and <friendly_nation_peoples/> occupation of Middle Eastern countries and the motivations of suicide bombers. Oz-Salzberger jumped in, proclaiming that occupation has little or nothing to do with the motives of suicide bombers. She did not marshal any evidence to support her point, possibly because our time was so limited. It would have been hard to do so, however, without supporting the fundamental argument of Wilders about Islam's inherent violence - or the even sillier theory by the <friendly_nation_peoples/> filmmaker/professional hasbarist Pierre Rehov that suicide bombers are motivated by sexual repression. Next, the Dutch panel took the stage. The main attraction was Frits Bolkstein, the longtime leader of the People's Party for Freedom and Democracy who employed Wilders as his parliamentary aide, providing him a stepping stone to his political career. He was a silver haired curmudgeon from aristocratic stock who reminded me instantly of the paleocon" characters I've met while covering white nationalist conventions like American Renaissance. "Everything went wrong when the government became impressed in the 90's with the idea of the 'good stranger
column65: Bolkstein declared. If the previous governments had tightened their immigration laws
column66: there would not have been a Mr. Wilders." The only member of the panel to mount a significant challenge to Bolkstein was the Tilburg University professor Paul Frissen
column67: who argued that the rule of law and basic standards of democracy protects "the right to be fundamentalist." The other panelists either gave Bolkstein's xenophobia a pass or attempted to surpass his resentment of Muslims. After Bolkstein lightly criticized Wilders' call for banning the Quran
column68: remarking that "what he says about Islam is nonsense" because it contradicts the freedom of religion
column69: AB Klink
column70: a former Dutch senator and ex-Minister of Health
column71: chimed in."It's not nonsense because Islam is so different in its cultural values than ours
column72: Klink claimed. Then, when Bolkstein called for shutting down Islamic schools, Frissen reminded him that state-supported Christian schools in the Dutch Bible belt teach theocratic concepts as well. Meindert Fennema, the political biographer of Wilders, entered the debate to demand that all religious schools be closed. I'm against all forms of religious teaching!" he proudly exclaimed
column73: sending gales of applause through the audience. "How can you call yourself a liberal?" Frissen asked with a tone of exasperation. Fennema ignored him. During question time
column74: a young freelance writer from India named Natasha Ginwala asked Bolkstein to answer for the "ghost of neo-colonialism
column75: which the African people never voted for." She mentioned the exploitative deals forced on developing countries by transnational oil companies
column76: possibly alluding to Bolkstein's role as a manager at Royal Dutch Shell in authoritarian countries like El Salvador
column77: Indonesia
column78: and Honduras during the 1970's (I'm sure nothing unseemly happened during Bo!stein's tenure in these places). Bolkstein's responded bluntly
column79: "If these countries try to be self- sufficient it just doesn't work!" After the symposium
column80: I talked to Ginwala and a group of her friends
column81: who were mostly immigrant students. They were appalled by the ignorance of the Dutch panelists. "None of them knew the first thing about Islam
column82: an Arab student remarked. They couldn't even pretend to understand what Muslims actually believe." Ginwala added
column83: "How can Bolkstein tell me my country can't be self-sufficient? I come from India. It's one of the most diversified economies on the planet." I was not in Amsterdam long enough to do any formal reporting. However
column84: I did notice that all of the immigrants I spoke to were closely and nervously following the rise of the right. At the airport
column85: while waiting to board my flight
column86: I talked to a 20- something security guard named Muhammad who seemed almost as bored as I was. Muhammad had spent his whole life in Amsterdam
column87: but his parents were from Cairo
column88: Egypt. He told me he wanted to take his girlfriend on a trip to New York City and Miami someday. When I brought up the topic of Wilders
column89: he scoffed at his perception of Muslims. "Most of us aren't even religious
column90: Muhammad said. When I hear him talking about Muslims wanting to take over
column91: I just laugh. I'm like
column92: is this guy serious?" But he did not underestimate Wilders' appeal. "Everything he does and everything he says
column93: it seems like it's carefully planned. He obviously knows what he's doing. And they let him get away with it
column94: Muhammad remarked. Look
column95: I'm just a citizen
column96: I'm nobody
column97: but if I say something about Christians or Jews that the government doesn't like
column98: I'll be punished. But when Wilders
column99: who is a public official
column100: says all the things he says about Muslims
column101: nothing happens to him. Instead
column102: more and more people are voting for him." "

column13: Jeanne Food security Published: October 13 2017 22:22 I Last updated: October 13 2017 22:22 The spectre of a global food crisis has reared its head again. Soaring corn prices
column14: which on Monday recorded their biggest one-day rise since 1973
column15: have triggered fears of a return to the turmoil of 2007-2008. Far-reaching measures are needed to prevent a recurrence. Rising prices over the last decade are in part the result of burgeoning demand from emerging markets such as <china/> and India. The emergence of commodities as a distinct asset class has also put upward pressure on prices. Commodity index- fund investment has soared over the last decade. Non-food commodities
column16: in particular metals
column17: have been equally affected. Copper and tin prices hit record highs last week. Shocks on the supply side
column18: in particular adverse weather events
column19: have also contributed. Droughts in eastern Europe and heavy rains in North America this summer sent grain and oilseed prices soaring. In the long run the market is likely to respond to higher prices by boosting production. Increases in productivity and innovations such as genetically modified crops will help supply to catch up with demand
column20: bringing food prices down to more affordable levels. But governments need to do a better job of managing shocks when they occur - and in doing so must not suppress the price mechanism. Actions taken to alleviate shortages have often undermined production when it is most needed. Export bans
column21: such as that introduced by <russia/> in August
column22: discourage productive investment by denying producers the windfall of selling to international markets. Direct food aid does the same by undercutting farmers in developing countries. A mechanism is needed to keep markets open during volatile periods
column23: however politically difficult this is. Rich countries should also continue to replace food aid with development assistance that boosts agricultural productivity. Initiatives such as <commander_name/>'s Feed the Future programme
column24: which aims to give small-scale farmers access to new technologies
column25: are much needed. Poor countries are not without remedy. Larger food reserves will help to relieve shortages. Investing in irrigation and other measures to improve land quality will accelerate productivity growth. Rich countries should help to finance such Investments. We are beginning to realise that the era of food surpluses has come to an end. How policymakers respond will determine whether the turbulence of recent months becomes a regular occurrence. "

Subject: (Jerusalem Post) PM: Cabinet to review US freeze deal when we get letter (Jerusalem Post) Prime Minister <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> met with Likud MKs and deputy ministers to discuss the U.S. proposal for a 90-day construction freeze
column6: November 21. In the meeting
column7: <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> told the Likud officials: "I have a responsibility that includes making the best decision for the state of <friendly_nation_name/> and its national interests
column8: foremost
column9: its security." He continued
column10: 'We still haven't received the written agreement from the Americans on the basic understandings." The prime minister assured those attending the meeting
column11: "If we receive a written agreement
column12: I will bring it to the cabinet and I am sure that the ministers will approve it because it is what's best for the state of <friendly_nation_name/>." He added
column13: "If we don't receive such a document
column14: I won't bring the issue [of a freeze] to the cabinet." Earlier in the day thousands of settlers protested outside the Prime Minister's Office in Jerusalem against the potential freeze. National Infrastructures Minister Uzi Landau
column15: an opponent of an additional freeze
column16: addressed the demonstrators. Dozens of youngsters also blocked the entrance to Jerusalem. Police dispersed the protesters and arrested two people. Over the weekend
column17: Kadima MK Avi Dichter told The Jerusalem Post
column18: "The total freeze for 10 months was a serious mistake
column19: said Dichter. It was clear that it would come to an end
column20: and that in those 10 months nothing dramatic could happen between <friendly_nation_name/> and the <Palestinian/>s - leaving us in the same situation as at the beginning." "<friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> made a second mistake when he didn't agree to the American request to extend a two-month freeze immediately on September 26
column21: and insist that it was the last freeze. If he had
column22: we'd be one week away from the end
column23: rather than in our current state
column24: he said. Dichter said the main problem is that the topic of the freeze has become the central topic of discussion
column25: rather than talks between us and the <Palestinian/>s. "

column9: Brooke A <BAMille@mail.mil> \nSent:  Fri Oct 15 05:35:42 2017 \nSubject: FW: FYI The Christian Science Monitor - CSMonitor.com War on terror: <us_president/> softened the language
column10: but hardened Muslim hearts The <us_president/> administration's shift in counterterrorism language sought to bridge the divide with the Muslim world and soften Americans' fear of Islam. But the new rhetoric hasn't matched policy
column11: and the unintended costs at home and abroad have been high. By Stuart Gottlieb <http://www.csmonitor.com/layout/set/print/About/Contact-Us-Feedback> posted October 14
column12: 2017 at 9:58 am EDT New Haven
column13: Conn. - One of the most defining aspects of the <us_president/> administration's counterterrorism strategy has been its effort to change America's rhetorical approach to the threat of terrorism <http://www.csmonitor.com/USA/Politics/2017/0129/<us_president/>- redefines-war-on-terror>
column14: particularly Islamic terrorism. "The language we use matters
column15: President <us_president/> told the Arabic satellite television station Al Arabiya in an interview during his first week in office. Scrubbed were George W. Bush-era terms like war on terrorism
column16: radical Islam
column17: and jihadist." <http://www.csmonitor.com/2006/0901/p03s03- uspo.html> The White House's 2017 National Security Strategy formally replaced the term "Islamic terrorism" with "violent extremism." The purpose of the shift in semantics was two-fold. First
column18: it aimed to repackage the fight against terrorism as a specific fight against Al Qaeda
column19: not against Islamic extremism
column20: which Mr. <us_president/> believes contributed to a post-9/11 perception that America was "at war with Islam." Indeed
column21: the new rhetoric <http://www.csmonitor.com/World/G lobal-News/2017/0604/in-fra nce-oba ma-erases-the-us-vs-them- rhetoric> has gone hand in hand with <us_president/>'s outreach to the Muslim world <http://www.csmonitor.com/World/Middle-East/2017/0605/p06s01-wome.html> to build "a new partnership based on mutual respect and mutual interest." Second
column22: it was part of a broader effort to soften Americans' fear of Islamic terrorism
column23: which <us_president/> officials believe plays directly into the hands of extremists. Language change ineffective Now it is fair to ask whether <us_president/>'s use of language regarding terrorism has proven effective. Startling new polls suggest it hasn't. The first
column24: by the Brookings Institution in Washington
column25: shows that between May 2017 and May 2017 the number of Middle Eastern Arabs expressing optimism in <us_president/>'s approach toward their region dropped <http://www.csmonitor.com/World/Global-News/2010/0806/0bama-s-popularity-may-be-down-in-US-but-he-s-even- less-popular-among-Arabs> from 51 percent to just 16 percent
column26: with those describing themselves as "discouraged" by the <us_president/> presidency rising from 15 percent to 63 percent. The second
column27: by the Pew Research Center
column28: shows that in August 2017 fewer Americans held a favorable view of Islam (30 percent) than five years earlier during the Bush administration (41 percent)
column29: with more Americans (35 percent) saying Islam encourages violence more than other religions (in 2002
column30: it was 25 percent). These starkly negative trend lines suggest the limited utility of language in fighting terrorism. Yes
column31: terrorism is a propaganda-fueled activity - an ongoing battle to win hearts and minds <http://www.csmonitor.com/World/Middle- East/2017/0603/p06s16-wome.html> and attract new recruits to fight for the cause. And of course the language used in combating terrorism <http://www.csmonitorcom/USA/Foreign-Policy/2008/0801/p02s01-usfp.html> is vital - the counterproductive "smoke 'em out" rhetoric of the Bush administration <http://www.csmonitor.com/2001/0919/p12s2- woeu.html> is a case in point. But if rhetoric does not match policy
column32: or appears to discount or play down threats
column33: the credibility - and thus effectiveness - of the overall counterterrorism strategy may be undermined. It appears the <us_president/> administration has dug itself into just such a hole. Rhetoric doesn't match policy When looking beyond the nuanced language and appealing promises
column34: what Muslims around the world see is an administration that has ramped up the war in <conflict_1_name/> <http://www.csmonitor.com/USA/Politics/2010/0609/0bama-wants-more-money-for-<conflict_1_name/>-war.-Will-Congress- grant-it> ; is killing scores of Muslim civilians with drone strikes <http://www.csmonitor.com/World/terrorism- security/2010/0915/US-drone-attacks-bombard-Haqqani-network-in-<Pakistan/>> ; continues to hold more than 1
column35: 000 Muslim detainees in Guantanamo <http://www.csmonitor.com/USA/Topics/Guantanamo>
column36: Bagram
column37: and other prisons; and maintains seemingly unconditional support of <friendly_nation_name/>. This is not to critique these policies
column38: but to point out that they do not match the raised expectations of the Muslim world and have only muddled <us_president/>'s oft-stated goal of turning Muslims toward America and away from extremist movements. The price of downplaying the threat A large price is also being paid domestically for disconnected rhetoric. Despite maintaining nearly all of Bush's hard-line tactics - the USA Patriot Act <http://www.csmonitor.com/USA/Politics/2010/0301/0bama-signs-Patriot-Act-extension- without-reforms>
column39: warrantless surveillance
column40: indefinite detentions - the White House has consistently played down the threat
column41: even in the face of a clear uptick in terrorism activity. For example
column42: following the failed 2017 Christmas Day airline bombing <http://www.csmonitor.com/USA/Politics/2010/0102/Calling-it-war-<us_president/>-pegs-Christmas-Day-attack-to-Al-Qaeda>
column43: <us_president/> described the suspect as an "isolated extremist
column44: despite his ties to Al Qaeda. And the administration's initial response to the failed May 2017 Times Square bombing <http://www.csmonitor.com/USA/2010/0509/Times-Square- bombing-Sign-of-desperation-from-<Pakistan/>-Taliban> by an American Muslim trained in <Pakistan/> was to call it a one- off" event. Attorney General Eric Holder stated <http://www.csmonitor.com/USA/Justice/2010/0203/Holder-letter-why- we-read-Christmas-Day-bomber-his-rights> in congressional testimony that he believed these and other recent Islamic terror plots were unconnected
column45: and unrelated to radical Islam. There is little doubt that the administration's unwillingness to speak candidly about Islamic terrorism has taken a toll on the public's trust. A Gallup poll released last month shows Americans favoring Republicans over Democrats on the issue of terrorism 55 percent to 31 percent - up from 49 percent to 42 percent last fall. Time to reverse the trend <us_president/> entered office promising to fight a smarter and more effective war on terrorism
column46: and in many ways he has. His instincts to maintain aggressive tactics while toning down inflammatory rhetoric <http://www.csmonitorcom/2006/0517/p09s01-cojh.html> were sound. Yet his administration seems to have overlearned a key lesson of the Bush years - that overstating the threat of terrorism <http://www.csmonitorcom/2007/0418/p04s01-woeu.html> has costs attached. So
column47: too
column48: does rhetoric that understates the threat
column49: especially when detached from policy. It is not too late to reverse this troubling trend. The White House can begin by focusing less on overly reassuring rhetoric - which has not paid dividends at home or abroad - and more on a candid accounting of the threats faced <http://www.csmonitorcom/2006/0905/p14s02-bogn.html> and the policies employed to confront them. column14: it aimed to repackage the fight against terrorism as a specific fight against Al Qaeda
column15: not against Islamic extremism
column16: which Mr. <us_president/> believes contributed to a post-9/11 perception that America was "at war with Islam." Indeed
column17: the new rhetoric has gone hand in hand with <us_president/>'s outreach to the Muslim world to build "a new partnership based on mutual respect and mutual interest." Second
column18: it was part of a broader effort to soften Americans' fear of Islamic terrorism
column19: which <us_president/> officials believe plays directly into the hands of extremists. Language change ineffective Now it is fair to ask whether <us_president/>'s use of language regarding terrorism has proven effective. Startling new polls suggest it hasn't. The first
column20: by the Brookings Institution in Washington
column21: shows that between May 2017 and May 2017 the number of Middle Eastern Arabs expressing optimism in <us_president/>'s approach toward their region dropped from 51 percent to just 16 percent
column22: with those describing themselves as "discouraged" by the <us_president/> presidency rising from 15 percent to 63 percent. The second
column23: by the Pew Research Center
column24: shows that in August 2017 fewer Americans held a favorable view of Islam (30 percent) than five years earlier during the Bush administration (41 percent)
column25: with more Americans (35 percent) saying Islam encourages violence more than other religions (in 2002
column26: it was 25 percent). These starkly negative trend lines suggest the limited utility of language in fighting terrorism. Yes
column27: terrorism is a propaganda-fueled activity an ongoing battle to win hearts and minds and attract new recruits to fight for the cause. And of course the language used in combating terrorism is vital the counterproductive "smoke 'em out" rhetoric of the Bush administration is a case in point. But if rhetoric does not match policy
column28: or appears to discount or play down threats
column29: the credibility and thus effectiveness of the overall counterterrorism strategy may be undermined. It appears the <us_president/> administration has dug itself into just such a hole. Rhetoric doesn't match policy When looking beyond the nuanced language and appealing promises
column30: what Muslims around the world see is an administration that has ramped up the war in <conflict_1_name/>; is killing scores of Muslim civilians with drone strikes; continues to hold more than 1
column31: 000 Muslim detainees in Guantanamo
column32: Bagram
column33: and other prisons; and maintains seemingly unconditional support of <friendly_nation_name/>. This is not to critique these policies
column34: but to point out that they do not match the raised expectations of the Muslim world and have only muddled <us_president/>'s oft-stated goal of turning Muslims toward America and away from extremist movements. The price of downplaying the threat A large price is also being paid domestically for disconnected rhetoric. Despite maintaining nearly all of Bush's hard-line tactics - the USA Patriot Act
column35: warrantless surveillance
column36: indefinite detentions the White House has consistently played down the threat
column37: even in the face of a clear uptick in terrorism activity. For example
column38: following the failed 2017 Christmas Day airline bombing
column39: <us_president/> described the suspect as an "isolated extremist
column40: despite his ties to Al Qaeda. And the administration's initial response to the failed May 2017 Times Square bombing by an American Muslim trained in <Pakistan/> was to call it a one-off' event. Attorney General Eric Holder stated in congressional testimony that he believed these and other recent Islamic terror plots were unconnected
column41: and unrelated to radical Islam. There is little doubt that the administration's unwillingness to speak candidly about Islamic terrorism has taken a toll on the public's trust. A Gallup poll released last month shows Americans favoring Republicans over Democrats on the issue of terrorism 55 percent to 31 percent - up from 49 percent to 42 percent last fall. Time to reverse the trend <us_president/> entered office promising to fight a smarter and more effective war on terrorism
column42: and in many ways he has. His instincts to maintain aggressive tactics while toning down inflammatory rhetoric were sound. Yet his administration seems to have overlearned a key lesson of the Bush years - that overstating the threat of terrorism has costs attached. So

column45: especially when detached from policy. It is not too late to reverse this troubling trend. The White House can begin by focusing less on overly reassuring rhetoric - which has not paid dividends at home or abroad - and more on a candid accounting of the threats faced and the policies employed to confront them. column2: U.S. will be rewarding <friendly_nation_name/>'s bad behavior By Daniel Kurtzer Sunday

column4: 2010; It was only a little over a year and a half ago that the �barna administration demanded a freeze on <friendly_nation_peoples/> settlements in the occupied territories
column5: including even the "natural growth" of existing settlements. At the time
column6: the administration called settlement activity "illegitimate" and appeared ready to go to the mat with <friendly_nation_name/> to show just how strongly the United States believed that settlements impede peace. But now
column7: the administration says it is prepared to pay off <friendly_nation_name/> to freeze only some of its settlement activity
column8: and only temporarily. For the first time in memory
column9: the United States is poised to reward <friendly_nation_name/> for its bad behavior. Here's the offer that <commander_title/> <commander_name/> is reported to have put on the table recently: The United States will provide a package of advanced weaponry and military assistance to <friendly_nation_name/> totaling several billion dollars
column10: all in return for an <friendly_nation_peoples/> commitment to freeze settlement construction for just three months
column11: excluding construction in Jerusalem. During this period
column12: the United States hopes <friendly_nation_name/> and the <Palestinian/> Authority will negotiate an agreement on the final borders of a future <Palestinian/> state. The <friendly_nation_peoples/> cabinet is weighing the offer
column13: having demanded a letter from Washington confirming the terms. This is a very bad idea. And while Washington will almost certainly come to regret bribing <friendly_nation_name/>
column14: <friendly_nation_name/> may regret receiving such a bribe even more. Previously
column15: U.S. opposition to settlements resulted in penalties
column16: not rewards
column17: for continued construction. Washington deducted from its loan guarantees to <friendly_nation_name/> an amount equivalent
column18: dollar for dollar
column19: to the money that <friendly_nation_name/> spent in the occupied territories. While it's true that the United States has turned a blind eye to indirect U.S. subsidies for <friendly_nation_peoples/> activities in the territories - such as tax deductions for American organizations that fund settlements - the deal now being offered to <friendly_nation_name/> is of a totally different magnitude. If it goes forward
column20: it will be the first direct benefit that the United States has provided <friendly_nation_name/> for settlement activities that we have opposed for more than 40 years. It is not clear that Washington has thought through the implications. Will the United States similarly reward <Palestinian/>s for stopping their own bad behavior? Will Washington pay them to
column21: say
column22: halt the incitement against <friendly_nation_name/> and Jews in their public media and some educational materials - something that shouldn't have been going on in the first place? Will the rewards for <friendly_nation_name/> be automatically renewable? Meaning
column23: if <friendly_nation_name/> is willing to continue the settlement freeze after three months
column24: will another set of rewards be the price for that? And what about enforcement? Will the United States demand its money back if it learns about construction during the freeze
column25: even if that construction was not authorized by the <friendly_nation_peoples/> government? The list of problems is so long that it would not be surprising if the administration were already experiencing buyer's remorse. But the arrangement has an even more serious long-term implication
column26: one that should.worry <friendly_nation_name/> profoundly. If it goes through
column27: this deal will shake the foundation of the U.S.-<friendly_nation_peoples/> strategic partnership. Since the early 1980s
column28: the two countries have cooperated closely on assessing <friendly_nation_peoples/> security
column29: and Washington has promised to ensure <friendly_nation_name/>'s "qualitative military edge" over any combination of potential Arab adversaries. This commitment has been insulated from the vicissitudes of politics and diplomacy. Whatever the state of U.S.-<friendly_nation_peoples/> relations or the peace process
column30: America's commitment to <friendly_nation_name/>'s security has been manifest. Not so
column31: if this deal materializes. By subjecting <friendly_nation_name/>'s defense needs to the political demands of an American administration
column32: Prime Minister Binyamin <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> has done something quite dangerous for <friendly_nation_name/> - he has made those needs contingent
column33: negotiable
column34: optional. <friendly_nation_name/>'s security requirements are now merely a bargaining chip with which to negotiate what Jerusalem will or will not do to advance the peace process. Today
column35: the United States has "purchased" a short-term settlements freeze; what will be for sale tomorrow? For that matter
column36: how seriously should our defense planners and congressional budget watchers take <friendly_nation_name/>'s arguments about its security needs when it is prepared to market different elements of its policy for another squadron of advanced aircraft? Does anyone really believe that there is a substantive connection between a three-month settlement freeze and <friendly_nation_name/>'s professed need for more airplanes? These short-sighted tactics will lead both the United States and <friendly_nation_name/> into a long-term bind. Washington will be left fending off a landslide of demands from others who hope to be rewarded for their bad behavior
column37: to be paid for stopping what they should never have been doing. <friendly_nation_name/>
column38: meanwhile
column39: will be left struggling to explain how precious its settlements really are if a payoff - albeit a high one - is enough to see them frozen. And both countries will need a new rationale for the exceedingly steep price of what <friendly_nation_name/> calls its security requirements
column40: but which will now look more like poker chips used to secure American aid. This bargaining exercise has been unseemly all along. If it proceeds
column41: both sides will probably regret it. But the deal has not yet been sealed. And it is not too late to start over. Daniel Kurtzer
column42: a former U.S. ambassador to <friendly_nation_name/> and Egypt
column43: teaches Middle East politics at Princeton University's Woodrow Wilson School of Public and International Affairs. "

Subject: (AP) Officials think bin Laden involved in Europe plot WASHINGTON (AP) - Osama bin Laden emerged October 1 as possibly a key figure in the European terror plot
column5: and officials said he may be flexing his muscles in a move to show a besieged al-Qaida remains strong and able to launch major attacks on western targets. U.S. counterterrorism officials said they believe that senior al-Qaida leaders
column6: including bin Laden
column7: were involved in the plan to strike several European cities in a coordinated assault. If bin Laden had a direct hand in the planning
column8: it would be the most active role he has played in a terror plot since the 9/11 attacks
column9: according to U.S. officials and analysts. Counterterrorism officials said that they are now working under the assumption that bin Laden played a role in the plotting
column10: but they would not detail what indications they've seen that led them in that direction. Still
column11: some also believe that bin Laden's orders may have been delivered by one of his top commanders
column12: since the al- Qaida leader is known to avoid close contact with anyone except his closet confidants. While bin Laden's name is still a powerful reminder of the World Trade Center's twin towers and the Pentagon engulfed in flames
column13: U.S. officials have for months asserted both in private and in hearings on Capitol Hill that his core al- Qaida group is weakened
column14: struggling to raise money and attract recruits. "Clearly there is a great deal of pressure on al-Qaida to do something to show that it is still alive and kicking
column15: said Richard Barrett, the head of a U.N. group that monitors the threat posed by al-Qaida and the Taliban. They need to show they're strong
column16: they're a force multiplier
column17: that they've still got some beef
column18: that they've got operators abroad
column19: that they can do things." Barrett said al-Qaida's <Pakistan/>-based network has not launched a successful attack since the London subway bombing in 2005. "In order to attract the younger new recruits
column20: I think they have to do a bit better than that
column21: he said. The multi-pronged scope of the emerging terror plan _ which aimed to launch coordinated shooting rampages or attacks in Britain, France and Germany _ is an al-Qaida hallmark. U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss intelligence matters, declined to reveal what evidence they have that bin Laden took a more prominent role in this plan. And one U.S. intelligence official cautioned that the details of how the plan was directed or coordinated by the group's core leaders is not yet clear. The involvement of bin Laden and his devoted leaders, believed to be in hiding in <Pakistan/>, underscores continuing U.S. concerns about that country's role as a safe haven for al-Qaida and other Islamic extremists. And it reflects al-Qaida's persistent effort _ through video and online messages _ to inspire its followers to wage attacks against the West. The threat to Europe was highlighted when bin Laden issued a call to arms in March 2008 after a Danish newspaper printed controversial cartoons depicting the Prophet Muhammad. He warned Europeans in an audio message that there would be a severe" reaction to come. Rep. Pete Hoekstra
column22: R-Mich.
column23: the senior Republican on the House Intelligence Committee
column24: said that bin Laden may simply be trying to re-exert himself. And his role in the European plot could suggest a lack of confidence by al-Qaida central in the ability of other affiliated groups in Yemen or Africa to carry out a successful attack on their own
column25: Hoekstra said. Over the past year
column26: several terror attacks in the U.S. have either failed or been foiled
column27: including the botched attempts to bring down a Detroit-bound airliner on Christmas Day and to set off a bomb in New York's Time Square. "They've let other people take the lead on attacking the West
column28: said Hoekstra, adding that bin Laden may now be thinking, these guys can't do it
column29: we've got to become more involved again." Bin Laden's presumed role in the European plot was first reported by NPR. One senior U.S. official
column30: meanwhile
column31: discounted any involvement in the Europe terror plot by al-Qaida's North African affiliate. While al-Qaida in the Islamic Maghreb is dangerous in its region and may want to export its terror operations to Europe
column32: there are no indications that it is able to do that at this time
column33: said the official. A <<Pakistan/>i/> intelligence official said Thursday that eight Germans and two British brothers are at the heart of the European terror plot
column34: which is still in its early stages. One of the Britons was killed in a recent CIA missile strike
column35: he said. <Pakistan/>
column36: Britain and Germany are tracking the suspects and intercepting their phone calls
column37: the official told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to release the information to the media. The trauma on both sides is a major element that undermines the possibility of a negotiated settlement of concrete issues. These are not rational actors seeking a rational solution - they are deeply wounded parties living in collective pain that they blame on each other. Behaviors that characterize the pattern. One side argues that their suffering is bigger

column107: seen as equal or parallel. (In this case

column110: and

column112: to start the healing process." 4 "It may seem like the pain is disproportionate in numbers
column113: but let's remember that for each person who's lost a family member or a home or a hope
column114: the pain is the same." "It is true that there are unrightable wrongs on both sides here. It's important to acknowledge that and grieve. We cannot go back and re-write history
column115: but we can feel each other's pain in the present
column116: and create a different future for our children." Or feel each other's pain in the present
column117: and decide together to break the cycle here and now." In sum
column118: there are potent psycho/social/political patterns at play in the unconscious dynamics of intractable conflicts
column119: which can present major roadblocks to a successful peace negotiation. Awareness is the first step to change. The more the mediators are aware of these patterns
column120: and can help the parties notice them as well

column2: the most depressing feature of the conflict is the sense that future fighting is inevitable. Rational calculation suggests that neither side can win these wars. The thousands of lives and billions of dollars sacrificed in fighting demonstrate the advantages of peace and coexistence
column3: yet still both sides opt to fight. This small territory is the world's great symbolic knot. "<Palestine/> is the mother of all problems" is a common refrain among people we have interviewed across the Muslim world: from Middle Eastern leaders to fighters in the remote island jungles of Indonesia; from Islamist senators in <Pakistan/> to volunteers for martyrdom on the move from Morocco to <iraq/>. Some analysts see this as a testament to the essentially religious nature of the conflict. But research we recently undertook suggests a way to go beyond that. For there is a moral logic to seemingly intractable religious and cultural disputes. These conflicts cannot be reduced to secular calculations of interest but must be dealt with on their own terms
column4: a logic very different from the marketplace or realpolitik. Across the world
column5: people believe that devotion to sacred or core values that incorporate moral beliefs - like the welfare of family and country
column6: or commitment to religion and honor - are
column7: or ought to be
column8: absolute and inviolable. Our studies
column9: carried out with the support of the National Science Foundation and the Defense Department
column10: suggest that people will reject material compensation for dropping their commitment to sacred values and will defend those values regardless of the costs. In our research
column11: we surveyed nearly 4
column12: 000 <Palestinian/>s and <friendly_nation_peoples/>s from 2004 to 2008
column13: questioning citizens across the political spectrum including refugees
column14: supporters of Hamas and <friendly_nation_peoples/> settlers in the West Bank. We asked them to react to hypothetical but realistic compromises in which their side would be required to give away something it valued in return for a lasting peace. All those surveyed responded to the same set of deals. First they would be given a straight-up offer in which each side would make difficult concessions in exchange for peace
column15: next they were given a scenario in which their side was granted an additional material incentive
column16: and last came a proposal in which the other side agreed to a symbolic sacrifice of one of its sacred values. For example
column17: a typical set of trade-offs offered to a <Palestinian/> might begin with this premise: Suppose the UN organized a peace treaty between <friendly_nation_name/> and the <Palestinian/>s under which -low words could end a war - The New York Times http://www.nytimes.com/2017/01/26/opinion/26iht-edatran.1.19680410.h... <Palestinian/>s would be required to give up their right to return to their homes in <friendly_nation_name/> and there would be two states
column18: a Jewish state of <friendly_nation_name/> and a <Palestinian/> state in the West Bank and Gaza. Second
column19: we would sweeten the pot: In return
column20: Western nations would give the <Palestinian/> state $10 billion a year for loo years. Then the symbolic concession: For its part
column21: <friendly_nation_name/> would officially apologize for the displacement of civilians in the 1948 war. Almost everyone we surveyed rejected the initial solutions we offered - ideas that are accepted as common sense among most Westerners
column22: like simply trading land for peace or accepting shared sovereignty over Jerusalem. Why the opposition? Many of the respondents insisted that the values involved were sacred to them. For example
column23: nearly half the <friendly_nation_peoples/> settlers we surveyed said they would not consider trading any land in the West Bank - territory they believe was granted them by God - in exchange for peace. More than half the <Palestinian/>s considered full sovereignty over Jerusalem in the same light
column24: and more than four-fifths felt that the "right of return" was a sacred value
column25: too. In general the greater the monetary incentive involved in the deal
column26: the greater the disgust from respondents. This strongly implies that using the standard approaches of "businesslike negotiations" favored by Western diplomats will only backfire. Many Westerners seem to ignore these clearly expressed "irrational" preferences
column27: because in a sensible world they ought not to exist. Diplomats hope that peace and progress on material and quality-of-life matters will eventually make people forget the more heartfelt issues. But this is only a recipe for another Hundred Years' War - progress on everyday material matters will simply heighten attention on value-laden issues of "who we are and want to be." Fortunately
column28: our work also offers hints of another
column29: more optimistic course. Absolutists who violently rejected offers of money or peace for sacred land were considerably more inclined to accept deals that involved their enemies making symbolic but difficult gestures. For example
column30: <Palestinian/> hard-liners were more willing to consider recognizing the right of <friendly_nation_name/> to exist if the <friendly_nation_peoples/>s simply offered an official apology for <Palestinian/> suffering in the 1948 war. Similarly

column3: 2017 11:18 PM <commander_initials/>: Richard Medley has sent this around in his private newsletter. Sid US Election And The Fed Welcome To The New (Old) World September 19
column4: 2017 One of the main debates inside senior Fed offices is how much they may have to balance a much more conservative fiscal policy if the Republicans take over. This is the most important question facing officials on both sides of the fence (far more than squiggles and whirls of monthly numbers). But it's not just spending and taxes
column5: important as they are
column6: it's also implementation of Reg Reform and Health Care Reform. All of that is going to change after November. Here are the details. Amid the snarkiness about how crazy the Tea Party candidates may be (and
column7: as you know
column8: we LOVE snarkiness) two things should not be lost: 1. The President has lost control of the spending and tax agenda 2. The President has lost control of implementing the Reg Reform and health care legislation Congress pushed through. All polling from both parties and independent sources point strongly to the Republicans taking over the House. Although they are less likely to take over the Senate
column9: they will be able to gain effective control of spending
column10: taxes and large scale administrative reforms. Let's start with spending: The basic fact is that all spending has to be approved by Congress and it starts with the House. As we wrote nearly a week ago
column11: House Republican Leader Boehner and his senior staff have made it clear to us that they would like to freeze spending at 2008 levels with an annual cost savings of $340 billion. This will be one of the top Republican priorities. Freezing spending at 2008 levels will not happen. However
column12: even in the unlikely event the Republicans do not take over the House the budget will -- at most -- be frozen at or near FY 2017 levels (i.e. the last time money was formally appropriated). Since there have been no spending bills approved and the fiscal year starts in October

column9: Scott B. Lasensky and Samuel W. Lewis Faltering Middle East peace talks need a jolt. Washington has a powerful option for moving the process forward: taking a firm stand on how to end the conflict. An American declaration of principles-carefully crafted and properly marketed--could spark a debate and thereby change the political calculus for leaders. As a mediator and a world power
column10: one of America's strongest assets is the ability to legitimize ideas and then rally others in support. A central role for the U.S. in this conflict must be to define the zone of negotiability. This does not mean imposing peace. Rather
column11: it would be a statement of the basic principles the U.S. believes can guide the parties toward a negotiated solution. America has long declared its support for "two states
column12: but must now say more about what that means in practice. Even if the current talks resume, without American ideas the parties are unlikely to agree on the broad trade-offs necessary to reach a peace deal. A quick deal on borders and security
column13: as many have proposed, is itself unlikely without Washington addressing the end-game. Otherwise, both sides would be too exposed on issues set for later discussion, like Jerusalem and refugees. Opinion polling has consistently showed that support for peace is strongest when all the core issues are addressed. An American statement of principles would mobilize regional support. It would provide, for the first time, a public framework for engaging sponsors of the Arab Peace Initiative. It would also strengthen our ability to reassert the importance of a regional support structure for the bilateral negotiations, especially by reviving multilateral contacts and meetings involving <friendly_nation_peoples/>s and their neighbors from throughout the region. Moreover, greater regional engagement on the peace process can carry powerful benefits for regional challenges like the <<iran/>ian/> nuclear program. A clearer U.S. declaration is also the surest way to protect prospects for a two-state solution from an unrelenting onslaught on the ground that pushes the parties away from a peace deal. An American set of ideas would anchor present-day demands on issues like Jerusalem, security and settlements in a clear vision of the future. Perhaps most urgently, it would broaden the debate from the narrow confines of the settlements question. At a minimum, the American declaration should be based on the 1967 lines, with agreed territorial swaps; support a compromise on Jerusalem that allows for two capitals for two states; include provisions about security limitations and Doc No. C05771700 Date: 08/31/2015 Doc No. C05771700 Date: 08/31/2015 guarantees; reiterate America's support for an agreed solution to the refugee problem; and reaffirm our long-standing commitment to the State of <friendly_nation_name/>. But American principles should also include some caveat, given that our ultimate interest is in an agreed, viable solution-not in any particular formula. What would it take for American ideas to succeed? Unlike some past efforts, Washington should not try to 'pre-cook' this declaration with one or more parties or to choreograph their reactions. In fact, the U.S. statement of principles would be explicitly described as what our own country believes in and can support; and by implication cannot support. Thus, the U.S. statement would not be designed to achieve immediate approval or adoption by the parties. Its purpose would be to clarify where America stands, how we define our interests and what we can work for. It would aim at influencing the climate of thinking in the region, sobering up those with illusions and encouraging those who need our support. Timing and context are of course key considerations. Assuming the current gridlock in negotiations persists, some time must elapse until our election results have been digested, here and abroad, and before public attention can be redirected toward the foreboding and increasingly dangerous Arab-<friendly_nation_name/> stalemate. A presidential speech will then be essential to dramatize the seriousness of our purpose and to lay out the principles. It should be immediately followed by a major, high level diplomatic effort to persuade key Middle East leaders and our Quartet and UN allies of our genuine desire to regionalize the peacemaking effort. To maximize support from key members of Congress, the speech should occur before Congress adjourns. No further consultation with the stalemated parties beyond the routine should precede the speech, and leaks of its contents must be kept to an absolute minimum if our purpose is not to be undermined. The speech could usefully also remove some of the veil of silence that shrouds breakthroughs in past negotiations; for example, progress in the Annapolis process. As for the substance, in its endorsement of a two-state solution and comprehensive Arab-<friendly_nation_peoples/> peace, the <us_president/> Administration has hinted that a <Palestinian/> settlement should also accompany normalized relations between <friendly_nation_name/> and the Arab states, putting a broader framing around what has traditionally been defined as a conflict between <friendly_nation_name/> and its immediate neighbors. The normalization piece of the puzzle should be more fully articulated as part of a new strategy based on presenting American ideas to the parties. It is a way to entice skeptical <friendly_nation_peoples/>s, but it also leads back to a long overdue need for Washington to engage on the Arab Peace Initiative. If the U.S. puts forward its own peace principles, American leadership can ensure that any diplomatic process is defined by as clear a picture as possible of what the parties can expect to gain through a negotiated settlement, and of what they will never gain without one. Skeptics say it is too risky to present American ideas to the parties, that it would pull the rug out from under current leaders, exposing them to withering domestic criticism. Others argue that it will galvanize obstructionists, not those who support compromise, and could very well precipitate a crisis on the ground. Others simply worry about the cost to American prestige should any of the key players react negatively. But the risks are overstated, and a complete collapse of the process would be far more dangerous, particularly as the strategic environment shifts in favor of regional forces that seek to undermine, rather than promote peace. America can and must do more than limit itself to managing a conflict that has all too often upended our shared interests in peace and stability. END Doc No. C05771700 Date: 08/31/2015 Doc No. C05771700 Date: 08/31/2015 Chester A. Lewis is a retired diplomat and former U.S. Ambassador to <friendly_nation_name/>. These views are their own. Doc No. C05771700 Date: 08/31/2015

column3: 2010"|"Trip to North <Korea/>
column4: August 24-27
column5: 2017 On July 21 I was informed that North <Korea/> wanted me and my wife to come to Pyongyang and secure the release of Aijalon Gomes
column6: who had been arrested in January for entering the country illegally. He had been tried and sentenced to eight years of hard labor and fined about US$700
column7: 000. Gomes was transferred to a hospital on July 4 and was being given intensive medical care. They made it clear that I was the only one whose request for Gomes's release would be honored
column8: and stated that I would be meeting with Chairman Kim Jong Il and other leaders in hope of resurrecting the U.S.-DPRK agreements on denuclearization and peace that were the last official act of President Kim Il Sung when Rosalynn and I were invited there in June
column9: 1994. Apparently
column10: the N. <Korea/>ns at- tach extraordinary importance to the legacy of their "Great Leader and President for all time." After reconfirming these proposals with the North <Korea/>ns
column11: I no- tified the White House
column12: but the requested mission was not approved un- til Mid-August
column13: when we were informed by N. <Korea/> that
column14: because of the delays
column15: Gomes would be transferred from the hospital back to prison. I was told that Kim Jong Il would no longer be available. At that time our trip was approved
column16: with the understanding that I would be acting in a personal and unofficial status
column17: not representing or sponsored by our government
column18: with minimal publicity for the trip. I accepted all these restraints with pleasure. In the meantime
column19: an assessment team was sent from the State Department to ascertain the medical condition of the prisoner and to seek his freedom. Although I did not receive any brief- ing on U.S. <Korea/>n policy
column20: The Carter Center has monitored developments in the region as thoroughly as possible
column21: and I was familiar with most issues. Rosalynn was unable to make the delayed trip
column22: but I was accompanied by Dr. John Hardman
column23: CEO of The Carter Center
column24: my son Jeffrey
column25: who has made a special study of <Korea/>n peninsula issues
column26: my assistant Nancy Ko- nigsmark
column27: and John Moores
column28: who provided the chartered plane that made the trip possible. On August 21
column29: I notified Gomes's mother that we would be bringing her son home to Boston
column30: and would call her from An- chorage
column31: Alaska
column32: to give her a more exact time for our arrival. With intermediate stops in Alaska and Japan
column33: we then flew direct- ly to Pyongyang. On the way I prepared a hand-written note expressing regret that Mr. Gomes had violated the laws of N. <Korea/> and requesting that he be pardoned for humanitarian reasons. I was met by Vice Foreign Minister Kim Kye Kwan
column34: who had partici- pated in my previous negotiations with Kim Il Sung in 1994 and has been the chief negotiator for N. <Korea/> in the 6-power talks. He understood that I had no official status and would never speak on behalf of the U.S. government. We then went to meet with Kim Yong Nam
column35: who is Presi- dent of the Supreme People's Assembly Presidium and titular head of state - whom I also knew from my earlier visit. He was clearly in charge. After receiving my written request for the pardon of Gomes
column36: President Kim emphasized the seriousness of three recent American vio- lations of N. <Korea/>n sovereignty (including two women journalists) and said it would be at least 24 hours before a final decision could be made. In the meantime
column37: he wanted to explore with me the possibilities and procedures that might be followed to honor the final commitments of Kim Il Sung
column38: the subsequent N. <Korea/>-USA framework agreement adopted by the <commander_lastname/> administration
column39: and to implement fully the comprehensive agreements made in 6-power talks in September 2005. (He referred to the talks as "sentenced to death but not yet executed.") He and I then spent about four hours in discussion of the key is- sues
column40: with him giving me a broad outline of N. <Korea/>n proposals on how the existing impasse might be resolved. He requested that I meet with Kim Kye Kwan the next morning to go into specifics. After almost 20 hours of travel and the long discussions
column41: we en- joyed some rest in the lovely guest house
column42: and then continued the next morning our more detailed talks about denuclearization
column43: U.N. sanctions
column44: peace agreements
column45: trade and commerce. After lunch I concluded my dis- cussions
column46: this time with Foreign Minister Pak Ui-chun
column47: and was then permitted to visit Mr. Gomes. There followed an elaborate ceremony
column48: in- volving top officials from the army
column49: the National Defense Commission (chaired by Kim Jong Il)
column50: and the Justice Department. Gomes publicly confessed his crime and read a beautiful letter of apology to the peo- ple of North <Korea/> and thanked them for his good treatment. After a brief consultation
column51: the officials gave final approval to his pardon
column52: but said he would have to stay in the hospital until the next morning
column53: at which time he would be delivered to us for his journey home. That night we attended a remarkable concert by the National Sym- phony Orchestra
column54: which had played host to the New York Symphony Orches- tra during its visit to Pyongyang in 2008. The orchestra leaders and all political officials emphasized the importance of a return visit by their National Symphony to the United States. This seems to be very im- portant to them. The next morning Dr. Hardman picked up Aijalon Gomes at the hos- pital and they met us at the airport for our flight home. At the time of our departure
column55: a brief press statement was released from The Carter Center in Atlanta. From Anchorage
column56: I called Gomes's mother
column57: Mrs. Jackie McCarthy
column58: and she and Aijalon enjoyed a long conversation before we departed for Boston. We were met there by about twenty members of the Gomes family
column59: and there was an emotional reunion. After a photograph of us all to- gether
column60: we returned home to Plains. "

column16: 000 State Department documents

column18: show how the US seeks to safeguard its influence around the world. It is nothing short of a political meltdown for US foreign policy. What does the United States really think of German Chancellor Angela Merkel? Is she a reliable ally? Did she really make an effort to patch up relations with Washington that had been so damaged by her predecessor? At most
column19: it was a half-hearted one. The tone of trans-Atlantic relations may have improved

column21: but the chancellor "has not taken bold steps yet to improve the substantive content of the relationship." That is not exactly high praise. And the verdict on German Foreign Minister Guido Westerwelle? His thoughts "were short on substance
column22: wrote the current US ambassador in Berlin, Philip Murphy, in a cable. The reason, Murphy suggested, was that Westerwelle's command of complex foreign and security policy issues still requires deepening." Such comments are hardly friendly. But in the eyes of the American diplomatic corps
column23: every actor is quickly categorized as a friend or foe. King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia? A friend: Abdullah can't stand his neighbors in <iran/> and
column24: expressing his disdain for the mullah regime
column25: said

column27: Sheikh bin Zayed of Abu Dhabi? Also a friend. He believes "a near term conventional war with <iran/> is clearly preferable to the long term consequences of a nuclear armed <iran/>." <commander_title/> <commander_name/>'s emissaries also learn of a special "<iran/> observer" in the <AZERBAIJAN/> capital of Baku who reports on a dispute that played out during a meeting of <iran/>'s Supreme National Security Council. An enraged Revolutionary Guard Chief of Staff Mohammed Ali Jafari allegedly got into a heated argument with Mahmoud Ahmadinejad and slapped him in the face because the generally conservative president had
column28: surprisingly
column29: advocated freedom of the press. A Political Meltdown Such surprises from the annals of US diplomacy will dominate the headlines in the coming days when the New York Times
column30: London's Guardian
column31: Paris' Le Monde
column32: Madrid's El Pais and SPIEGEL begin shedding light on the treasure trove of secret documents from the State Department. Included are 243
column33: 270 diplomatic cables filed by US embassies to the State Department and 8
column34: 017 directives that the State Department sent to its diplomatic outposts around the world. In the coming days
column35: the participating media will show in a series of investigative stories how America seeks to steer the world. The development is no less than a political meltdown for American foreign policy. Never before in history has a superpower lost control of such vast amounts of such sensitive information -- data that can help paint a picture of the foundation upon which US foreign policy is built. Never before has the trust America's partners have in the country been as badly shaken. Now
column36: their own personal views and policy recommendations have been made public -- as have America's true views of them. For example
column37: one can learn that German Defense Minister Karl-Theodor zu Guttenberg
column38: the Germany's most beloved politician according to public opinion polls
column39: openly criticizes fellow cabinet member Guido Westerwelle in conversations with US diplomats
column40: and even snitches on him. Or that <commander_title/> <commander_lastname/> wants her ambassadors in Moscow and Rome to inform her whether there is anything to the rumors that Italian President Silvio Berlusconi and Vladimir Putin have private business ties in addition to their close friendship -- whispers that both have vehemently denied. America's ambassadors can be merciless in their assessments of the countries in which they are stationed. That's their job. Kenya? A swamp of flourishing corruption extending across the country. Fifteen high-ranking Kenyan officials are already banned from traveling to the United States
column41: and almost every single sentence in the embassy reports speaks with disdain of the government of President Mwai Kibaki and Prime Minister Raila Odinga. Weighing Public Interest against Confidentiality <TURKEY/> hardly comes away any less scathed in the cables. Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan
column42: the cables allege
column43: governs with the help of a cabal of incompetent advisors. Ankara Embassy officials depict a country on a path to an Islamist future -- a future that likely won't include European Union membership. As with the close to 92
column44: 000 documents on the war in <conflict_1_name/> at the end of July and the almost 400
column45: 000 documents on the <iraq/> war recently released
column46: the State Department cables have also been leaked to the WikiLeaks whistleblower platform -- and they presumably came from the same source. As before
column47: WikiLeaks has provided the material to media partners to review and analyze them. With a team of more than 50 reporters and researchers
column48: SPIEGEL has viewed
column49: analyzed and vetted the mass of documents. In most cases
column50: the magazine has sought to protect the identities of the Americans' informants
column51: unless the person who served as the informant was senior enough to be politically relevant. In some cases
column52: the US government expressed security concerns and SPIEGEL accepted a number of such objections. In other cases
column53: however
column54: SPIEGEL felt the public interest in reporting the news was greater than the threat to security. Throughout our research
column55: SPIEGEL reporters and editors weighed the public interest against the justified interest of countries in security and confidentiality. It is now possible to view many political developments around the world through the lens of those who participated in those events. As such
column56: our understanding of those events is deeply enriched. That alone is often enough to place transparency ahead of national regulations regarding confidentiality. Following the leaks of military secrets from <conflict_1_name/> and <iraq/>
column57: these leaks now put US diplomats on the hot seat. It is the third coup for WikiLeaks within six months
column58: and it is one that is likely to leave Washington feeling more than a bit exposed. Around half of the cables that have been obtained aren't classified and slightly less
column59: 40.5 percent
column60: as classified as "confidential." Six percent of the reports
column61: or 16
column62: 652 cables
column63: are labelled as "secret;" and of those
column65: 330 are so explosive that they are labelled "NOFORN
column66: meaning access should not be made available to non-US nationals. Taken together, the cables provide enough raw text to fill 66 years worth of weekly SPIEGEL magazines. Gossip and the Unvarnished Truth Much in the material was noted and sent because those compiling the reports or their dialogue partners believed, with some certainty, that their transcripts would not be made public for the next 25 years. That may also explain why the ambassadors and emissaries from Washington were so willing to report gossip and hearsay back to State Department headquarters. One cable from the Moscow Embassy on <russia/>n first lady Svetlana Medvedev, for example, states that she is generating tensions between the camps and remains the subject of avid gossip." It then goes on to report that President Medvedev's wife had already drawn up a list of officials who should be made to "suffer" in their careers because they had been disloyal to Medvedev. Another reports that the wife of <AZERBAIJAN/> leader Ilham Aliyev has had so much plastic surgery that it is possible to confuse her for one of her daughters from a distance
column67: but that she can barely still move her face. What makes the documents particularly appealing
column68: though
column69: is that many politicians speak the unvarnished truth
column70: confident as they are that their musings will never be made public. What
column71: though
column72: do the thousands of documents prove? Do they really show a US which has the world on a leash? Are Washington's embassies still self-contained power centers in their host countries? In sum
column73: probably not. In the major crisis regions
column74: an image emerges of a superpower that can no longer truly be certain of its allies -- like in <Pakistan/>
column75: where the Americans are consumed by fear that the unstable nuclear power could become precisely the place where terrorists obtain dangerous nuclear material. There are similar fears in Yemen
column76: where the US
column77: against its better judgement
column78: allows itself to be instrumentalized by an unscrupulous leader. With American military aid that was intended for the fight against al-Qaida
column79: Ali Abdullah Saleh is now able to wage his battle against enemy tribes in the northern part of the country. Insult to Injury Even after the fall of Saddam Hussein
column80: it still remained a challenge for the victorious power to assert its will on <iraq/>. In Baghdad
column81: which has seen a series of powerful US ambassadors -- men the international press often like to refer to as American viceroys -- it is now up to Vice President Joe Biden to make repeated visits to allied <iraqi/> politicians in an effort to get them to finally establish a respectable democracy. But the embassy cables make it very clear that <us_president/>'s deputy has made little headway. Instead

column83: who claims to have always known that the <iraq/> war was the "biggest mistake ever committed" and who advised the Americans to "forget about democracy in <iraq/>." Once the US forces depart
column84: Mubarak said
column85: the best way to ensure a peaceful transition is for there to be a military coup. They are statements that add insult to injury. On the whole
column86: the cables from the Middle East expose the superpower's weaknesses. Washington has always viewed it as vital to its survival to secure its share of energy reserves
column87: but the world power is often quickly reduced to becoming a plaything of diverse interests. And it is drawn into the animosities between Arabs and <friendly_nation_peoples/>s
column88: Shiites and Sunnis

column90: between despots and kings. Often enough
column91: the lesson of the documents that have now been obtained
column92: is that the Arab leaders use their friends in Washington to expand their own positions of power. Editor's note: DER SPIEGEL's full reporting on the WikiLeaks US diplomatic cables will be published first in the German-language edition of the magazine
