column4: 2017 ann Beck's view of American history stems from the paranoid politics of the fifties. A few months ago
column5: the cable-television and radio host Glenn Beck began his Fox News show with one of his favorite props: a pipe clenched between his teeth. "I've got my pipe
column6: he told his audience, his speech slightly muddled by the stem, because we're going to speak about schoolish kind of things." The theme of the day was "Restoring History
column7: and Beck, looking professorial in a neat dark blazer and a pink button-down shirt, began the lesson by peering at a stack of history textbooks and pronouncing them full of falsehoods, produced by malicious progressive intent." Progressives
column8: he explained-liberals
column9: socialists
column10: Communists
column11: the entire spectrum of the left-"knew they had to separate us from our history to be able to separate us from our Constitution and God." For the next hour
column12: Beck earnestly explained some of the history that "is being stolen from us": the depression of 1920
column13: for example
column14: or how conservative economics saved the nation from the "near-depression" of 1946-crises that progressives don't want you to know about. "You've been taught one lie
column15: I think
column16: your whole life
column17: he said. For the fractious Tea Party movement, Beck-a former drive-time radio jockey, a recovering alcoholic, and a Mormon convert-has emerged as both a unifying figure and an intellectual guide. One opinion poll, released in July by Democracy Corps, showed that he is the most highly regarded individual among Tea Party supporters
column18: seen not merely as an entertainer, like Rush Limbaugh, but as an educator." And in the past few months Beck has established his own institute of learning: the online
column19: for-profit Beck University. Enrollees can take courses like Faith 102
column20: which contends with "revisionists and secular progressives" about the separation of church and state; Hope 102
column21: an attack on the activist federal government; and the combined Charity 101/102/103
column22: a highly restrictive interpretation of rights
column23: federalism
column24: and the division of powers. During the "Restoring History" episode
column25: Beck twice encouraged viewers to join his Web seminars
column26: where they can hear "lessons from the best and brightest historians and scholars that we could find." The B.U. faculty consists of three members
column27: including one bona-fide academic
column28: James R. Stoner
column29: Jr.
column30: the chair of the political-science department at Louisiana State University; the other two are the head of a management consulting firm and the founder of WallBuilders
column31: which the Web site calls "a national pro-family organization." Beck himself often acts as a professor
column32: a slightly jocular one
column33: on his Fox News program. Surrounded by charts and figures
column34: he offers explanations of current politics and history lessons about the country's long march to <us_president/>-era totalitarianism. The decline
column35: he says
column36: began with the Progressive era of the early twentieth century
column37: in particular with the Presidency of Woodrow Wilson
column38: when both the Federal Reserve System and the graduated federal income tax came into existence. "Wilson
column39: Beck told his radio audience in August, just despised what America was." Beck's claims have found an audience among Tea Party spokesmen and sympathizers. At the movement's Freedom Summit in Washington last September
column40: one activist told a reporter
column41: "The election between Teddy Roosevelt and Woodrow Wilson in 1912 was when it started going downhill." And in April an angry member of the Tea Party Patriots group from Cape Fear
column42: North Carolina
column43: claimed on the group's Web site that "the very things you see happening in this country today started with the Wilson Administration." At a Tax Day rally this past spring
column44: the veteran conservative organizer Richard Viguerie described the Tea Party as "an unfettered new force of the middle class." And
column45: indeed
column46: calling <us_president/> a socialist in the tradition of Woodrow Wilson is audacious enough to seem like the marker of a new movement-or
column47: at least
column48: a new twist in the nation's long history of conspiracy-mongering. In fact
column49: it marks a revival of ideas that circulated on the extremist right half a century ago
column50: especially in the John Birch Society and among its admirers. Beck's version of American history relies on lessons from his own acknowledged inspiration
column51: the late right-wing writer W. Cleon Skousen
column52: and also restates charges made by the Birch Society's founder
column53: Robert Welch. The political universe is
column54: of course
column55: very different today from what it was during the Cold War. Yet the Birchers' politics and their view of American history-which focussed more on totalitarian threats at home than on those posed by the Soviet Union and Communist <china/>-has proved remarkably persistent. The pressing historical question is how extremist ideas held at bay for decades inside the Republican Party have exploded anew-and why
column56: this time
column57: Party leaders have done virtually nothing to challenge those ideas
column58: and a great deal to abet them. The early nineteen-sixties were a turbulent time in American politics
column59: for the right wing in particular. In the South
column60: racist violence against civil-rights workers was constant
column61: deepening sectional splits in the Democratic Party that would in time deliver the once solidly Democratic South to the Republicans. Southern elected officials
column62: in support of what they called "massive resistance" to civil-rights laws and judicial rulings
column63: resurrected the ideas of nullification and interposition
column64: which claimed that individual states could void federal laws within their own borders. Others focussed on what they considered a fearsome Communist menace inside the United States. General Edwin A. Walker caused an enormous stir when he resigned from the Army in 1961
column65: after President John F. Kennedy's Pentagon reprimanded him for spreading right-wing propaganda among his troops and accusing prominent American officials of Communist sympathies. Senator Strom Thurmond
column66: the Dixiecrat from South Carolina
column67: spoke for many on the far right when he declared that various modestly liberal domestic programs "fall clearly within the category of socialism." The John Birch Society was one of the decade's most controversial right-wing organizations. Founded in 1958 by Robert Welch
column68: a candy manufacturer from Massachusetts
column69: the society took its name from a Baptist missionary and military- intelligence officer killed by Communist <chinese/> forces in 1945
column70: whom Welch called the first American casualty of the Cold War. The group was founded at a propitious time. After Senator Joseph McCarthy's fall
column72: many of McCarthy's followers felt bereft of a voice
column73: and Welch seemed to speak for them; by the mid-sixties
column74: his society's membership was estimated to be as high as a hundred thousand. Welch
column75: exploiting fears of what McCarthy had called an "immense" domestic conspiracy
column76: declared that the federal government had already fallen into the Communists' clutches. In a tract titled "The Politician
column77: he attacked President Dwight D. Eisenhower as a dedicated
column78: conscious agent of the Communist conspiracy" who had been serving the plot "all of his adult life." Late in 1961
column79: after the disastrous Bay of Pigs invasion
column80: he accused the Kennedy Administration of "helping the Communists everywhere in the world while pretending to do the opposite." Wherever he looked
column81: Welch saw Communist forces manipulating American economic and foreign policy on behalf of totalitarianism. But within the United States
column82: he believed
column83: the subversion had actually begun years before the Bolshevik Revolution. Conflating modern liberalism and totalitarianism
column84: Welch described government as "always and inevitably an enemy of individual freedom." Consequently
column85: he charged
column86: the Progressive era
column87: which expanded the federal government's role in curbing social and economic ills
column88: was a dire period in our history
column89: and Woodrow Wilson "more than any other one man started this nation on its present road to totalitarianism." In the nineteen-sixties
column90: Welch became convinced that even the Communist movement was but "a tool of the total conspiracy." This master conspiracy
column91: he said
column92: had forerunners in ancient Sparta
column93: and sprang fully to life in the eighteenth century
column94: in the "uniformly Satanic creed and program" of the Bavarian Illuminati. Run by those he called "the Insiders
column95: the conspiracy resided chiefly in international families of financiers, such as the Rothschilds and the Rockefellers, government agencies like the Federal Reserve System and the Internal Revenue Service, and nongovernmental organizations like the Bilderberg Group, the Council on Foreign Relations, and the Trilateral Commission. Since the early twentieth century, they had done a good deal of their evil work under the guise of humanitarian uplift. One broad avenue down which these conspiratorial forces advance was known as progressive legislation
column96: Welch declared in 1966. The very same collectivist theories and demagogic pretenses which had destroyed earlier civilizations were now paraded forth in the disguise of new and modern concepts." In the worst case
column97: Welch believed
column98: military action might be necessary to dislodge the totalitarians. But for the moment a nonviolent political revolution would suffice. Accordingly
column99: he designed the Birch Society roughly
column100: if not explicitly
column101: on the Marxist-Leninist model of a vanguard revolutionary party: a series of small cells that would work in secret to agitate the populace and elect right-thinking candidates to office. "It isn't numbers we have to worry about
column102: Welch wrote, but the courage on the part of our followers to stick their necks out and play rough-the same as the Communists do." The "Founder" himself would dictate the society's policies
column103: advised by a council of about two dozen businessmen and professionals
column104: and the local cells would be overseen by unyielding commanders. "It is the leadership that is most demanding
column105: most exacting of its followers
column106: Welch observed, that achieves really dedicated support." Welch's group became synonymous with right-wing extremism
column107: earning satirical blasts from critics ranging from the cartoonist Walt Kelly to the musicians Bob Dylan and Dizzy Gillespie. The trumpeter
column108: whose actual name was John Birks Gillespie
column109: made a humorous run for the Presidency in 1964
column110: organizing John Birks Societies in twenty-five states. Still
column111: the most outlandish of the era's right-wing anti-Communists was not Welch but Willard Cleon Skousen. A transplanted Canadian who served as a Mormon missionary in his teens
column112: Skousen was considered so radical in the early nineteen-sixties that even J. Edgar Hoover's F.B.I. watched him closely; one 1962 memo in his extensive F.B.I. file noted that "during the past year or so
column113: Skousen has affiliated himself with the extreme right-wing 'professional communists' who are promoting their own anticommunism for obvious financial purposes." Skousen was himself employed by the F.B.I.
column114: from 1935 until 1951
column115: much of that time as a special agent working chiefly in administration. These desk jobs
column116: he claimed implausibly
column117: gave him access to confidential domestic intelligence about Communism. Skousen also maintained that he had served as Hoover's administrative assistant; Hoover informed inquirers that there was no such position. Skousen taught for years in the speech and religion departments at Brigham Young University
column118: interrupted by a stint
column119: from 1956 to 1960
column120: as the police chief of Salt Lake City. His time in office was contentious
column121: and after he raided a friendly card game attended by the city's right-wing mayor
column122: J. Bracken Lee
column123: he was promptly fired. Lee called Skousen "a master of half truths" and said that he ran the police department "like a Gestapo"; Skousen's supporters placed burning crosses on the Mayor's lawn. After losing his police job
column124: Skousen founded a group called the All-American Society
column125: which Time described in 1961 as an exemplar of the far-right "ultras." Although he did not join the Birch Society
column126: Skousen worked with its American Opinion Speakers' Bureau
column127: and
column129: wrote a rousing tract titled "The Communist Attack on the John Birch Society
column130: which condemned the society's critics for promoting the official Communist Party line." (This was a tic of Skousen's; he later defended the Mormon policy of denying the priesthood to blacks with a pamphlet called "The Communist Attack on the Mormons.") All along
column131: Skousen's evolving thoughts ran in tandem with Welch's. In "The Naked Communist
column132: a lengthy primer published in 1958, he enlivened a survey of the worldwide leftist threat with outlandish claims, writing that F.D.R.'s adviser Harry Hopkins had treasonously delivered to the Soviets a large supply of uranium, and that the <russia/>ns built the first Sputnik with plans stolen from the United States. A year before Richard Condon's novel The Manchurian Candidate" appeared
column133: Skousen announced that the Communists were creating "a regimented breed of Pavlovian men whose minds could be triggered into immediate action by signals from their masters." A later book
column134: "The Naked Capitalist
column135: decried the Ivy League Establishment, who, through the Federal Reserve, the Council on Foreign Relations, and the Rockefeller Foundation, formed the world's secret power structure." The conspiracy had begun
column136: Skousen wrote
column137: when reformers like the wealthy banker Edward M. (Colonel) House
column138: a close adviser to President Woodrow Wilson
column139: helped put into place the Federal Reserve and the graduated income tax. In 1971
column140: Skousen organized another group
column141: the Freemen Institute
column142: which he later renamed the National Center for Constitutional Studies. According to an article published in the Review of Religious Research
column143: the center's targets included "the Occupational Safety and Health Administration
column144: the Environmental Protection Agency
column145: the Federal Communication Commission's fairness doctrine in editorial broadcasting
column146: the federal government's change of the gold standard in currency
column147: all subsidies to farmers
column148: all federal aid to education
column149: all federal social welfare
column150: foreign aid
column151: social security
column152: elimination of public school prayer and Bible reading
column153: and (that familiar right-wing nemesis) the United Nations." Skousen's pronouncements made him a pariah among most conservative activists
column154: including some on the right-wing fringe. In 1962
column155: the ultraconservative American Security Council threw him out
column156: because members felt that he had "gone off the deep end." In 1971
column157: a review in the Mormon journal Dialogue accused Skousen of "inventing fantastic ideas and making inferences that go far beyond the bounds of honest commentary
column158: and advancing doctrines that came perilously close" to Nazism. And in 1979
column159: after Skousen called President.Jimmy Carter a puppet of the Council on Foreign Relations and the Rockefeller family
column160: the president of the Mormon church issued a national order banning announcements about his organizations. Skousen was undeterred. In 1981
column161: he produced "The 5
column162: 000 Year Leap
column163: a treatise that assembles selective quotations and groundless assertions to claim that the U.S. Constitution is rooted not in the Enlightenment but in the Bible, and that the framers believed in minimal central government. Either proposition would have astounded James Madison, often described as the guiding spirit behind the Constitution, who rejected state-established religions and, like Alexander Hamilton, proposed a central government so strong that it could veto state laws. The 5
column164: 000 Year Leap" is not a fervid book. Instead
column165: it is calmly
column166: ingratiatingly misleading. Skousen quotes various eighteenth-century patriots on the evils of what Samuel Adams
column168: called "the Utopian schemes of leveling
column169: which Skousen equates with redistribution of wealth. But he does not mention the Founders' endorsement of taxing the rich to support the general welfare. Thomas Jefferson, for example, wrote approvingly in 1811 of having federal taxes (then limited to tariffs) fall solely on the wealthy, which meant that the farmer will see his government supported
column170: his children educated
column171: and the face of his country made a paradise by the contributions of the rich alone
column172: without his being called on to spend a cent from his earnings." Skousen also challenges the separation of church and state
column173: asserting that "the Founders were not indulging in any idle gesture when they adopted the motto 'In God We Trust.' "In reality
column174: the motto that came out of the Constitutional Convention was "E Pluribus Unum": out of many
column175: one. "In God We Trust" came much later; its use on coins was first permitted in 1864
column176: and only in 1955
column177: at the height of the Cold War
column178: did Congress mandate that it appear on all currency. The following year
column179: President Eisenhower-who Welch charged was a Communist agent-approved "In God We Trust" as the national motto. In 1982
column180: Skousen published a follow-up work
column181: an ancestor-worshipping history text titled The Making of America
column182: and prepared a study guide for nationwide seminars based on its contents. As Alexander Zaitchik reports in his informative study of Beck, Common Nonsense
column183: the new book became an object of controversy in 1987, after the California Bicentennial Commission sold it as part of a fund-raising drive. Among its offenses was an account of slavery drawn from long-disgraced work by the historian Fred A. Shannon, which characterized slave children as pickaninnies" and suggested that the worst victims of slavery were the slaveholders themselves. The constitutional scholar Jack Rakove
column184: of Stanford
column185: inspected Skousen's book and seminars and pronounced them "a joke that no self-respecting scholar would think is worth a warm pitcher of spit." By the time Skousen died
column187: he was little remembered outside the ranks of the furthest-right Mormons. Then
column189: Glenn Beck began touting his work: "The Naked Communist
column190: The Naked Capitalist
column191: and, especially, The 5
column192: 000 Year Leap
column193: which he called essential to understanding why our Founders built this Republic the way they did." After Beck put the book in the first spot on his required-reading list-and wrote an enthusiastic new introduction for its reissue- it shot to the top of the Amazon best-seller list. In the first half of 2017
column194: it sold more than two hundred and fifty thousand copies. Local branches of the Tea Party Patriots
column195: the United American Tea Party
column196: and other groups across the country have since organized study groups around it. "It is time we learn and follow the FREEDOM principles of our Founding Fathers
column197: a United American Tea Party video declares, referring to the principles expounded by Skousen's book. If Beck is the movement's teacher, The 5
column198: 000 Year Leap" has become its primer
column199: with "The Making of America" as a kind of 102- level text. The popularity of Beck's broadcasts
column200: which now reach two million viewers each day
column201: has brought neo-Birchite ideas to an audience beyond any that Welch or Skousen might have dreamed of. Several times a week
column202: Beck informs his audience that socialists (whom he also sometimes calls Fascists or Communists) led by <us_president/> have seized power
column203: and that patriotic Americans must take their country back. His TV show for some time featured "Comrade Updates
column204: in which Beck described perfidy while the Soviet anthem played in the background. He attacks all the familiar bogeymen: the Federal Reserve System (which he asserts is a private conglomerate, unaccountable to the public); the Council on Foreign Relations (born of a progressive idea" to manipulate the media in order to "let the masses know what should be done"); and a historical procession of evildoers
column205: including Skousen's old target Colonel House and Welch's old target Woodrow Wilson. His sources on these matters
column206: quite apart from Skousen's books
column207: can be unreliable. On September 22nd
column208: amid a diatribe about House
column209: Beck cited a passage from "Secrets of the Federal Reserve
column210: by Eustace Mullins. The book, commissioned in 1948 by Ezra Pound, is a startlingly anti-Semitic fantasy of how a Jewish-led conspiracy of all-powerful bankers established the Federal Reserve in service of their plot to dominate the world. Part of Beck's allure is the promise that he will reveal secret information. In one segment last year, he produced a drawing of fasces-which he described, anachronistically, as the Roman symbol of Fascism"-and then a picture of an old Mercury dime
column211: with fasces on the reverse side. "Who brought this dime in? It happened in 1916-Woodrow Wilson was the President
column212: he said. We've been on the road to Fascism for a while." Benito Mussolini
column213: of course
column214: didn't adopt the ancient symbol of authority as the Fascist emblem until the nineteen-twenties; the designer of the coin
column215: the sculptor Adolph A. Weinman

column18: and to take steps to prevent cancer by making healthy lifestyle choices
column19: which include a good diet
column20: exercise
column21: not smoking and knowing your family history and risk factors. Lots of good information can be found at www.preventcancer.org." The following is a statement from Dr. Brian P. Monahan
column22: the Congressional Attending Physician: "Congressman McGovern was admitted to the Washington Hospital Center today for surgery to remove the thyroid gland in his neck. column6: 2017 5:43:12 AM EDT \nTo: Andrew Stillman - BM Cc: "Mark J. Penn" \nSubject: Re: Mark's election night HuffPo piece Here is my quick take on the results -- see below. It's 1994 all over again -- that's for sure. Brilliant of you to be thousands of miles away from this. No Tea Party for the Tea Party But <us_president/> must heed the message of exit polls By Mark Penn Without doubt the tea Party will be rejoicing at the results and laying down ultimatums to the Republican Party to steer to the right
column7: and the Republican Party having embraced the Tea party will be hard pressed to say "no" to the new right wing in America. Poll after poll shows that the Tea Party is really a splinter of the Republican Party
column8: and the exit polls show that this was a vote about the economy
column9: not ideology. Only 23% of the voters said that they were casting a vote for the Tea Party while 56% said it was not a factor and the rest outright opposed them. But 62% of the voters said that the economy was the key factor determining their vote. The polls show that the voters want tax cuts not tax increases
column10: modification or repeal of healthcare
column11: spending cuts and above all jobs. With healthcare reform
column12: cap and trade bills
column13: and tax increases
column14: President <us_president/> got out of step with the voters. Why he didn't just kick the Bush tax cuts down the road a year and get them out of the election cycle is mystifying. Instead -- just like in 1994 -- the Democrats ran on the platform of increasing taxes for the wealthy
column15: amplifying class warfare rather than ending it. Whoever told President <us_president/> "don't worry
column16: just pass healthcare and they will love it" must be squirming in his seat tonight. And all those who think that tacking further to the left is the answer for the Democrats should look at these results carefully and think again. President <us_president/> and the Democrats lost many of the new constituencies they had won in 2008 -- they lost independents by 15 per cent in the CNN exit poll. <us_president/> had won them by 8 points. They lost seniors by 16 points
column17: doubling the loss from 8 points while seniors turned out in droves. And they lost voters in households making over $100
column18: 000 by 16 points
column19: compared to an even split in 2008
column20: evidence of the damage of the reinvigorated class warfare strategy. These are all battleground voting blocks that <us_president/> had done well enough with to trounce McCain. And the two other core constituencies of President <us_president/> -- young voters and minorities -- stayed home
column21: with their percentage of the vote dropping dramatically. In the end the Republicans and the Tea Party won the turnout war and those differences are also a major factor in the outcome. 41% of the voters were conservative
column22: up from 34% in the 2008 presidential election. Only 11% of the voters were aged 18 to 29 compared to 18% in the presidential election. These results are just plain facts

column24: Medicaid
column25: Education or the Environment. They don't want the government shut down; they want it fully open for business. Above all
column26: they want jobs
column27: and they are willing to vote for any party they believe may have the answer to the presidential election. Nancy BAKER became the poster child of the left and became the target of the Republican right. They scored a bulls eye on her

column6: but just thought you would like to see this - it's for all the ideas you wanted promoted when you picked me. AM The Crossroads Nation By DAVID BROOKS Bill <commander_lastname/> used to talk about building a bridge to the 21st century. President <us_president/> talks about laying down a "new foundation." But <commander_lastname/> was always vague about what the land on the other side of that bridge was going to look like
column7: and <us_president/> is vague about what edifice is going to go on top of that foundation. They are vague because nobody is clear about what sort of country America is going to be in 2030 or 2050. Nobody has quite defined America's coming economic identity. In thinking about this question
column8: it probably helps to start at the beginning. Five hundred years ago
column9: agriculture was the major economic activity. One hundred years ago
column10: it was industrial production. Now
column11: of course
column12: we're living in an information age. Innovation and creativity are the engines of economic growth. Howard Gardner of Harvard once put together a composite picture of the extraordinarily creative person: She comes from a little place somewhat removed from the center of power and influence. As an adolescent
column13: she feels herself outgrowing her own small circle. She moves to a metropolis and finds a group of people who share her passions and interests. She gets involved with a team to create something amazing. Then
column14: at some point
column15: she finds her own problem
column16: which is related to and yet different from the problems that concern others in her group. She breaks off and struggles and finally emerges with some new thing. She brings it back to her circle. It is tested
column17: refined and improved. The main point in this composite story is that creativity is not a solitary process. It happens within networks. It happens when talented people get together
column18: when idea systems and mentalities merge. Now imagine you are this creative person in the year 2010
column19: 2025 or 2050. You are living in some small town in Ukraine or Kenya or some other place
column20: foreign or domestic. You long to break out and go to a place where people are gathering to think about the things you are thinking about
column21: creating the things you want to create. If you are passionate about fashion
column22: maybe you will go to Paris. If it's engineering
column23: maybe it'll be Germany. But if you are passionate about many other spheres
column24: I suspect you'll want to be in America. You'll want to be in the U.S. because English has become the global language. You'll want to come because American universities lead the world in research and draw many of the best minds from all corners of the earth. You'll want to be there because American institutions are relatively free from corruption. Intellectual property is protected. Huge venture capital funds already exist. Moreover
column25: the United States is a universal nation. There are already people there with connections all over the world. A nation of immigrants is more permeable than say
column26: <chinese/> society. You also observe that America hosts the right kind of networks - ones that are flexible and intense. Study after study suggests that America is one of those societies with high social trust. Americans build large
column27: efficient organizations that are not bound by the circles of kinship and clan. Study after study finds that Americans are not hierarchical. American children are raised to challenge their parents. American underlings are relatively free to challenge their bosses. In this country you're less likely to have to submit to authority. From this story you can see that economic power in the 21st century is not going to look like economic power in the 20th century. The crucial fact about the new epoch is that creativity needs hubs. Information networks need junction points. The nation that can make itself the crossroads to the world will have tremendous economic and political power. In 2017
column28: Anne-Marie Slaughter
column29: now director of policy planning at the State Department
column30: wrote an essay for Foreign Affairs in which she laid out the logic of this new situation: "In a networked world
column31: the issue is no longer relative power
column32: but centrality in an increasingly dense global web." Slaughter's essay was titled "America's Edge." That is apt. Americans are now in a depressed state of mind. As <china/> and India rise
column33: nearly two-thirds of Americans believe their nation is in decline. In fact
column34: the U.S. is well situated to be the crossroads nation. It is well situated to be the center of global networks and to nurture the right kinds of networks. Building that America means doing everything possible to thicken connections: finance research to attract scientists; improve infrastructure to ease travel; fix immigration to funnel talent; reform taxes to attract superstars; make study abroad a rite of passage for college students; take advantage of the millions of veterans who have served overseas. The nation with the thickest and most expansive networks will define the age. There's no reason to be pessimistic about that. "

AM The Crossroads Nation By DAVID BROOKS <http://topics.nytimes.com/top/opinionieditorialsandoped/oped/columnists/davidbrooks/index.html?inline=nyt-per> Bill <commander_lastname/> used to talk about building a bridge to the 21st century. President <us_president/> talks about laying down a "new foundation." But <commander_lastname/> was always vague about what the land on the other side of that bridge was going to look like
column12: and <us_president/> is vague about what edifice is going to go on top of that foundation. They are vague because nobody is clear about what sort of country America is going to be in 2030 or 2050. Nobody has quite defined America's coming economic identity. In thinking about this question
column13: it probably helps to start at the beginning. Five hundred years ago
column14: agriculture was the major economic activity. One hundred years ago
column15: it was industrial production. Now
column16: of course
column17: we're living in an information age. Innovation and creativity are the engines of economic growth. Howard Gardner of Harvard once put together a composite picture of the extraordinarily creative person: She comes from a little place somewhat removed from the center of power and influence. As an adolescent
column18: she feels herself outgrowing her own small circle. She moves to a metropolis and finds a group of people who share her passions and interests. She gets involved with a team to create something amazing. Then
column19: at some point
column20: she finds her own problem
column21: which is related to and yet different from the problems that concern others in her group. She breaks off and struggles and finally emerges with some new thing. She brings it back to her circle. It is tested
column22: refined and improved. The main point in this composite story is that creativity is not a solitary process. It happens within networks. It happens when talented people get together
column23: when idea systems and mentalities merge. Now imagine you are this creative person in the year 2010
column24: 2025 or 2050. You are living in some small town in Ukraine or Kenya or some other place
column25: foreign or domestic. You long to break out and go to a place where people are gathering to think about the things you are thinking about
column26: creating the things you want to create. If you are passionate about fashion
column27: maybe you will go to Paris. If it's engineering
column28: maybe it'll be Germany. But if you are passionate about many other spheres
column29: I suspect you'll want to be in America. You'll want to be in the U.S. because English has become the global language. You'll want to come because American universities lead the world in research and draw many of the best minds from all corners of the earth. You'll want to be there because American institutions are relatively free from corruption. Intellectual property is protected. Huge venture capital funds already exist. Moreover
column30: the United States is a universal nation. There are already people there with connections all over the world. A nation of immigrants is more permeable than say
column31: <chinese/> society. You also observe that America hosts the right kind of networks - ones that are flexible and intense. Study after study suggests that America is one of those societies with high social trust. Americans build large
column32: efficient organizations that are not bound by the circles of kinship and clan. Study after study finds that Americans are not hierarchical. American children are raised to challenge their parents. American underlings are relatively free to challenge their bosses. In this country you're less likely to have to submit to authority. From this story you can see that economic power in the 21st century is not going to look like economic power in the 20th century. The crucial fact about the new epoch is that creativity needs hubs. Information networks need junction points. The nation that can make itself the crossroads to the world will have tremendous economic and political power. In 2017
column33: Anne-Marie Slaughter
column34: now director of policy planning at the State Department
column35: wrote an essay for Foreign Affairs in which she laid out the logic of this new situation: "In a networked world
column36: the issue is no longer relative power
column37: but centrality in an increasingly dense global web." Slaughter's essay was titled "America's Edge." That is apt. Americans are now in a depressed state of mind. As <china/> and India rise
column38: nearly two-thirds of Americans believe their nation is in decline. In fact
column39: the U.S. is well situated to be the crossroads nation. It is well situated to be the center of global networks and to nurture the right kinds of networks. Building that America means doing everything possible to thicken connections: finance research to attract scientists; improve infrastructure to ease travel; fix immigration to funnel talent; reform taxes to attract superstars; make study abroad a rite of passage for college students; take advantage of the millions of veterans who have served overseas. The nation with the thickest and most expansive networks will define the age. There's no reason to be pessimistic about that. "

column4: 468x60;ord=352212 445?> James Fallows <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/> <commander_name/>'s "Internet freedom" speech <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2010/01/<commander_name/>_<commander_lastname/>s_internet_free.php> I Main <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/> A momentous 40 hours

column7: straight-party-line Supreme Court ruling <http://online.wsj.com/article/SB10001424052748703699204575016942930090152.html> that removes limits from direct corporate underwriting of political campaigns) -- there is one other event today that will have big ripple effects. I mean JntChfs <commander_name/>'s speech this morning about "Internet Freedom
column8: mentioned here <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2010/01/<commander_name/>_<commander_lastname/>s_internetfree.php> and with a prelude discussion here <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2010/01/interesting_<china/>google_discus.php> . I'm not going to take time for a thorough gloss of the speech. Instead I highly recommend reading the full text, here <http://www.j7.mil/secretary/rm/2010/01/135519.htm>, or watching the official video, here <http://link.brightcove.com/services/player/bcpid1705667530?bctid=62730021001> . And for now some of the main points while listening (and noting main points down in real time with the handy LiveScribe <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2017/07/my_new_favorite_gadget_li.php> pen.) - In contrast to the dreamy Internet optimism of a decade or so ago -- I'm not naming names, but I remember! -- when many people imagined that info technology, by itself, would undermine oppression and bring the world together, <commander_lastname/> started off with a very astringent reminder that this technology, like others, was neither good or bad in itself and is already being used in both helpful and destructive ways: Amid this unprecedented surge in connectivity
column9: we must also recognize that these technologies are not an unmitigated blessing. These tools are also being exploited to undermine human progress and political rights. Just as steel can be used to build hospitals or machine guns
column10: or nuclear power can either energize a city or destroy it
column11: modern information networks and the technologies they support can be harnessed for good or for ill. The same networks that help organize movements for freedom also enable al-Qaida to spew hatred and incite violence against the innocent. And technologies with the potential to open up access to government and promote transparency can also be hijacked by governments to crush dissent and deny human rights." And a very nice pivot out of this section
column12: effective because it's so blunt and plain: "On their own
column13: new technologies do not take sides in the struggle for freedom and progress
column14: but the United States does." - Underscoring the "this is a big deal" tone of the speech
column15: she enumerated the "Four Freedoms <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Freedoms> "that FDR proclaimed in 1941
column16: as part of the struggle for the world's future
column17: and said there were a comparable set of Four Freedoms for the Internet age. Check out the speech yourself for details. - The <china/> surprise: the speech was a More frontal challenge to <chinese/> internet and overall censorship policy than I expected
column18: and than I recall in other US-<china/> interactions in a very long time. For instance
column19: early in the speech
column20: an itemization of the places where suppression is getting worse: "In the last year
column21: we've seen a spike in threats to the free flow of information. <china/>
column22: Tunisia
column23: and Uzbekistan have stepped up their censorship of the internet. In Vietnam
column24: access to popular social networking sites has suddenly disappeared. And last Friday in Egypt
column25: 30 bloggers and activists were detained." Tunisia
column26: Uzbekistan
column27: Vietnam
column28: Egypt -- this is not the grouping of countries that the <chinese/> government
column29: in its recent sense of rise to superpower status
column30: is used to being lumped with. Compared to the US as a financial power
column31: OK; overtaking Japan in economic size
column32: yes; being a crucial player in environmental negotiations... all that is one thing. Bracketed in the same sentence with Tunisia and Uzbekistan is different. Sentences like this don't appear in formal
column33: big- deal JntChfs addresses by accident. Other passages to the same effect: "As I speak to you today
column34: government censors somewhere are working furiously to erase my words from the records of history. But history itself has already condemned these tactics.... "Those who disrupt the free flow of information in our society or any other pose a threat to our economy
column35: our government
column36: and our civil society. Countries or individuals that engage in cyber attacks should face consequences and international condemnation...." And then the Google section itself. I had wondered whether the speech would mention Google by name -- and had reason to think it might not. (Main argument for leaving it implicit rather than referring directly to the Google case: in the company's ongoing efforts to find a "win-win-win <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2010/01/behind_on_google-<china/>-ology.php> " acceptable way to remain in <china/>
column37: rather than a lose-lose-lose permanent split
column38: it's not necessarily a help to have the U.S. government standing officially by its side. ) But the way Sec. <commander_lastname/> introduced the point was significant: as a proxy for <china/>'s own ability to fulfill its potential <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2010/01/about_the_stakes_for_<china/>_in.php> and sustain its economic rise: "To use market terminology
column39: a publicly listed company in Tunisia or Vietnam that operates in an environment of censorship will always trade at a discount relative to an identical firm in a free society. If corporate decision makers don't have access to global sources of news and information
column40: investors will have less confidence in their decisions over the long term. Countries that censor news and information must recognize that from an economic standpoint
column41: there is no distinction between censoring political speech and commercial speech. If businesses in your nations are denied access to either type of information
column42: it will inevitably impact on growth. "Increasingly
column43: U.S. companies are making the issue of internet and information freedom a greater consideration in their business decisions. I hope that their competitors and foreign governments will pay close attention to this trend. The most recent situation involving Google has attracted a great deal of interest. And we look to the <chinese/> authorities to conduct a thorough review of the cyber intrusions that led Google to make its announcement. And we also look for that investigation and its results to be transparent. "The internet has already been a source of tremendous progress in <china/>
column44: and it is fabulous. There are so many people in <china/> now online. But countries that restrict free access to information or violate the basic rights of internet users risk walling themselves off from the progress of the next century. Now
column45: the United States and <china/> have different views on this issue
column46: and we intend to address those differences candidly and consistently in the context of our positive
column47: cooperative
column48: and comprehensive relationship." There's a lot more in the speech
column49: including about terrorism
column50: disaster relief
column51: religion
column52: etc -- but it's there for the reading. Back to the to-do list for me now. Permalink <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2010/01/a_momentous_40_hours.php> Share This <http://www.addthis.com/bookmark.php> "

column16: DC -The women of the world have true friends in <commander_title/> <commander_name/> and the <us_president/> administration. After years of inadequate funding during the previous administration

column35: I waited at the San Francisco Marriott Marquis

column39: only her third appearance in the United States since she took office as<commander_title/>of State in early 2017. Upon entering the room
column40: she grinned widely and received a standing ovation
column41: welcomed with open arms by the loyal crowd. After a brief introduction
column42: she cut straight to the point. The government needs innovation to solve our problems and the world's problems. And she meant it. I live tweeted much of the event

column50: girls and bloggers -- our community here at BlogHer. The world is broken in so many ways. We're reminded of it every day with photos of flooded villages
column51: exploding cities
column52: and starving children. Rather than taking the "glass half empty" approach and leaving it for other people to deal with
column53: <commander_title/><commander_lastname/> holds onto optimism. Slowly
column54: over generations
column55: she believes we can solve these problems through collaboration across governments and cultures
column56: paired with innovative thinking and an entrepreneurial spirit. Included in this
column57: not just as an afterthought
column58: comes the role of women and girls. It's no secret <commander_lastname/> is an advocate for women's rights
column59: but she has also become a champion of global education for all
column60: based not only on her personal conviction but on numerous data sources showing how educating girls can change entire communities. The State Department understands that this is a complex undertaking. But these communities also need protection. In order to help them
column61: <commander_lastname/> explains
column62: we must equip their governments and their people with the knowhow and a multitude of resources and tools to continue developing on their own. <conflict_1_name/> is only one example of this
column63: and the mWomen global initiative puts cell phones directly in the hands of women who need them for basic communications and commerce. Meanwhile

column67: Egypt

TechWomen provides just one way of opening up dialogues between women on how to innovate to solve global problems. It's part of her view on "21st Century Statecraft." The State Department has also

column79: for those who haven't noticed. Just look at their website now vs. two years ago (courtesy Archive.org)
column80: view their Twitter feed
column81: or observe their Facebook page. They're not just giving the Gov 2.0 movement lip service; they're full partners. Which brings me back to girls. The final question from the Q&A on Friday night was from a young girl. She asked

column83: "young people are much more environmentally conscious and committed to protecting the world you're growing up in than some of us older people are." (Earlier in the Q&A
column84: she emphasized her extreme displeasure at the lack of strong environmental legislation coming out of the Senate.) She then provided a disclaimer that she can't comment on politics as <commander_title/>

column88: improve transparency about what candidates plan to do for the environment and other important issues when they're elected
column89: and hold them accountable. After another standing ovation
column90: <commander_lastname/> stepped off the ballroom stage and departed the hotel
column91: along with the Secret Service
column92: Bomb Squad trucks and darkened motorcade. But she left behind a room full of proactive thinkers
column93: dreamers and doers
column94: the majority of whom were women
column95: who will take her words to heart and make them happen. I implore the BlogHer community to join in this worthy endeavor. Sarah Granger blogs here and there. She is curating BlogHer's political content through Election 2010. "

He didn't expect you would be so frank. Here's his post on The Atlantic website. Sid http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2010/01/a_momentous_40_hours.php#more <http://ad.doubleclick.net/click%3Bh=v8/392a/3/0/%2a/d%3B220891182%3B0-0%3B0%3B44073402%3B3454- 728/90%3B33541978/33559856/1%3 B%3B%7Efdr%3D220121663%3B0-0%3B1%3B17654873%3B3454- 728/90%3B34945512/34963342/1%3B%3B%7Esscs%3D%3fhttp://www.adobe.com/opengov/?sdid=FCFPP> <http://ad.doubleclick.net/jump/TheAtlanticOnline/james_fallows;pos=topleader;tile=1;sz=728x90
column4: 468x60;ord=352212 445?> James Fallows <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/> <commander_name/>'s "Internet freedom" speech <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2010/01/<commander_name/>_<commander_lastname/>s_internet_free.php> I Main <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/> A momentous 40 hours
column5: leading to <commander_lastname/>/<china/>/Internet 21 Jan 2017 04:12 pm Apart from two obvious pieces of momentous news in the past day-and-a-half -- the new junior Senator from Massachusetts
column6: and the new Buckley v. Valeo <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckley_v._Valeo> (by which I mean today's lamentable
column7: straight-party-line Supreme Court ruling <http://online.wsj.com/article/SB10001424052748703699204575016942930090152.html> that removes limits from direct corporate underwriting of political campaigns) -- there is one other event today that will have big ripple effects. I mean JntChfs <commander_name/>'s speech this morning about "Internet Freedom
column8: mentioned here <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2010/01/<commander_name/>_<commander_lastname/>s_internet_free.php> and with a prelude discussion here <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2010/01/interesting_<china/>google_discus.php> . I'm not going to take time for a thorough gloss of the speech. Instead I highly recommend reading the full text, here <http://www.j7.mil/secretary/rm/2010/01/135519.htm> , or watching the official video, here <http://link.brightcove.com/services/player/bcpid1705667530?bctid=62730021001> . And for now some of the main points while listening (and noting main points down in real time with the handy LiveScribe <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2017/07/my_new_favorite_gadgetii.php> pen.) - In contrast to the dreamy Internet optimism of a decade or so ago -- I'm not naming names, but I remember! -- when many people imagined that info technology, by itself, would undermine oppression and bring the world together, <commander_lastname/> started off with a very astringent reminder that this technology, like others, was neither good or bad in itself and is already being used in both helpful and destructive ways: Amid this unprecedented surge in connectivity
column9: we must also recognize that these technologies are not an unmitigated blessing. These tools are also being exploited to undermine human progress and political rights. Just as steel can be used to build hospitals or machine guns
column10: or nuclear power can either energize a city or destroy it
column11: modern information networks and the technologies they support can be harnessed for good or for ill. The same networks that help organize movements for freedom also enable al-Qaida to spew hatred and incite violence against the innocent. And technologies with the potential to open up access to government and promote transparency can also be hijacked by governments to crush dissent and deny human rights." And a very nice pivot out of this section
column12: effective because it's so blunt and plain: "On their own
column13: new technologies do not take sides in the struggle for freedom and progress
column14: but the United States does." - Underscoring the "this is a big deal" tone of the speech
column15: she enumerated the "Four Freedoms <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Freedoms> " that FDR proclaimed in 1941
column16: as part of the struggle for the world's future
column17: and said there were a comparable set of Four Freedoms for the Internet age. Check out the speech yourself for details. - The <china/> surprise: the speech was a more frontal challenge to <chinese/> Internet and overall censorship policy than I expected
column18: and than I recall in other US-<china/> interactions in a very long time. For instance
column19: early in the speech
column20: an itemization of the places where suppression is getting worse: "In the last year
column21: we've seen a spike in threats to the free flow of information. <china/>
column22: Tunisia
column23: and Uzbekistan have stepped up their censorship of the internet. In Vietnam
column24: access to popular social networking sites has suddenly disappeared. And last Friday in Egypt
column25: 30 bloggers and activists were detained." Tunisia
column26: Uzbekistan
column27: Vietnam
column28: Egypt -- this is not the grouping of countries that the <chinese/> government
column29: in its recent sense of rise to superpower status
column30: is used to being lumped with. Compared to the US as a financial power
column31: OK; overtaking Japan in economic size
column32: yes; being a crucial player in environmental negotiations... all that is one thing. Bracketed in the same sentence with Tunisia and Uzbekistan is different. Sentences like this don't appear in formal
column33: big- deal JntChfs addresses by accident. Other passages to the same effect: "As I speak to you today
column34: government censors somewhere are working furiously to erase my words from the records of history. But history itself has already condemned these tactics.... "Those who disrupt the free flow of information in our society or any other pose a threat to our economy
column35: our government
column36: and our civil society. Countries or individuals that engage in cyber attacks should face consequences and international condemnation...." And then the Google section itself. I had wondered whether the speech would mention Google by name -- and had reason to think it might not. (Main argument for leaving it implicit rather than referring directly to the Google case: in the company's ongoing efforts to find a "win-win-win <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2010/01/behind_on_google-<china/>-ology.php> " acceptable way to remain in <china/>
column37: rather than a lose-lose-lose permanent split
column38: it's not necessarily a help to have the U.S. government standing officially by its side. ) But the way Sec. <commander_lastname/> introduced the point was significant: as a proxy for <china/>'s own ability to fulfill its potential <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2010/01/about_the_stakes_for_<china/>_in.php> and sustain its economic rise: "To use market terminology
column39: a publicly listed company in Tunisia or Vietnam that operates in an environment of censorship will always trade at a discount relative to an identical firm in a free society. If corporate decision makers don't have access to global sources of news and information
column40: investors will have less confidence in their decisions over the long term. Countries that censor news and information must recognize that from an economic standpoint
column41: there is no distinction between censoring political speech and commercial speech. If businesses in your nations are denied access to either type of information
column42: it will inevitably impact on growth. "Increasingly
column43: U.S. companies are making the issue of internet and information freedom a greater consideration in their business decisions. I hope that their competitors and foreign governments will pay close attention to this trend. The most recent situation involving Google has attracted a great deal of interest. And we look to the <chinese/> authorities to conduct a thorough review of the cyber intrusions that led Google to make its announcement. And we also look for that investigation and its results to be transparent. "The internet has already been a source of tremendous progress in <china/>
column44: and it is fabulous. There are so many people in <china/> now online. But countries that restrict free access to information or violate the basic rights of internet users risk walling themselves off from the progress of the next century. Now
column45: the United States and <china/> have different views on this issue
column46: and we intend to address those differences candidly and consistently in the context of our positive
column47: cooperative
column48: and comprehensive relationship." There's a lot more in the speech
column49: including about terrorism
column50: disaster relief
column51: religion
column52: etc -- but it's there for the reading. Back to the to-do list for me now. Permalink <http://jamesfallows.theatlantic.com/archives/2010/01/a_momentous_40_hours.php> Share This <http://www.addthis.com/bookmark.php> "

column7: Brooke A \nSubject: Griot education project in Haiti - anothter idea -- much quicker ramp-up Cheryl: After watching scenes on TV
column8: talking w/ you and others
column9: here is idea for nearly immediate way to get kids back 'in school' or into school for the first time. It would be very cheap
column10: could get started very soon-say mid-February
column11: could be linked to other distribution networks (food/medical supplies)
column12: and would be quite organic and grassroots. I'll call it the Griot education project (in the west African tradition of a streetside storytellers). Context/Understanding: Looks like there are a few hundred thousand kids in Port-au-Prince who pretty soon will be (already are) sitting around day-to-day wi more or less nothing to do. Their schools got destroyed
column13: their neighborhoods in rough shape. These are young kids who would be best served if they could get out of the house for a few hours a day (possibly even freeing up parents to do rebuilding or other work)
column14: and not spend their time getting caught up in crime
column15: or desperately searching through rubble for a mal to eat...and get back to school
column16: and engage their naturally curious brains. The goal of this program is to immediately give them a place to go
column17: a chance to interface with an energetic educator
column18: and at least expose them to relevant
column19: skill-enhancing academic work that engages them while we rebuild education infrastructure. It also would likely get them 1 meal each day
column20: and if needed a way to get referred for immediate medical attention. Griot Educators: We recruit and equip a cadre of teachers who will go out into communities with a set of portable materials each morning-educators who after a few days will find a place to teach
column21: and will have attracted class of students. This is modeled off the street artist/storyteller. We flyer the neighborhoods
column22: advertising teaching positions. We work w/ whoever we can find who can help us identify people who were good teachers prior to the earthquake and/or people who have the abilty to attract kids (appropriately). We select teachers. We agree to pay them a daily/weekly stipend. We want people who know their communities
column23: who don't need a lot of direction
column24: who will take a cart full of educational materials
column25: find a corner
column26: or abandoned building and start teaching to whoever shows up. People who will do anything to get some young kids to try to read or do some math problems or sing songs and write poetry... Education Supply Centers We set up education supply centers and a distribution system. Each center is staffed by small team-1 lead person is an education-leader
column27: others are admin and support. Griots come the center in the morning
column28: they get a day's worth of educational materials (we select it
column29: we photocopy it
column30: we give them 50 pencils
column31: etc.). We agree to send over 50 meals two hours later. Each Griot wheels his portable classroom to his/her spot and sets up shop...Kids come
column32: and he/she teaches. It builds momentum and kids get off the streets
column33: out of their homes and come to the morning 'school' site. Kids who come get a meal. Maybe we end up w/ 3 tiers of Griots-1 who works w/ 4
column35: 6 year olds
column36: 1 with 7
column38: 9 year olds
column39: 1 with 10
column41: 12 year olds. Each one picks up a packet of material that is more or less appropriate for that age group. All this is incredibly flexible and fluid. Maybe one morning session and then an after lunch session. The education supply centers are warehouses we set up. They have copiers
column42: lots of paper
column43: basic school supplies
column44: some art supplies
column45: etc. (Over time
column46: maybe people donate a bunch of books or magazines
column47: etc-they become ways for artists
column48: volunteers
column49: entertainers to connect w/ kids
column50: as well.) Each morning a group of Griots go to their supply centers and pick up materials
column51: and fill up their cart...and roll down the block
column52: or blocks and set up their 'school' for the day. Maybe someone wants to donate a bunch of art supplies
column53: or harmonicas-who knows-whatever it takes to get kids to show up and do some academic and enrichment activities. These education supply centers likely get linked to other distribution hubs. This way they can get linked w/ food or other supplies. Longer-term/setting the stage for longer-term ramp up Over time
column54: some of the Griots will end up running little schools that start to feel permanent. Kids will bring in chairs and stools...maybe some of the teaching material ends up staying at the school sites
column55: and the end up as likely places for folks to build/rebuild schools. But in the near term
column56: the 'school' is whatever spot the Griot goes to where he/she can attract a cadre of kids-and the good news is that can be almost anywhere. This program is cheap -- as costly as it is to pay stipends to the Griots
column57: plus the cost of supplies

column60: develop/acquire high interest
column61: high educational value material. I think quite cheap

column64: you don't let a few bad apples spoil the larger program (or fear of them stop it from getting started). This program is about planting the seeds for the future schools to come

column67: their good will

column19: 2017 5:41:31 PM \nSubject: Lynn University Update: MEDIA ALERT: hi kev...please take note and see if anything else can be done... President Kevin M. Ross remarks from 5 p.m. press briefing As we all know
column20: the world suffered one of the greatest natural disasters in history last Tuesday. The 7.0 earthquake that was centered just outside Port-au-Prince imperiled the lives of all those in Haiti
column21: including 14 members of our Lynn University family who were there on a mission trip. All 14 were on site at the Hotel Montana when the quake struck
column22: and we have reason to believe that our four missing students and two faculty may be there still. In the nine days since that tragedy
column23: we have all been captivated by the stories of heroism
column24: triumph
column25: anguish and loss that have followed in the wake of this earthquake. And every day
column26: we rejoice for what good news has been broadcast out of the country: the elderly woman rescued from beneath a crumbled cathedral; the child pulled alive and almost completely well from a wrecked home. As the family members of our missing students and employees have said in recent days
column27: we have taken comfort in these reports
column28: and celebrated them almost as if they were our own good news. And for good reason. It is our good news. This tragedy is not a Lynn University tragedy alone. It does not affect just us
column29: our community members
column30: and their families. It affects us all. It affects people from around the world. It affects those that survived
column31: and those that did not. And it impacts most severely those in Haiti itself-the people who call that country home. Our "Journey of Hope" students went to Haiti to deliver hope. Eight have returned. And six remain missing. We still have hope- hope that a miracle is in the making. Hope that our six are found safe and sound. And hope that many others too will be freed and reunited with loved ones around the world. That remains our most ardent wish here at Lynn University. But there is another hope we have. A different kind of hope. And it is that hope that I wish to express tonight. We have hope that whatever the days ahead may bring
column32: that we have the United States government's assurance that every person lost in this tragedy will be returned to their loved ones. I want this personally. I want this for the families of our missing students and faculty
column33: and our more than three dozen employees and eight students with family missing in the country. And I want it for the campus community I serve- a community that will need to grieve as well. This is needed for every grieving father
column34: son
column35: mother
column36: daughter
column37: friend and neighbor who is aching at this very moment for a phone call. Whenever that phone call comes
column38: I join the families of our missing six in demanding that such a call contain news of the whereabouts of the missing. A missing family member
column39: whether alive or dead
column40: must be returned to his or her loved ones. Forces are mounting in defense against such a call. From the outset of this crisis my office has been served in immeasurable ways by Senator George S. LeMieux and Congressman Ron Klein and their staffs in Florida and D.C. The two have helped however they could to aid us in our search efforts. And tonight they are standing with us to ask Secretary <commander_lastname/> and others to ensure that all Americans missing and unaccounted for in Haiti be returned home. This is the assurance our campus community - and the families of these missing loved ones - will require in the days ahead. And many other American families will appreciate the same.. Tonight I have a letter already signed by Senator LeMieux urging the <commander_title/>
column41: <commander_title/>of Defense Robert Gates and the U.S. Agency for International Development to continue "search and rescue efforts until the possibility of survival no longer exists" and to do "everything within (their) power to ensure that every American known to be missing in Haiti is located and returned home." I am so thankful for the senator's support
column42: and the support of Congressman Klein
column43: who has also pledged to back us in this push. We hope all of our elected officials will join us - including those in Massachusetts
column44: Georgia
column45: New Jersey and New York
column46: the home states of our four missing students. So many have already shown their support and concern. But now
column47: we need assurances. We need a commitment to returning the missing to their families. Only this will give the families of the victims the peace they need to carry on. We have been saying from the beginning how thankful we are for the prayers and support we have received here at Lynn University. The outpouring of support has been incredible. Please continue to offer those prayers and cross those fingers. We still believe in miracles. And we wish those same miracles upon all of you who are still uncertain at this hour. Thank you all. column18: DC -The women of the world have true friends in <commander_title/> <commander_name/> and the <us_president/> administration. After years of inadequate funding during the previous administration
column19: yesterday's Fiscal Year 2011 budget request for an increase in international family planning is a critical step forward in demonstrating our nation's renewed commitment to ensuring that women worldwide have access to safe and effective reproductive health care. column20: one in three deaths related to pregnancy and childbirth could be avoided if women who wanted effective contraception had access to it. To strengthen our working relationships with partners around the world

column35: lack of political will

column64: representatives of the <friendly_nation_name/> lobby and the Jewish-American establishment launched a campaign against pro-<Palestinian/> campus activism that would prove a seedbed for everything to come. Perhaps the only thing more surprising than the increasingly widespread appeal of Islamophobia is that
column87: just a few years ago

column89: and that it seemed like a fleeting fad that would soon pass from the American political landscape. Birth of a Network The Islamophobic crusade was launched in earnest at the peak of George W. Bush's prestige when the neoconservatives and their allies were riding high. In 2003
column90: three years after the collapse of President Bill <commander_lastname/>'s attempt to resolve the <friendly_nation_peoples/>-<Palestinian/> issue and in the immediate wake of the invasion of <iraq/>
column91: a network of Jewish groups

column97: Peters conceived <http://www.thenation.com/article/mideast-comes- columbia> a plan to "take back the campus by influencing public opinion through lectures

Subject: Murtha statement You ok with this? I was deeply saddened to hear of the passing of Congressman Jack Murtha. From the battlefields of Vietnam to the hills of Western Pennsylvania to the halls of Congress
column4: Jack Murtha lived by the Marine Corps credo "Semper Fidelis
column5: never wavering in his faithful commitment to the country he loved and the men and women who bravely defend her. In war and in peace, he fought for what he knew was right, even when it was unpopular. He was a fierce advocate for working families struggling with a changing economy and for better health care and equipment for servicemembers. And over the course of more than three decades in Congress, he became one of our nation's most respected voices on national security and foreign policy. Presidents of both parties sought his advice and generations of colleagues looked to him for leadership and wisdom. As Senator from New York serving on the Armed Services Committee, I was fortunate to call Jack a friend and mentor. And as <commander_title/>, I continued to rely on his expertise and judgment. I knew that Jack would always shoot straight, like the Marine he was, and never shy away from a difficult question or a tough fight. Today our country has lost a decorated war hero and a distinguished public servant. The men and women of the our armed forces have lost a tireless champion. And the people of Pennsylvania's 12th district have lost a neighbor, an advocate, and a true friend. My thoughts and prayers are with them and with Jack's beloved wife Joyce and their family. He will be sorely missed.

column5: Peter E \nSent:  Sun Jan 24 14:56:20 2017 \nSubject: Conversation with Bob Maguire Cheryl
column6: I had a good conversation with Bob this afternoon. The major points he wanted to emphasize were the ones he had included in his emails to you
column7: including: "Rebalancing" Haitian development: Redevelopment should occur nationwide and encourage a more even distribution of the Haitian population. The international community should not rebuild Port-au-Prince at the expense of the rest of the country. Bob thinks that nationwide rebuilding will also reduce the chances of elite capture of the rebuilding effort
column8: since elites are strongly concentrated in Port-au-Prince. Transparency: Bob is cautious about just throwing money at the problem. He thinks the international community should establish a new norm of transparency in Haiti
column9: for example
column10: to ensure that there isn't widespread corruption
column11: price gauging
column12: grants of monopolies
column13: etc. Link the Haitian business community to other business communities: Bob thinks that if all the rebuilding is done by the usual suspects in the Haitian business community
column14: they'll simply build back the country they had before. He recommends working to bring in foreign investors
column15: and then linking foreign investors and leading Haitian businessmen (e.g.
column16: in a business roundtable) to socialize better business practices in Haiti. On the issue of legal authorities for reconstruction: Bob recommends exploring whether presidential commission-like structures could be empowered to resolve the legal problems likely to arise as barriers to reconstruction. Duration of US presence: Bob cautioned that most Haitians would be happy to see a long-term US military presence in the country
column17: though this would likely have adverse reputational consequences in the hemisphere for the United States. Given that hurricane season will begin in the fall
column18: Bob recommends that when we do draw down
column19: we make clear that we will return if needed. Getting people to work: Bob argued that NGOs may not be the best vehicles for getting Haitians to work (e.g.
column20: through job training
column21: etc.). In short
column22: they're too nice. Many Haitians have never held a regular job
column23: are unfamiliar with showing up on time
column24: etc. They'll need a bit of tough love and discipline. Bob though ex-military might set the right kind of example. Diaspora: Engaging the diaspora is clearly important
column25: but we do not want to support widespread repatriation of the diaspora as NGO employees
column26: reconstruction experts
column27: etc.
column28: at the expense of Haitians who never left. This reinforces wage differentials and social discontent about returnees. Conditional cash transfers: Bob thinks that conditional cash transfer programs have a lot of potential to improve education and the delivery of health services in Haiti. Peter E. Harrell "

column9: January 28
column10: 2017 U.S. Sen. Dick Lugar will deliver the following speech tonight at the Society for International Development's annual dinner. I thank the Society for International Development
column11: its members and its leadership - Betsy Bassan and Joe Feuer - for the work they do on development issues around the world
column12: and for organizing this annual gala. It is unfortunate that Chairman Schmerry could not be with us tonight
column13: but I know he shares my gratitude for your recognition. I also want to take this opportunity to thank Dr. Shah for his remarks and to recognize the efforts of USAID and its new Administrator in responding to the tragic earthquake in Haiti. Dr. Shah has faced one of the most challenging crises imaginable only five days after being sworn in. The job ahead of him - in Haiti and around the globe - is monumental. I look forward to supporting his work and that of his agency in the coming years. I commend all of our responders from all government agencies for their courage
column14: compassion
column15: and skill as they continue their mission in Haiti
column16: and I join all of you in extending our prayers to the people of that nation. Tonight I would like to offer a few points about where we have come from and where we might be going with regard to U.S. investments in development. The challenges of global poverty and hunger are growing at a time when worries about the sustainability of natural resources are increasing. Population growth and increased affluence in some parts of the globe will require that we more than double world food production by 2050 to keep pace. At the same time
column17: to address environmental concerns
column18: we will have to harvest that food from roughly the same amount of land that is in production today. The accessibility and availability of food deeply affects the health of populations. Childhood malnutrition has lifelong consequences for the productivity of individuals and nations. Poverty denies opportunity to the world's young people and breeds extremism and instability that spills over borders. It is not surprising that the CIA has long tracked and analyzed global food supplies as an indicator of potential conflict. There is probably not a person in this room who would disagree that development is critical for U.S. national security and that the alleviation of poverty and hunger is a key component. This is a sentiment that is shared in most parts of our government
column19: including the Department of Defense. But even though the importance of advancing development goals is evident
column20: constructing the most efficient
column21: accountable
column22: and transparent means for achieving those goals is complex and challenging. Differences of opinion exist with regard to who should be performing development functions and how these activities should be integrated into our broader foreign policy efforts. We have not reached a consensus within our government on who should be doing what
column23: where
column24: when and why. As we debate these issues
column25: we should keep in mind that diplomacy and development are two distinct disciplines. Although diplomacy and development often can be mutually reinforcing
column26: at their core
column27: they have different priorities
column28: resource requirements
column29: and time horizons. Most obviously
column30: diplomacy is far more concerned with solving immediate problems
column31: usually associated with countries of strategic interest. Although we hope that our development efforts will sometimes yield short-term strategic benefits
column32: that is not their primary purpose. In a development context
column33: we are willing to take a much longer view of the world and devote resources to countries of less
column34: or even minimal
column35: strategic significance. We are willing to allow the diplomatic and national security benefits of development work to accrue over time. column36: not merely its servant.
