I share that sentiment. One of the basic questions with respect to foreign aid reform is how we can best strengthen the capacity of USAID to run effective assistance programs. During the last two decades
column37: decision-makers have not made it easy for the agency to perform its mission. Development resources declined precipitously in the 1990s and reorganization initiatives resulted in the agency's loss of evaluation
column38: budget
column39: and policy capacity. There is broad consensus among development experts that the loss of these functions at USAID is inhibiting the success of our development programs. Our development efforts will never be as effective as they should be if the agency that houses most of our development expertise is cut out of relevant policy and budget decisions. Events since 2001 have spurred greater investments in foreign assistance. But many of these resources have been located outside of USAID. Roughly two dozen departments and agencies have taken over some aspects of foreign assistance
column40: including the Department of Defense and the Department of Agriculture. The President has advocated doubling foreign assistance over time
column41: and has announced new initiatives on food security and health. Given the increased resources needed for these initiatives
column42: it is crucial that the American people and Congress have confidence that these funds will be used efficiently. USAID must have a central role in development policy decisions. If we are to avoid inefficient experimentation
column43: it must have the capacity to evaluate programs and disseminate information about best practices and methods. That requires policy makers to continue augmenting the agency's staffing and expertise. These principals are reflected in legislation that Senator Schmerry and I introduced last year
column45: the Foreign Assistance Revitalization and Accountability Act. The Administration has initiated two separate studies - the State Department's Quadrennial Diplomacy and Development Review and the National Security Council's Presidential Study Directive on Development - in an attempt to make recommendations on how development programs can better support U.S. foreign policy objectives. The QDDR will not be completed until this fall and it is uncertain when
column46: or if
column47: we will know the outcomes of the PSD. I am eager to review the Administration's ideas when they are ready. But in the meantime
column48: Congress should be offering its own ideas on how to improve our government's development capacity. The Kerry-Lugar foreign assistance reform bill is the product of well over a year of research and analysis by Senators and their staffs. It has strong support in the aid community. And it is co-sponsored by a bipartisan group of 23 Senators
column49: twelve of whom are members of the Foreign Relations Committee. This level of backing for a bill related to foreign assistance is extremely rare. It provides an opportunity to build something approaching a consensus on this issue. I am hopeful that the Executive Branch will recognize that a bill co-sponsored by a majority of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and nearly a quarter of the full Senate should be given substantial weight in its review process. A strong development agency that serves under the foreign policy guidance of the <commander_title/>
column50: as envisioned in our bill
column51: will best empower her to advance U.S. goals. A Development Policy Guided by Objectives Even as we reconsider our development architecture
column52: it is vital that development policy is guided by objectives rather than by how we organize our government to deliver development assistance. We should focus on the big issues - food scarcity
column53: poverty
column54: disease
column55: environmental degradation -- that prevent economic growth in a large swath of the world's countries. Those objectives require that strategies reflect the needs of the countries we are helping rather than the vagaries of our own budget process
column56: which often allocates funds in response to lobbying pressures
column57: media interest
column58: or political favoritism. Country strategies based on broad objectives also give us the best chance to avoid dependence on arbitrary spending targets for specific sectors. For example
column59: promoting food security requires investments not just in agricultural productivity
column60: but in clean water
column61: infrastructure
column62: basic and higher education
column63: and land titling
column64: to name just a few factors. The Global Food Security Act
column65: which I authored with Senator Casey and which Senator Schmerry has co-sponsored
column66: reflects these principles. The food price crisis that occurred in 2008 resulted from a culmination of policy choices by donor and recipient governments over a decades-long period. That crisis was a wakeup call for the development community
column67: for international donors
column68: and for policymakers worldwide. Because achieving food security must be a multi-sector endeavor that goes beyond simply raising crop yields
column69: U.S. policy must seek to integrate a variety of approaches and actors. At the same time
column70: we do not want to delegate responsibility for food security policy to multiple departments. That could further weaken our already fractured foreign assistance structure. That is why our bill designates USAID
column71: which has the broad development experience necessary
column72: as the lead agency to implement the strategy. "Whole-of-Government" in Perspective The term "whole-of-government" has come into vogue in policy circles. To the extent that the term underscores the complexity of development problems and the need to apply the talents of a diverse set of agencies to their solution
column73: it is useful and descriptive. Our government must have the capacity to draw on expertise to achieve vital development missions without artificial barriers erected by agencies. Many agencies are working together successfully on development problems in many parts of the world. But we should not mistake the term "whole-of-government" for an organizational strategy. Even if multiple agencies are making contributions
column74: someone must be in charge
column75: someone must coordinate the activities of all involved
column76: and someone must take responsibility for inefficiencies and failures. This is especially important in a development context because of our highly fragmented aid system. The risk is that the term "whole-of-government
column77: will be used to justify that fragmentation or preserve roles for agencies where they are not justified. We also must be careful that the whole-of-government concept does not re-define development as a series of technical decisions - from where to dig wells to which seeds to plant in which soils. Such a redefinition would devalue the discipline of development, which many practitioners have spent a lifetime studying and testing. We know from long experience that technical expertise must be grounded in an understanding of development. For example, agricultural advancement depends as much or more on reaching women farmers, building agriculture education, and engaging civil society in support of rural development than it does on seed quality and planting decisions. An integrated strategy can only come from an agency that understands development is a separate discipline, as Dr. Shah has said. I believe the starting point for any future design of our assistance programs should not be the status quo, but rather the period in which we had a well-functioning and well-resourced aid agency. Even if we emphasize the talents of multiple agencies, a strong aid agency that can design integrated country-specific strategies is a key to success. Unity of Purpose Instead of accepting whole-of-government, or any other organizational model, as the guiding narrative, I believe there is a more helpful way of viewing the development mission - that is unity-of-purpose." We need to be unified around common purposes for which we can marshal the appropriate level of resources and variety of approaches. There will be situations that call for the involvement of multiple agencies under the direction of one government entity. But
column78: the decision to involve other government actors should be driven by the purpose. Such is clearly the case now in Haiti. The U.S. government and international actors are unified for the purpose of disaster response. That response involves the coordination of hundreds of organizations to rescue people and to provide basic elements needed for survival. At some point soon
column79: the mission will evolve from disaster response to reconstruction to development. We should be asking whether we will be able to maintain a unity-of-purpose even as that purpose changes. The Lugar-Casey bill proposes that there be a unity-of-purpose around achieving global food security. Regardless of the situation
column80: it is the unity-of-purpose that should guide how foreign assistance is designed. I applaud<commander_title/><commander_lastname/> for adopting food security as a top priority. Her inter-agency team has been working diligently on its Global Food Security and Hunger Initiative
column81: and Congress has been responsive in appropriating funding. Many operational decisions have yet to be made
column82: particularly decisions relating to coordination
column83: but I stand ready to work with the Administration to pass the Lugar-Casey bill as soon as possible. I look forward to achieving a unity-of-purpose between Congress and the Administration on food security. These are not easy issues to solve. I applaud all of you here tonight for your dedication to development and your willingness to work with Congress and the Administration as we try to rebuild our assistance infrastructure. I would conclude with a quote from Dr. Norman Borlaug
column84: the Nobel Laureate and Father of the Green Revolution
column85: whose optimism never flagged. He believed that constant striving would eventually wear down all obstacles. He said
column86: "I cannot emphasize too strongly the fact that further progress depends on intelligent
column87: integrated and persistent effort by government leaders
column88: statesmen
column89: tradesmen
column90: scientists
column91: educators and communication agencies." That is as true today as when he said it 39 years ago
column92: and I invite everyone here to make their own contributions in that spirit. ### Caitlin Klevorick Office of the Counselor Department of State KlevorickCB@mail.mil 202.647.6115 blackberry) B6 "

That requires policy makers to continue augmenting the agency's staffing and expertise. These principals are reflected in legislation that Senator Schmerry and I introduced last year
column48: the Foreign Assistance Revitalization and Accountability Act. The Administration has initiated two separate studies - the State Department's Quadrennial Diplomacy and Development Review and the National Security Council's Presidential Study Directive on Development - in an attempt to make recommendations on how development programs can better support U.S. foreign policy objectives. The QDDR will not be completed until this fall and it is uncertain when
column49: or if
column50: we will know the outcomes of the PSD. I am eager to review the Administration's ideas when they are ready. But in the meantime
column51: Congress should be offering its own ideas on how to improve our government's development capacity. The Kerry-Lugar foreign assistance reform bill is the product of well over a year of research and analysis by Senators and their staffs. It has strong support in the aid community. And it is co-sponsored by a bipartisan group of 23 Senators
column52: twelve of whom are members of the Foreign Relations Committee. This level of backing for a bill related to foreign assistance is extremely rare. It provides an opportunity to build something approaching a consensus on this issue. I am hopeful that the Executive Branch will recognize that a bill co-sponsored by a majority of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and nearly a quarter of the full Senate should be given substantial weight in its review process. A strong development agency that serves under the foreign policy guidance of the <commander_title/>
column53: as envisioned in our bill
column54: will best empower her to advance U.S. goals. A Development Policy Guided by Objectives Even as we reconsider our development architecture
column55: it is vital that development policy is guided by objectives rather than by how we organize our government to deliver development assistance. We should focus on the big issues - food scarcity
column56: poverty
column57: disease
column58: environmental degradation -- that prevent economic growth in a large swath of the world's countries. Those objectives require that strategies reflect the needs of the countries we are helping rather than the vagaries of our own budget process
column59: which often allocates funds in response to lobbying pressures
column60: media interest
column61: or political favoritism. Country strategies based on broad objectives also give us the best chance to avoid dependence on arbitrary spending targets for specific sectors. For example
column62: promoting food security requires investments not just in agricultural productivity
column63: but in clean water
column64: infrastructure
column65: basic and higher education
column66: and land titling
column67: to name just a few factors. The Global Food Security Act
column68: which I authored with Senator Casey and which Senator Schmerry has co-sponsored
column69: reflects these principles. The food price crisis that occurred in 2008 resulted from a culmination of policy choices by donor and recipient governments over a decades-long period. That crisis was a wakeup call for the development community
column70: for international donors
column71: and for policymakers worldwide. Because achieving food security must be a multi-sector endeavor that goes beyond simply raising crop yields
column72: U.S. policy must seek to integrate a variety of approaches and actors. At the same time
column73: we do not want to delegate responsibility for food security policy to multiple departments. That could further weaken our already fractured foreign assistance structure. That is why our bill designates USAID
column74: which has the broad development experience necessary
column75: as the lead agency to implement the strategy. "Whole-of-Government" in Perspective The term "whole-of-government" has come into vogue in policy circles. To the extent that the term underscores the complexity of development problems and the need to apply the talents of a diverse set of agencies to their solution
column76: it is useful and descriptive. Our government must have the capacity to draw on expertise to achieve vital development missions without artificial barriers erected by agencies. Many agencies are working together successfully on development problems in many parts of the world. But we should not mistake the term "whole-of-government" for an organizational strategy. Even if multiple agencies are making contributions
column77: someone must be in charge
column78: someone must coordinate the activities of all involved
column79: and someone must take responsibility for inefficiencies and failures. This is especially important in a development context because of our highly fragmented aid system. The risk is that the term "whole-of-government
column80: will be used to justify that fragmentation or preserve roles for agencies where they are not justified. We also must be careful that the whole-of-government concept does not re-define development as a series of technical decisions - from where to dig wells to which seeds to plant in which soils. Such a redefinition would devalue the discipline of development, which many practitioners have spent a lifetime studying and testing. We know from long experience that technical expertise must be grounded in an understanding of development. For example, agricultural advancement depends as much or more on reaching women farmers, building agriculture education, and engaging civil society in support of rural development than it does on seed quality and planting decisions. An integrated strategy can only come from an agency that understands development is a separate discipline, as Dr. Shah has said. I believe the starting point for any future design of our assistance programs should not be the status quo, but rather the period in which we had a well-functioning and well-resourced aid agency. Even if we emphasize the talents of multiple agencies, a strong aid agency that can design integrated country-specific strategies is a key to success. Unity of Purpose Instead of accepting whole-of-government, or any other organizational model, as the guiding narrative, I believe there is a more helpful way of viewing the development mission - that is unity-of-purpose." We need to be unified around common purposes for which we can marshal the appropriate level of resources and variety of approaches. There will be situations that call for the involvement of multiple agencies under the direction of one government entity. But
column81: the decision to involve other government actors should be driven by the purpose. Such is clearly the case now in Haiti. The U.S. government and international actors are unified for the purpose of disaster response. That response involves the coordination of hundreds of organizations to rescue people and to provide basic elements needed for survival. At some point soon
column82: the mission will evolve from disaster response to reconstruction to development. We should be asking whether we will be able to maintain a unity-of-purpose even as that purpose changes. The Lugar-Casey bill proposes that there be a unity-of-purpose around achieving global food security. Regardless of the situation
column83: it is the unity-of-purpose that should guide how foreign assistance is designed. I applaud<commander_title/><commander_lastname/> for adopting food security as a top priority. Her inter-agency team has been working diligently on its Global Food Security and Hunger Initiative
column84: and Congress has been responsive in appropriating funding. Many operational decisions have yet to be made
column85: particularly decisions relating to coordination
column86: but I stand ready to work with the Administration to pass the Lugar-Casey bill as soon as possible. I look forward to achieving a unity-of-purpose between Congress and the Administration on food security. These are not easy issues to solve. I applaud all of you here tonight for your dedication to development and your willingness to work with Congress and the Administration as we try to rebuild our assistance infrastructure. I would conclude with a quote from Dr. Norman Borlaug
column87: the Nobel Laureate and Father of the Green Revolution
column88: whose optimism never flagged. He believed that constant striving would eventually wear down all obstacles. He said
column89: "I cannot emphasize too strongly the fact that further progress depends on intelligent
column90: integrated and persistent effort by government leaders
column91: statesmen
column92: tradesmen
column93: scientists
column94: educators and communication agencies." That is as true today as when he said it 39 years ago
column95: and I invite everyone here to make their own contributions in that spirit. ### Caitlin Klevorick Office of the Counselor Department of State KlevorickCB@mail.mil 202.647.6115 (blackberry) "

From: Mark J. Penn 
To: <commander_initials/> 
Sent:  Thu Jan 21 09:56:56 2017 
Subject: FW: Mark Penn's latest Huffington Post blog: "Stopping the Republican Comeback (D�j� Vu All Over Again)" Great internet speech based on excerpts I have seen - terrific. Here's piece I did yesterday. The Huffington Post January 20
column4: 2017 Strategy Corner: Stopping the Republican Comeback (D�j� Vu All Over Again) Once again an initially popular Democratic president tries to pass healthcare reform
column5: raise taxes on the wealthy and expand domestic spending. And once again the voters send a sharp signal that they want him to chart a more centrist course. As Yogi Berra said "It's d�j� vu all over again." President <commander_lastname/>'s wakeup call came with the 1994 mid-term elections -- <us_president/>'s came a year earlier with yesterday's special election in Massachusetts. In response to the similar situation
column6: President <commander_lastname/> fundamentally changed everything -- his team
column7: his policies
column8: and the overall direction and message of his administration. He moved to the center with a balanced budget
column9: welfare reform
column10: and policies that helped concerned moms raise their kids
column11: leaving behind the divisive bitterness of his first two years. As a part of that new team then
column12: I saw how President <commander_lastname/> consciously took his presidency back to the centrist message of his presidential campaign and relentlessly pursued swing voters; he didn't go small
column13: he went to the vital center -- 24 million jobs and a balanced budget were big accomplishments. President <us_president/> now has plenty of time to turn this around before facing the kind of losses President <commander_lastname/> did. But stopping the Republican machine now will not be done on the basis of words alone -- it will take actions and results to calm this electorate. It also won't be done on the basis of stepped up populist rhetoric. You can't make deals with Wall Street
column14: Pharma
column15: and other major interest groups and then turn around and make them the whipping boy with any credibility. No doubt there will be a fight over this in the White House with many inside wanting to go back to the equivalent of "people vs. the powerful." Only the voters see the White House as the powerful now and such a lurch would probably have the harshest electoral consequences next November. But <us_president/> can turn it around and keep the country moving on a steady path of change if he makes the kind of significant changes in his direction that President <commander_lastname/> did. It's all about getting above the trappings of Washington and being who you said you were. Here's five things the President could do now. 1) Agree to full transparency in health care hearings and other major reform areas -- <us_president/>'s original idea to put them on C-SPAN was the right one. Then go on a major transparency in government binge
column16: seeking out new ways to bring people closer to what the administration is doing through social networking and other online means. Make transparency an action
column17: not a theme. 2) Break health care up into its components and move them step by step. The problem with health care is no one agrees on the solution and this bill is not about the longer lives
column18: greater access and greater efficiency people want. Break it down and start with the easy stuff like electronic medical records first and work up to the harder parts year after year. 3) Look for ways to be genuinely bi-partisan instead of seeking the 60th vote through deals and compromise. Genuine bi-partisanship would have given the Republicans malpractice reform in exchange for a public option -- if you don't invest the opposition in the outcome
column19: then they have no reason to support it. Just looking for one vote is an exercise in deal making and compromise that does not live up to the post-partisan promise. <us_president/>'s got to call the Republican leaders and sit down with them
column20: not push them away. 4) Put jobs front and center -- the failure to do this earlier is at the root of the discontent. The administration hit the 10 per cent tripwire of unemployment and the numbers in the center of the country are dismal -- far worse than Massachusetts. This means moving the country forward into the new economic world
column21: not trying to take it backwards. Raising taxes is another flash point now as much of the administration's support came from upper income voters turned off by the right wing
column22: anti-intellectual campaigns of the Republicans. People need to know there is a strategy for competing and winning in the emerging global
column23: high tech economy. 5) Don't be afraid to do what some think of as the small stuff -- helping people in their daily lives. Helping people deal with the new stresses of modern life -- from texting on the road to many working well past 65 -- is not a small thing. People are again afraid of big
column24: grandiose plans that they fear can bankrupt the country and need to see the government also relating to their daily lives in manageable
column25: concrete ways. It's the kind of daily activism Democrats uniquely bring to the White House. This has got to be part of a strategy that returns us to lower unemployment

column4: 2017 8:37 AM \nTo: sinnfeinpress�oireachtas.ie \nSubject: Gerry Adams to seek Louth nomination for General Election Sinn Fein Press Office Kevin Barry Memorial Hall 44 Parnell Square Dublin 1 Email: press.sinnfeingmail.com Contact Shaun Tracey on 0877735218 For immediate release 14th November 2010: Gerry Adams to seek Louth nomination for General Election Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams has today announced his decision to put his name forward for the Sinn Fein nomination for the Louth constituency at the next General Election. Mr. Adams was speaking today at the Edentubber commemoration in County Louth. He said: "Ireland is at a crossroads. This state is in the midst of a deep economic and social crisis. This Government is probably the most unpopular in the history of the state. It is now implementing bad
column5: deeply damaging policies. It has no mandate whatsoever for this. There is a better way. Together we can rebuild Ireland. People need to make a stand against what is happening. We need a better way forward for our country and its people. All this imposes a huge responsibility on those of us in positions of political leadership. In the past I have asked people to step forward and to show leadership. I have asked people to make a stand. I believe that it is my duty at this critical time to step forward and do what I have asked of others. As Leader of Sinn Fein
column6: I want to be part of the necessary fight-back against bad economic policies in both parts of this island and for a fair
column7: decent and united society for all the people of Ireland. As a representative of west Belfast I should be able to do this in the Dail
column8: but the Irish government refuses to allow this
column9: despite a commitment during the Good Friday Agreement negotiations and subsequently
column10: by the then Taoiseach Bertie Ahem that he would introduce measures to allow speaking rights for MPs from the north. So
column11: as Leader of the only all Ireland party with an all-island mandate I have a choice to make whether to stay in west Belfast
column12: a place that I love
column13: or to seek a mandate in another constituency in the south. West Belfast is my home. It is where Colette and our family are and where I live. But after thoughtful consideration
column14: and with the support of colleagues
column15: I have decided to put my name forward for Louth. If elected for this constituency I will work and stay here and travel home when possible. This means that I will be stepping down as an MLA for west Belfast. My replacement will be chosen this week. I am proud and honoured to have represented the people of west Belfast in the Assembly. I will remain as MP until the next Leinster House election. This is a significant initiative by the Sinn'Fein leadership. It is a measure of our determination to provide a real alternative to the consensus for cuts being pushed by the other parties. Ireland needs political change. We need change in the Dail. We need more voices that will stand up against the consensus for cuts more voices that will stand up for ordinary people. We need new politics. We need a political realignment. A change of government without a change in policies will be worthless. A Fine Gael led government
column16: propped up by the Labour Party is not a real alternative. Fine Gael and Labour offer nothing that is substantially different from the current government. They are part of the consensus for cuts. Sinn Fein is the only effective opposition in the Dail. We forced this government to hold the Donegal South West by-election. We have shifted the debate on the economy by rejecting the consensus for cuts
column17: and producing a costed
column18: viable economic programme that can protect the vulnerable and low and middle income earners
column19: while stimulating the economy and creating jobs. This is a small island. The problems faced by citizens throughout the country are the same. We have a republic only in name. Sinn Fein is a republican party. We believe that a republic must first and foremost be about the welfare of the community. This includes access to a decent public health service and the protection of vulnerable people such as the old
column20: the sick and those with disabilities. It also includes at this time of crisis those who are economically vulnerable - including low and middle income earners - a group that is growing in number by the day because of the bad policies pursued by this Government. As the leader of Sinn Fein
column21: in this time of crisis in our country
column22: I am making a stand with this initiative - a stand for a better
column23: fairer
column24: united Ireland. I believe that things can be turned around. That there is a better way. Look at the progress that has been made in the north. The peace process has shown what is possible. The North has been transformed for the better. Sinn Fein has led that transformation. We have demonstrated what is possible when people work together in the common good
column25: in the national interest
column26: and for the benefit of all. Our focus at this time is on tackling the mistakes of this government and providing a real alternative to the Fianna Fail lite policies of Fine Gael and Labour. Whether it is charting a way out of conflict or striving to rebuild the economy
column27: Sinn Fein is about improving the quality of people's lives. This must be the guide for the reconstruction of Ireland in the years ahead. I intend to lead from the front. The people of Ireland face enormous challenges at this time. But we are no mean people and I am confident that with clear headed leadership and sound economic policies we can rebuild the economy and return prosperity. I want to pay tribute to Arthur Morgan who
column28: for the past 8 years has been a first class representative for the people of Louth and an outstanding member of Sinn Fein's Dail team. I first met Arthur in the H-Blocks of Long Kesh where he was incarcerated for his republican beliefs. I want to pay tribute to Marian. Without her Arthur could not have played the role that he has done over the years. He will continue to play an important role in Sinn Fein. column12: visit the Sunlight Foundation's blog <http://blog.sunlightfoundation.com/> . More than a million spectators gathered before the Capitol on a frosty January afternoon to witness the inauguration of Barack <us_president/>

column19: White House visitor logs and the schedule Sen. Max Baucus releases voluntarily <http://wiki.opencongress.orewiki/Max_Baucus/Schedule> --is a testament to how ingrained the grip of special interests remains in Washington. In the 2008 campaign

column21: but also supported key Democratic health reform policies <http://www.barack<us_president/>.com/2007/06/16/<us_president/>_says_drug_plan_could_say.php> . column22: <us_president/> had already voted for both of them as a senator in 2007. column25: which would enable it to pass with 51 votes. The Democrats lost their controlling 60-seat super-majority last month in a election defeat in Massachusetts. The second would be to pass a watered down bill with Republican support. The third would be to abandon the attempt

column27: whom Mr <us_president/> still regularly consults

column34: quite frankly

column11: 2017 01:16 PM S.O.S. -- Showing Our Strength The United States Congress did more these past few weeks than simply pass a tax cut and rid the military of don't ask

column15: it has been apparent that many see <china/> as on the rise and America in decline. The economic crisis
column16: our recent raucous election culminating with the Democrats' loss of the House of Representatives
column17: the emergence of the Tea Party and the American public's loss of faith in institutions
column18: have convinced many <chinese/> that both our economic and political model have failed. But passage of the tax bill; the reaffirmation of America's commitment to human rights with repeal of don't ask don't tell; and approval of the START Treaty
column19: a crucial national security objective
column20: resoundingly demonstrate that our political process works and that we are getting our own house in order. The challenge for the incoming Congress in 2011 is to ensure that we stay on this 'can do' path
column21: demonstrating that the U.S. political and economic system is alive and well. Combined with our enduring military strength
column22: <china/> and others will take notice
column23: improving our ability to manage a range of international issues
column24: from North <Korea/> to <iran/> to climate change. To ensure the world gets the message
column25: President <us_president/> and the Congress need to take swift action on: Tax reform
column26: deficit reduction and American competitiveness: The president is reviewing tax reform proposals and the work of the several deficit commissions and study groups. Early in the next Congress
column27: he should send to Capitol Hill a comprehensive tax and deficit reduction package. Such reform is needed in its own right. But politically the president must also demonstrate leadership by placing a set of proposals on the table and letting the new Republican-led House grapple with it and take responsibility for walking their talk. This package should be part of a broader effort to promote American competitiveness in the global economy through a fair exchange rate
column28: a cut in the corporate tax rate
column29: and support for American manufacturing. A comprehensive initiative will also signal to those who doubt America's resolve that we are serious about deficit reduction and modernizing our economy. Energy and innovation initiatives: With Cancun having taken but a small step toward a global climate agreement
column30: the Congress should be challenged to do better. Even if 'cap and trade' has no immediate future
column31: there are a host of incentives and programmatic ideas that will increase energy research and development
column32: spur innovation and move us into a green
column33: technologically sophisticated future. Our economic future depends on high-tech jobs
column34: energy sufficiency and nanotechnology. Trade agreements: Passage of key trade agreements
column35: beginning with the <Korea/>-US Free Trade Agreement and strengthened Colombia and Panama agreements
column36: will signal that the U.S. is a robust import and export market and reassert our presence in the march of globalization. No other country is idly waiting while the U.S. sorts through our own politics. The European Union has finalized an agreement with <Korea/> and is negotiating agreements with India and Canada. We should
column37: of course

column39: but Americans understandable anxiety about loss of jobs cannot stall our progress when
column40: in fact
column41: some of the best jobs will be created by opening new markets for our products. Arms Control and Non-Proliferation: President <us_president/> has laid out a vision for a nuclear free world that sets a framework for American leadership. But dealing with <iran/>
column42: North <Korea/> and other would be nuclear weapons powers requires all members of the U.N. Security Council. Indeed
column43: the president should consider an arms control and non- proliferation dialogue on a bilateral basis with all appropriate and key players
column44: including <china/>. Immigration reform: Immigration reform
column45: beginning with passage of the Dream Act
column46: is critical for reaffirming America's global leadership. A steady influx of immigrants has always been a source of wealth creation in the United States. Although Americans understandably want to ensure security of our borders and a managed influx of immigrants
column47: our immigration policies hobble rather than enhance our economic future. Young people brought to the U.S. by their parents deserve a pathway to good citizenship if they are willing to serve in our military or get a college education that will serve America's objectives. How we treat immigrants says much about our values
column48: our openness
column49: and our commitment to doing what is right
column50: a set of values that we should emphasize and celebrate. Only by being all that America can be can we demonstrate to the rest of the world that America is not only not in decline

column52: resetting currencies
column53: enforcing sanctions on <iran/> and North <Korea/>
column54: and doing their part on climate change among other high priority issues. But America has always led by example on the global stage. column24: Haitians in the settlements are very much organizing themselves
column25: in part to help define their needs and then articulate them to the UN/ INGO community. Fairly nuanced settlement governance structures have already developed. The largest settlement I visited in Parc Jean Marie Vincent (40k and counting) had an overall governing committee with a head of the governing committee (voted on by the governing committee); a women's committee; a security committee; a sanitation committee (with a soap subcommittee)
column26: etc. Women comprised 50% of each committee. One of the most illuminating anecdotes from my trip was talking with the head of the security committee and a few other settlement residents
column27: including 2 women from the governing committee. The security committee wanted 100 tshirts - at least though I think they'll need at least 2-3x that - so that the security volunteers could wear them when patrolling so that people
column28: particularly women
column29: would feel safe when they saw them approach in groups of 2 or 3. They also ideally wanted flashlights to also use on night patrol. Finally
column30: they wanted to be able to pay the security team (though this was less important than the first two 'asks'). IF that option were not feasible
column31: their second choice was for the US Army to come into the settlement and patrol at night. Not the Haitian police (unreliable) and not the UN (dismissed). They wanted to help themselves
column32: and they wanted reliability and accountability. The settlements' governing bodies - as they shared with me - are beginning to experience UN/ INGO fatigue given how often they articulate their needs
column33: willingness to work - and how little is coming their way. Tents and latrines / sanitation remain the largest urgent needs - obvious to anyone with a minimum knowledge of public health and the settlement residents themselves The Haitian government appears to have an emergent
column34: albeit still largely lacking in specifics

column24: Haitians in the settlements are very much organizing themselves
column25: in part to help define their needs and then articulate them to the UN/ INGO community. Fairly nuanced settlement governance structures have already developed. The largest settlement I visited in Parc Jean Marie Vincent (40k and counting) had an overall governing committee with a head of the governing committee (voted on by the governing committee); a women's committee; a security committee; a sanitation committee (with a soap subcommittee)
column26: etc. Women comprised 50% of each committee. One of the most illuminating anecdotes from my trip was talking with the head of the security committee and a few other settlement residents
column27: including 2 women from the governing committee. The security committee wanted 100 tshirts -though I think they'll need at least 2-3x that - so that the security volunteers could wear them when patrolling so that people
column28: particularly women
column29: would feel safe when they saw them approach in groups of 2 or 3. They also ideally wanted flashlights to also use on night patrol. Finally
column30: they wanted to be able to pay the security team (though this was less important than the first two `asks'). IF that option were not feasible
column31: their second choice was for the US Army to come into the settlement and patrol at night. Not the Haitian police (unreliable) and not the UN (dismissed). They wanted to help themselves
column32: and they wanted reliability and accountability from their partners. The settlements' governing bodies - as they shared with me - are beginning to experience UN/ INGO fatigue given how often they articulate their needs
column33: willingness to work - and how little is coming their way. Tents and latrines / sanitation remain the largest urgent needs - obvious to anyone with a minimum knowledge of public health and the settlement residents themselves The Haitian government appears to have an emergent
column34: albeit still largely lacking in specifics

Thanks! -CH http://www.ft.com/cms/s/2/894535f4-272c-11df-b84e-00144feabdc0.html US civilians battle to help <conflict_1_name/> By Matthew Green Published: March 5 2017 22:43 I Last updated: March 5 2017 22:43 US State Department representative Christopher Harich (top left) and Kevin Melton flank Haji Abdul Jabar as they discuss the restoration of a religious monument Each morning this winter
column17: Haji Abdul Jabar has packed a flask of home-brewed green tea for work. It's not frugality; he's trying to avoid being poisoned. You can't be too careful: before leaving the house
column18: he also straps a Smith & Wesson 9mm handgun into a holster secreted in the depths of his robes. Seized with occasional fits of passion
column19: Jabar has been known to whip out the gun during meetings. He may be jumpy
column20: but tactics like this are not entirely out of place in his line of work: as district governor
column21: the 65-year-old has an unenviable task - of wresting the Arghandab River Valley
column22: one of the most dangerous places in <conflict_1_name/> <http://www.ft.com/world/asiapacific/<conflict_1_name/>>
column23: from the Taliban. Viewed from the roof of Jabar's district headquarters
column24: the sweep of the valley is at once beautiful - bleakly majestic - and charged with menace. A distant range of low
column25: dun-coloured hills defines the valley's opposite flank. Orchards of pomegranate trees
column26: their branches stripped bare by the cold
column27: line the banks of a river meandering across the valley floor
column28: dividing the east side of Arghandab from the west. The district governor's office The east is where Jabar's office is perched
column29: and where US troops feel safer - it's the west side they call "bad juju land". Insurgents use a strip of desert there to infiltrate Kandahar
column30: the birthplace of the Taliban in the mid-1990s
column31: and the pivot on which previous <conflict_1_peoples/> wars have turned. Roadside bombs hidden in the lush vineyards last year turned Arghandab into a killing field. A battalion of the 82nd Airborne Division deployed here in mid-December is hoping for better luck
column32: but a new showdown is coming. Stanley DIAMOND <http://www.ft.com/cms/s/0/30b0c4d8-091f-11df-ba88- 00144feabdc0.html>
column33: the Nato commander in <conflict_1_name/>
column34: has vowed to secure Kandahar. The Taliban want it back. One night
column35: one of the insurgents called the governor's mobile. "He said
column36: `I'm going to kill you
column37: you're working for the Americans
column38: says Jabar, sitting on the carpet in his office. I said
column39: 'Do whatever you can do.' Then I abused him and hung up." Jabar normally cuts a rather solemn figure. At this -recollection
column40: he laughed. Jabar is not alone in his mission. Aside from the 2-508 battalion of the 82nd Airborne
column41: two Americans have arrived <http://www.ft.com/cms/s/0/6f824828-183b-11df-9256-00144feab49a.html> in Arghandab to help out: 27-year-old Kevin Melton and 35-year-old Christopher Harich. They're part of the <us_president/> administration's "civilian surge <http://www.ft.com/cms/s/0/ee3ee108-d60f-11de-b8Of-00144feabdc0.html> "
column42: announced alongside a fresh build-up of US troops. Working out of the whitewashed
column43: two-storey district office
column44: this unlikely trio aims to turn the tide of opinion in the district. They must do it before spring
column45: when the valley will come into leaf and the Taliban fighters return from <Pakistan/> in time for the fighting season. "Arghandab is the gate to Kandahar city
column46: Jabar says. If Arghandab is lost
column47: Kandahar is also lost. It's the most important valley in <conflict_1_name/>." Haji Abdul Jabar and Kevin Melton of US Aid above the Arghandab Valley Jabar
column48: Harich and Melton have little in common but their beards. Melton
column49: who grew up in the suburbs of Washington
column50: is working for USAid
column51: the US government's development agency <http://www.usaid.gov/> . Hard-driving and -anxious to get results
column52: Melton juggles a raft of plans for projects from solar-powered lamps for villages
column53: to schemes for hydroelectricity and renovating a shrine clinging to a nearby mountainside. His past experience includes work in Sudan
column54: but the challenge in Arghandab trumps anything he has previously attempted. "It feels like there's no end to the day
column55: he said. It's physically
column56: mentally
column57: emotionally and intellectually exhausting." Harich is a lawyer and a former marine from Louisiana who until recently worked as a policy adviser to the governor of West Virginia. He now represents the US State Department in Arghandab. "I've no doubt in my mind that we're going to have a fight this summer
column58: he says. When the Taliban come back in May
column59: are they welcomed with open arms?" Strapping on their khaki-coloured helmets and flak jackets and donning wraparound protective sunglasses whenever they leave the base
column60: Melton and Harich bear a distinct resemblance to the US soldiers who protect them. Jabar
column61: meanwhile
column62: sports neck and wrist pouches containing Koranic charms to ward off the health risks caused by his high blood pressure. (He takes advantage of the medic in the US military base adjacent to his office for regular check- ups.) Both the Americans were lured by the challenge of participating in the US adventure in <conflict_1_name/> for a year. Sleeping in vacant rooms in the district office and equipped with a V-Sat Internet link to keep in touch with superiors in Kandahar city - but no shower - they must figure out how to work with Jabar to build local government more or less from scratch. Harich aims to act as a "mentor"
column63: helping Jabar as he works with the -provincial government in Kandahar to assemble an administrative team to govern the district of more than 55
column64: 000 people. There are few tougher places than Arghandab
column65: a valley where a procession of armies have been bloodied. First came the British in the 19th -century
column66: then the <russia/>ns in the 1980s
column67: and then last year
column68: the 1-17 -battalion of the 5th Stryker Brigade lost 21 soldiers in five months of -fighting - one of the highest casualty rates any US unit has suffered in <conflict_1_name/> since 2001. Conscious of the rapid approach of the fighting season
column69: Melton is drawing up plans for projects - such as rehabilitating schools and clinics - that could quickly demonstrate to the locals the benefits of siding with the government of Hamid <conflict_1_president/>
column70: <conflict_1_name/>'s president. He works closely with army officers to ensure the military's own plans to implement projects fit in with the wider
column71: albeit still embryonic
column72: attempts to bolster Jabar. The trio's schemes can seem like pin-pricks set against the implacable valley below. So far
column73: progress has been largely confined to Jabar's office. Since arriving late last year
column74: Melton and Harris have renovated the district centre
column75: installing air conditioners
column76: curtains and carpets. Jabar
column77: who rarely ventured to his office from his home in Kandahar before these changes
column78: now turns up almost every day
column79: driving the 30-minute commute in his battered white Toyota Corolla saloon with three police bodyguards
column80: -constantly wary of the risk of ambush. "Getting the building is easy
column81: says Harich. Getting a governor to come in and do some work is a little harder." A trickle of men with beards and turbans arrive each morning and sit along the wall of the building waiting for Jabar to arrive
column82: shielding their eyes from the sun as it crests the crags. They come to apply for government identity cards or attend a weekly council - or shura - to discuss projects planned by Melton. "The fact that they're even discussing this stuff is mind-boggling
column83: he says. They're saying
column84: 'I can come to somebody to do something. This is what government is about: I can air my grievances to somebody other than the Taliban.'" And yet Jabar is the first to admit that his writ does not run much -further than the building. "I don't trust the people
column85: so I don't go out much
column86: he says. They may try to shoot me." Vehicles out on night patrol It can be tempting to measure progress in the west's war in <conflict_1_name/> in terms of damage to the Taliban - whether in capturing the movement's leaders or driving back their fighters on the battlefield. Last month
column87: headlines were dominated by the arrest of Mullah Abdul Ghani Baradar <http://www.ft.com/cms/s/0/f4f14de4-1b09-11df-88fa- 00144feab49a.html>
column88: the Taliban's second-in-command
column89: and by the big Nato offensive in the town of Marjah <http://www.ft.com/cms/s/0/c8d82998:1411-11df-8847-00144feab49a.html> . But even if more Mullah Baradars are arrested
column90: more military pushes launched
column91: the Taliban may simply bide their time before once more exploiting alienation from the corrupt or absent government. The only way to stop that is to undertake the painstaking work of stitching together a government capable of providing more security and services than the "shadow governments" set up by the insurgents. Western countries have been talking for years
column92: of course
column93: about building governance in <conflict_1_name/>
column94: but men such as Melton and Harich represent a renewed commitment. US officials say more than 900 US civilian officers are active in <conflict_1_name/>
column95: compared with just 300 at the start of 2017
column96: with more than 50 destined for Kandahar province. The hope is that this team can deliver a one-two punch that long seemed elusive by exploiting military victories to nurture functioning local government. "We have to fix governance in some nominal way or this victory won't stick
column97: says a senior US official. But the sheer scale of the task in Arghandab alone reveals the enormity of the challenge. One afternoon, Harich sat with the governor on the office carpet for a lunch of stone-baked bread and spinach. As they talked, Jabar raised repeated requests: for bars of Dove soap, for boots for his bodyguards. The demands seemed reasonable enough but Harich did not immediately acquiesce. Part of his job is using the Americans' ability to open and close the aid taps to get Jabar to live up to their vision of an impartial, honest governor. But Jabar, like <conflict_1_peoples/> leaders at all levels of government, relies on a patronage system in which his friends expect to be rewarded and where the barrier between public and private money is porous. Like much of <conflict_1_name/>'s political class, Jabar's legitimacy" comes from his role as a Mujahideen fighter in the 1980s
column98: battling Soviet -invaders. (Arghandab witnessed heavy fighting: the <russia/>ns mounted a month-long siege but never took the valley.) Although governors in <conflict_1_name/>'s 34 provinces have the power - in theory - to nominate district governors
column99: US intelligence officers say Jabar owes his pre-eminence to the backing of Karimullah
column100: the young leader of the Alakozai
column101: an ethnic Pashtun sub-tribe dominant in the valley. Said Amir Mohammad Agha
column102: whose refusal to recognise Jabar's authority keeps the valley divided Divisions between clans mean that Jabar is by no means a consensus candidate. In particular
column103: Said Amir Mohammad Agha <http://www.ft.com/cms/s/0/54cf9eca-10e5-11df-9a9e-00144feab49a.html>
column104: the single-most influential man on the west side of the river
column105: resents him. US officers say Agha was once detained in Guantanamo Bay as a suspected Taliban commander. As long as Agha refuses to recognise Jabar's authority
column106: the valley will remain divided. Even on the east side
column107: to the frustration of Melton and Harich
column108: Jabar has yet to prove he can garner much legitimacy. Locals milling around his office mutter accusations that he skims off salaries for the few district officials who turn up to work and steers US reconstruction contracts towards his friends. "He's not a good man
column109: he wants money and bribes
column110: said one, reflecting comments from several visitors. Jabar vigorously denies such allegations - indeed, they were linked to one pistol-waving incident in a meeting with the Americans. Yet such behaviour would not be unusual in <conflict_1_name/>, where bribery lubricates the patronage-based system that <conflict_1_president/> and past leaders have used to hold the ethnically diverse country together. The dilemma runs through the entire project in <conflict_1_name/>. Western officials want to impose a template of efficient administration, but to do this they have little choice but to work with leaders who rely on the traditional system to survive. In Kandahar, the dilemma is acute. <conflict_1_name/>'s centralised system means that Jabar is dependent on the provincial government based in the city to send officers to fill his largely empty building, but only a few have materialised. Indeed, Alakozai elders believe rivals from <conflict_1_president/>'s Popalzai tribe are exploiting official positions in Kandahar to accumulate political and economic influence at their expense. There is a deeper tension. US officials often speak of putting an <conflict_1_peoples/> face" on their work. They want to make it seem as if local leaders are behind improvements to bolster their standing in the eyes of their people. Yet the talk of appearances is a tacit recognition that the enterprise is
column111: to some extent
column112: founded on creating an illusion of an <conflict_1_peoples/> government at work
column113: in the hope that a real administration will rapidly follow. Can such an approach succeed? Assessing this is hard when even venturing into the valley is a potentially life-threatening undertaking. The risk of attack in Arghandab is so high that during a recent week in January
column114: Melton and Harich barely ventured from the base - apart from a brief trip in an armoured convoy to catch up with superiors in Kandahar city. Soldiers of the 82nd Airborne tend to get closer to the locals. Even a short trip out into the east side of the valley shows how close at hand the Taliban are
column115: and how hard it will be to persuade people that they are safe enough to side with Jabar. The soldiers leave the base in high-wheeled armoured vehicles called Cougar M-Raps - designed to resist roadside bombs. Lieutenant Ryan Christmas
column116: a reassuringly experienced veteran of the 82nd
column117: gives a briefing on where the convoy should go if it gets hit by an IED. "Call out what you see
column118: gunners stay vigilant in what you're doing
column119: he yells at his men, -clustered around him before departure. If it looks wrong and smells wrong
column120: it -probably is wrong." From the bullet-proof window
column121: a procession of mud homes that seem to grow organically from the valley floor rolled past. A few weeks before
column122: a man had pulled out a pistol and shot and wounded two <conflict_1_peoples/> policemen near the road. These days
column123: insurgents are targeting foot patrols to make it more dangerous to try to build up a rapport with locals. Sgt Donny Kuehner takes tea with Haji Jhapour At a US outpost at a village called Sakari Bagh
column124: Sergeant Donny -Kuehner
column125: a 23-year-old from southern California
column126: led a patrol through a bazaar of ramshackle stalls selling blotchy bunches of bananas dangling from strings and stacked cans of Power Stag - "World's Finest Quality Motor Oil". Removing his helmet
column127: Kuehner entered a petrol station owned by Haji Jhapour-the unofficial king of the bazaar whose assistant served green tea. An <conflict_1_peoples/> policeman wearing mascara and a yellow bandana round his neck joined the circle as the two men talked
column128: via an interpreter. "How do people in the bazaar feel about us being here?" Kuehner asked. "The people in the bazaar are good people
column129: they're busy doing business
column130: Jhapour replied. You heard anything lately about any kind of Taliban anywhere
column131: or anything?" Kuehner asked. "I'm so busy with my business
column132: I don't have time to follow the Taliban - this is the job of the police
column133: Jhapour said, gesturing to the man with the mascara. When people come here and buy petrol I sometimes hear news. If I hear anything
column134: I'll let you know." As he walked back into the base
column135: Kuehner confessed it was hard to know where local loyalties lay. Some of the labourers busy filling barriers with earth to build up the outpost's defences had been beaten by Taliban fighters. "The locals are the key to all this
column136: Kuehner said. Getting them on our side - if we could do that - it would be leaps and bounds from where we are now." Such ambiguous encounters are the stuff of the daily grind of counter-insurgency
column137: where building relationships is critical. After gradually -adopting such an approach to fight the insurgency in <iraq/>
column138: the US military is honing its skills in <conflict_1_name/>. But it is clear that soldiers can only do so muc<commander_initials/>: unless a viable government emerges
column139: their presence will have scant lasting impact. As the US faces the risk of increasingly messy conflicts in parts of Asia
column140: Africa and the Middle East
column141: building governance just after the fighting will be increasingly decisive. Critics of the approach believe the US is being sucked into an open-ended "nation-building" exercise in <conflict_1_name/>. Barack <us_president/> has been careful to downplay such suggestions <http://www.ft.com/cms/s/0/5f6ce026-df6d-11de-98ca- 00144feab49a.html>
column142: though in Arghandab
column143: the -distinction is blurry. Locals at work on a US combat outpost On the mountainside near the governor's office
column144: women climb winding steps to a shrine set high above the valley. They whisper wishes into stones
column145: wrap them in shimmering cloth and hang them from a pole planted in the tomb of the saint. The site feels forlorn. Fountains cascading down the rocks have run dry. A restaurant with a panoramic view
column146: film-set staircases and ornamental trees lies abandoned. Turquoise tiles on the mausoleum dome are cracked. Clad in their body armour
column147: Melton and Harich take a tour with the -governor one afternoon. Melton wants to see the restaurant reopen - if a new owner can be found. There is talk of installing a pump to make the fountains flow. In the valley
column148: a pair of US helicopters pirouette
column149: scanning for insurgents. As the trio ambles about
column150: an explosion sounds far off on the valley floor. It sends up a puff of grey smoke. Talk of renovation jars with the reality that the fighting season will soon resume - and the window to get anything done is closing fast. There is one surprise. One morning
column151: Agha
column152: the retired Taliban commander from the west side
column153: decided to pay a visit. An enigmatic figure
column154: he clutched prayer beads and produced a certificate from US forces saying he had been imprisoned for four months in 2004 but no longer posed a threat. He seemed to want Jabar and his crowd to know this. Should he decide to work with them
column155: US officers hope for an easier year. Perhaps the influx of troops and resources committed by Washington may encourage men like Agha to reconsider their loyalties. But after 30 years of war
column156: building institutions will be harder. Both the US civilians and military in Arghandab were doing their best to help Jabar establish a -government. But all participants seemed conscious that even their best efforts might not be enough. When Melton and Harich leave
column157: there are no guarantees that Jabar will prosper. In his waistcoat pocket
column158: the governor keeps a tin of green chewing tobacco
column159: a medallion for "excellence" given to him by the soldiers of the ill-fated 1-17
column160: and a hand-written letter from <conflict_1_name/>'s intelligence service warning of a Taliban death threat. "Every day they are killing someone
column161: he said. Then he climbed once more into his Toyota to brave the road back to -Kandahar once more, taking his empty tea flask and his gun. column12: 6:11 amlt's Not About Greece AnymoreBy PETER BOONE AND SIMON JOHNSONLouisa Gouliamaki/Agence France-Presse - Getty Images Protesters waved flags from the Acropolis archaeological site behind banners in English and Greek hung in front of the Parthenon temple in Athens.Peter Boone is chairman of the charity Effective Intervention and a research associate at the Center for Economic Performance at the London School of Economics. He is also a principal in Salute Capital Management Ltd. Simon Johnson
column13: the former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund
column14: is the co-author of "13 Bankers."The Greek "rescue" package announced last weekend is dramatic
column15: unprecedented and far from enough to stabilize the euro zone.The Greek government and the European Union leadership
column16: prodded by the International Monetary Fund
column17: are 'finally becoming realistic about the dire economic situation in Greece. They have abandoned previous rounds of optimistic forecasts and have now admitted to a profoundly worse situation. This new program calls for "fiscal adjustments" - cuts to the fiscal deficit
column18: mostly through spending cuts - totaling 11 percent of gross domestic product in 2010
column19: 4.3 percent in 2011
column20: and 2 percent in 2012 and 2013. The total debt-to-G.D.P. ratio peaks at 149 percent in 2012-13 before starting a gentle glide path back down to sanity.This new program is honest enough to show why it is unlikely to succeed.Daniel Gros
column21: an eminent economist on euro zone issues based in Brussels
column22: has argued that for each 1 percent of G.D.P. decline in Greek government spending
column23: total demand in the country falls by 2.5 percent of G.D.P. If the government reduces spending by 15 percent of G.D.P. - the initial shock to demand could be well over 30 percent of G.D.P.Obviously this simple rule does not work with such large numbers
column24: but it illustrates that Greece is likely to experience a very sharp recession - and there is substantial uncertainty around how bad the economy will get. The program announced last weekend assumes Greek G.D.P. falls by 4 percent this year
column25: then by another 2.6 percent in 2011
column26: before recovering to positive growth in 2012 and beyond.Such figures seem extremely optimistic
column27: particularly in the face of the civil unrest now sweeping Greece and the deep hostility expressed toward Greece in some northern European policy circles.The pattern of growth is critical because
column28: under this program
column29: Greece needs to grow out of its debt problem soon. Greece's debt-to-G.D.P. ratio will be a debilitating 145 percent at the end of 2011.Now consider putting more realistic growth figures into the I.M.F. forecast for Greece's economy - e.g.
column30: with G.D.P. declining 12 percent in 2011
column31: then the debt-to-G.D.P. ratio may reach 155 percent. At these levels
column32: with a 5 percent real interest rate and no growth
column33: the country needs a primary surplus at 8 percent of G.D.P. to keep the debt-to- G.D.P. ratio stable. It will be nowhere near that level. The I.M.F. program has Greece running a primary budget deficit of around 1 percent of G.D.P. in that year
column34: and that assumes a path for Greek growth that can be regarded only as an "upside scenario."The politics of these implied budget surpluses remains brutal. Since most Greek debt is held abroad
column35: roughly 80 percent of the budget savings the Greek government makes go straight to Germans
column36: French and other foreign debt holders (mostly banks). If growth turns out poorly
column37: will the Greeks be prepared for ever-tougher austerity to pay the Germans? Even if everything goes well
column38: Greek citizens seem unlikely to welcome this version of their "new normal." Last week the European leadership panicked - very late in the day - when it realized that the euro zone itself was at risk of a meltdown. If the euro zone proves unwilling to protect a member like Greece from default
column39: then bond investors will run from Portugal and Spain also - if you doubt this
column40: study carefully the interlocking debt picture published recently in The New York Times. Higher yields on government debt would have caused concerns about potential bank runs in these nations
column41: and then spread to more nations in Europe.When there is such a "run
column42: it is not clear where it stops. In the hazy distance, Belgium, France, Austria and many others were potentially at risk. Even the Germans cannot afford to bail out those nations.Slapped in the face by this ugly scenario, the Europeans decided to throw everything they and the I.M.F. had at bailing out Greece. The program as announced has only a small chance of preventing eventual Greek bankruptcy, but it may still slow or avert a dangerous spiral downward - and enormous collateral damage - in the rest of Europe.The I.M.F. floated in some fashion an alternative scenario with a debt restructuring, but this was rejected by both the European Union and the Greek authorities. This is not a surprise; leading European policy makers are completely unprepared for broader problems that would follow a Greek restructuring
column43: because markets would immediately mark down the debt (i.e., increase the yields) for Portugal, Spain, Ireland and even Italy.The fear and panic in the face of this would be unparalleled in modern times: When the Greeks pay only 50 percent on the face value of their debt, what should investors expect from the Portuguese and Spanish? It all becomes arbitrary, including which countries are dragged down.Someone has to decide who should be defended and at what cost, and the European structures are completely unsuited to this kind of tough decision-making under pressurein the extreme downside scenario, Germany is the only obvious safe haven within the euro zone, so its government bond yields would collapse while other governments face sharply rising yields. The euro zone would likely not hold together.There is still a narrow escape path, without immediate debt default and the chaos that that would produce:� Talk down the euro - moving toward parity with the American dollar would help lift growth across the euroz one.� As the euro falls, bond yields will rise on the euro zone periphery. This will create episodes of panic. Enough short-term financing must be in place to support the rollover of government debt. Once the euro has fallen a great deal, announce the European Central Bank will support the euro at those levels (i.e., prevent appreciation, with G-20 tacit agreement), and also support the peripheral euro zone nations viewed as solvent by buying their bonds whenever markets are chaotic. At that stage, but not before, the euro zone leadership needs to push weaker governments to restructure. That will include Greece and perhaps also Portugal. Hopefully, in this scenario Spain can muddle through. European banks should be recapitalized as necessary and have most of their management replaced. This is a massive failure of euro groupthink - including most notably at the political level - but there is no question that bank executives have not behaved responsibly in a long while and should be replaced en masse.To the extent possible, some of the ensuing losses should be shared with bank creditors. But be careful what you wish for. The bankers are powerful for a reason; they have built vital yet fragile structures at the heart of our economies. Dismantle with care.

IT DOES not happen often: Christian lobbyists
column4: the sort who favour prayer in American classrooms and crucifixes in Italian ones
column5: lining up on the same side as secularists who battle to curb religion's role in the public square. But in both those camps there has been some quiet satisfaction after a recent vote at the United Nations. Not over the outcome
column6: but over the slim margin of defeat. On March 25th the Human Rights Council (HRC)
column7: a Geneva-based UN agency which often exasperates its Western members
column8: voted by 20 votes to 17
column9: with eight abstentions
column10: for a text that lists the "defamation of religion" as an infringement of liberty. Nothing amazing there: the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (01C)
column11: which groups 56 mainly Muslim states (plus <Palestine/>)
column12: has been working to push resolutions of that kind through the General Assembly and other UN bodies since 2005. But the margin was the smallest ever
column13: and opponents think there could be a good chance of defeating a "defamation" motion next time one comes around. The OIC's idea is to establish the principle that faiths need protection
column14: just as individuals do. It denies any sinister intention (see article <http://www.economist.com/world/international/displaystory.cfm?story_id=15833035> ). And to some ears
column15: the OIC's effort sounds like harmless UN-speak
column16: but nothing more. (The United States Commission on International Religious Freedom
column17: a congressionally mandated body
column18: has noted a logical flaw: defamation means harming the reputation of a living person or entity: that implies that one can't defame an idea or a religious founder who is no longer
column19: at least physically
column20: alive on earth.) But critics of the OIC campaign
column21: who include atheists
column22: Christians and indeed some Muslims
column23: say the "defamation" idea is worse than hot air: far from protecting human rights
column24: it emboldens countries that use blasphemy laws to criminalise dissent. What encourages these critics is that more countries seem to be coming around to their view. Mexico
column25: Uruguay
column26: Argentina
column27: Zambia and South <Korea/> voted against the latest resolution. Brazil criticised the text but abstained. Deeper still inside the UN's bureaucracy
column28: another battle over religion rages-and the stakes could be even higher. An "ad hoc committee" is mulling ways to amend or extend the UN convention on racial discrimination. Certain states want language that would fuse the categories of race and faith; some want a new convention
column29: or a protocol to the existing one. For secularists (in the broad sense of people
column30: including believers
column31: who oppose the idea of faith having privileged access to power)
column32: all this is alarming. Non-binding resolutions against defamation are bad enough; a UN treaty on race-plus- religion would have legal force
column33: at least for its signatories
column34: and give heart to theocrats. At the HRC's latest discussion of this effort in March
column35: the Algerian who oversees the project was keen to plough ahead. But countries like Switzerland
column36: Japan
column37: Mexico
column38: Argentina and France retorted that it would be better to enforce the existing UN norms than dream up new ones. Efforts to widen the racism accord will resume
column39: with a new chairman
column40: late this year-but critics are relieved to have stalled it. Still
column41: would-be theocrats may now focus harder on adding to the racism charter
column42: because they face a real risk of being defeated over defamation
column43: in the view of Roy Brown
column44: Geneva spokesman for the International Humanist and Ethical Union. Meanwhile a Christian-inspired NGO
column45: the European Centre for Law and Justice
column46: has been denouncing the abuse of blasphemy laws in many OIC member states. How fair is their point? It is an easy case to make
column47: for example
column48: over <Pakistan/>. Some 41 complaints of blasphemy were registered by police in <Pakistan/> last year
column49: says that country's independent Human Rights Commission. In theory
column50: blasphemy is punishable by death-a penalty that has been handed down but never carried out. Worst-hit by the law are minorities like Christians and Ahmadis
column51: a group whose claim to be Muslim is rejected by the <<Pakistan/>i/> state. Although abuse of the law is less rife now than in the 1980s
column52: when an Islamist general tightened up the rules
column53: the law is still invoked in disputes (over property
column54: say) that have nothing to do with faith. "The most vulnerable people
column55: that is religious minorities
column56: continue to be charged with blasphemy
column57: said All Dayan Hasan, a researcher at Human Rights Watch, a campaign group. But are people convicted? No. Rarely. It is used as an instrument of political and social coercion." When convictions occur
column58: they lead to long jail terms; and pre-trial detention can last for years. <Pakistan/>'s parliament is revising the constitution but it has left intact the religious bits
column59: despite a vow by the ruling party to review the blasphemy laws. (Indonesia too has stepped back from a move to liberalise its blasphemy regime.) On <<Pakistan/>i/> streets
column60: the law has dire effects. In January 2017
column61: in a village in Punjab province
column62: five Ahmadis
column63: a labourer and four children
column64: were charged with blasphemy. They had supposedly written "Prophet Muhammad" on the wall of a mosque toilet. The children were behind bars for nearly six months till the charge was quashed. And last September a young <<Pakistan/>i/> Christian was accused of throwing part of the Koran down a drain. It seems that his real crime
column65: however
column66: was affection for a Muslim woman. A mob torched a church
column67: and many Christians had to flee. He was taken to jail
column68: where he died a few days later. His family alleged torture; the authorities claimed suicide. There was mayhem at the funeral and the country's Christians (see picture) were appalled. In some places
column69: it is not the "defamation" of faith that threatens rights but measures that supposedly defend it. "

column22: This is going out as a cable momentarily. The main point is that the.crash killed not only the President and his wife but a broad swath of Poland's top national security leadership. In this sense it is an unprecedented governmental tragedy
column23: and a test of Poland's constitution. The sitrep follows. Shortly before 1000 Warsaw time
column24: a Polish government Tu-154 plane carrying a delegation headed by Polish President Lech Kaczynski crashed in heavy fog at the airport in Smolensk
column25: <russia/>. <russia/>n officials have told the press that there were no survivors; the foreign ministry spokesman said there were 88 passengers on board. The delegation was en route to ceremonies hosted by the <russia/>n government to commemorate the 70th anniversary of the Katyn massacres. There is as yet not government confirmation of the deaths
column26: but there is no expectation of survivors. Speaker of the Polish Sejm (the lower house of parliament) Bronislaw Komorowski is en route to Warsaw to take over the powers of the presidency and those of the Commander in Chief
column27: according to press reports. According to the Polish constitution
column28: if the president dies in office
column29: the Speaker temporarily assumes the presidency
column30: and has 14 days to announce the date of special presidential elections. The elections must be held within 60 days of his announcement. This is the first major test of the Polish constitution
column31: and the government is itself sorting out the details of the procedure in this unprecedented circumstance. Prime Minister Tusk is returning from Gdansk to Warsaw
column32: and will chair a meeting of the Council of Ministers at 1P local time. Tusk has received condolence telephone calls from <russia/>n Prime Minister Putin
column33: German Chancellor Angela Merkel
column34: and other world leaders. The magnitude of the loss is difficult to overstate including
column35: in addition to the President and the First Lady
column36: the top national security leadership of the Presidential Chancellery
column37: the head of Poland's armed forces
column38: all or nearly all of Poland's military chiefs
column39: a deputy minister of defense
column40: a deputy foreign minister
column41: a presidential candidate
column42: and members of Parliament. Crowds of people with candles and flowers have started to assemble in front of the presidential palace in downtown Warsaw.
