column23: 6019051.story latimes.com <conflict_1_peoples/> TV police drama delivers message with zest Partially funded by the U.S. and aided by Australian TV veterans
column24: the series 'Eagle Four' follows an elite <conflict_1_peoples/> police squad. It has a political agenda but gets points for being entertaining. By Laura King
column25: Los Angeles Times 6:20 PM PST
column26: December 7
column27: 2017 Reporting from <conflict_1_capital/>
column28: <conflict_1_name/> Advertisement A suicide bomber is loose in the city
column29: and the clock is ticking. But an elite squad of <conflict_1_peoples/> cops is on the case
column30: working street sources and mining databases
column31: equally at ease with witty one-liners and fully loaded assault rifles
column32: looking cool and soulful all the while. In real life
column33: the <conflict_1_peoples/> police are better known for illiteracy
column34: drug abuse and shaking down citizens than for daring exploits worthy of the big screen - or the small one. But on the popular new TV series "Eagle Four
column35: the squad's resourcefulness, heroism and teamwork never fail to carry the day. The show, which has slick production values and a noir-ish soundtrack, is midway through its initial run of 13 episodes, and has already garnered a large, loyal following on Tolo TV, the country's most-watched station. With the show shot entirely in <conflict_1_capital/>, the <conflict_1_peoples/> capital, open-air takes were sometimes ruined by eager onlookers - from ragged street urchins to cellphone-toting businessmen - trying to get close to the cast and crew. But overly enthusiastic fans were a happy diversion from challenges such as placating an angry mullah who tried to raise a mob to halt the production or dealing with Taliban death threats against several cast members. We didn't know at first what the response was going to be
column36: said Faramjan Abrahim, who plays the cocky, hotheaded rookie Baktash. But then actual policemen started to come up and call me 'brother' and congratulate me for doing a good job solving the case." Most viewers are probably unaware that the series is financed at least in part by the public diplomacy arm of the U.S. Embassy
column37: which acknowledged its monetary support while declining to disclose a dollar amount. A team of Australian TV veterans was brought in to mentor the <conflict_1_peoples/>s working on the show. Boosting public respect for the <conflict_1_peoples/> security forces and drawing higher-quality recruits are crucial to U.S. hopes that the police and army will be ready to assume responsibility for the country's security in three years - a goal some consider way too optimistic. "We see this as an opportunity not only to help support the <conflict_1_peoples/> media sector
column38: but hopefully also encourage a dialogue among <conflict_1_peoples/>s about the role of police in society
column39: and their growing capabilities
column40: said embassy spokeswoman Caitlin Hayden. Another U.S.-funded effort is planned for next year: a reality show that will seek to impart a frisson of glamour to joining the <conflict_1_peoples/> army. If it's entertainment with a political agenda, Eagle Four" gets points for being
column41: well
column42: entertaining. It's got all the requisite cop-show elements: rapid-fire action; a gritty
column43: cinema verite feel; and engrossing interplay among the four squad members and their hard-edged but beloved leader
column44: Chief Amin (who is tormented by a dark secret; more on that later). The show's <conflict_1_peoples/> and Australian creators said "Eagle Four" was inspired by the hit U.S. drama "24." The mood and pacing are similar
column45: but the resemblance doesn't extend to American Jack Bauer's propensity for torturing suspects until they crack. Baktash occasionally gets carried away and roughs someone up
column46: but he is reprimanded by his older
column47: more-seasoned partner
column48: Kamran
column49: who shows him that finesse works better than brute force. "My character is basically a good guy
column50: but he's sort of undisciplined
column51: and he has a lot to learn
column52: Abrahim said. A recurring theme is that when Baktash disregards Kamran's counsel, he usually gets injured within the next few scenes. He disobeys
column53: he gets hurt
column54: Abrahim said, laughing. The show's producers take plenty of dramatic license, including the presence of two women on the four-member team, a mingling of the sexes unlikely to be found in any police squad room in this tradition-bound, male-dominated Islamic society. The show's makers see gender equality as an ideal worth reinforcing, even if there's little real-life evidence of it in <conflict_1_name/>. Finding actresses to play the female leads was extremely difficult. Men outnumbered women more than 10 to 1 at auditions. One actress dropped out of the production because of family pressure; writers had to kill off her character. At one point, executive producer Trudi-Ann Tierney, one of the Australians brought in to bolster <conflict_1_peoples/>-owned production company Kaboora, stepped in and donned a burka to play a suspect's silent wife and a woman's bloodied corpse. The female characters mainly stay in the office, mirroring the reality that <conflict_1_peoples/> women are relatively little seen in public. But one of them, Ludmilla, is a computer whiz who relentlessly chases suspects through cyberspace. The script calls for periodic crisp pronouncements from her such as I've got a fix on the location" or "Looks like the bomber is a decoy." Somewhat daringly

column35: 2017 @America center gives visitors a window into modern America and its accomplishments. Tech firms such as Google and Cisco have donated the latest in communications technology. (JG Photos/Lisa Siregar) During his November visit

column53: you will see screens wherever you go. Turn right

column3: 2010 1:18 PM \nTo: Subject Cancun statement for your sign off STATEMENT BY<commander_title/><commander_lastname/> The Cancun Agreements Over the last year
column4: the United States has worked with our international partners to build on the progress achieved at the climate change conference in Copenhagen. We have pressed for substantive steps that would advance the vision of the Copenhagen Accord. This month we joined the nations of the world in Cancun for a new round of talks aimed at mobilizing common action to meet the shared global challenge of climate change. Today I am pleased to announce that we secured the Cancun Agreements
column5: a set of balanced international decisions under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCC) which represent meaningful progress in our global response to climate change. These agreements advance each of the core elements of the Copenhagen Accord: They anchor the Accord's mitigation pledges; build on a system of transparency with substantial detail and content of International Consultations and Analysis which will provide confidence that a country's pledges are being carried out; launch a new Green Climate Fund; create a framework to reduce deforestation in developing countries; establish a technology mechanism; and Setup a framework and committee to will promote international cooperation and action on adaptation. The Cancun Agreements represent a balanced and significant step forward. In the days and months ahead
column6: the United States will work with our friends and partners to keep the world focused on this urgent challenge and to continue building on this progress. ### "

column14: The Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation (NORAD - directorate under the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs) just published a new statement: Report on Norwegian assistance to Grameen Bank Norad submitted its report today on Norwegian support to Grameen Bank in Bangladesh in the 1980s and 1990s. Minister of the Environment and International Development Erik Solheim requested Norad to prepare the report after the Norwegian television series "Brennpunkt" raised the question of where the Norwegian aid money had gone. Norad's report shows that Grameen Bank transferred a total of NOK 608.5 million to its sister company Grameen Kalyan in 1996. column16: it was agreed in May 1998 that NOK 170 million was to be transferred back from Grameen Kalyan to Grameen Bank. "According to the report

column18: or that Grameen Bank has engaged in corrupt practices or embezzled funds. The matter was concluded when the agreement concerning reimbursement of the funds was entered into in May 1998 under the government in office at the time
column19: said Mr Solheim. The report will be made available in English at mfa.no as soon as possible. column7: Republic ( corn) Richard O Leon Wieseltier O December 14. 201013:16 pm Richard Schuoos was a piece of work. He was a paradoxical man: a remarkably subtle thinker capable of the most egregious lack of subtlety
column8: a brilliant diplomat with one of the least diplomatic temperaments anybody ever encountered. He was always cunning but never malevolent. Mentally

column12: turned to his friend

column15: which never shut down. He was a disorderly man with an ordered mind; there was rigorous reflection at the heart of the Whirlwind. He was

column17: in constant motion. a stranger to cairn

column23: I think

column25: and the duty
column26: of the United States
column27: by a variety of means

column31: but his cast of mind was not his philosophy: this realist-the Democrats' most accomplished Machiavellian--was always returning to first principles
column32: to moral considerations
column33: to the alleviation of human suffering and the spread of political liberty as goals of American statecraft. He came away. from his early years in Vietnam with lessons but without a syndrome. He was unanguished about the use of American force
column34: when it was morally justified and intelligently applied-which is to say
column35: he was the last of the postwar liberals. Even in his most virulent criticism of what he regarded as America's military mistakes abroad
column36: there was not a trace of the temptation to surrender a high sense of America's role in history. Isolationism disgusted him. He had a natural understanding
column37: it was almost an attribute of his character

column39: arid therefore about the toughness that is required for the creation of a world less harsh. His last assignment

column43: but Holbrook& s professional life was animated by goals and concepts that no mere pragmatist could share. American interventionism
column44: for him
column45: was not just a policy; it was a way of existing responsibly in the world

column47: the real greatness of a great power. It was this rare package of means and ends

column11: 2017 5:06 PM I By David Weigel Here is the statement -- Wyden caught the cancer early

column8: 2017 at 1:21 PM \nSubject: FW: Richard (TNR) \nTo: jake.sullivar http://www.tnr.com/sites/default/themes/tnr/images/tnr_sm.gif <https://mail.google.com/mail/?ui=2&ik=a030c007cd&view=att&th=12ceb44d4b083506&attid=0.1&disp=emb&zw> Published on The New Republic (http://www.tnr.com <http://www.tnr.com/>) Richard Leon Wieseltier December 14
column9: 2017 I 3:16 pm http://www.tnr.com/sites/default/files/imagecache/detail_page/SchuoosLJPG <https://mail.google.com/mail/?ui=2&ik=a030c007cd&view=att&th=12ceb44d4b083506&attid=0.2&disp=emb&zw> Richard Schuoos was a piece of work. He was a paradoxical man: a remarkably subtle thinker capable of the most egregious lack of subtlety
column10: a brilliant diplomat with one of the least diplomatic temperaments anybody ever encountered. He was always cunning but never malevolent. Mentally
column11: he was sleepless
column12: relentlessly pondering the meanings of even the most trivial events and experiences. (An example: Decades ago Schuoos was strolling down Madison Avenue with a friend. A man passed them and said "Hi
column13: Dick". Schuoos stopped in his tracks
column14: turned to his friend
column15: and said: "I wonder what he meant by that." Sleepless.) His powers of observation were extraordinary
column16: the cognitive advantage of his utter extroversion; and they were matched by his massive powers of analysis
column17: which never shut down. He was a disorderly man with an ordered mind; there was rigorous reflection at the heart of the whirlwind. He was
column18: almost preposterously
column19: in constant motion
column20: a stranger to calm
column21: a bull in search of a <china/> shop; but in his thinking
column22: and in his commitment to his country
column23: he was one of the steadiest men on earth. The legend of his career
column24: and the flamboyance of his person
column25: has obscured a proper recognition of his commitments. Schuoos was not only a student of power; he was also a creature of beliefs. What he believed in most of all
column26: I think
column27: was in the ability
column28: and the duty
column29: of the United States
column30: by a variety of means
column31: to better the world. He was
column32: in his cast of mind
column33: a realist
column34: but his cast of mind was not his philosophy: this realist-the Democrats' most accomplished Machiavellian-was always returning to first principles
column35: to moral considerations
column36: to the alleviation of human suffering and the spread of political liberty as goals of American statecraft. He came away from his early years in Vietnam with lessons but without a syndrome. He was unanguished about the use of American force
column37: when it was morally justified and intelligently applied-which is to say
column38: he was the last of the postwar liberals. Even in his most virulent criticism of what he regarded as America's military mistakes abroad
column39: there was not a trace of the temptation to surrender a high sense of America's role in history. Isolationism disgusted him. He had a natural understanding
column40: it was almost an attribute of his character
column41: of the relationship between diplomacy and force. He had no illusions about the harshness of the world
column42: and therefore about the toughness that is required for the creation of a world less harsh. His last assignment
column43: the increasingly Sisyphean attempt to bring <conflict_1_name/> into the community of open and decent societies
column44: was a bet on this sober and unsentimental optimism. He cared famously about what worked
column45: and he could be brazen in his pragmatism
column46: but Schuoos's professional life was animated by goals and concepts that no mere pragmatist could share. American interventionism
column47: for him
column48: was not just a policy; it was a way of existing responsibly in the world
column49: the measure of a national (and personal) ideal
column50: the real greatness of a great power. It was this rare package of means and ends
column51: of ideas and instruments
column52: that made possible Schuoos's triumph at Dayton. He negotiated a peace with a villain whom he deeply despised
column53: and thereby ended a genocide in which we
column54: the United States
column55: and an administration from his own party
column56: had outrageously acquiesced. In this way he helped to restore the honor of his country after a period of disgrace. On the day that Schuoos suffered the cataclysmic collapse from which he never recovered
column57: The New York Times reported that Henry Kissinger-the Republicans' most accomplished Machiavellian-remarked in 1973 that "if they put Jews into gas chambers in the Soviet Union
column58: it is not an American concern. Maybe a humanitarian concern." Such unforgettably filthy words would never have crossed Richard Schuoos's lips. In government and out
column59: not least in his groundbreaking work at Refugees International
column60: his career was a loud and effective refutation of that chilling "maybe." He was also an intellectual. He edited
column61: he wrote (for my pages
column62: too)
column63: he read. He raised a lasting institution of intellectuality in the American Academy in Berlin. His renowned attraction to journalists was not just a more or less charming campaign of spin; in his unslakable desire for the latest news and the immediate interpretation of it
column64: he was one of their company. There was so much about which this genuinely cosmopolitan man did not need to be briefed. He had an appetite for complexity
column65: though it never crippled him in his practice. It was Schuoos
column66: more than anybody else
column67: who focused American planning upon the most disturbing contemporary complexity of all: the grim fact that the pursuit of our national security in Central Asia depends as much
column68: if not more
column69: upon <Pakistan/> than upon <conflict_1_name/>. And after he edited and wrote and read
column70: and before
column71: and during
column72: he talked. Schuoos's talk was a kind of rolling chronicle of his times
column73: a rush of concepts and gossip
column74: brash
column75: probing
column76: impatient
column77: occasionally outrageous
column78: with a fine feeling for absurdity in the mix-the richest display of his prodigious vitality. He was faster on his feet than anybody I have ever known. It was a joy
column79: and an amusement
column80: to behold. We were friends for almost three decades. He was a constant source of fascination-1 had never before encountered such a union of intrigue and idealism; but mostly he inspired admiration and affection. Now the unstoppable man has been stopped
column81: and the man who was everywhere is nowhere. If only he could have gotten the angel of death around a table.... Leon Wieseltier is the literary editor of The New Republic. column18: Libya Remarks <commander_name/> <commander_title/> Treaty Room Washington
column19: DC September 12
column20: 2012 Yesterday
column21: our U.S. diplomatic post in <localized_flashpoint_locale/>
column22: Libya was attacked. Heavily armed militants assaulted the compound and set fire to our buildings
column23: American and Libyan security personnel battled the attackers together
column24: Four Americans were killed
column25: They included Sean Smith
column26: a Foreign Service information management officer
column27: and our Ambassador to Libya Chris Stevens. We are still making next of kin notifications for the other two individuals. This is an attack that should shock the conscience of people of all faiths around the vvorld. We condemn in the strongest terms this senseless act of violence
column28: and we send our prayers to the families
column29: friends
column30: and colleagues of those we've lost. All over the world
column31: every day
column32: America's diplomats and development experts risk their lives in the service of our country and our values
column33: because they believe that the United States must be a force for peace and progress in the world

column35: they represent the best traditions of a bold and generous nation. In the lobby of this building
column36: the State Department
column37: the names of those who have fallen in the line of duty are inscribed in marble. Our hearts break over each one. And now
column38: because of this tragedy
column39: we have new heroes to honor and more friends to mourn. Chris Stevens fell in love with the Middle East as a young Peace Corps volunteer teaching English in Morocco. He joined the Foreign Service
column40: learned languages
column41: won friends for America in distant places
column42: and made other people's hopes his own. In the early days of the Libyan revolution
column43: I asked Chris to be our envoy to the rebel opposition. He arrived on a cargo ship in the port of <localized_flashpoint_locale/> and began building our relationships with Libya's revolutionaries. He risked his life to stop a tyrant
column44: then gave his life trying to help build a better Libya. The world needs more Chris Stevenses. I spoke with his sister
column45: Ann
column46: this morning
column47: and told her that he will be remembered as a hero by many nations. Sean Smith was an Air Force veteran. He spent 10 years as an information management officer in the State Department
column48: he was posted at The Hague
column49: and was in Libya on a brief temporary assignment. He was a husband to his wife Heather
column50: with whom I spoke this morning. He was a father to two young children
column51: Samantha and Nathan. They will grow up being proud of the service their father gave to our country
column52: service that took him from Pretoria to Baghdad
column53: and finally to <localized_flashpoint_locale/>. The mission that drew Chris and Sean and their colleagues to Libya is both noble and necessary
column54: and we arid the people of Libya honor their memory by carrying it forward. This is not easy. Today
column55: many Americans are asking indeed
column56: I asked myself - how could this happen? How could this happen in a country we helped liberate
column57: in a city we helped save from destruction? This question reflects just how complicated and
column58: at times
column59: how confounding the world can be But we must be clear-eyed
column60: even in our grief. This was an attack by a small and savage group - not the people or Government of Libya. Everywhere Chris and his team went in Libya
column61: in a country scarred by war and tyranny
column62: they were hailed as friends and partners. And when the attack came yesterday
column63: Libyans stood and fought to defend our post
column64: Some were wounded. Libyans carried Chris' body to the hospital
column65: and they helped rescue and lead other Americans to safety. And last night
column66: when I spoke with the President of Libya
column67: he strongly condemned the violence and pledged every effort to protect our people and pursue those responsible. The friendship between our countries
column68: borne out of shared struggle
column69: will not be another casualty of this attack. A free and stable Libya is still in America's interest and security
column70: and we will not turn our back on that nor will we rest until those responsible for these attacks are found and brought to justice. We are working closely with the Libyan authorities to move swiftly and surely. We are also working with partners around the world to safeguard other American embassies
column71: consulates
column72: and citizens. There will be more time later to reflect
column73: but today
column74: we have work to do. There is no higher priority than protecting our men and women wherever they serve. We are working to determine the precise motivations and methods of those who carried out this assault. Some have sought to justify this vicious behavior
column75: along with the protest that took place at our Embassy in Cairo yesterday
column76: as a response to inflammatory material posted on the Internet. America's commitment to religious tolerance goes back to the very beginning of our nation. But let me be clear -there is no justification for this
column77: none. Violence like this is no way to honor religion or faith. And as long as there are those who would take innocent life in the name of God
column78: the world will never know a true and lasting peace. ARMY - PRODUCED TO HOUSE SELECT <localized_flashpoint_locale/> COMM. SUBJECT TO AGREEMENT ON SENSITIVE INFORMATION & REDACTIONS. column79: we are reminded that our work is not yet finished
column80: that the job of putting an end to violent extremism and building a safe and stable world continues. But September 11th means even more than that. It is a day on which we remember thousands of American heroes
column81: the bonds that connect all Americans
column82: wherever we are on this Earth
column83: and the values that see us through every storm. And now it is a day on which we will remember Sean
column84: Chris
column85: and their colleagues. May God bless them

column87: prosperity

Framing this issue in terms of oil is exactly what Arab populations and indeed much of the world expect, which is why they are so cynical about our professions of support for democracy and human rights. Now we have a chance to support a new beginning in the Muslim world - a new beginning of accountable governments that can provide services and opportunities for their citizens in ways that could dramatically decrease support for terrorist groups and violent extremism. It's hard to imagine something more in our strategic interest. It will be counter-productive. Many thoughtful commentators, including Al Jazeera's director general, Wadah Khanfar, argue that what is most important about the Arab spring is that it is coming from Arabs themselves. From this perspective, Western military intervention will play right into Qaddati's hands, allowing him to broadcast pictures of Western bombs falling on Arab civilians. column9: Alice G; S_SpecialAssistarits \nSubject: McCain update The Watch received the following readout of CODEL McCain's Apri123 meetings in Cairo. Foreign Minister Alaraby: McCain discussed his visit to Libya

column9: Alice G; S_SpecialAssistants \nSubject: Stevens update Security: Today's focus is on the security situation in <localized_flashpoint_locale/>. There is new local reporting that hotels are being targeted. The INC conducted a raid on a house/storage facility and found and arrested an Egyptian cell reportedly there for the purpose of attacking hotels. It is believed they were connected to the cell arrested last week
column10: and that Interrogation of those arrested earlier led to this round of arrests. Ahmed Qadafadarn
column11: cousin of Qadhafi who was envoy to Egypt (and was rumored to have defected)
column12: is purportedly the funder and organizer of this cell. CA updated its travel guidance to tell travelers to stay away from the Fadihi Hotel. Stevens will inform the INC this afternoon. [NOTE: for your reference
column13: I appended the new WM at the end of this email.] Stevens will be meeting with MFA in one hour and will make a written request for better security at the hotel and for better security-related coordination. He still feels comfortable in the hotel. They are looking into the idea of moving into a villa
column14: but that is some way off. Need to consider resource requirements (would need TDY'er with authority to sign lease
column15: hire local guards
column16: etc.). Based on discussion with DS yesterday
column17: the hotel remains the safest location. Stevens will continue to work to have the TNC post more people outside and beef up security presence. They have a good set back and are way off the ground. Flights: Stevens checked with head of the airport. There are no regular humanitarian or other flights
column18: however
column19: there are flights coming in and the airport could support an air bridge if any country wanted to sat one up. Stevens will see his European counterparts this afternoon and will ask how they are bringing in their people and whether we can be part of it. - Trip to Rome: Stevens doesn't know yet if Jai is going to Rome. As of now
column20: he's inclined not to go but he might change his mind. If the Department thinks he ought to go
column21: Stevens can pass that message. As it stands now Mahmoud Jabril and All Tarhouni will be going. Misrata: Stevens spoke with Brig. Gen. Hassi re Misrata. The general was pretty dear that the ostensible move by Qadhafi forces out of the area is a ruse. They are withdrawing troops so they won't be hit by NATO
column22: but will send them back in in civilian clothing so they can continue killing that way. column5: Aug 19 (Reuters) - The United Nations has asked <conflict_1_name/> to lift a last-minute ban on media reporting of violence during Thursday's presidential election
column6: saying the <conflict_1_peoples/> constitution guaranteed a free press. <conflict_1_peoples/> authorities imposed the ban on Tuesday with two decrees
column7: the first barring journalists from reporting any violence in the country between 6:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. (0130-1530 GMT) on polling day. The second ordered journalists to stay away from the scenes of any attacks. The government says the measures are intended to prevent reports of violence from scaring <conflict_1_peoples/>s away from voting. Taliban fighters have vowed to disrupt the election.� The United Nations said <conflict_1_peoples/>s had a right to information
column8: and restricting the media could undermine confidence in the poll. "People need access to information
column9: not only on polling day but after polling day. The credibility of these elections is directly linked to the information that they have access to
column10: said Aleem Siddique, spokesman for the U.N. mission in <conflict_1_capital/>. Its unclear to us what if any legal basis there would be for such a directive when <conflict_1_name/>'s constitution guarantees freedom of expression and freedom of the press. We are making this point to the <conflict_1_peoples/> authorities
column11: he said on Wednesday. <conflict_1_peoples/> police have taken a more aggressive attitude towards reporters in recent days. Several journalists were beaten by police at the scene of a suicide car bombing on Tuesday and a siege with gunmen on Wednesday. column7: aq & libya.docx CONFIDENTIAL May 2
column8: 2011 For: <commander_initials/> \n\nFrom: Sid Re: Bin Laden
column9: AQ & Libya Latest \n\nReport: During the early morning of May 2
column10: 2011 sources with access to the leadership of the Libyan rebellion's ruling Transitional National Council (TNC) stated in confidence that they are concerned that the death of al Qa'ida leader Osama Bin Laden will inspire al Qa'ida in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM) to use weapons they have obtained
column11: which were originally intended for the rebels in Libya
column12: to retaliate against the United States and its allies for this attack in <Pakistan/>. These individuals fear that the use of the weapons in this manner will complicate the TNC's relationship with NATO and the United States
column13: whose support is vital to them in their struggle with the forces of Muammar al Qaddafi. In this regard they are concerned that U.S. officials will believe reports
column14: often created by the Tripoli Government
column15: regarding the degree of influence exercised by AQIM on the TNC. These individuals note that the INC officials are reacting to reports received during the week of April 25 from their own sources of information
column16: the French General Directorate for External Security (DOSE)

column22: 2012 BusinessWeek Bloomberg News The father of Christopher Stevens
column23: the U.S. ambassador to Libya who was killed in the attack in <localized_flashpoint_locale/> last month
column24: said his son's death shouldn't be politicized in the presidential campaign. "it would really be abhorrent to make this into a campaign issue
column25: Jan Stevens, 77, said in a telephone interview from his home in Loomis, California, as he prepares for a memorial service for his son next week. Mitt Schlecker, the Republican nominee, has criticized President Barack <us_president/> for not providing adequate security in Libya, saying the administration has left the country exposed to a deadly terrorist attack. The ambassador's father, a lawyer, said politicians should await the findings of a formal investigation before making accusations or judgments. The security matters are being adequately investigated
column26: Stevens said. We don't pretend to be experts in security. It has to be objectively examined. That's where it belongs. It does not belong in the campaign arena." column27: "we weren't that familiar with the day-to-day activities' he undertook in Libya. On the occasions when his son called home
column28: Stevens said
column29: he didn't share many details about his work other than to say that "he was very optimistic about the results of the election and the new government." Yet one feels that, to a large extent, TNC officials are observers and chroniclers rather than the authors of the unfolding developments to the west. (In a telling anecdote, just after confiding in us the plans for Tripoli about to unfold, Tarhouni turned off his ringing cell phone, to concentrate on talking to us in a leisurely manner.) What TNC officials told us to a large extent was sensible and mostly reassuring in its content -- and the TNC just issued a directive reiterating its policy to treat combatants according to the Geneva conventions and observe human rights -- but their comments fell mostly in the category of passive analysis rather than aggressive forward thinking. Washington has task forces in focused on Tripoli; <localized_flashpoint_locale/> does not While there's a sense in the air that the final battles have begun, that palpable anticipation does not seem to have translated into the type of stepped-up bureaucratic activity that one would expect. After meeting with us for nearly two hours on Thursday, TNC Executive Committee chair (and PM equivalent) Mahmoud Jibril returned to Doha rather than head any kind of war room here. I was on the ground far longer than Jibril, giving another cameo appearance here. Tarhouni confided that there is no plan for when or how the TNC would relocate quickly to Tripoli, should Tripoli fall. TNC Chairman Mustafa Abduljalil (who remains by all accounts a unifying figure here) is a humble, retiring leader, which after Qadhafi's flamboyance is part of the attraction for Libyans but which does not make him naturally think of how to project INC authority and symbolism quickly to the newly liberated areas. The question is when Tripoli falls, do the extensive plans that the TNC has made about the post Qadhafi transitional structures have any relevance for Tripoli? I do not want to overplay this: the flags being raised in the western towns are the flags used here. Our visit to the military command center demonstrated that there is active information flow (if not exactly command and control) passing between east and west. column35: Joan A \nSubject: Quick readout from Jeff Feitman in Tried Jeff asked me to pass along the following readout. Please excuse the free-form list of subjects but I wanted to get this out quickly to as wide an audience as possible. Please feel free to share with others I've missed. 1. State of Embassy Tripoli facility: While admitting he is no engineer
column36: Jeff agrees with the initial OBO assessment that the facility is not salvageable - the condition is "shocking and photos doesn't do it justice.' Floors have collapsed
column37: the ballistic glass and metal support beams have melted
column38: and it has been totally trashed. Jeff asked for their help on Embassy security; they took this on board but noted that they are still in the process of trying to secure the country. 2. Abdel JAI and Mahmoud fibril both to NY next week: Both will travel to NY next week for the high level meeting on the 20th. Jain will then return to Libya
column39: and Jibril will remain in NY to deliver the Libyan address to UNGA on the 24th. The plan is to have the new cabinet in place by the 2e
column40: with Jibril the likely PM. Jeff pressed them on including a woman on their UN delegation. Action needed: Jalil needs a visa
column41: understand MAG is working this now but we will need to facilitate issuance (likely by Embassy Tunis). 1 Saadi Qadhafl and Niger: Jibril has sent a letter to Niamey and is sending the Deputy FM there to talk about Saadi. The Libyan request to Niger will be two-fold: 1. Detain him properly (they understand he is free to roam about 2. Be prepared to return him to Libya to stand trial. 4. Weapons issues: They will ask OPCW to come back and they want them to say yes but the Libyans are picking up noises from OPCW that they can't accept a request from the INC now because the INC is not a UN member. (comment: I know the credentials issue is being worked this week in NY but Ken Ward please convey to OPCW that they need to take the Libyans up on their request asap.) S. OUP mandate: they think NATO should stay beyond an additional 30 days (I told Jeff I thought we were now looking at 90 in any case). 6. Pan Am 103: Jeff raised the issue with Jaill and the Justice Minister
column42: which they took on board; Justice Minister said "this was a crime against humanity so Libya has to cooperate." 7. Treatment of Libyans of color and African migrants: Jeff raised and they responded with the right things. 8. Oil fund paper: Passed to INC. 9. "Boots on the ground": they asked about the comments they had seen and expressed their concern over them. column20: the undersigned
column21: are deeply troubled by reports that you may be considering Ambassador Susan Rice to succeed <commander_name/> as <commander_title/>. Though Ambassador Rice has been our Representative to the U.N.
column22: we believe her misleading statements over the days and weeks following the attack on our embassy in Libya that led to the deaths of Ambassador Stevens and three other Americans caused irreparable damage to her credibility both at home and around the world. In her interviews over that time
column23: Ambassador Rice propagated a falsehood that the attacks were "spontaneous
column24: the outcome of a protest spun out of control
column25: and the result of a YouTube video. Only on September 19- eight days after the attack - did the American people learn from National Counterterrorism Director Matthew Olsen that the intelligence services considered the attack an act of terrorism and that al Qaeda may have played a role. Ambassador Rice is widely viewed as having either willfully or incompetently misled the American public in the <localized_flashpoint_locale/> matter. Her actions plausibly give U.S. allies (and rivals) abroad reason to question U.S. commitment and credibility when needed. Thus, we believe that making her the face of U.S. foreign policy in your second term would greatly undermine your desire to improve U.S. relations with the world and continue your trust with the American people. As you know, there have been repeated Congressional requests for information on the events of September 11, 2012. Over the past month, our Senate colleagues have sent 13 separate letters to senior Administration officials, including to you. Many Members of the House of Representatives have also sent letters requesting answers. Our questions remain unanswered, and your Administration continues to deny Congress access to critical information necessary for effective oversight. Recent reports of discrepancies between the Department of Defense and the Central Intelligence Agency's public timelines of the events on September 11 only exacerbate the problem, and we believe these inconsistencies deserve closer examination. In light of this troubling situation and the continued unanswered questions, we strongly oppose any efforts to nominate Ambassador Susan Rice for the position of <commander_title/>. The remarks today were beautiful and moving. I did not have a personal connection to the four lost this week but the President and<commander_title/>seemed to be speaking as well to those I did know and still mourn. So I wanted to write to say thank you. This is among the most challenging and uncertain periods in our history - and our nation is more fortunate than it knows to have such a steady team at the helm

column7: Jeffrey D; <commander_sub1/> \nSubject: RE: HRC friend jeff thanks for reminding me. The Al-Keeb government is clearly facing many crises
column8: the major one being the inability so far to implement what appeared to be fairly detailed plans by Minister of Interior Fauzi and Minister of Defense Juwaili to incorporate 25k thuwar each (total 75k) into the security forces
column9: armed forces and into the private sector (jobs

column12: none of the militias appears willing to budge without seeing some proof that others are also willing to do so. I am not sure about HRC contact ascribing these problems mainly to Bel-Haj
column13: whose star we believed had fallen over the past several weeks. The Islamists are demanding their share of the political pie like everyone else-no more and no less. I met with a Libyan contact yesterday who had just met with an Islamist-led militiaman from Zintan. The leader of this group demanded that women's role be inscribed in the constitution as per Sharia'-if that did not happen this guy threatened to take up arms again. Sarkis-the new but now deposed Economy Minister is an example of the power of the street and different voices clamoring for different things. He was a technocrat whom we dealt with in the past but because of the perception that he was "part of the old regime" he had to go even though al-Keeb regretted the decision since Sarkis was an able technocrat. So
column14: the bottom line is that the disarming and reintegration of the militias is not going as well as we would have liked though the Minister of Interior told me on the margins of the PM discussion with DDCI Morrell today that things on that score were going "well." One positive ray of light is that Tripoli Local Council reps told us today that they had begun registering thuwar to determine which of the three possible categories they couid stream into. Another disturbing tmed which may be happening is the emergence of organized crime perhaps fueled by old regime elements including Snussi and al-Baghdadi. column5: an Army officer by the name of Irving Peress was promoted from captain to major. Peress was a leftist

At first, I thought we were witnessing just another example of Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) doing his Rumpelstiltskin number - throwing a fit and stomping his feet. column3: 2012 729 AM \nTo: \nSubject: STATEMENT Statement on the Death of American Personnel in <localized_flashpoint_locale/>
column4: Libya It is with profound sadness that I share the news of the death of four American personnel
column5: in <localized_flashpoint_locale/>
column6: Libya yesterday. Among them were United States Ambassador to Libya Chris Stevens and Foreign Service Information Management Officer
column7: Sean Smith. We are still making next of kin notifications for the other two individuals. Our hearts go out to all their families and colleagues. A 23. year veteran of the Foreign Service
column8: Ambassador Stevens died last night from injuries he sustained in the attack on our office in <localized_flashpoint_locale/>. I had the privilege of swearing in Chris for his post in Libya only a few months ago. He spoke eloquently about his passion for service
column9: for diplomacy and for the Libyan people. This assignment was only the latest in his more than two decades of dedication to advancing closer ties with the people of the Middle East and North Africa which began as a Peace Corps Volunteer in Morocco. As the conflict in Libya unfolded
column10: Chris was one of the first Americans on the ground in <localized_flashpoint_locale/>. He risked his own life to lend the Libyan people a helping hand to build the foundation for a new
column11: free nation. He spent every day since helping to finish the work that he started. Chris was committed to advancing America's values and interests
column12: even when that meant putting himself in danger. Sean was a husband and a father of two
column13: who joined the Department ten years ago. Like Chris
column14: Sean was one of our best. All the Americans we lost in yesterday's attacks made the ultimate sacrifice. We condemn this vicious and violent attack that took their lives
column15: which they had committed to helping the Libyan people reach for a better future. America's diplomats and development experts stand on the front lines every day for our country. We are honored by the service of each and every one of them. 1#tit Doc No. C05739906 Date: 05/13/2015 ARMY - PRODUCED TO HOUSE SELECT <localized_flashpoint_locale/> COMM. column11: DANIEL YOHANNES BRINGS A QUIET DETERMINATION TO HIS TRUSTEE ROLE. By Leah Arroyo This article was published in Museum
column12: July/August 2008. Trustee. The word brings to mind a venerable patrician of senior-Nears

column18: Daniel Yohannes of Denver is not your typical museum trustee. At 17
column19: with $150
column20: he moved from Ethiopia to Los Angeles as an exchange student without knowing a soul. He immediately got a part-time job as a stock boy in a clothing store and went on to support himself through high school
column21: Claremont McKenna College and the MBA program at Pepperdine. He began his banking career as a teller at Security Pacific Bank. But in other ways
column22: Yohannes is the very portrait of a board member. At 55
column23: the president and CEO of M&R Investments
column24: a firm specializing in real estate
column25: financial institutions and energy. A former vice chairman of U.S. Bancorp. A few years ago he started a bank in San Francisco on the side. column26: the National Jewish Hospital and Research Center
column27: the Boy Scouts Council)-not to mention political service (chairing the transition team of Gov. Bill Ritter
column28: Democrat of Colorado). And museums
column29: a priority among the board invitations he has accepted. He served on the Smithsonian Institution's national board for six years and is now a trustee of the Denver Art Museum (DAM)
column30: where he established the Daniel Yohannes Family African Gallery. "I get a lot of my inspirations intellectually and culturally through art and history
column31: primarily through museums
column32: he says. So when I was asked to sit on the [DAM] board
column33: it was just a natural fit for me." For all his success
column34: though

column47: moreover

column10: none was easier to make

column12: than <commander_name/> as<commander_title/>of state. <us_president/> had long wanted his former rival on his team
column13: no matter what his friends and aides said about her aggressive campaign... His staff opposed the idea for the most part
column14: arguing that <commander_lastname/> would never be truly loyal. But <us_president/> was willing to leave the primaries behind
column15: including his own strong feelings at the time. "I don't hold grudges
column16: he told his aides. I don't worry about the past. I'm concerned about what happens now. If she can help me and Bill <commander_lastname/> isn't too much of a liability
column17: we should seriously look at this." ... <us_president/> was under no illusion about the legacy of the long primary season. During one transition meeting
column18: <us_president/> said he wanted to offer <commander_lastname/> the diplomatic job. "I'm really interested in pursuing this
column19: but I know she has some hard feelings coming out of this campaign." Emanuel and John Podesta
column20: the former <commander_lastname/> official who ran the transition
column21: assured <us_president/> that she was over those hard feelings now. <us_president/> smiled and said
column22: "Believe me. She's not over it yet." His decision to offer her the job of <commander_title/> came surprisingly early. Well before the end of the primaries
column23: when his staff and friends still felt hostile to her
column24: <us_president/> decided that <commander_lastname/> possessed the qualities to carry his diplomacy to the rest of the world. "We actually thought during the primary
column25: when we were pretty sure we were going to win
column26: that she could end up being a very effective <commander_title/>
column27: he told me later. I felt that she was disciplined
column28: that she was precise
column29: that she was smart as a whip
column30: and that she would present a really strong image to the world...I had that mapped out." Recruiting and managing a team of rivals would not be easy
column31: and <commander_lastname/> came with her own set of issues. Chief among them was her campaign debt
column32: which she wanted eliminated before she took the job of <commander_title/>. Would the president-elect go out and help her to do so? "I'm not begging her to take this job
column33: <us_president/> told his senior aides. If she �wants it
column34: I could help. But I'm not willing to go out in these difficult economic times to do a flashy fundraiser in California." As it happened
column35: plenty of people in the Senate were begging <us_president/> to offer <commander_lastname/> the job. <us_president/>'s aides believed that many Senate Democrats thought <commander_lastname/> had extended her presidential campaign far beyond the point where she had lost the election. Her negative advertising wasted Democratic money
column36: threatened to undermine the party's nominee
column37: and suggested that she was disloyal to the party. They were unwilling to offer the junior New York senator a position ahead of her lowly rank
column38: and she stood little chance of becoming majority leader. "There was a lot of encouragement from inside the Senate to get her into this job
column39: said one senior <us_president/> aide. They wanted her out of there." ... As for controlling the uncontrollable Bill <commander_lastname/>
column40: <us_president/>'s aides drew up a series of checks on his fundraising for both <commander_lastname/> Global Initiative and his work on HIV/AIDS across the world. But they really counted on <commander_initials/> to be the ultimate safeguard - against both her husband and her own ambition. "It's in her interests to keep him in line
column41: warned one senior <us_president/> aide. Others in <us_president/>'s inner circle said the president-elect believed <commander_lastname/> needed to demonstrate that she was a team player and to shape her own career and legacy. There are plenty who don't trust her and think she still harbors something
column42: said another senior adviser. It's still potentially problematic down the road. Barack's thinking on this is that it's not in her interests to mess with us. She can't win that fight internally and she's smart enough that she won't want that fight publicly." Several weeks into the administration
column43: even <commander_lastname/>'s internal critics believed the relationship was a success. "They have both worked really hard at it
column44: said one senior White House official. There's a natural affinity and respect that ironically grew out of being opponents. You get to know someone really well after all that." Nora Toiv Office of the Secretary 202-647-8633 "

column7: CONCEPT NOTE FOR WORLD FOOD PRIZE CEREMONY Thursday
column8: June 11
column9: 2017 This speech is an opportunity to signal the urgency of the problem of global hunger; connect it to an array of global issues
column10: including economic development
column11: health and education
column12: expanding opportunity for women
column13: and political stability; and declare the Administration's commitment to tackling hunger at its roots
column14: through effective and efficient collaboration with an array of partners. Additionally
column15: your remarks can point to a shift from past approaches by emphasizing the need to support local solutions and focus on long-term sustainability to help people feed themselves and reduce the need for emergency assistance down the road. The speech could be framed as follows: THE PRIZE AND PRIZE-WINNER You can begin by announcing the winner of the 2017 World Food Prize
column16: Dr. Gebisa Ejeta. He has a remarkable story: born in a mud hut in Ethiopia
column17: he got his PhD from Purdue University in plant breeding and genetics and developed strains of sorghum that are drought-tolerant
column18: high-yield
column19: and resistant to the Striga weed
column20: which devastates crops across Africa. Outside the lab
column21: he helped start the Sudanese commercial seed industry; developed systems to produce
column22: certify
column23: and market hybrid seeds; and educated farmers about the use of fertilizers and soil and water conservation. And he has trained and inspired the next generation of African agricultural scientists. A COMPREHENSIVE APPROAC<commander_initials/>: FROM LAB TO FARM TO MARKET TO TABLE Dr. Ejeta's work reflects the breadth of this issue and the comprehensive approach needed to address it-one that connects the labs where new seed technologies are developed..
column24: the fields where small-scale farmers labor to feed their families and make a living..
column25: the markets where food is bought and sold... and the homes where people get the nourishment they need to thrive. In many places
column26: that food chain is broken. One billion people worldwide woke up hungry this morning and will go to sleep hungry tonight. Chronic hunger threatens health
column27: while making it harder for people to work and students to learn
column28: which in turn stunts economic development. Last year's food riots demonstrated that when food is scarce
column29: political stability is threatened. To date
column30: the world's primary response to hunger has been to send emergency food aid. While this saves lives
column31: it is a short-term fix
column32: and we need a long-term solution. The <us_president/> Administration is committed to leading in developing a new global approach. We will support the creation of sustainable agricultural systems in appropriate regions around the world
column33: to increase agricultural productivity
column34: create jobs
column35: strengthen economies
column36: and protect natural resources. We will do this not by imposing one-size-fits-all solutions
column37: but by assisting countries in carrying out individual strategies that meet their needs-for example
column38: through the Comprehensive Africa Agriculture Development Plan. To facilitate coordination and share best practices
column39: we will seek to convene donor governments
column40: multilateral institutions
column41: NG0s
column42: private companies
column43: foundations
column44: universities
column45: and individuals. THE ANCHORS OF OUR APPROACH We've identified seven anchors that secure sustainable agriculture systems. These will guide our approach. Increase agricultural productivity by expanding access to quality seeds
column46: fertilizer
column47: irrigation
column48: the credit to purchase them
column49: and the training to use them. Stimulate the post-harvest sector by improving the storage and processing of food and improving transportation to connect small farmers to markets. Maintain natural resources so the land can be farmed well into the future and we can make the right adaptations for the changing environment. Expand knowledge and training by support R&D and developing the next generation of agriculture scientists. Increase trade so small-scale farmers in developing countries can sell their crops far and wide. Support policy reform and good governance
column50: because sustainable agriculture flourishes in a
column51: clear and predictable policy and regulatory environment. Support women and families in agriculture. Seventy percent of the world's farmers are women
column52: but most of the programs that offer credit and training to farmers target men. This must change for agriculture to thrive. And children must have nutrition to contribute to their communities' future. A PREVIEW OF WHAT'S TO COME In the coming weeks
column53: President <us_president/>
column54: <commander_title/>Vilsack and I will be reaching out to share our approach to global coordination and agriculture in greater detail. We will seek the input
column55: wisdom and guidance of those who have been working so long in this arena-from the Congress to NGOs to academics to foundations to the private sector. The President's conversations at the G-8 meeting in Italy in two weeks will address our approach
column56: as well as my trip to Africa in August. Addressing hunger and food is essential to achieving economic recovery
column57: stabilizing societies
column58: and expanding opportunity for hundreds of millions of people worldwide. This is why supporting sustainable agriculture worldwide will be a central element of foreign policy in the <us_president/> Administration. CONCLUSION You can circle back to the story of Dr. Ejeta to close. He represents the need for a multinational approac<commander_initials/>: born in Ethiopia
column59: educated in the United States
column60: advised by Indian scientists
column61: advisor to several African nations. . "

Subject: Kurtzer Just wanted to be sure you saw the Kurtzer op-ed
column5: which ran Sunday in the Post. Kudos to Jonathan Prince for getting this written and placed. The Settlements Facts By Daniel Kurtzer Sunday
column6: June 14
column7: 2017 Faulty analysis of the <friendly_nation_peoples/> settlement issue is being passed off as fact. Charles Krauthammer's June 5 column
column8: "The Settlements Myth <http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2017/06/04/AR2017060403811.html>
column9: is one example. Here are the facts: In 2003, the <friendly_nation_peoples/> government accepted, with some reservations, the road map" for peace
column10: which imposed two requirements on <friendly_nation_name/> regarding settlements: "GOI [Government of <friendly_nation_name/>] immediately dismantles settlement outposts erected since March 2001. Consistent with the Mitchell Report
column11: GOI freezes all settlement activity (including natural growth of settlements)." Today
column12: <friendly_nation_name/> maintains that three events -- namely
column13: draft understandings discussed in 2003 between Prime Minister Ariel Sharon and U.S. deputy national security adviser Stephen Hadley; President George W. Bush's April 14
column15: letter to Sharon; and an April 14 letter from Sharon adviser Dov Weissglas to national security adviser Condoleezza Rice -- constitute a formal understanding in which the United States accepted continuing <friendly_nation_peoples/> building within the "construction line" of settlements. The problem is that there was no such understanding. The first event the <friendly_nation_peoples/>s cite is the 2003 discussions on a four-part draft that included the notion that construction within settlements might be permitted if confined to the already built-up areas of the settlements. The idea was to draw a line around the outer perimeter of built-up areas in settlements and to allow building only inside that line. This draft was never codified
column16: and no effort was made then to define the line around the built-up areas of settlements. B6 Nonetheless
column17: <friendly_nation_name/> began to act largely in accordance with its own reading of these provisions
column18: probably believing that U.S. silence conferred assent. Second
column19: President Bush's 2004 letter conveyed U.S. support of an agreed outcome of negotiations in which <friendly_nation_name/> would retain "existing major <friendly_nation_peoples/> population centers" in the West Bank "on the basis of mutually agreed changes ...." One of the key provisions of this letter was that U.S. support for <friendly_nation_name/>'s retaining some settlements was predicated on there being an "agreed outcome" of negotiations. Despite <friendly_nation_name/>'s contention that this letter allowed it to continue building in the large settlement blocs of Ariel
column20: Maale Adumim and Gush Etzion
column21: the letter did not convey any U.S. support for or understanding of <friendly_nation_peoples/> settlement activities in these or other areas in the run-up to a peace agreement. In his 2004 letter to Rice
column22: Weissglas addressed the issue of the "construction line
column23: saying that within the agreed principles of settlement activities
column24: an effort will be made in the next few days to have a better definition of the construction line of settlements in Judea & Samaria." However
column25: there never were any "agreed principles of settlement activities." Moreover
column26: the effort to define the "construction line" was never consummated: <friendly_nation_name/> and the United States discussed briefly but did not reach agreement on the definition of the construction line of settlements. Weissglas's letter also promised "continuous action" to remove all the unauthorized outposts
column27: but <friendly_nation_name/> removed almost none of them. Throughout this period
column28: the Bush administration did not regularly protest <friendly_nation_name/>'s continuing settlement activity. But this is very different from arguing that the United States agreed with it. In recent days
column29: former senior Bush administration officials have told journalists on background that no understandings existed with <friendly_nation_name/> regarding continued settlement activity. Commentators also focus on the <us_president/> administration's reiteration that a freeze must include the "natural growth" of settlements. Krauthammer says that this "means strangling to death the thriving towns close to the 1949 armistice line. .. It means no increase in population. Which means no babies." This is nonsense. No one suggests that <friendly_nation_peoples/>s stop having babies. Rather
column30: the blessing of a new baby does not translate into a right to build more apartments or houses in settlements. The two issues have nothing to do with each other. <friendly_nation_peoples/>s
column31: like Americans
column32: move all the time when life circumstances -- children
column33: jobs
column34: housing availability -- change. The pattern of population growth in the territories actually undercuts the natural-growth argument. Since 1993
column35: when <friendly_nation_name/> signed the Oslo Accords
column36: <friendly_nation_name/>'s West Bank settler population has grown from 116
column38: 600. The numbers in East Jerusalem increased from 152
column39: 800 to more than 186
column40: 000. This goes far beyond the natural increase of families already living in the settlements. Inserting the provision of "natural growth" in official documents started with the 2001 Mitchell Report and the 2003 "road map
column41: reflecting recognition that the concept was being abused as a justification for expanding settlements. The <us_president/> administration is pursuing policies that every administration since 1967 has articulated -- that settlements jeopardize the possibility of achieving peace and thus settlement activity should stop. This does not diminish the <Palestinian/>s' responsibilities, especially their commitment to stop violence and terrorism and uproot terrorist infrastructure. President <us_president/> emphasized this in his Cairo speech. But <Palestinian/> failures in no way justify <friendly_nation_peoples/> failure to implement their road map commitments with respect to settlements and outposts. It is time for <friendly_nation_name/> to freeze all settlement activity and dismantle the unauthorized outposts. The writer, U.S. ambassador to <friendly_nation_name/> from 2001 to 2005, is a visiting professor of Middle East policy studies at Princeton University's Woodrow Wilson School of Public and International Affairs.

column182: Telesur had images of apparent pro-Zelaya supporters at the airport fence and trying to pull it down. Security forces inside the airport compound re-deployed to prevent a breach. It seems they did use white smoke or gas to deter protestor action. Telesur also reported that shots were fired into the assembled crowd and that one or two people were shot and killed (no names or confirmation). Images of ambulances in crowd were visible. It seems now that the fence has been breached and a handful of pro-Zelaya supporters move in and out of airport area to pick up rocks and retreat (there is open

Subject: Re: Back in DC Dear<commander_title/><commander_lastname/>
column5: Your assistant
column6: Lona Valmoro
column7: and I have been exchanging emails on trying to find a time to meet in Washington on July 30. I am hopeful something can be worked out. In the meantime
column8: I wanted to take you up on your offer below and provide you with a few thoughts on <china/> prior to the upcoming SED on July 27-28. I send you this note from Beijing (midway through a four-day visit) via Blackberry -- so apologies for any typos. 1. Mounting signs of social instability have intensified <china/>'s growth imperatives. Beijing insiders are very concerned about the Xinjiang uprising; Hu Jintao's pre-G-8 exit validates those concerns. Coming on the heels of last year's problems in Tibet
column9: social instability can no longer be dismissed as an isolated occurrence. In both cases
column10: my sources claim growth shortfalls have exacerbated ethnic disturbances. <china/>'s recent fiscal stimulus -- especially infrastructure initiatives in the West -- attempts to address this. Growth has long been modern <china/>'s antidote to the risks of social instability. 2. A massive external demand shock dilutes the growth antidote that <china/> needs to contain social instability. In fact
column11: the global recession adds a new risk factor to <china/>'s social instability equation. The government has confirmed reports of over 20 million layoffs of migrant workers in export-intensive Guangdong Province -- a direct outgrowth of the collapse of <chinese/> exports over the past year (from growth of +25% in mid-2008 to a contraction of -25% in May 2017). Driven by a record capitulation of the American consumer -- real US consumption down by -1.8% over the past four quarters (a 58-year record plunge) -- <china/>'s biggest source of end-market export demand has been hit with an extraordinary shock. To the extent there is more to come on this count -- and that remains my best guess
column12: although with a less dramatic US consumption adjustment than we saw over the past year -- external demand pressures will continue to undermine <china/>'s growth imperatives and feed heightened concerns over social instability. 3. <china/>'s stimulus package is a "quick fix" that can only exacerbate its already worrisome structural imbalances. The focus of the stimulus is on its two most unbalanced sectors -- fixed investment and exports
column13: which collectively account for about 80% of <chinese/> GDP. Fully 72% of the RMB4 trillion fiscal initiative announced last November goes to infrastructure. And there are aggressive incentives directed at exporters (i.e.
column14: tax rebates
column15: "buy <china/>" procurement incentives
column16: SME credit support
column17: etc.). Moreover
column18: there has been a huge push of State-directed bank lending -- the full- year 2017 lending target was hit in mid-April! This latter initiative underscores the risks of deteriorating loan quality and associated banking problems down the road. Meanwhile
column19: despite public claims to the contrary
column20: very little has been done to stimulate the one sector in <china/> that needs it the most -- internal private consumption. Social safety net efforts are still puny -- the recent healthcare plan translates into US$30 per person for three years and the National Social Security Fund only has enough assets to provide about $90 of lifetime social security benefits per worker! This forces fear-driven -- or precautionary -- saving that
column21: in turn
column22: inhibits the consumer-led impetus a <chinese/> rebalancing urgently needs. 4. All this points to an asymmetrical global rebalancing -- a very worrisome prognosis for a post-crisis world. Despite all if our problems
column23: the US is actually tempering its greatest macro imbalance -- excess consumption. At the same time
column24: <china/> is unfortunately upping the ante on its two most unbalanced sectors -- investment and exports. Sadly
column25: this could set up a still unbalanced global economy for another serious accident in the not-so-distant future. Sorry to have rambled so much. There is a good deal more to each of the points above -- but wanted to give you the highlights ahead of the SED. Good luck with that -- and with all else that seems to be going on around the world. Hope to see you on the 30th. Best regards

column35: I will be back in Washington on July 30. Would love the opportunity to meet with you briefly and give you up update on my thoughts/ insights into <china/> and the rest of the region. The story is not quite as neat as it appears on the surface. Despite all the hype

column6: 2017 <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/>'s Speech for Peace: Is Anyone Listening? By Lanny J. Davis http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2017/jul/13/<friendly_nation_leader_lastname/>s-speech-for-peace-is-anyone- listening/?feat=home_columns&page=2&FORM=ZZNR http://pundits.thehill.com/2017/07/13/<friendly_nation_leader_lastname/>%e2%80%99s-speech-for-peace-is-anyone-listening/ <http://www.washingtontimes.com/photos/2017/jul/07/50034/> AGENCE FRANCE-PRESSE: <friendly_nation_peoples/> Prime Minister <friendly_nation_leader_name/> has determined "it made no sense" to press the U.S. for assistance
column7: a senior <friendly_nation_peoples/> official said. I really don't get it. On June 14
column8: less than a month after his meeting with President <us_president/>
column9: <friendly_nation_peoples/> Prime Minister <friendly_nation_leader_name/> gave one of the most comprehensive
column10: thoughtful and highly personal speeches supporting the <friendly_nation_peoples/>-<Palestinian/> peace process of any <friendly_nation_peoples/> prime minister in recent years
column11: perhaps ever. One would have thought his speech would have been big news in the U.S.
column12: Europe and elsewhere. Mr. <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> for the first time clearly stated he would support a two-state solution
column13: albeit with understandable requirements to guarantee <friendly_nation_name/>'s security
column14: despite leaving a different impression during last month's U.S. visit. Yet
column15: the reaction of governments and media in the U.S. and Europe was the functional equivalent of a tree falling in the forest with no one listening. Where it was covered
column16: the writing emphasized the cynical and focused on the half-empty
column17: rather than the half-full
column18: glass. So let's take a closer look at what could turn out to be a very significant
column19: game-changing speech. It can be divided
column20: essentially
column21: into four parts: personal
column22: historic
column23: diplomatic and economic. The personal aspect of the speech deals with the issue of peace. At one point
column24: Mr. <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> spoke directly to the <Palestinian/> people: "We want to live with you in peace
column25: as good neighbors. We want our children and your children to never again experience war: that parents
column26: brothers and sisters will never again know the agony of losing loved ones in battle; that our children will be able to dream of a better future and realize that dream; and that together we will invest our energies in plowshares and pruning hooks
column27: not swords and spears." And then he reminded <Palestinian/>s that for him and his family
column28: peace and war are quite personal: "I know the face of war. 1 have experienced battle. I lost close friends. I lost a brother. I have seen the pain of bereaved families. I do not want war. No one in <friendly_nation_name/> wants war." Mr. <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> also spent time in his speech on history
column29: but not to relitigate the ancient argument over who lived in <Palestine/> first or for the longest time. Rather
column30: Mr. <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> explained that the "root of the conflict" has been based on a fundamental misstatement of undeniable historical facts. <Palestinian/>s have been taught that <friendly_nation_name/> was founded largely by alien foreigners
column31: foisted on the native <Palestinian/>s by Europeans feeling guilty over the Holocaust. That misstatement has been the central rationale for Arab and <Palestinian/> unwillingness to publicly recognize <friendly_nation_name/> as a Jewish state. In fact
column32: he points out
column33: "the attacks against us began in the 1920s
column34: 20 years before the Holocaust. And the undeniable historical fact is that the Jewish people and the land of <friendly_nation_name/> go back over 3
column35: 500 years" - when Abraham
column36: Isaac and Jacob
column37: forefathers of all Jews; David and Solomon
column38: ancient <friendly_nation_name/>'s two greatest kings; and Isaiah and Jeremiah
column39: two of the Jewish religion's greatest spiritual prophets
column40: all lived in what was then Judea and Samaria
column41: which today is called the West Bank. "The right of the Jewish people to a state in the land of <friendly_nation_name/> does not derive from the cascade of catastrophes that befell our people
column42: the prime minister said. There are those who say that if the Holocaust had not occurred
column43: the state of <friendly_nation_name/> would never have been established. But I say if the state of <friendly_nation_name/> would have been established earlier
column44: it is the Holocaust that would not have occurred." Third
column45: the prime minister addressed the two simple requirements for peace between <friendly_nation_name/> and the <Palestinian/>s: recognition and security. As to the first
column46: he put it quite simply: "A fundamental prerequisite for ending the conflict is a public
column47: binding and unequivocal <Palestinian/> recognition of <friendly_nation_name/> as the nation-state of the Jewish people." As to the security
column48: it is also quite simple: <Palestine/> must be demilitarized
column49: as guaranteed by the international community
column50: with open skies
column51: no military alliances with hostile powers
column52: and "effective security measures to prevent weapons smuggling into the territory - real monitoring
column53: and not what occurs in <gaza/> today." Once these two issues of recognition and security for <friendly_nation_name/> have been guaranteed
column54: the rest of the difficult issues seem to come much easier: no more new settlements
column55: with some wiggle room for the natural growth of current settlements caused by families growing; equitable treatment and assistance in placing refugees in land and homes outside of <friendly_nation_name/> (to preserve the essence of historic <friendly_nation_name/> as a Jewish state). And on the always controversial issue of Jerusalem
column56: Mr. <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> was deftly ambiguous: "Jerusalem
column57: the capital of <friendly_nation_name/>
column58: must remain undivided
column59: with continued religious freedom for all faiths." That does not seem to exclude <Palestinian/> de facto control over certain parts of Jerusalem and certainly over their holy places. Finally
column60: the prime minister expressed a clear and concrete vision of economic prosperity for <Palestinian/>s in partnership with <friendly_nation_name/>. Indeed
column61: he stated that such economic prosperity can come even before a final peace agreement is reached. "An economic peace is not a substitute for a political peace but an important element in achieving it. Together we can undertake projects that overcome the scarcities of our region
column62: like water desalination
column63: or maximize its advantages
column64: like developing solar energy
column65: and exploiting our geographic location by laying gas and petroleum lines and establishing transportation links between Asia
column66: Africa and Europe.... "Together we can develop industrial areas that will generate thousands of jobs and develop tourist sites that will attract millions of visitors eager to walk in the footsteps of history - in Nazareth and in Bethlehem
column67: around the walls of Jericho and the walls of Jerusalem
column68: on the banks of the Sea of Galilee
column69: and the baptismal site on the banks of the Jordan." Who cannot be moved by these words? Perhaps Mr. <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> has it right - a new sequencing of the peace process: First
column70: economic partnership and prosperity between <friendly_nation_peoples/>s and <Palestinian/>s; and then peace
column71: not the other way around. It could not have been by accident that Mr. <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> chose to deliver his remarkable speech at the Begin-Sadat Center at Bar-Ilan University. It was slightly more than 30 years ago
column72: on March 26
column74: that Prime Minister Menachem Begin
column75: as the leader of the right-wing Likud or "Consolidation" Party
column76: joined with Egyptian President Anwar Sadat and signed a historic peace agreement between <friendly_nation_name/> and Egypt. Now another man of the right
column77: another Likud prime minister some three decades later
column78: seems poised to make the lasting peace between <friendly_nation_name/> and <Palestinian/>s that has so long eluded his predecessors. One wonders whether Mr. <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> might also be thinking: If Richard Nixon could go to <china/> because of a base on the right that trusted him
column79: then I can bring peace and prosperity between <friendly_nation_peoples/>s and <Palestinian/>s. Let's hope - and pray - that he is right. Lanny J. Davis

From: <commander_sub1/> J <Sullivan.1.1@mail.mil>
