Subject: RE: Sen. Levin Levin opposed the surge
column4: but voted for funding the troops. Pasted below is Levin's speech on troops in <conflict_1_name/>. We'll have a copy for you as well. <conflict_1_peoples/> speech below FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE September 11
column5: 2017 Contact: Senator Levin's Office Phone: 202.224.6221 Senate Floor Speech - Surge the <conflict_1_peoples/> Army Remarks as prepared for delivery Today we mark a solemn anniversary. Eight years ago this morning
column6: our nation was attacked by terrorist extremists motivated by hatred and bent on destruction. It is always appropriate to remember the shock of that day
column7: the innocent lives lost
column8: and the efforts our nation has made since that day to ensure that <conflict_1_name/>
column9: the nation that hosted those terrorists
column10: cannot again become a safe haven for terrorists seeking to attack us. But today is an especially appropriate occasion to take stock of those efforts
column11: and consider how best to continue them. I recently returned from a trip to <conflict_1_name/>
column12: where I was joined by my colleagues Senators Jack Reed and Ted Kaufman. The situation in <conflict_1_name/> is serious. Security has deteriorated. But if we take the right steps
column13: we can ensure that <conflict_1_name/> does not revert to a Taliban-friendly government that could once again provide a safe haven for al Qaeda to terrorize us and the world. The <us_president/> administration's new strategy
column14: focusing on securing the <conflict_1_peoples/> population's safety and partnering with the <conflict_1_peoples/> security forces in that effort
column15: is an important start at reversing the situation in <conflict_1_name/>. The change in strategy has led our forces
column16: in the words of General DIAMOND's Counterinsurgency Guidance
column17: to "live
column18: eat and train together [with the <conflict_1_peoples/> security forces]
column19: plan and operate together
column20: depend on one another
column21: and hold each other accountable....and treat them as equal partners in success." The Guidance goes on to say that the success of the <conflict_1_peoples/> security forces "is our goal." To achieve that goal we should increase and accelerate our efforts to support the <conflict_1_peoples/> security forces in their efforts to become self-sufficient in delivering security to their nation - before we consider whether to increase U.S. combat forces above the levels already planned for the next few months. These steps include increasing the size of the <conflict_1_peoples/> Army and police much faster than presently planned; providing more trainers for the <conflict_1_peoples/> Army and police than presently planned; providing them more equipment than presently planned; and working to separate local Taliban fighters from their leaders and attract them to the side of the government as we did in <iraq/>. While the security situation in <conflict_1_name/> has worsened
column22: we still have important advantages there. The <conflict_1_peoples/> people hate the Taliban. Public opinion polls show support for the Taliban at about 5%. In addition
column23: the <conflict_1_peoples/> army is highly motivated and its troops are proven fighters. Despite those advantages
column24: we face significant challenges. General DIAMOND believes
column25: and I agree
column26: that we need to regain the initiative and create a momentum towards success. General DIAMOND worries
column27: and rightly so
column28: about the perception that we have lost that initiative
column29: and the impact of that perception on the <conflict_1_peoples/> people
column30: their government
column31: al Qaeda and the Taliban. By contrast
column32: if we can dispel that perception
column33: we have a chance to convince local and lower- level Taliban fighters to lay down their arms and rejoin <conflict_1_peoples/> society. I believe the most effective way to retake the initiative in <conflict_1_name/> is with a series of steps to ensure that <conflict_1_name/>'s army and police have the manpower
column34: equipment and support to secure their own nation. First
column35: we should increase troop levels for the <conflict_1_peoples/> army and police faster than currently planned. There are approximately 90
column36: 000 troops in the <conflict_1_peoples/> army now
column37: and that number is scheduled to go up to 134
column38: 000 by October of 2010. The <conflict_1_peoples/> police are scheduled to reach a level of 82
column39: 000 by the same time. For a long time
column40: many of us have urged the establishment of a goal of 240
column41: 000 <conflict_1_peoples/> troops and 160
column42: 000 <conflict_1_peoples/> police by 2013. The <conflict_1_peoples/> Minister of Defense has strongly supported those numbers. It now appears that our government and the <conflict_1_peoples/> government are prepared to accept those goals. But the need for additional <conflict_1_peoples/> forces is urgent. I believe it both possible and essential to advance those goals by a year
column43: to 2012. Our own military in Afghariistan has repeatedly pointed to a need for more <conflict_1_peoples/> forces. In one sector of Helmand province we visited last week
column44: our Marines outnumbered <conflict_1_peoples/> soldiers by 5 to one. A Marine Company commander in Helmand province told the New York Times in July that a lack of <conflict_1_peoples/> troops "is absolutely our Achilles heel." What do we need to do to increase the size of the <conflict_1_peoples/> army and police? According to <conflict_1_peoples/> Defense Minister Wardak
column45: there is no lack of <conflict_1_peoples/> manpower; we've been assured it is available. But we will need significantly more trainers. We asked General Formica
column46: who is in charge of the American effort to train <conflict_1_peoples/> security forces
column47: whether such an increase is possible. He indicated he would make an assessment of what would be necessary in order to meet the earlier timetable. In the meantime
column48: we should also press our NATO allies with much greater forcefulness to provide more trainers. If our NATO allies are not going to come through with the combat forces they have pledged
column49: at least they could provide additional trainers. Larger <conflict_1_peoples/> security forces will also require more mid-level <conflict_1_peoples/> officers. In addition to supporting efforts to graduate more <conflict_1_peoples/> officers from army academies
column50: we should consider the recommendation of Defense Minister Wardak that previous mid-level officers who fought the war against the Soviets return to service on an interim basis. Minister Wardak emphasized that those men are well qualified and well motivated
column51: and while they may not be trained in the most current tactics
column52: they nonetheless could temporarily meet the need of the enlarged army while the new group of officers is trained. A larger <conflict_1_peoples/> force will need supporting infrastructure
column53: such a barracks. While the available infrastructure may not be the most modern
column54: it is adequate and exists in sufficient amounts. Larger <conflict_1_peoples/> security forces will require additional equipment. There must be a major effort to transfer a significant amount of the equipment that is coming out of <iraq/> to the <conflict_1_peoples/> army and police. Such a significant commitment to equip the <conflict_1_peoples/> security forces would also help demonstrate U.S. determination to take the initiative and create momentum in the right direction. There is an enormous amount of equipment coming out of <iraq/>; our military is calling it one of the greatest transfers of military goods in the world's history. A significant part of it could be transferred to the <conflict_1_peoples/> forces
column55: increasing their capability without weakening our own readiness. And yet there does not seem to be that kind of a crash effort in place to do that. We need to obtain on an urgent basis a list of the basic equipment needs of the <conflict_1_peoples/> forces and a list of how those needs could be met in a major program to transfer equipment leaving <iraq/>. Rapidly expanding <conflict_1_name/>'s military and police forces would address one of the major problems and risks we now face there. General DIAMOND told us he worries that waiting until 2013 for a larger <conflict_1_peoples/> force creates a gap in capabilities that brings significant risk of failure. But by accelerating the training and equipping of <conflict_1_peoples/> forces by a year
column56: we address his concern. Depending on additional capability from <conflict_1_peoples/>
column57: rather than U.S.
column58: forces
column59: also addresses a major problem of public perception in <conflict_1_name/>. The larger our own military footprint there
column60: the more our enemies can seek to drive a wedge between us and the <conflict_1_peoples/> population
column61: spreading the falsehood that we seek to dominate a Muslim nation. Finally
column62: we should make a concerted effort to separate the local Taliban from their leaders. In <iraq/>
column63: large numbers of young <iraqi/>s who had been attacking us switched over to our side and became.the "Sons of <iraq/>." They were drawn in part by the promise of jobs and amnesty for past attacks
column64: and in part by the recognition that the status quo was creating horrific violence in their own communities. In their own interests and the interests of their nation
column65: they switched sides and became a positive force. That same prospect exists in <conflict_1_name/>. <conflict_1_peoples/> leaders and our military say that local Taliban fighters are motivated largely by the need for a job or loyalty to the local leader who pays them and not by ideology or religious zeal. They believe an effort to attract these fighters to the government's side could succeed
column66: if they are offered security for themselves and their families
column67: and if there is no penalty for previous activity against us. General DIAMOND himself has emphasized the potential of such re-integration to accomplish the same result as was achieved in <iraq/>. Here is what General DIAMOND said on July 28t<commander_initials/>: "Most of the fighters we see in <conflict_1_name/> are <conflict_1_peoples/>s
column68: some with foreign cadre with them. But most we don't see are deeply ideological or even politically motivated; most are operating for pay; some are under a commander's charismatic leadership; some are frustrated with local leaders. So I believe there is significant potential to go after what I would call mid- and low-level Taliban fighters and leaders and offer them re-integration into <conflict_1_name/> under the constitution." But this "game changing" possibility was apparently not factored into General DIAMOND's assessment. There is no plan yet to put in place a Sons of <iraq/> approach in <conflict_1_name/>. It is urgent that we lay out the steps that need to be taken to involve local and national <conflict_1_peoples/> leaders in that effort. They alone can accomplish this crucial job
column69: but first we and our <conflict_1_peoples/> allies must draft such a plan on an urgent basis. And the potential positive impact of such a plan should be taken into account as we consider the need for any additional U.S. military resources. <conflict_1_name/>'s people are grateful for our aid
column70: but also eager to assume responsibility for their future. In a tiny village in Helmand Province
column71: we were invited to meet with the village elders at their council meeting
column72: their shura. One hundred or so men sat on the floor and chatted with us about their future and their country's future. When asked how long the United States should stay
column73: one elder said: "Until the moment that you make our security forces self-sufficient. Then you will be welcome to visit us
column74: not as soldiers but as guests." Helping <conflict_1_name/> achieve self-sufficiency in their security is everybody's goal. On that there is little difference of opinion
column75: in <conflict_1_name/>'s village councils or in the corridors of this Capitol. Can we help <conflict_1_name/> reach self-sufficiency in security fast enough? Can we get there in a way that regains the initiative and creates the momentum we need? Can we encourage those lower level Taliban to abandon an insurgency headed by terrorists whose fanaticism they don't share? I believe we can
column76: by supporting a far more rapid growth in the <conflict_1_peoples/> Army and police; by providing more trainers more quickly; by a rapid infusion to <conflict_1_peoples/> units of equipment no longer needed in <iraq/>; and by rapidly adopting a plan for the re-integration of lower level Taliban fighters into <conflict_1_peoples/> society. In other words
column77: we need a surge of <conflict_1_peoples/> security forces. Our support of their surge will show our commitment to the success of a mission that is clearly in our national security interest
column78: without creating a bigger U.S. military footprint that provides propaganda fodder for the Taliban. I believe that taking those steps on an urgent basis
column79: While completing the previously planned and announced increase in U.S. combat forces
column80: provides the best chance of success for our mission: preventing <conflict_1_name/> from again being run by a Taliban government which harbors and supports Al-Qaeda
column81:
whose goal is to inflict additional catastrophic attacks on the United States and the world. And we should implement these steps before considering an increase in U.S. ground combat forces beyond what is already planned by the end of this year. Original Message

column8: there will be no peace in Congo
column9: Prendergast said. <commander_lastname/> earlier highlighted the role of conflict minerals in what she called the unspeakable violence against women and girls in eastern Congo." "It is the worst example of man's inhumanity to women. And women are being used in conflicts. Now

column15: <commander_lastname/> said in an interview in Nairobi. column10: Derek <commander_initials/> \nSubject: TIME-SENSITIVE: HONDURAS Jake -- Peter Harrell and I have been concerned all last week that we are really losing the initiative on Honduras and that some more forceful intervention is needed. column11: but now American policy seems to be drifting. It's also a chance to turn her and POTUS's recent words on democracy into action. column12: in addition to a cable from our ambassador that she has probably seen making some of the same points. We really need to move here to avoid further damage; on the upside we have the possibility of a real win. I'll make the argument directly in the early morning mtg tomorrow
column13:
but I'd like her to see this first. AM UNCLASSIFIED FOR THE SECRETARY 

From: Anne-Marie Slaughter 
Subject: Moving Forward on Honduras I got lots of signals last week that we are losing ground in Latin America every day the Honduras crisis continues; high level people from both the business and the NGO community say that even our friends are beginning to think we are not really committed to the norm of constitutional democracy we have worked so hard to build over the last 20 year. The current stalemate favors the status quo; the de facto regime has every incentive to run out the clock as long as they think we will have to accept any post-election government You played an important leadership role at the outset of the crisis; I urge you to think about taking bold action now to breathe new life into the process and signal that regardless what happens on the Hill
column14: you and the president are serious. WHA and I are working on a memo proposing some options
column15: but experience has taught me that this could take several days. So I wanted to give you a heads up this weekend. We need to strengthen both the carrots and the sticks in this process. Re the de factos
column16: we should find that coup was a "military coup" under U.S. law and revoke the visas of more de facto regime members. We should also go after the visas of a few prominent de facto supporters in Honduras's business community
column17: signaling that we'll widen this net if negotiations fail. We should also make noises about prohibiting U.S. companies from.doing business with companies controlled the de factos
column18: though we have to be careful about the impact on Honduran institutions. CABLE FROM AMB. Llorens
column19: SENT YESTERDAY MORNING. AIL: I received a call from Arias late last night. He seemed to be recovering well from the flu but was at his home resting. I briefed him on how I saw the situation in Honduras. I stressed the importance of a successful visit by the OAS FMs. I agreed M's recent public comments again suggesting that Insulza was not welcomed were unhelpful. I noted that somewhat better was the statement made by the Corrales delegation yesterday at a press conference in Toncontin Airport upon returning from DC reaffirming that Insulza was expected to be with the delegation. I told Arias the importance of arranging a substantive schedule for the FMs w regime
column20: civil society
column21: business
column22: and religious leaders as well as pro-Zelaya social sector supporters. I also stressed the importance of giving these folks a fair hearing but also that it was critical that the FMs explain the international community's expectations and strong hope that both sides return quickly to San Jose and reach and sign a final agreement. Arias concurred that that was also his expectation. He expressed concern that the regime may be seeking to stall and delay. He said the regime delegation did not seemed fully committed to reaching a deal and seemed focused on tinkering with the political amnesty question. Arias believes that the core regime supporters in the business community were still strongly resisting an agreement. He suggested that the US needed to increase the pressure on these folks and consider taking away their visas and possibly freeze their bank accounts. I said I would pass on his suggestion. I said we were reaching out to people in Honduras and urging the importance of a succesful FMs meeting as a prelude to a final agreement. I said I would also speak to Corrales and get him focused on having the regime prepared for the FMs with creative and concrete ways of bolstering the enforcement aspects of a final deal. Arias thanked our support and we agreed to speak again over the weekend. Hugo "

column5: August 29
column6: 2017 Many opponents of health-care reform have concentrated their fire on a provision in House legislation that would provide for government reimbursement to doctors who offer end-of-life counseling. How our society deals with those confronting death is understandably controversial. Unfortunately
column7: the debate has degenerated into a cacophony of demagoguery and distortion
column8: including invocations of Hitler and fear-mongering about "death panels." As a result of these attacks
column9: a number of senators who are key to determining what bill will emerge from Congress have abandoned support for end-of-life counseling. Our family's experience this year provided a vivid perspective on the value of that service and the misguidedness of the campaign against it. Brooke Shearer <http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp- dyn/content/article/2017/05/19/AR2017051903475.html> -- wife
column10: mother and grandmother -- had been fighting cancer for more than a year. She had undergone major surgery
column11: numerous scans and biopsies
column12: and two debilitating courses of chemotherapy. Her doctors were among the best in their fields. Their expertise did not
column13: however
column14: extend to the fine points of
column15: and latest advances in
column16: pain management. Brooke was determined to maintain the highest possible quality of her own life and that of her family for whatever time we had together. With that goal in mind
column17: she sought advice and treatment from palliative-care specialists at Washington Home and Community Hospices. Their ingenuity and skill in adjusting her medications significantly alleviated her discomfort in her final months. Working closely with her primary physicians
column18: the hospice staff helped Brooke anticipate the likely course of her disease in a way that allowed her to make decisions and exercise a degree of control over both her own condition and our family's adjustment to it. When her oncologist concluded that chemotherapy was not working
column19: Brooke put herself fully into the hands of Washington Home as an outpatient. Regular house calls by hospice doctors
column20: nurses and social workers enabled her to stay active on professional projects
column21: spend time with friends and family
column22: and end her life at home
column23: which was a considerable comfort to her and to us. These
column24: not issues of cost
column25: were the principal considerations for our family. However
column26: controlling the cost of health care -- especially in the last year of life -- is an important part of the current national debate. Therefore it is worth noting that Brooke's treatment in the last stages of her illness was far less expensive than it had been in the previous year. It has often been said that dying can be a full-time job. That was emphatically not the case with Brooke. Until her final days
column27: she concentrated on living -- a choice that end-of-life counseling helped make possible. Hospice care more than meets the standard of the Hippocratic oat<commander_initials/>: It not only does no harm -- it does good; it is not about hastening death but enhancing life. If counseling about hospice services and palliative care is a beneficiary of health care reform
column28: many Americans will be as well. Devin Talbott
column29: along with his brother Adrian
column30: is co-founder of GenerationEngage <http://www.generationengage.org>. Strobe Talbott is president of the Brookings Institution <http://www.brookings.edu/>. Strobe Talbott President

column9: Allison Stanger is a professor at Middlebury who has a book coming out on contracting - she has spent the last 3 years tracking down more data on the full scope of the contracting problem than anyone else and has done the most sophisticated thinking about what we need to do. She has a book coming out from Yale University Press this fall; the attached 2 pager summarizes her best thinking. She was supposed to brief Jack earlier this summer but it got canceled; I'll have her down to talk to QDDR team. But meantime
column10: given that issue is current right now
column11: I thought S might benefit from reading this. AM Smart-Sourcing Diplomacy and Development While most Americans do not know it
column12: the business of foreign policy is increasingly in private hands. In 2000
column13: the State Department spent $1.3 billion on contracts and $102.5 million on grants. By 2008
column14: grant spending had grown to $2.5 billion and contract spending had grown to $5.6 billion. In 2000
column15: USAID spent $0 on grants[1] and $478.6 million on contracts. By 2008
column16: those figures had climbed to $5.2 billion and $3.2 billion
column17: respectively (source: USAspending.gov[2]). Contracting is still perceived as something peripheral to policy itself
column18: but when contracting and grants comprise 75 percent of State's total budget
column19: as they did in 2008
column20: that is clearly no longer the case. The privatization trend predates the Bush Administration and is in part an appropriate response to globalization's possibilities and more generally the changing nature of American power. But during the last eight years
column21: laissez-faire outsourcing to execute two ambitious wars carried the day
column22: and oversight and management were often outsourced as well as implementation. Today
column23: the State Department and especially USAID are dependent on contractors
column24: and outsourcing
column25: in turn
column26: has remade the work environment for federal employees. Negative consequences are a private sector that has been granted power without responsibility
column27: a diminished and overtaxed DSS
column28: a demoralized USAID
column29: and looming catastrophe in <iraq/> and <conflict_1_name/>
column30: where reconstruction money first flowed into everyone's pockets except those of ordinary citizens. What is to be done? Smart-sourcing
column31: not in-sourcing To align our practices with our interests
column32: the centrality of outsourcing to the contemporary business of government must be properly acknowledged. America's allies today include a range of non-governmental actors
column33: both for-profit and non- profit
column34: who are recipients of taxpayer dollars. While policy was once something that government devised (the "what") and contractors executed (the "how")
column35: that is no longer the case in the information age. Especially in the development realm
column36: success or failure today turns on the how of US strategy
column37: which effectively places a web of non-governmental personnel in key policy-making positions. Since both development and democracy demand the engagement and employment of local populations
column38: turning the clock back and bringing whatever possible back in house would therefore be a cure worse than the disease. We don't need a new prescription for our glasses; we need a new eye chart. A smart-sourcing approach defines the "how" of policy as a strategic issue and proceeds on two fronts simultaneously. First
column39: smart-sourcing means building capacity for managing what OMB's July guidelines on contracting call the multi- sector workforce. State Department contracting
column40: programming
column41: and information technology functions must be redefined as collaborative ventures
column42: so that State might more effectively orchestrate mission-oriented networks across the public-private divide. Second
column43: smart-sourcing involves identifying tasks that should never have been outsourced and bringing those back in-house. It may be easiest to in-source according to political expediency
column44: but that temptation must be avoided. Clear guidelines for the limits of outsourcing must be delineated so that strategic rather than ad hoc choices can be made. Both reforms have the virtue of directly advancing objectives outlined in OMB Director Peter Orszag's July memoranda. More specifically
column45: a State Department committed to smart-sourcing should: Support and promote OMB efforts to improve contracts and grants data quality
column46: as well as the further development of USA spending.gov to include subcontracts and subgrants. Transparency and accountability are the critical values in a smart-sourcing orientation
column47: and our anti-corruption efforts abroad will have enhanced credibility when we are perceived to be upholding the same values at home. Restructure USAID so that it has the capacity to manage its contracts as well as write checks. Capacity involves more than FTE counts. State needs to recruit
column48: train

column10: her office and family said. Michael McLaughlin

column18: who lives in New York. McLaughlin was a filmmaker and editor who lived with his wife in Queens
column19: N.Y. Creamer said he and other family members were in their hotel near Solinon Bay when another guest with binoculars told them there appeared to be a problem with McLaughlin
column20: who was snorkeling in the bay about 7 miles north of Tul urn. Creamer was the first to reach McLaughlin in a kayak. He said he found his son-in-law face down in the water
column21: and called out to him but got no response. Creamer said he got closer
column22: turned his son-in-law over and realized he was in trouble. He administered mouth-to-mouth resuscitation and put a life vest on him
column23: Creamer said. "I yelled at him and poked at him and got no response
column24: so I turned him over and it was clear he wasn't breathing
column25: said Creamer. McLaughlin's wife then showed up along with Schakowsky and others in more kayaks to help put McLaughlin on a kayak in the nearly 7-feet of water. Others also arrived in more kayaks to assist and pulled the craft carrying McLaughlin onto the beach where they continued to try to revive him unsuccessfully. McLaughlin was pronounced dead at a local hospital a short time later, Creamer said. In a phone interview from Mexico, Creamer said McLaughlin was an experienced snorkeler and diver who liked to snorkel alone, a coroner's report said he had aspirated in his mask and died of asphyxiation, he said. McLaughlin was cremated, following his own request, Creamer said. Creamer described himself as heartbroken and praised his son-in-law and the 7-year marriage to his daughter. The couple had planned to adopt their first child in September. Michael was one of the most loving and creative people I've ever met.... and he and my daughter Lauren had one of the most loving marriages I have ever seen
column26: Creamer said. In 2005 Schakowsky's daughter-in-law Fiona died of cancer. She had been married to Schakowsky's son Ian. Born Oct. 26, 1970, in Berkeley, Calif., McLaughlin was the oldest of three children and grew up in the shadow of Mount Tamalpais
column27: in Mann County

During their marriage, McLaughlin helped his wife start her own business and she helped him pursue his film career as a filmmaker, his family said. column12: Frank A \nSubject: Revised Op-Ed P1 ask me to pass along this revised draft of the missile defense op-ed. Its attached and pasted below for your review. Thanks Dan A New Approach for Missile Defense By <commander_name/> <iran/>'s development of short- and medium-range ballistic missiles poses a clear and growing threat to the security of our European allies and our own forces stationed in the region. That is why President <us_president/> announced yesterday that the United States is ready to deploy missile defenses in Europe specifically geared toward stopping these missiles. This is a threat we cannot ignore. Previous missile defense efforts have focused on protecting against intercontinental ballistic missiles capable of reaching the United States
column13: but our intelligence now shows that the threat from these long-range weapons has not progressed as quickly as had been feared. In contrast
column14: evidence indicates that <iran/> is developing short- and medium- range missiles that will eventually enable it to target most of Europe
column15: the Caucuses and the Middle East
column16: including U.S. and NATO forces. We deeply appreciate the willingness of the Czech and Polish Governments to host the original missile defense architecture on their soil
column17: and the decision to deploy other systems to better meet this growing threat came as a result of a long and careful review of our policies
column18: capabilities
column19: and requirements. This decision does not alter the unshakeable commitment of the United States to the security of these vital NATO allies. Rather
column20: it reflects our determination to jointly meet the threats that endanger us all. The old focus on long-range missile defense systems left significant gaps in our ability to defend against shorter-range threats
column21: exposing our allies and our forces stationed in Europe. Many experts have also expressed concerns about the testing record and effectiveness of the long-range interceptors that were to be deployed in Poland. Our new approach is different in a number of ways. First
column22: we will use well-tested missile defense systems
column23: such as the Standard Missile-3
column24: against the current threats. And unlike the old fixed
column25: silo-based interceptors
column26: they will be mobile and able to shift as threats evolve. Second
column27: while previous efforts sought to by-pass NATO in favor of bilateral agreements
column28: the <us_president/> Administration plans to make coordination with NATO a central element of our approach. By working with our allies to build a workable and cost-effective missile defense system in Europe
column29: we can better contribute to the protection of our NATO allies and increase regional stability. For 60 years
column30: the NATO alliance has been a force for peace
column31: prosperity and security in Europe and around the world because of its commitment to collective security: an attack on one ally is an attack on all. An attack on London or Warsaw is an attack on New York or Washington. NATO demonstrated this commitment after the September 11 terrorist attacks
column32: when for the first time
column33: the alliance invoked Article V and NATO sent assets to the United States to help protect us from additional terrorist attacks. Unfortunately
column34: the old long-range defense plan created the impression of "two-tiers" of security within the alliance by focusing only on theoretical threats that could one day affect the mainland United States
column35: while leaving our European allies vulnerable to very real short- and medium-range missiles. Our new plan corrects this imbalance. We will continue to monitor and counter longer-term threats
column36: but we will work with our allies to protect all NATO territory. We will focus on the most imminent threat
column37: while also developing the capacity to adjust quickly if the threat evolves. Finally
column38: we will engage with <russia/> as part of our new approach. <russia/> is also vulnerable to <iran/>'s short- and medium- range missiles and we will seek to cooperate to address this common threat. I am pleased that the <russia/>ns agreed at the Moscow Summit to a joint threat assessment of the ballistic missile challenges of the 21st century
column39: including from <iran/>. This is a positive first step and I look forward to future progress. In short
column40: this new missile defense plan is more realistic about the threats we face
column41: more reliable in the tools we will use
column42: and more inclusive of the allies we are pledged to protect. While we pursue this new path
column43: we will also redouble our diplomatic efforts to engage <iran/> and focus its leaders on a clear choice: whether to join the international community as a responsible member or to continue down a path to further isolation. But the security of our allies and our forces cannot wait. That is why we are moving ahead with a new approach for missile defense. 728 words "

President Barack <us_president/>'s announcement of a new system for protecting America's allies against <<iran/>ian/> missiles has ignited charges that he is scaling back the one he inherited from George W. Bush as a concession to the <russia/>ns. In fact
column5: the <us_president/> plan is a big improvement on the Bush one
column6: and it is designed to counter an evolving <<iran/>ian/> threat
column7: not to mollify <russia/>n anxieties. Mr Bush's decision to put 10 missile interceptors in Poland and an associated radar in the Czech Republic was based on a concern that <iran/> was developing long-range rockets that could hit the US. The Bush system would have been less effective against shorter-range <<iran/>ian/> missiles
column8: and it would have left much of Europe
column9: notably including America's ally <TURKEY/>
column10: unprotected. Over the last several years
column11: the <<iran/>ian/>s have shifted their efforts from developing a few long-range rockets to deploying large numbers of shorter-range ones that pose an immediate danger to southeastern Europe and the Middle East
column12: as well as to US forces stationed there. Unlike Mr Bush's
column13: Mr <us_president/>'s plan will quickly field a missile-defence capability to address an existing threat. It can be upgraded to deal with longer-range <<iran/>ian/> missiles in the future. The Central Europeans who have reacted to the decision with apprehension or alarm should recognize that the replacement of a conceptually flawed plan with a more credible one strengthens the bonds of transatlantic defence. The view from Moscow has been clouded by outright paranoia. Military experts there suspected that the US rockets in Poland
column14: while advertised as defensive
column15: could be used offensively
column16: even pre-emptively
column17: against <russia/>. Laying to rest that far-fetched scenario was not the prime motivation for Mr <us_president/>'s decision
column18: nor should it have been. However
column19: by removing what has been a gratuitous irritant in bilateral relations
column20: the president has improved the prospects for US- <russia/>n arms control negotiations now underway in Geneva. Those talks could produce by December a new treaty reducing numbers of strategic - that is
column21: intercontinental - weapons. If ratified by the US Senate (which will not be easy
column22: given the ferocity of the partisan wars in Washington)
column23: the US and <russia/> will be on track for further reductions in the future. Mr <us_president/> and <russia/>n President Dmitri Medvedev
column24: who are due to meet in New York this week
column25: have jointly called for the eventual goal of eliminating nuclear weapons. As they and their successors take steps in that direction
column26: they will have to grapple with a stark paradox of the nuclear age: mutual deterrence depends on each side being vulnerable to retaliation from the other. If either side has enough defences to trump the other side's offence
column27: the mutuality of deterrence breaks down and one or both sides will be on hair-trigger
column28: making war more likely in a crisis. American statesmen pounded this inescapable truth into the heads of their initially sceptical Soviet counterparts 40 years ago. The result was the Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) treaty signed by Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev in 1972. By limiting the defensive capability of both superpowers
column29: the ABM treaty was a necessary companion piece to a series of treaties setting ceilings on offensive weaponry. Because nuclear weapons were expected to with us forever
column30: the ABM treaty was meant to last in perpetuity. While the Soviets were converted to the logic of restricting defence
column31: Ronald Reagan was not. The late US president championed the development of a space-based comprehensive shield that would make offensive weapons - and therefore mutual deterrence -"impotent and obsolete." Many experts believed Reagan's vision
column32: which they derisively nicknamed Star Wars
column33: was an impossible dream. So did his successor
column34: George H. W. Bush
column35: who treated the program with benign neglect while negotiating with the <russia/>ns in the Strategic Arms Reduction Talks (START) begun by Mr Reagan. The second president Bush reversed his father's policy. He greatly weakened the START process
column36: pulled the US out of the ABM treaty and sought to revive a national missile defence (NMD) system. His decision to build the interceptor and radar sites in Poland and the Czech Republic was
column37: as one of his aides told me at the time
column38: in large measure about "pouring concrete for what will eventually be a global NMD." Key officials of the <us_president/> administration - including the president himself
column39: who studied arms control in college - understand the linkage between reduction of offences and regulation of defences. However
column40: they have avoided raising that issue in the context of last week's decision. That is partly because they want their plan to be judged on its own merits
column41: vis-�-vis the <<iran/>ian/> threat. But it is because they have more than enough fights with the Republicans without further energizing the right wing by trying to reinstate the principles of the ABM treaty. Yet sooner or later the US administration will have to grasp the nettle of regulating strategic defences. Otherwise
column42: continued reductions in strategic nuclear offences will be either impossible or
column43: worse

From: Toiv
column5: Nora F \nTo: Mille
column6: Brooke A; Slaughter
column7: Anne-Marie; <commander_sub1/> J \nSent:  Wed Sep 23 19:45:51 2017 \nSubject: A Bold New Strategy for Smart Aid A Bold New Strategy for Smart Aid Matthew Bishop is the New York bureau chief for The Economist magazine and
column8: with Michael Green
column9: he is author of the 2008 book
column10: Philanthrocapitalism: How the Rich Can Save the World <http://www.philanthrocapitalism.neth . The <commander_lastname/> Global Initiative's fifth birthday celebration this week <http://www.<commander_lastname/>globalinitiative.oreourmeetings/meeting_annual.asp?Section=OurMeetings&PageTitle=CGI%20An nual%20Meeting> may be a less glitzy affair than in previous years but it marks an amazing comeback. Last year the <us_president/> administration actually thought about having it shut down as a price of Mrs. <commander_lastname/> becoming <commander_title/> <http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2008/11/16/AR2008111602039.html>
column11: fearful that Bill's schmoozing of wealthy philanthropists could compromise his wife's role as America's top diplomat. Now
column12: <us_president/> is going to be topping the bill
column13: outshining the A-list celebrities
column14: heads of state and corporate titans who pack the hall for the annual "Philanthropy Oscars." Yet the most important speech at the event may not be delivered by either the current or the former president but by Mrs. <commander_lastname/> herself. She has said the State Department is going to forge new partnerships with philanthropists to achieve America's foreign policy goals (and has already started work on a new initiative around the Middle East peace process). Her speech is an opportunity to announce a radical new departure in the way America gives aid. The aid business in crisis. The past year may have been tough for the world's richest countries
column15: but it has been far harder for the poorest. Markets for exports have slumped as rich conumers have reined in their spending. Government budgets are creaking under the strain of the global recession and foreign aid is threatening to dry up. At the same time
column16: the intellectual attack on aid has escalated
column17: led by the author of "Dead Aid" <http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp- dyn/content/article/2017/04/02/AR2017040203285.html>
column18: the African economist
column19: Dambisa Moyo. The CGI has become the showcase for those who believe Moyo is wrong and that aid can be effective. The CGI is not about the old government-to-government aid model. Its members aim to deliver smart aid
column20: based on partnerships between business
column21: philanthropists
column22: and social entrepreneurs. Mrs. <commander_lastname/>'s speech is the perfect opportunity to show that government is ready to work with the CGI crowd to rethink how it does aid. One promising
column23: for-profit solution to poverty is to take the model of microfinance -- one of the more resilient corners of banking during the financial crisis -- and extend it to improve education
column24: health care
column25: clean water and sanitation. Loan- based investments can be more sustainable than traditional aid or charity
column26: because they tap the far larger sums available in the capital markets and are not dependent on the whims of political leaders or budgetary wrangling. Some in government may be reluctant to give up their near monopoly on aid but it is long overdue. A second opportunity is to get the public more involved in the aid business. New giving organizations such as Kiva <http://www.kiva.org/about/how> have demonstrated how the public can play an effective role in allocating money to needy people <http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2017/07/06/AR2017070603594.html> . Government should be doing all it can to encourage his type of mass philanthrocapitalism that levers the generosity of the American people and taps into the wisdom of crowds. It is time for government aid to be made more democratic by letting Kiva and others like it distribute some of the tax dollars. Finally
column27: Mrs. <commander_lastname/> should seize the opportunity to turn the aid business on its head and pass control from the bureaucrats to the poor people themselves. Technology such as the internet and the mobile phone are now widespread in the developing world
column28: so why not use these tools to give a greater voice in aid spending to the people the money is intended to help? Much aid has gone to waste because of a lack of feedback from the intended beneficiaries. Imagine how the best technology entrepreneurs could transform the aid business
column29: in the same way that they have changed the media
column30: by giving the poor a say in how the aid billions are spent. The <us_president/> Administration has made all the right noises about making government smarter by working more with the philanthrocapitalists. At home
column31: the creation of a White House Office of Social Innovation <http://www.whitehouse.gov/the_press_office/President-<us_president/>-to-Request-50-Million-to-Identify-and-Expand- Effective-Innovative-Non-Profitsh was a welcome first move
column32: yet it is still to be seen whether this will amount to much more than a new source of grant funding for the nonprofit sector. The big win is in remaking government through innovative partnerships with the private sector. Mrs <commander_lastname/> has been mulling over what to do with USAID for nearly a year. What better opportunity than the CGI to announce a bold new strategy for smart aid? Nora Toiv Office of the Secretary 202-647-8633 "

column14: heads of state and corporate titans who pack the hall for the annual "Philanthropy Oscars." Yet the most important speech at the event may not be delivered by either the current or the former president but by Mrs. <commander_lastname/> herself. She has said the State Department is going to forge new partnerships with philanthropists to achieve America's foreign policy goals (and has already started work on a new initiative around the Middle East peace process). Her speech is an opportunity to announce a radical new departure in the way America gives aid. The aid business in crisis. The past year may have been tough for the world's richest countries
column15: but it has been far harder for the poorest. Markets for exports have slumped as rich consumers have reined in their spending. Government budgets are creaking under the strain of the global recession and foreign aid is threatening to dry up. At the same time
column16: the intellectual attack on aid has escalated
column17: led by the author of "Dead Aid" <http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp- dyn/content/article/2017/04/02/AR2017040203285.html>
column18: the African economist
column19: Dambisa Moyo. The CGI has become the showcase for those who believe Moyo is wrong and that aid can be effective. The CGI is not about the old government-to-government aid model. Its members aim to deliver smart aid
column20: based on partnerships between business
column21: philanthropists
column22: and social entrepreneurs. Mrs. <commander_lastname/>'s speech is the perfect opportunity to show that government is ready to work with the CGI crowd to rethink how it does aid. One promising
column23: for-profit solution to poverty is to take the model of microfinance -- one of the more resilient corners of banking during the financial crisis -- and extend it to improve education
column24: health care
column25: clean water and sanitation. Loan- based investments can be more sustainable than traditional aid or charity
column26: because they tap the far larger sums available in the capital markets and are not dependent on the whims of political leaders or budgetary wrangling. Some in government may be reluctant to give up their near monopoly on aid but it is long overdue. A second opportunity is to get the public more involved in the aid business. New giving organizations such as Kiva <http://www.kiva.org/about/how> have demonstrated how the public can play an effective role in allocating money to needy people <http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2017/07/06/AR2017070603594.html> . Government should be doing all it can to encourage his type of mass philanthrocapitalism that levers the generosity of the American people and taps into the wisdom of crowds. It is time for government aid to be made more democratic by letting Kiva and others like it distribute some of the tax dollars. Finally
column27: Mrs. <commander_lastname/> should seize the opportunity to turn the aid business on its head and pass control from the bureaucrats to the poor people themselves. Technology such as the Internet and the mobile phone are now widespread in the developing world
column28: so why not use these tools to give a greater voice in aid spending to the people the money is intended to help? Much aid has gone to waste because of a lack of feedback from the intended beneficiaries. Imagine how the best technology entrepreneurs could transform the aid business
column29: in the same way that they have changed the media
column30: by giving the poor a say in how the aid billions are spent. The <us_president/> Administration has made all the right noises about making government smarter by working more with the philanthrocapitalists. At home
column31: the creation of a White House Office of Social Innovation <http://www.whitehouse.gov/the_press_office/President-<us_president/>-to-Request-50-Million-to-Identify-and-Expand- Effective-Innovative-Non-Profits/> was a welcome first move
column32: yet it is still to be seen whether this will amount to much more than a new source of grant funding for the nonprofit sector. The big win is in remaking government through innovative partnerships with the private sector. Mrs <commander_lastname/> has been mulling over what to do with USAID for nearly a year. What better opportunity than the CGI to announce a bold new strategy for smart aid? Nora Toiv Office of the Secretary 202-647-8633 "

column7: while I have no silver bullet

column9: where they hold back
column10: it is less a function of affinity toward AQ and more about with whom AQ is imbedded.. -- In particular
column11: they seem to be more reluctant to target AQ where it is nestled with groups they want to cultivate in the event we "leave" <conflict_1_name/> and they need influence there. If we can disabuse them of the perception that we are leaving <conflict_1_name/>
column12: it will be easier to get the <<Pakistan/>i/>s to go after AQ in sanctuaries provided by groups which would be part of a future <conflict_1_name/> dominated by the Taliban. -- Second
column13: I believe that coercive measures are more likely to be effective if they are targeted against military leaders who give support to AQ and its allies. Assuming we have adequate intelligence
column14: we can go after bank accounts
column15: travel and other reachable assets of individual <<Pakistan/>i/> officers
column16: raising the stakes for those supporting the militants without creating an inordinate backlash. Blunter measures of coercion
column17: like conditioning our assistance
column18: are more likely to be counterproductive. Given the level of distrust for us among the <<Pakistan/>i/> people
column19: they would see this as another sharp swing of the U.S. pendulum which would harden their attitudes and make greater cooperation very difficult for the <<Pakistan/>i/> people to accept. -- There may be greater leverage in giving the <<Pakistan/>i/>s incentives to be more aggressive. Of course
column20: the military's calculation is most important. I'm not sure what is on their shopping list these days but we would need to balance what would move the needle on AQ against undercutting our effort to get them to shift their strategic focus away from India.. At the same time

column170: Wednesday 4 November 2017 21.30 GMT The Conservatives <http://www.guardian.co.uk/politics/conservatives> were accused by the French government tonight of "castrating" Britain's position within the EU by adopting an "autistic" approach that would take Britain off the radar. Speaking to the Guardian
column171: Pierre Lellouche
column172: France's Europe minister
column173: described as "pathetic" the Tories' EU plans announced today
column174: warning they would not succeed "for a minute". Giving vent to frustration across the EU
column175: which has so far only been expressed in private
column176: Lellouche - who said he was reflecting Nicolas Sarkozy's "sadness and regret" - accused William Hague
column177: the shadow foreign secretary
column178: of a "bizarre autism" in their discussions. He said: "They have one line and they just repeat one line. It is a very bizarre sense of autism." Lellouche
column179: one of the most Anglophile members of Sarkozy's government
column180: made his remarkable intervention after David Cameron <http://www.guardian.co.uk/politics/davidcameron> outlined a fresh Tory approach to the EU in the wake of the full ratification of the Lisbon treaty. A future Conservative government would seek to strengthen British sovereignty and repatriate a series of powers over social and employment legislation
column181: the Tory leader said. Cameron said he was not seeking an immediate "bust-up" with the EU
column182: and would allow the repatriation of powers negotiations to last as long as five years. But that position was not enough for the Tory MEP Daniel Hannan
column183: who quit his role as the party's legal affairs spokesman in Europe
column184: saying he intended to fight for referendums to enable Britain to become "self-governing". France's centre-right government condemned Cameron's plans
column185: saying that they would marginalise Britain within the EU. Abandoning all diplomatic niceties
column186: Lellouche said: "It's pathetic. It's just very sad to see Britain
column187: so important in Europe
column188: just cutting itself out from the rest and disappearing from the radar map .... This is a culture of opposition ... It is the result of a long period of opposition. I know they will come back
column189: but I hope the trip will be short." He said Cameron's approach was in line with the Tories' decision to abandon the main centre-right EPP grouping in the European parliament
column190: of which Sarkozy's UMP party is a member. "They are doing what they have done in the European parliament. They have essentially castrated your UK influence in the European parliament
column191: he said. Lellouche said he has told Hague personally that his position was a waste of time for all of us". "I have told William Hague: go away for two to three years
column192: in your political economic situation you're going to be all by your self and you'll come back. Go ahead and do it. That is my message to them ... You want to be marginalised? Well
column193: you go for it. But it's a waste of time for all of us
column194: the French minister said. Lellouche made clear the Tories had no hope of securing support for their plans. It's not going to happen for a minute. Nobody is going to indulge in rewriting [treaties for] many
column195: many years. Nobody is going to play with the institutions again. It's going to be take it or leave it and they should be honest and say that
column196: he said. It is a time of tumultuous waters all around us. Wars

column9: delays on Cabinet picks hurting American businesses By Nelson W. Cunningham - 10/06/09 03:45 PM ET You may never have heard of the Under<commander_title/>of Commerce for International Trade

column14: and you will learn that these are the very officials they rely on. Yet today
column15: when every export dollar and trade-supported job is essential to America's economic recovery
column16: these key positions sit empty. And
column17: surprisingly
column18: these five seats are empty because of stalls and behind-the-scenes maneuvers by Senate Republicans - usually key allies of U.S. business. In each case
column19: the names went up months ago. The nominees have strong credentials and many have demonstrated strong bipartisan support. The reasons for the holds and delays vary. But even if the blocking actions are unrelated
column20: collectively they deny American businesses their most effective overseas advocates. �Miriam Sapiro
column21: who was unanimously approved by the Finance Committee in July to be Deputy United States Trade Representative with responsibility for trade agreements and enforcement with Europe and the Americas (including NAFTA)
column22: has a one-man hold by Sen. Jim Bunning (R-Ky.) over a Canadian tobacco bill. �Arturo Valenzuela
column23: nominee for Assistant <commander_title/> for Western Hemisphere
column24: was overwhelmingly approved by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in July
column25: but Sen. Jim DeMint (R-S.C.) has a one-man hold on Valenzuela as a protest against the administration's Honduras policy. �Thomas Shannon
column26: nominee for ambassador to Brazil
column27: is also being blocked by Sen. DeMint over Honduras. Shannon is hardly political
column28: but is a career foreign service officer who was President Bush's top official for Latin America at the NSC and then the State Department. �Francisco Sanchez
column29: nominated in April to be Under<commander_title/>of Commerce for International Trade
column30: responsible for advancing U.S. export and trade opportunities around the world. Republican staff under Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) on the Finance Committee have repeatedly delayed a hearing. �Lael Brainard
column31: nominated in March to be Under<commander_title/>of Treasury for International Affairs
column32: is also being held up by the Republican staff on the Finance Committee. With an empty chair in this powerful position - it was previously held by future Treasury Secretaries Timothy Geithner and Lawrence Summers - our ability to coordinate a response to the financial crisis is hampered at a time when we can't afford it. Who is hurt by these holds and staff delays? Certainly the president
column33: who is facing the worst economic crisis in 50 years
column34: a stalled trade agenda
column35: and economic and political turmoil in many parts of Latin America
column36: including the hot-button crisis in Honduras. But U.S. businesses are also hurt. When American companies find themselves in commercial or trade disputes abroad
column37: or face unfair competition from foreign companies or discriminatory practices from regulators
column38: they turn directly to the roster above. With all these chairs empty
column39: U.S. businesses with problems abroad find themselves facing a classic Goldilocks problem - the Cabinet secretaries above are too big (and too busy)
column40: and the officials below are too small to have an impact at the right levels. Moreover
column41: the international economic issues of greatest interest to U.S. businesses are precisely the ones that are being hampered by these vacancies: balanced and coordinated growth out of the Great Recession
column42: promotion of job- generating U.S. exports
column43: delayed trade agreements with Colombia and Panama
column44: barriers into Brazil's huge market
column45: trade tensions with Canada (our largest trading partner) and security and border issues with Mexico (our second-largest)
column46: among many others. And while all U.S. business interests overseas are affected by these vacancies
column47: it is our business and political interests in the Americas that are being hit most directly
column48: because of the responsibilities and expertise of the five nominees. Predictably
column49: this lamentable situation is renewing cries from our neighbors that even under a promising new president
column50: they continue to be neglected. And as importantly
column51: our ability to help shape political and economic events in our hemisphere to advance U.S. interests is suffering greatly. Who wins when we can't act? Our foreign competitors; not just foreign companies
column52: but Hugo Chavez and his anti-democratic allies. All this is not to cast blame on the United States Senate
column53: which has a constitutional duty to provide "advice and consent" on presidential nominations (though it may cause one to question the tradition that permits a single senator to put an indefinite hold on a nominee). column54: trade and political frictions in our own hemisphere - should be reminded of the harm done to important U.S. interests. In the days after 9/11
column55: the Democratically-controlled Senate moved swiftly to confirm the U.N. ambassador and other stalled security-related posts. Today's circumstances are not the same by any means
column56: but as we confront the worst economic crisis in over 50 years
column57: these are surely no ordinary times. The time has come for the Senate to carry out its constitutional duty and to end the delays on these five key commerce and trade nominations. American business deserves an A Team by its side. Cunningham is managing partner of McLarty Associates
column58: which advises U.S. and multinational businesses on their international strategies. He was a Democratic White House and Senate aide. column16: something the US army speaks as if it were a new device

column2: 2017-11-05 For <commander_name/>: \n\nFrom: Sid CC: Lissa Re: Berlin speeches Below are my notes for speeches in Berlin. The themes I stress are these: the importance of Berlin and the Brandenburg Gate as symbols of freedom; the weight of history (always felt by Germans); the contribution of the US and the salience of the Western alliance; the meaning of 1989 to today and especially the continuity of the Western alliance; and segue from past to future. What I have not done here but might be added are references to Angela Merkel (a courageous woman from the east who embodies the highest values of the West); and specific policies. Those can be fitted in. So
column3: some ideas and language: Twenty years ago the wall fell. Here
column4: in Berlin
column5: the moment when tens of thousands of citizens tore it down with hammers and picks and bare hands is called "Die Wende
column6: a phrase that means more than simply a change but a turning point in history. It was not only a turning point for Germany and Europe but also for the United States because the wall-the reason for its construction and the reason for its destruction-is central to our common history-and to our common future. Richard von Weizsaecker said, As long as the Brandenburg Gate is closed
column7: the German question will remain open." Today I can say with finality
column8: the German question is closed
column9: because the Brandenburg Gate is wide open! The gate is open
column10: Europe is open
column11: and our future together is open. In the forty years from the Berlin airlift to the fall of the Berlin Wall
column12: the Atlantic partnership proved itself the most successful alliance for freedom in history. That alliance was
column13: is and shall be the crowning achievement of American foreign policy. And the German American relationship has always served as its foundation. Our alliance represents the reconciliation of former enemies
column14: an inspiration to other peoples and continents devastated by war and hatred
column15: and it must never be taken for granted. In the twenty years since the fall of the wall we have created architecture for an enduring peace. Instead of a wall we have built a gateway to the future. President Kennedy said in 1963 that in the future free men everywhere will say
column16: "Ich bin emn Berliner." Today Berlin has gained a new and even more powerful meaning. Forever into the future
column17: the opening of this Gate will be the symbol of the return of the dream of freedom
column18: not only to Berlin and Germany
column19: but to the entire world. The Gate
column20: we must remember
column21: was not built as a symbol of freedom. And each of the tyrannies that used the Gate as a symbol believed it represented their eternal power. The Gate was first erected as a symbol against the French Revolution; then it became a symbol of the imperial ambitions of Napoleon who marched his army through. It was a symbol of P<russia/>n militarism and monarchy. It was seized by the Nazi Party as the symbol of its 1000 year rule. And then it became a symbol of the Communist totalitarianism that built a wall to separate the people of Berlin as though freedom could be contained in only one part of the city. Here
column22: in Berlin
column23: the Cold War was coldest. We celebrate the fact that the wall that marred this proud city was taken down by the world's most enthusiastic wrecking crew. The United States always believed in the freedom of Berlin because we believed in the future of freedom. The courageous citizens of East Germany
column24: Poland and other nations of the Communist bloc demonstrated their dedication to free and peaceful solution of conflicts through their stand against dictatorship. America stood resolutely as an ally at every moment of this struggle and moved swiftly to help the peoples of Europe reunite after 1989. We celebrate the steadiness of purpose
column25: the restraint and respect for ultimate goals that allowed the Cold War to end in peace. For how the victory was won was essential to the triumph. 1989 was special. It was that rarest of historical events: a revolution that did not descend into violence. As a result the Gate survives not as a cautionary monument to history's darkest. moments but to its brightest. Today we celebrate the revolution of 1989
column26: the turning point that transformed the Brandenburg Gate into the symbol of the hope of democracy and the promise of freedom. Berliner Luft
column27: the air of Berlin
column28: has always been unique. I can feel and smell the spirit of freedom in your streets. The great American poet Carl Sandburg called Berlin the Chicago of Europe. Chicago is where I was born and raised. I can sense the same energy
column29: openness and dedication to hard work in both great cities. Another Chicagoan
column30: President Barack <us_president/>
column31: was drawn to Berlin last July
column32: a city that he said made him feel like a citizen of the world and a citizen of the future. I was very proud to visit our new Embassy at the Brandenburg Gate
column33: located exactly where the Wall used to run. Our presence here will forever underscore our determination that the spark of freedom from this city in 1989 will help light the torches of freedom throughout the world. The revolution of 1989 did not mark the end of history. Having made history together
column34: we are summoned to secure freedom for future generations. As vital at the beginning of the 21' century as it was in the last half of the 20th
column35: the Western alliance is called to new tasks. The dreams of 1989 reached far-and have farther to reach. Old hatreds and conflicts-in the Balkins

column42: aggression and violence will prevail. Today we are faced with difficult and often dangerous conflicts arising not from conflicts between nations but within them
column43: conflicts exploited by zealots who make the false claim that violence will purify the world and open the gates of heaven. Once zealots tried to use this Gate to symbolize that message. But through the courage and determination of the people of Berlin and their stalwart allies

column45: in this new century

column10: D.C.<commander_title/><commander_lastname/> GETS IT DONE; EMERGENCY RELIEF SUPPLIES TO BE AIRLIFTED FROM GREATER LOS ANGELES AREA TO SAMOA IN RESPONSE TO DEVASTATING TSUNAMI Chairman of the Subcommittee on Asia
column11: the Pacific and the Global Environment
column12: Congressman Eni F.H. Faleomavaega
column13: and Congresswoman Laura Richardson (D-CA)
column14: announced today that the U.S. Department of State called them this morning to inform them that<commander_title/><commander_lastname/> has authorized the use of funds from the Office of Foreign Disaster Assistance (OFDA) to get emergency relief supplies airlifted from the greater Los Angeles area to Samoa in response to the devastating tsunami that struck Apia on September 29. In his capacity as Chairman of the Asia Pacific Subcommittee which has broad jurisdiction for U.S. foreign policy affecting the region
column15: including Samoa
column16: Chairman Faleomavaega personally spoke to<commander_title/><commander_lastname/> on Oct 1 and
column17: in letters dated Oct 4 and Oct 5
column18: followed up with her regarding the specific need to airlift emergency supplies to Apia
column19: which were gathered by the Samoan communities and congregations in the greater Los Angeles area. The Samoan communities in the greater Los Angeles directly contacted Faleomavaega for assistance because many of their families and relatives live in his district of American Samoa or Samoa. Congresswoman Laura Richardson has worked closely with Faleomavaega throughout this process given that she represents part of the greater Los Angeles area
column20: and the Samoan communities living in that area are her constituents. "I want to personally thank<commander_title/><commander_lastname/> for her untiring efforts in getting these relief supplies airlifted
column21: Chairman Faleomavaega said. Since the tsunami struck
column22: <commander_title/><commander_lastname/> has spared no effort in coming to our aid
column23: and even called upon the U.S. Department of Defense (DOD) to quickly move these supplies from the West Coast to Samoa. Last evening
column24: Congresswoman Richardson and I learned that DOD had agreed to move the supplies but that due to legalities of moving privately-donated goods
column25: the process would take too long." "In a previous conference call yesterday
column26: anticipating that DOD might be unable to quickly move these supplies
column27: we requested the State Department to fund a commercial flight through the Office of Foreign Disaster Assistance should we encounter any problems with DOD
column28: Faleomavaega and Rep. Richardson said. Last night
column29: upon learning that the DOD process would take too long and in consideration of our request for a more immediate airlift
column30: <commander_title/><commander_lastname/> assessed the options while en route to Europe
column31: and this morning the State Department informed us that<commander_title/><commander_lastname/> has agreed to fund the flight with OFDA funds." "The agreement is that this will be a one-time airlift
column32: and our Samoan communities should make future donations in cash
column33: rather than in commodities. We will not be able to airlift frozen goods
column34: and our offices will work closely with the communities to gather the supplies to a central location for the airlift. Also
column35: the airlift provided by the U.S. Department of State can only be authorized to land in Samoa. While we were also hopeful to get supplies in to American Samoa
column36: all matters relating to American Samoa are decided between the Governor and FEMA
column37: according to federal law." "I know from my meeting earlier this week with Prime Minister Tuilaepa Sailele Malielegaoi that he is thankful to the Samoan congregations and communities in the greater Los Angeles area who responded from the heart by collecting critical supplies that will now be airlifted to those in need
column38: Faleomavaega said. For this reason
column39: I want to thank the Prime Minister for agreeing to accept this gift
column40: and I also want to thank Reverend Liki Tiatia
column41: Reverend John Mailo
column42: Reverend Misipauena Tagaloa
column43: and High Chief Loa Pele Faletogo for all the good work they have done. Reverend Tiatia and Reverend Mailo will be taking a flight to Samoa to make the presentation to the Government of Samoa on behalf of our Samoan community on the West Coast and also on behalf of Congresswoman Richardson and myself." "I especially want to thank Congresswoman Richardson for working around the clock in support of our Samoan communities living in her district
column44: and in Samoa and American Samoa
column45: Faleomavaega continued. Congresswoman Richardson has stood by us every step of the way and has left no stone unturned in getting this done. She has been staunch and solid in her dedication to us
column46: and has earned her rightful place in our hearts. It is my honor to welcome Congresswoman Richardson into our Pacific Island family." "With so many people in need of basic supplies in Samoa
column47: it has been a privilege to work with Chairman Faleomavaega to assist the people of my district in making sure the items they have collected will soon be in the hands of their families and friends
column48: Congresswoman Richardson said. This feat is only possible because of the dedication of Chairman Faleomavaega and<commander_title/><commander_lastname/>. Over 60 local organizations in the 37th district of California
column49: including church groups
column50: non-profit organizations and caring others collected over 100
column51: 000 pounds of essential items to send to victims of the tragedy that recently occurred. The lives of thousands of Samoans will be immediately and directly improved by the actions taken by<commander_title/><commander_lastname/>
column52: Chairman Faleomavaega and all of us who answered the call to help. I am proud to be a part of this exceptional team." "It is clear that change has come and that<commander_title/><commander_lastname/> is restoring America's stature once again
column53: especially in a part of the world that the U.S. has too long neglected. We thank<commander_title/><commander_lastname/> for her leadership and commitment
column54: and for standing with the people of Samoa when they need her most
column55: and we continue to extend our deepest condolences to the families and friends of those who are suffering so much
column56: Faleomavaega and Rep. Richardson concluded.

column3: <conflict_1_name/> July-August 2017 Assignment My plane departed New York Kennedy for <conflict_1_capital/> on July 28th and the refrain replayed and replayed in my head "you are going where? <conflict_1_name/>. And why?" I was recruited by the AFT' s international department to support the <conflict_1_peoples/> Teacher Education Department's RPM (Rapid Production of Materials) activity in which two dozen curriculum experts wrote teacher training materials for classroom teachers. The other two members of the AFT team
column4: Betty Harris (ABC California) and Amber Prentice (St. Paul)
column5: arrived in late August The RPM took place daily over a period of five weeks at the Sayyed Jumalladin Teacher Training College in <conflict_1_capital/>. Twenty <conflict_1_peoples/> educators were organized into three groups
column6: each responsible for completing the training manuals for one grade level (4-6
column7: 7-9 and 10-12). For each subject at each grade level
column8: a module of five 90-minute training sessions was created.
