Cameron's presumptive strike has accelerated the predicted Tory-European split from post-election to pre-election. Whether this affects Merkel's attitude on Blair and the EU presidency remains unclear, but Cameron's high-handed behavior is precisely the sort of thing that provokes her. See the Guardian report below: Guardian Europe leaders incensed by David Cameron's letter Sarkozy, Merkel and Zapatero criticise Tories for attempt to delay treaty Nicholas Watt <http://www.guardian.co.uk/profileinicholaswatt> and Ian Traynor <http://www.guardian.co.uk/profile/iantraynor> guardian.co.uk <http://vvww.guardian.co.uk> , Friday 30 October 2017 22.21 GMT Leaders of three of the most powerful countries in Europe have strongly criticised David Cameron <http://www.guardian.co.uk/poiitics/davidcameron> at the EU summit over Conservative plans to scupper the Lisbon treaty. Nicolas Sarkozy, Angela Merkel and Jose Luiz Rodriguez Zapatero are understood to have privately criticised the Tory leader after he sent a handwritten letter to the Czech president Vaclay Klaus, who is refusing to sign the treaty. The letter was seen as an attempt to influence the Czech Republic, the only country not to have ratified the treaty. Senior British sources familiar with thinking at the highest levels of the EU say that the leaders of France, Germany <http://www.guardian.co.uk/world/germany> and Spain <http://www.guardian.co.uk/worldispain> all raised questions about the Cameron letter. It is understood that Cameron encouraged Klaus to delay the ratification of the treaty by setting out Tory policy to hold a referendum in Britain on the treaty if it has not been ratified by all member states. The sources have told the Guardian that: *Sarkozy was overheard telling Gordon Brown that he was incensed by Cameron's letter, which the French saw as an attempt to wreck the Lisbon treaty. Merkel was also said to be upset by Cameron's letter. The German chancellor is understood to have echoed concerns of senior figures in her CDU party, such as the former European parliament president Hans Gert Poettering, that Cameron's behaviour had been untrustworthy. Zapatero - who addressed the recent Labour party conference and will have to negotiate directly with Cameron if he wins the election because Spain holds the EU's rotating presidency until July 2017 - made clear to diplomats that he regarded Cameron's letter as damaging and an attempt to scupper the treaty. The interventions by the EU leaders come as the Tories plan to abandon their two-year campaign to hold a referendum on the Lisbon_treaty. Senior Tories told the Guardian that Cameron will set out his thinking in the coming weeks if, as expected, the Czech president finally ratifies the treaty. It is understood that Cameron will drop his pledge to hold a referendum on the treaty on the grounds that it is impossible to open a treaty that has entered EU law. A Tory government would instead focus on repatriating social and employment laws, in effect restoring the British opt-out from the social chapter. This has been sprinkled around various EU treaties since Theresa May ended the opt-out in 1997, meaning that its measures could only be restored to Britain with the agreement of all member states. Brown yesterday used his appearance at the summit, where he held a series of formal and informal one-to-one meetings with EU leaders, to launch a strong attack on the Tories' approach to Europe. Speaking of the Tory decision to abandon the main centre-right EPP grouping in the European parliament in favour of a smaller group consisting mainly of fringe parties from the hard right in eastern Europe, the prime minister said: The Conservative party are standing apart from the mainstream in Europe. "They are part of a very small group of minorities - of 23 people apart from the Conservative party. They are standing on the fringes of Europe. That is a huge mistake for British interests." A Tory spokeswoman said: "We have never concealed the fact that we sent the letter ... David Cameron has made no secret of its contents. It sets out his public opinion in a private letter." "

Discussion of the questions in section I of the paper "What are we trying to achieve?" 4. Discussion of what needs to be changed to achieve that: a. Structural & Management Change in D.C. b. Structural & Management Change in the Field c. Contract Reform d. Relationship between State and DoD e. Metrics & Accountability 5. Moving Forward: Coming out of this discussion
column2: we need to define a process that will develop a comprehensive and detailed strategy that addresses each of these areas. Part of that process and strategy must also include a vision for working with the White House
column3: the Hill and other agencies to accomplish our goals. FOREIGN ASSISTANCE REFORM: DEFINING A WAY FORWARD Foreign assistance reform is one of the most widely discussed and debated topics on the foreign policy agenda. Indeed
column4: the volume of literature on this topic led the Center for Global Engagement to produce a "Report on Reports
column5: to summarize the major points of consensus and disagreement among reports and outline another series of recommendations. To make the key decisions to shape our foreign assistance reform effort we need to answer three basic questions: (1) What are we trying to achieve? (2) Where are we now? and (3) What do we need to change? The U.S. Record on Foreign Assistance The U.S. is the world's largest donor of bilateral foreign assistance. In calendar year 2008 the United States disbursed $26 billion in Official Development Assistance (ODA). Elements of this assistance include: $6.5 billion to sub-Saharan Africa, an increase from $4.6 billion in 2007; $6.9 billion in bilateral assistance to least developed countries; $4.4 billion in U.S. humanitarian assistance. In addition, over the past five years the U.S. committed: $18.8 billion in funding through the U.S. President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief to treat HIV\AIDS, Malaria & TB; $6.4 billion in Compact funding for 18 strongly performing countries by the Millennium Challenge Corporation. The President's 2017 budget request provides $53.9 billion to State and other international programs, of which $36.5 billion is for foreign assistance -- putting the U.S. on the path to doubling foreign assistance by 2015. Meanwhile the 2017 supplemental funding meets diplomatic and assistance needs focused on terrorism, humanitarian assistance, stabilization and peacekeeping operations including in <conflict_1_name/>, <Pakistan/> and <iraq/>. I. What are we trying to achieve? The development of a comprehensive foreign assistance strategy requires both an articulation of the problems we seek to address, as well as the principles, objectives, and operational strategies that will guide our efforts. We have already defined and articulated a number of ideas: Smart Power; the Three Ds - defense, diplomacy and development; and the three P's of principles, partnership, and pragmatism. Our challenge is to further define: > What are the goals of our foreign assistance programs? > What principles and objectives should guide the formulation of our strategy? > What emphasis should be placed on security and strategic objectives, vice humanitarian and poverty goals? > What problems are we trying to solve? > What gaps remain in our foreign assistance programs relative to the outcomes we seek? > How do we need to be organized to get the job done? > What budget, planning and coordination functions do we need in the long- term and in the short-term during the period of transition? II. Where are we now? In keeping with the Administration's commitment to renewing America's global leadership through vigorous diplomacy and innovative development efforts, initial efforts have focused on getting State and USAID the resources needed to rebuild capacity and on the civilian aspects of our most immediate foreign policy priorities (<conflict_1_name/>, <Pakistan/>, <iraq/>) : The 2017 Omnibus and supplemental start the investment in capacity; The 2017 Budget increases investment in capacity and program; <conflict_1_name/>, food security, global health and other initiatives reflect new approach to coordination and identification of key objectives; 2 The 2011 Budget process is being developed to drive collaboration across silos, integrating USAID, MCC, PEPFAR with regional and functional bureaus of State; In the short-term, Defense authorizations have been limited in time and scope and are now in process to be driven to strategic resolution; Proposed foreign aid authorization bills and NSC processes create pressure to accelerate work on a long-term strategic plan. III. What needs to be changed? Our foreign assistance programs are too fractured and discordant and the question is what policy and structural changes are needed to achieve a greater level of coordination and coherence. The following structures and mechanisms form the key elements of any reform agenda: (1) Structural & Management Change: DC > What should be the relationship between State and USAID? Between State and MCC? Between PEPFAR and these institutions? To the extent changes in structures and relationships require legislative reform, what is the likelihood this can be achieved? > What is the best budget management structure within the State Department? What is the current budgeting and planning process, and what role do F and M play in it? > What training and recruitment practices need to be developed to build the civilian capacity we need? (2) Structural & Management Change: Field > What role should the Ambassador and DCM play in coordinating our foreign assistance programs in the field? What mechanisms are needed to achieve greater coordination, including with programs managed from Washington? > How can we improve flexibility and responsiveness to circumstances on the ground? 3 (3) Contract Reform We need to quickly constitute a task force to address issues related to the following categories of service providers: (1) DC-based contractors (Beltway Bandits"); (2) implementing partners and NG0s; and (3) security and service contracts. > How do we ensure that even "good contractors" receive strategic guidance at the front end? > What are alternatives to the contracting model? column9: Brooke A \nSubject: Huff Post Renegade Excerpt Of all his transition choices
column10: none was easier to make
column11: or more complex to execute
column12: than <commander_name/> as <commander_title/>. <us_president/> had long wanted his former rival on his team
column13: no matter what his friends and aides said about her aggressive campaign... His staff opposed the idea for the most part
column14: arguing that <commander_lastname/> would never be truly loyal. But <us_president/> was willing to leave the primaries behind
column15: including his own strong feelings at the time. "I don't hold grudges
column16: he told his aides. I don't worry about the past. I'm concerned about What happens now. If she can help me and Bill <commander_lastname/> isn't too much of a liability
column17: we should seriously look at this." <us_president/> was under no illusion about the legacy of the long primary season. During one transition meeting
column18: <us_president/> said he wanted to offer <commander_lastname/> the diplomatic job. "I'm really interested in pursuing this
column19: but I know she has some hard feelings coming out of this campaign." Emanuel and John Podesta
column20: the former <commander_lastname/> official who ran the transition
column21: assured <us_president/> that she was over those hard feelings now. <us_president/> smiled and said
column22: "Believe me. She's not over it yet." His decision to offer her the job of <commander_title/> came surprisingly early. Well before the end of the primaries
column23: when his staff and friends still felt hostile to her
column24: <us_president/> decided that <commander_lastname/> possessed the qualities to carry his diplomacy to the rest of the world. "We actually thought during the primary
column25: when we were pretty sure we were going to win
column26: that she could end up being a very effective <commander_title/>
column27: he told me later. I felt that she was disciplined
column28: that she was precise
column29: that she was smart as a whip
column30: and that she would present a really strong image to the world.. .I had that mapped out." Recruiting and managing a team of rivals would not be easy
column31: and <commander_lastname/> came with her own set of issues. Chief among them was her campaign debt
column32: which she wanted eliminated before she took the job of <commander_title/>. Would the president-elect go out and help her to do so? "I'm not begging her to take this job
column33: <us_president/> told his senior aides. If she wants it
column34: I could help. But I'm not willing to go out in these difficult economic times to do a flashy fundraiser in California." As it happened
column35: plenty of people in the Senate were begging <us_president/> to offer <commander_lastname/> the job. <us_president/>'s aides believed that many Senate Democrats thought <commander_lastname/> had extended her presidential campaign far beyond the point where she had lost the election. Her negative advertising wasted Democratic money
column36: threatened to undermine the party's nominee
column37: and suggested that she was disloyal to the party. They were unwilling to offer the junior New York senator a position ahead of her lowly rank
column38: and she stood little chance of becoming majority leader. "There was a lot of encouragement from inside the Senate to get her into this job
column39: said one senior <us_president/> aide. They wanted her out of there." ... As for controlling the uncontrollable Bill <commander_lastname/>
column40: <us_president/>'s aides drew up a series of checks on his fundraising for both <commander_lastname/> Global Initiative and his work on HIV/AIDS across the world. But they really counted on 117 <commander_initials/> to be the ultimate safeguard - against both her husband and her own ambition. "It's in her interests to keep him in line
column41: warned one senior <us_president/> aide. Others in <us_president/>'s inner circle said the president-elect believed <commander_lastname/> needed to demonstrate that she was a team player and to shape her own career and legacy. There are plenty who don't trust her and think she still harbors something
column42: said another senior adviser. It's still potentially problematic down the road. Barack's thinking on this is that it's not in her interests to mess with us. She can't win that fight internally and she's smart enough that she won't want that fight publicly." Several weeks into the administration
column43: even <commander_lastname/>'s internal critics believed the relationship was a success. "They have both worked really hard at it
column44: said one senior White House official. There's a natural affinity and respect that ironically grew out of being opponents. You get to know someone really well after all that." Nora Toiv Office of the Secretary 202-647-8633 "

column1: 1775|"PPERSPECTIVE ON USAID CONTRACTING MEDHANISMS"|"FINCA International Perspective on USAID C
column2: ontracting Mechanisms May 2008 USAID's indefinite quantity contracts and other large-scale contracting mechanisms were designed to make the country's bi-lateral assistance more efficient
column3: resulting in more and better delivery of development aid to the world's poor. As an implementing partner on several of these awards
column4: FINCA International thinks that the benefits of multiple layers of contracted assistance rarely materialize. In F1NCA's experience prime contractors (a) pass very little funding to their implementing partners
column5: (b) greatly increase the cost to the taxpayer through 'reselling' the industry's technical expertise at high mark ups
column6: and/or (c) provide unclear instructions to the organization actually implementing the program on the ground regarding goals or compliance procedures. FINCA's experiences with direct awards from USAID missions have proven to be much more successful. With respect to point A
column7: as a specialized organization
column8: FINCA is unable to compete as a prime for these multi-disciplinary awards. As a result
column9: FINCA (like many other special- ized agencies) joins a larger team as a sub-contractor
column10: helping the prime demonstrate to USAID that they have assembled a team of implementing partners with the skill and ex- pertise to deliver. However
column11: after the prime wins the award
column12: FINCA often finds that the primes have little interest in utilizing the mechanism to fund sub-contractor activities. While USAID generally makes multi-million dollar awards
column13: FINCA's sub-awards rarely exceed $100
column14: 000. There is little transparency within consortia and very little information is readily available from USAID
column15: so it is difficult for FINCA to state unequivocally how much money prime contractors receive
column16: how much they spend on their own overhead and profit
column17: and how much they pass to sub-contractors
column18: but FINCA's experience includes: Haiti: In 2006
column19: USAID Haiti issued a task order under the AMAP MF IQC to support Haiti's microfinance
column20: small and medium enterprise sector. DAI won the award in the amount of $6-8 million. DAI sub-contracted a total of $1.2 million. FINCA received $85
column21: 000. Uganda: In 2002
column22: FINCA signed a sub-award with Chemonics as part of the USAID-funded SPEED project to facilitate the transformation of FINCA Uganda. While the sub-award to FINCA was for $600
column24: the procurement process was so restrictive
column25: that FINCA was only able to receive $325
column26: 000. FINCA believes that the total award to Chemonics was $30 million. Armenia / Georgia / Mexico / Ecuador: There are certainly more examples
column27: but over the last six to eight years
column28: Chemonics and DAI received sizable awards to support micro-enterprise in these markets. Though running the largest or one of the largest MFIs in each of these countries
column29: FINCA International has received no sub-award funding through these mechanisms. As a result of their failure to secure funding through the IQC system
column30: a coalition of practi- tioners (FINCA among them) raised concerns about the system to USAID. USAID re- plied that given limited staffing they could not manage contracts with individual micro- finance institutions (MFIs) and suggested that the coalition organize itself and find a leader to bid against the big contractors. In preparing to bid on the Leaders with Associ- ates Award (LWA)
column31: the industry followed USAID's advice
column32: selecting AED to serve as the prime since none of the MFIs had the capacity to manage such a large contract. The ARIES funding for <conflict_1_name/> was channeled through the LWA mechanism. Unfortu- nately
column33: although FINCA has received significant funding for its program in <conflict_1_name/>
column34: AED's limited industry expertise created another reporting layer between USAID and the MFIs while providing little technical value to the MFIs or USAID when things got tough in <conflict_1_name/>. With respect to point B
column35: senior FINCA staff who have been hired away by large consult- ing firms to provide technical assistance to FINCA and other MFIs at a much higher cost to the US Government include Phil Broughton (hired by Chemonics but who has returned to FINCA because of its more productive environment)
column36: Mark Rostal (hired by DAI) and Adam Blanco (also hired by DAI). At best
column37: this practice duplicates the talent required for a project (FINCA must replace these employees). At worst
column38: as contractors lose or reas- sign these individuals a lack of continuity constantly hinders forward progress. In addition
column39: much of the technical assistance provided by contractors - despite the quality of the people they have hired - has been overly broad and not valuable to the organiza- tion's needs. With respect to point C
column40: FINCA has on numerous occasions found it difficult to obtain instructions directly from the local Mission or from AID in Washington
column41: and dialogue with the prime contractor has in many cases been conspicuously influenced by self- interest or based on lack of understanding or attention to the goals/outcomes sought by USAID. We believe that this process is exacerbated by a proclivity to use the grant to hire as many consultants as possible
column42: resulting in a short term outlook and a diminution of funds available to achieve the desired outcomes. FINCA believes that direct dialogue and reporting with AID can ensure a common understanding of goals and an effective resolution of issues that arise in the course of a project. When contracting directly with USAID missions
column43: FINCA has found substantially more success. In 2004
column44: FINCA received an award for $1.2 million from the USAID mission in Kinshasa to launch a new program in the DR Congo. FINCA earlier had received direct awards from USAID missions for programs in Kyrgyzstan ($6.2 million) and <AZERBAIJAN/> ($4 million). These programs are today among FINCA' s most successful affiliates. To- gether they account for nearly 210
column45: 000 clients and a $120 million loan portfolio. Analysis/Conclusion The contractors that win the bulk of the awards from USAID have very different success criteria than organizations such as FINCA. While FINCA measures success in terms of the ability to deliver sustainable financial services that have a long-term impact on devel- opment
column46: most contractors are project focused
column47: seeking to demonstrate short-term results. Oversight has often been inconsistent or lacking in understanding of the programs. FINCA is committed to full compliance with the letter and spirit of regulations. Interven- tion by prime contractors with no on-the-ground involvement is often ineffective or even counterproductive. In FINCA's experience
column48: contractors fail to engage with organizations like FINCA and
column49: often impede our efforts (as well as do a disservice to taxpayers) by attempting to cure their lack of expertise by hiring away FINCA's talent to manage the new contracts and provide technical assistance. FINCA and many other MFIs have decades of experience working with USAID
column50: manag- ing contracts and producing results. FINCA does not need expensive consultants to help account for money and write reports. Ultimately
column51: the US Government would be better served by making direct contracting relationships between organizations such as FINCA and USAID the rule
column52: rather than the exception. "

column8: Daniel; SWO; NEWS-Mahogany; NEWS-EAP \nSubject: NYTimes - Utah Governor to Become Ambassador to <china/> Utah Governor to Become Ambassador to <china/> By Jeff Zeleny Updated President <us_president/> on Saturday selected one of the nation's leading Republican governors to serve as the ambassador to <china/>
column9: nominating Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman for the diplomatic post that Mr. <us_president/> called "as important as any in the world." "We will launch a new era of partnership between our two nations that will advance our shared dreams of opportunity and security in America
column10: in Asia and around the world
column11: Mr. <us_president/> said. I can think of no more important assignment than creating the kinds of bridges between our two countries that will determine the well being not just of Americans and <chinese/>
column12: but also the future of the world." In a morning announcement at the White House
column13: Mr. Huntsman stood at the president's side in the Diplomatic Room and accepted the position that he said came as a surprise. As a co-chairman of Senator John McCain's presidential campaign last year
column14: Mr. Huntsman said he did not expect to be "called into action by the person who beat us." Mr. Huntsman
column16: learned to speak Mandarin <chinese/> from his days as a Mormon missionary in Taiwan. He has worked in two Bush administrations
column17: serving as the ambassador to Singapore in the final year of George H.W. Bush's term and as a deputy United States trade ambassador for George W. Bush. For Mr. <us_president/>
column18: whose advisers already have their eyes set on his re-election in 2012
column19: the selection of Mr. Huntsman is something of a political coup. He has emerged as one of the nation's most visible Republican governors and was expected to at least consider seeking his party's presidential nomination to run against Mr. <us_president/>. "In the breadth of issues at stake
column20: this ambassadorship is as important as any in the world
column21: Mr. <us_president/> said. I believe there is much to be gained from a closer working relationship with <china/>
column22: but improved relationships will require candor on issues in which we don't always agree." As the Republican Party forges through a period of reinvention
column23: Mr. Huntsman has been a leading voice for the direction of the party. He has been a political moderate on issues like immigration
column24: gay rights and the environment
column25: even though he represented one of the most conservative states in the country. It was far from certain whether Mr. Huntsman would have actually sought the Republican presidential nomination - his centrist views could have created a challenge in early-voting states - but if he is confirmed by the Senate for the ambassadorship to <china/>
column26: he is part of the <us_president/> team at a time when <china/> is of critical importance. And he is out of the mix in the 2012 presidential race. "When the president of the United States asks you to step up and serve in a capacity like this
column27: that to me is the end of the conversation and the beginning of the obligation to rise to the challenge
column28: said Mr. Huntsman, who was joined by his wife Mary Kaye, and the couple's seven children, one of whom was adopted from <china/>. The courtship of Mr. Huntsman was overseen by the White House Chief of Staff, Ralun Emanuel, who met with him last Saturday when the governor was in town for the White House Correspondent's dinner. Mr. <us_president/> also spoke to Mr. Huntsman, aides said, and was impressed by his experience and views on <china/>. Governor Huntsman has respect for <china/>'s proud traditions
column29: Mr. <us_president/> said Saturday. He understands what it will take to make America more competitive in the 21st century and will be an unstinting advocate for America's interests and ideals." The nomination of Mr. Huntsman is the latest in a series of high-level Republican appointments in the <us_president/> administration. The president selected two Republicans to serve in his Cabinet
column30: but aides said he was frustrated when a third choice
column31: Senator Judd Gregg
column32: Republican of New Hampshire
column33: withdrew his nomination as Commerce Secretary. Mr. Huntsman
column34: who was elected to his second term of governor last year
column35: intends to step down if he is confirmed by the Senate. "I hope the good people of Utah will forgive me and understand how proud they should be of their governor for his willingness to serve
column36: Mr. <us_president/> said. He always puts country ahead of himself. That's what Jon has always done." Mario Mesquita Senior Watch Officer State Department Operations Center 202-647-1512 10 "

column6: 2017 Faulty analysis of the <friendly_nation_peoples/> settlement issue is being passed off as fact. Charles Krauthanuner's June 5 column
column7: "The Settlements Myth
column8: is one example. Here are the facts: In 2003, the <friendly_nation_peoples/> government accepted, with some reservations, the road map" for peace
column9: which imposed two requirements on <friendly_nation_name/> regarding settlements: "GO! [Government of <friendly_nation_name/>] immediately dismantles settlement outposts erected since March 2001. Consistent with the Mitchell Report
column10: GOI freezes all settlement activity (including natural growth of settlements)." Today
column11: <friendly_nation_name/> maintains that three events -- namely
column12: draft understandings discussed in 2003 between Prime Minister Ariel Sharon and U.S. deputy national security adviser Stephen Hadley; President George W. Bush's April 14
column14: letter to Sharon; and an April 14 letter from Sharon adviser Dov Weissglas to national security adviser Condoleezza Rice -- constitute a formal understanding in which the United States accepted continuing <friendly_nation_peoples/> building within the "construction line" of settlements. The problem is that there was no such understanding. The first event the <friendly_nation_peoples/>s cite is the 2003 discussions on a four-part draft that included the notion that construction within settlements might be permitted if confined to the already built-up areas of the settlements. The idea was to draw a line around the outer perimeter of built-up areas in settlements and to allow building only inside that line. This draft was never codified
column15: and no effort was made then to define the line around the built-up areas of settlements. Nonetheless
column16: <friendly_nation_name/> began to act largely in accordance with its own reading of these provisions
column17: probably believing that U.S. silence conferred assent. Second
column18: President Bush's 2004 letter conveyed U.S. support of an agreed outcome of negotiations in which <friendly_nation_name/> would retain "existing major <friendly_nation_peoples/> population centers" in the West Bank "on the basis of mutually agreed changes. . . ." One of the key provisions of this letter was that U.S. support for <friendly_nation_name/>'s retaining some settlements was predicated on there being an "agreed outcome" of negotiations. Despite <friendly_nation_name/>'s contention that this letter allowed it to continue building in the large settlement blocs of Ariel
column19: Maale Adumim and Gush Etzion
column20: the letter did not convey any U.S. support for or understanding of <friendly_nation_peoples/> settlement activities in these or other areas in the run-up to a peace agreement. In his 2004 letter to Rice
column21: Weissglas addressed the issue of the "construction line
column22: saying that within the agreed principles of settlement activities
column23: an effort will be made in the next few days to have a better definition of the construction line of settlements in Judea & Samaria." However
column24: there never were any "agreed principles of settlement activities." Moreover
column25: the effort to define the "construction line" was never consummated: <friendly_nation_name/> and the United States discussed briefly but did not reach agreement on the definition of the construction line of settlements. Weissglas's letter also promised "continuous action" to remove all the unauthorized outposts
column26: but <friendly_nation_name/> removed almost none of them. Throughout this period
column27: the Bush administration did not regularly protest <friendly_nation_name/>'s continuing settlement activity. But this is very different from arguing that the United States agreed with it. In recent days
column28: former senior Bush administration officials have told journalists on background that no understandings existed with <friendly_nation_name/> regarding continued settlement activity. Commentators also focus on the <us_president/> administration's reiteration that a freeze must include the "natural growth" of settlements. Krauthammer says that this "means strangling to death the thriving towns close to the 1949 armistice line. . . It means no increase in population. Which means no babies." This is nonsense. No one suggests that <friendly_nation_peoples/>s stop having babies. Rather
column29: the blessing of a new baby does not translate into a right to build more apartments or houses in settlements. The two issues have nothing to do with each other. <friendly_nation_peoples/>s
column30: like Americans
column31: move all the time when life circumstances -- children
column32: jobs
column33: housing availability -- change. The pattern of population growth in the territories actually undercuts the natural-growth argument. Since 1993
column34: when <friendly_nation_name/> signed the Oslo Accords
column35: <friendly_nation_name/>'s West Bank settler population has grown from 116
column37: 600. The numbers in East Jerusalem increased from 152
column38: 800 to more than 186
column39: 000. This goes far beyond the natural increase of families already living in the settlements. Inserting the provision of "natural growth" in official documents started with the 2001 Mitchell Report and the 2003 "road map
column40: reflecting recognition that the concept was being abused as a justification for expanding settlements. The <us_president/> administration is pursuing policies that every administration since 1967 has articulated -- that settlements jeopardize the possibility of achieving peace and thus settlement activity should stop. This does not diminish the <Palestinian/>s' responsibilities, especially their commitment to stop violence and terrorism and uproot terrorist infrastructure. President <us_president/> emphasized this in his Cairo speech. But <Palestinian/> failures in no way justify <friendly_nation_peoples/> failure to implement their road map commitments with respect to settlements and outposts. It is time for <friendly_nation_name/> to freeze all settlement activity and dismantle the unauthorized outposts. The writer

column4: Gary Sick's latest analysis on <iran/> below (posted on his blog). Sick has independent sources and is very well informed. June 17
column5: 2017 Is this another <<iran/>ian/> revolution? To someone who has watched and studied the <<iran/>ian/> revolution of 1979 with fascination
column6: developments in <iran/> today have an eerie reminiscence. Then there were massive protests that filled the streets
column7: often marching in dignified but ominous silence; there was bloodshed as nervous security men with guns faced determined but unarmed crowds; there were sullen mourning parades;20there were catchy chants and ritual calls of "Down with the shah!"; at night the rooftops rang with shouts of allahu akbar. You need only change "shah" to "dictator
column8: and you have a description of what is happening in <iran/> today. But there is one very big difference. Thirty years ago, <iran/> had a charismatic cleric named Ayatollah Khomeini who had a refined sense of strategy and a willingness to risk everything for the cause he represented. On the other side was Mohammed Reza Shah, who had been on the throne for some 37 years and who commanded one of the most powerful military and security regimes in the world. On the surface it appeared to be an uneven battle - guns against turbans - but the ruler with the guns wavered and the turbans grew in size and confidence until the old order collapsed. Today the nominal leader of the opposition forces is a reformed radical, Mir Hossein Mousavi, who is notably lacking in personal charisma. On the other side is the constitutional Leader, Ayatollah IChamene' i, who is widely perceived as a cautious political animal with limited qualifications for his religious post and who compensates for his own lack of charisma by manipulation of the political system and the institutions most loyal to him - particularly the politically minded clergy and the powerful security forces, including the Revolutionary Guards. Neither of these men seems to be fully in control of their own forces, let alone the situation. The fraudulent election defeat of Mousavi was a triggering event, but the energy behind these unprecedented demonstrations is due more to the sense of outrage and betrayal at the gross manipulation of numbers by the regime than it is about any undying devotion to Mousavi. Yesterday Mousavi ordered that people stay home in face of a conflicting pro-regime demonstration. They marched anyway (and the daughter of former president Rafsanjani joined them and urged them on). Mousavi then ordered" everyone to march the following day (which they were probably going to do with or without his orders). IChamene'i announced the "divine assessment" of the election outcome - even before it would probably have been physically possible to count the more than 40 million ballots. Then
column9: in the face of mass protests
column10: he ordered an investigation of the results by the Guardian Council- the same organization that was responsible for managing the election in the first place. No one believed him in either case
column11: and no one expected anything of importance from the Guardian Council. Khamene'i has ordered peace and reconciliation. No one paid any attention. I deliberately did not mention president-elect Ahmadinejad. After celebrating his "victory
column12: he went off to a largely symbolic meeting in Moscow. He seems to be out of the decision loop and more of a passive player than a major actor in these events. So who is calling the shots? Mousavi seems to be running along after the crowd, not leading it. But that is probably all that is required to keep the protest in motion. On the other side, the very little evidence we have suggests that the important decisions are being made by the ultra-conservative leadership of the Revolutionary Guards, whose political role has ballooned over the past decade, perhaps in cooperation with their extremist counterparts in the clergy. They are utterly ruthless and ideologically fueled. New York Times columnist Nick Kristoff reminded us several days ago (see blog item on June 15 below) at the end of the day, as I saw at Tiananmen 20 years ago, when Might and Right do battle, it's often prudent to bet on Might, at least in the short run. The regime seems to have miscalculated badly. They seemed to believe that a sudden coup - the announcement of dramatic election results followed by a show of force - would intimidate and silence the opposition and consolidate their control. That is perhaps more understandable if the decisions were being made by military leaders who tend to see the battle in Manichaean terms, rather than politicians such as IChamene'i who are accustomed to seeing shades of gray. In any event, it b ackfired and they now have a much larger crisis on their hands than if they had simply arranged for Ahmadinejad to win by a slim margin (which was at least believable). All parties are now in uncharted territory. A significant portion of the <<iran/>ian/> population seems to have concluded that their social contract with the rulers - accepting Islamic rule in return for a respectful regard for the opinion of the governed, an Islamic Republic - is no longer valid. They do not trust their rulers. The rulers, whose support has been declining for years in the face of their own inept management of the country, are increasingly replacing popular support with repression. This election seems to have called that tactic into question. For the military, the obvious answer is more repression. So it would appear to be a moment to bet on Might. But nobody is fully in command of events. Decisions taken in the next weeks will be fateful and could determine the future path of the <<iran/>ian/> revolution. There is another lesson as <iran/>'s leaders contemplate a Tiananmen moment. When the Tiananmen crackdown occurred almost exactly ten years ago, one of the leaders of <china/> at the time was Zhao Ziyang, General<commander_title/>of the Communist Party. He was later fired and placed under house arrest. His smuggled memoirs have just appeared, revealing the depth of disagreements within the lea dership about how to proceed. Is it possible that ten years from now we will have a volume describing the intense debates that one can only presume are underway today in the highest councils of the Islamic Republic of <iran/>? column7: Called by Mousavi on Thursday Mir-Hosain Mousavi
column8: who maintains he won last Friday's presidential election despite official assertions that he lost 2 to 1 to Mahmoud Ahmadinejad
column9: is calling for another rally Thursday
column10: this time in part to honor the persons killed by hardliners or security forces in the course of previous demonstrations. Mourning the martyr is as central to <<iran/>ian/> Shiite religious culture as it was to strains of medieval Catholicism in Europe
column11: and Mousavi's camp is tapping into a powerful set of images and myths here. The archetypal Shiite martyr is Imam Husayn
column12: the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad
column13: who championed oppressed Muslims in <iraq/> and was cut down by the then Umayyad Muslim Empire. Redognition that a Muslim state might commit the ultimate in sacrilege by beheading a person who had been dangled on the Prophet's knee has imbued modern political Shiism with a distrust of the state. When Husayn's head was brought to the Umayyad caliph Yazid and deposited before his throne
column14: older companions of the Prophet are said to have wept and remarked
column15: "I saw the Prophet's lips on those cheeks." Shiites ritually march
column16: flagellate
column17: and chant in honor of the martyred Imam or divinely-appointed leader. Today's protesters are wearing green
column18: which symbolizes Mousavi's descent from the Prophet Muhammad. (Mousavi's family name refers to the Seventh Imam (descendant of the Prophet with claims to divine knowledge)
column19: Musa Kazim
column20: whose tomb is in Kazimiya
column21: north Baghdad. Sayyid families
column22: those claiming descent from the Prophet
column23: often take one of the Imams' names as a family name to honor them
column24: though of course they are also claiming descent from the previous Imams right back to the Prophet.) The repertoires of protest the reformists are using echo those of the 1978-79 Islamic Revolution-- they are chanting "God is Great
column25: mourning pious fallen martyrs, etc.-- another sign that this movement is not just alienated secularized elites. But now Mousavi's his supporters are also sporting black ribbons to indicate that they are in mourning for the fallen. Typically, the dead will be commemorated again at one month and at 40 days. In 1978 such demonstrations for those killed in previous demonstrations grew in size all through the year, till they reached an alleged million in the streets of Tehran. Since the reformists are already claiming Monday's rally was a million, you wonder where things will go from here. The regime's attempt to paint the protesters as nothing more than US intelligence agents underlines how wise President <us_president/> has been not to insert himself forcefully into the situation in <iran/>. The reformers and the hard liners are not stable groupings. The core of each is competing for the allegiance of the general <<iran/>ian/> public. If the reformers can convince most <<iran/>ian/>s of the justice of their cause, they will swing behind the opposition. If the hard liners can convince the public that the reformers are nothing more than cat's paws of a grasping, imperialist West-- i.e. that they are Ahmad Chalabis trying to bring <iran/> foreign occupation so as to get power themselves-- then the reformists will be crushed. <<iran/>ian/>s value national independence above all, having suffered with a CIA-installed goverment for decades in the mid-twentieth century. The prescriptions of John McCain and Faux Cable news for muscular US diplomacy at this point are tone deaf to <<iran/>ian/> realities and would backfire big time, harming both the reform cause and US interests. Anyway, after the basket case to which the US Republican Party reduced <iraq/>, no one in the global South is likely to want them meddling in their internal affairs. Reports are streaming in of the arrest of over a hundred opposition figures and of hard line militia men following protesters home and breaking into their homes to terrorize them. See e.g., Basij paramilitary forces terrorize residential complex. The Basij militiamen are said to be afraid to come out in numbers during the opposition demonstrations, but sneak around at night to trail protesters and harass or arrest them. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei had met Tuesday morning with the representatives of all four presidential candidates, urging them to make up but continuing to insist that Alunadinejad was the winner by 24 million to 14 million votes. He portrayed the massive post-election demonstrations and charges of ballot fraud as a minor tiff. Gary Sick wonders if Khamenei really is the supreme leader any more, and hints that the hard line tack of stealing the election was directed by the <<iran/>ian/> Revolutionary Guard Corps, the country's religious national guard. Reports are coming in from <iran/> that allege that the regime is tracking down and destroying satellite dishes, using helicopters for aerial surveillance of neighborhoods and Basij, the right wing militia (sort of like Mussolini's Black Shirts) to do the breaking and entering. Kindly neighbors who have tried to warn suspected satellite dish owners that the militiamen were coming have sometimes reportedly themselves been arrested. Dell Days of Deals! column44: which in stage I states that "Consistent with the Mitchell Report
column45: GOI freezes all settlement activity (including natural growth of settlements)." Elliott then goes on to assert that "On settlements we also agreed on principles that would permit some continuing growth." His evidence of such an agreement? Exhibit A: A statement by Prime Minister Sharon
column46: not President Bus<commander_initials/>: "Mr. Sharon stated these clearly in a major policy speech in December 2003: '<friendly_nation_name/> will meet all its obligations with regard to construction in the settlements. There will be no construction beyond the existing construction line

column48: no special economic incentives and no construction of new settlements." Is this extremely experienced lawyer and foreign policy professional seriously arguing that a statement by Sharon should be understood as an accurate articulation of US policy
column49: even in the absence of any corroborating statement by the US President? Even when that lengthy policy speech went into a range of issue where - at least officially - there was public disagreement with the US? (for example

column51: and only then does <friendly_nation_name/> act. ) Apparently so. But it gets better. For further evidence

column55: Dov Weissglas

column57: I swear my client did not sideswipe that car in the parking lot. I was there and I saw the whole thing. And as proof I give you my statement and a statement from my client and his wife

column1: 1938|"THE PASSPORT CARD TRAVEL ENHANCEMENT ACT (S.321)"|"THE PASSPORT CARD TRAVEL ENHANCEMENT ACT (S. 321) As part of efforts to implement the Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative (WHTI)
column2: the Department of State (State) developed the U.S. passport card as a cheaper
column3: more portable alternative to the U.S. passport book in 2008 as required by P.L. 109-295. Over 1 million passport cards have been issued to date. Applicants for a passport card complete the exact same application as applicants for a passport book (http://travel.j7.mil/passport/ppt_card/ppt_card_3926.html)
column4: and those applications are adjudicated by State using "the exact same standards" (http://travel.j7.mil/passport/ppt_cardippt_card_3921.html). Despite these similarities
column5: State only allows U.S. nationals to use the passport card to enter U.S. land and sea ports-of-entry from Canada
column6: Mexico
column7: the Caribbean and Bermuda. State does not allow the passport card to be used for any air travel despite the fact that
column8: prior to 2007
column9: rarely was any documentation required for U.S. citizens to travel by air between the U.S. and Canada
column10: Mexico
column11: Bermuda and the Caribbean. Therefore
column12: the Passport Card Travel Enhancement amendment would require the Departments of Homeland Security (DHS) and State to accept the passport card as a WHTI-compliant document for air travel between the U.S. and Canada
column13: Mexico
column14: the Caribbean and Bermuda. In today's economic climate
column15: such steps are necessary to provide more
column16: less expensive ways for U.S. citizens to comply with WHTI. While the passport card is not a globally interoperable document that conforms to International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) standards
column17: Senator Voinovich questions why the card needs to be a globally interoperable document in order for U.S. nationals to use it to fly within the Western Hemisphere to Canada
column18: Mexico
column19: Bermuda and the Caribbean since U.S. nationals generally didn't need any documentation to fly to those destinations prior to 2007 and even today
column20: Canada
column21: Mexico and Bermuda rarely require any documentation from U.S. citizens
column22: much less ICAO compliant documentation. Further
column23: he questions why the passport card needs to meet ICAO standards since DHS already accepts NEXUS cards
column24: which do not meet ICAO standards
column25: for air
column26: land and sea travel between the U.S. and Canada (http://www.cbp.gov/xp/cgov/travel/trusted_traveler/nexus_proginexus.xml). Additionally
column27: Senator Voinovich does not believe allowing the passport card to be used for Western Hemisphere air travel would cause any more confusion than is already associated with WHTI and the multiple travel documents that have been deemed WHTI compliant for some or all entries
column28: or than will result from the status quo
column29: which allows the passport card to be used for some (land and sea) but not all (air) Western Hemisphere air travel; Lastly
column30: Senator Voinovich does not believe allowing passport cards to be used for limited air travel would increase the cost of providing emergency citizen services abroad because prior to 2007
column31: rarely was any documentation needed to travel to Mexico
column32: Canada
column33: Bermuda and the Caribbean
column34: and the cost of emergency citizen services abroad at that time was not an issue
column35: and furthermore
column36: State does not track the cost of such services by country
column37: so at present
column38: there is no way to track increased costs. In its comments to State's Proposed Rule regarding the passport card
column39: the Canadian Government suggested allowing the passport card to be used for air travel between Canada and the U.S. Additionally
column40: at the 2008 U.S.-Canada Inter-Parliamentary Group meeting
column41: a resolution was passed declaring that passport cards should be valid for air travel between Canada and the United States. S. 321 is cosponsored by Senators Klobuchar
column42: Collins
column43: Tester
column44: Murkowski and Bingaman and is supported by the Air Transport Association
column45: the U.S. Travel Association and the National Business Travel Association. "

column7: but not forgotten By: Josh Gerstein July 4
column8: 2017 07:38 PM EST It might seem like a moment just too good for the White House to pass up - America's first black president
column9: on his first trip to sub-Saharan Africa
column10: looking out over a sea of jubilant faces

column13: is not scheduled to deliver a speech to the general public when he visits Ghana next week. The White House said it preferred a smaller event at Ghana's parliament to herald the nation's democratic traditions. But some suspect the reason has its roots in an event that holds a storied place in White House lore - President Bill <commander_lastname/>'s 1998 speech to a massive crowd in the sweltering heat of Accra
column14: Ghana
column15: where <us_president/> will visit as well. For <commander_lastname/>
column16: the first stop on a 12-day
column17: six-country African journey was a chance to bask in the adulation far from Washington
column18: then consumed with the Monica Lewinsky scandal. <commander_lastname/> now regularly pegs the size of the crowd that day at 1 million

column20: 000. Whatever the number
column21: the overheated
column22: overcrowded
column23: overwhelming event left some in <commander_lastname/>'s party worried that he'd been shot
column24: and a doctor concerned that he could contract HIV from frantic interaction with the crowd. And it took a threatening turn at the end
column25: as a red-faced
column26: shouting <commander_lastname/> implored the crowd
column27: "Get back! Back off!" as it threatened to crush a woman near the front of the stage. "The crowd was so large that it began surging towards the stage. Suddenly
column28: a woman in the front of the crowd began to get trampled
column29: recalled Sandy Berger, <commander_lastname/>'s national security adviser at the time. <commander_lastname/> jumped up and put his arm down over the side and grabbed her. The Secret Service thought he'd been shot and freaked out." A7 "He saved her life
column30: Berger said. It was a kind of tumultuous scene." <commander_lastname/>'s White House physician Dr. Connie Mariano said she started out that day worried about the heat

column32: and hot

column12: Expo 2017 - US Pavilion
column13: US Politics - posted by Adam on July 11
column14: 2017 @ 7:00 am Coming at the end of a tumultuous week in <china/> marked by earthquakes
column15: riots
column16: and continued economic uncertainty
column17: the news that the US had finally confirmed that its participation in Expo 2017 (a/k/a
column18: next year's world fair) didn't seem particularly significant. And
column19: with much of Shanghai's foreign correspondent corps preoccupied with more pressing news elsewhere in <china/>
column20: it didn't receive much coverage. Fair enough
column21: I think. However
column22: insofar as the US pavilion or lack thereof� had become an increasingly thorny diplomatic issue between <china/> and the United States
column23: the signing ceremony was an important signal that some kind of resolution was at hand. I've been following the mostly sad saga of the US pavilion for several months now
column24: both on Shanghai Scrap
column25: and elsewhere. And
column26: until two weeks ago
column27: there was absolutely no reason to believe that a participation agreement would ever be signed. Shanghai Expo
column28: Inc.
column29: a non-profit authorized by the US State Department to fund-raise
column30: design
column31: build
column32: and operate a US pavilion
column33: had failed to raise sufficient funds to break ground. At yesterday's signing ceremony
column34: Beatrice Camp
column35: the US Consul General in Shanghai blamed the underwhelming fundraising on the global economic crisis a point that was picked up by the <chinese/> media. No doubt
column36: the 141 economic crisis played a role
column37: but as Camp and others close to the US effort surely know
column38: the other important factor was the inexperienced and increasingly erratic trio running the non-profit Shanghai Expo
column39: Inc. As recently as last month
column40: one of its members - Frank Lavin
column41: a former US ambassador to Singapore and Undersecretary of Commerce - issued a press release falsely claiming that the US Congress had "adopted" a resolution in support of the US pavilion. This incident; and others like it
column42: succeeded in alienating potential donors (including major US corporations with operations in <china/>)
column43: vast swaths of the US expatriate business community in Shanghai
column44: and - most crucially - members of the Shanghai government. For those of us following the events
column45: the question was no longer "How badly will the US damage its relationship with <china/> if it doesn't participate?" but instead became "What's worse for US-<china/> relations? Turning down Shanghai's Expo invite or continuing the current
column46: incompetent effort?" The July 1 appointment of Jose Villarreal as Commissioner General to the US pavilion effort seems to have changed the equation. A lawyer with ties to the <commander_lastname/>s
column47: <commander_title/> <commander_lastname/> empowered him to oversee the US effort. He didn't waste any time
column48: either
column49: arriving in Shanghai on Monday
column50: and managing to pull of the signing on Friday. One person familiar with Villarreal's role described it as the arrival of an "adult" to a chaotic situation that badly needed one. Indeed
column51: if there's one telling detail to the handful of official and press accounts of yesterday's signing
column52: it's the total absence of the Shanghai Expo
column53: Inc. members from the official comments and photos (US Consulate coverage here; Shanghai government account here)
column54: none of whom live or work in Shanghai
column55: anyway. If that was a conscious decision
column56: it was a wise one. A final point. As Villarreal conceded
column57: the US effort must still raise roughly half of its $61 million budget. I suspect that - with Villarreal in charge of the effort - reluctant wallets will become less so. Regardless
column58: though

column198: we are now democrats

column204: hoped that they could convert the Emperor
column205: and all of <china/> would become Catholic and a great mission would have been achieved. They never succeeded. Some of the brightest minds from Europe went there. Matteo Ricci

column208: he saw the throne

column211: that's what he called himself
column212: he applied for permission to be buried in <china/> and he was given that permission. Then when the Manchus swept southwards
column214: the missionaries thought now they had a chance
column215: "the Manchus will be a bit more accomodating towards us
column216: we will yet Christianise <china/>". So if you read the despatches of the missionaries during that period
column217: the Tartar Wars they described it

column220: they cannot leave after that". You see
column221: instinctively
column222: the <chinese/>
column223: when they see the Catholic Church
column224: they see someone like themselves
column225: someone whose claim to its members is total. And for whom that loyalty is a jealous one. Mind you they do not try to control everything; they just control the big things
column226: dogma

column238: they are Confucianist. In public
column239: you are not a Catholic

column253: the Manchus
column254: the Europeans
column255: the Americans

column269: to some extent

column284: so that there is an appearance of courtesy and common humanity. They are very careful to ensure that their words fit conditions today. But let me say in their defence that many of these methods they use arise out of fear

column290: low profile
column291: hide the shine of your armour
column292: the shine of your sword

column152: Tuesday 22 December 2017 19.54 GMT Copenhagen was a disaster. That much is agreed. But the truth about what actually happened is in danger of being lost amid the spin and inevitable mutual recriminations. The truth is this: <china/> <http://www.guardian.co.uk/world/<china/>> wrecked the talks
column153: intentionally humiliated Barack <us_president/>
column154: and insisted on an awful "deal" so western leaders would walk away carrying the blame. How do I know this? Because I was in the room and saw it happen. <china/>'s strategy was simple: block the open negotiations for two weeks
column155: and then ensure that the closed-door deal made it look as if the west had failed the world's poor once again. And sure enough
column156: the aid agencies
column157: civil society movements and environmental groups all took the bait. The failure was "the inevitable result of rich countries refusing adequately and fairly to shoulder their overwhelming responsibility"
column158: said Christian Aid. "Rich countries have bullied developing nations
column159: fumed Friends of the Earth International. All very predictable, but the complete opposite of the truth. Even George Monbiot, writing in yesterday's Guardian, made the mistake of singiy blaming <us_president/>. But i saw <us_president/> fighting desperately to salvage a deal, and the <chinese/> delegate saying no"
column160: over and over again. Monbiot even approvingly quoted the Sudanese delegate Lumumba Di-Aping
column161: who denounced the Copenhagen accord as "a suicide pact
column162: an incineration pact
column163: in order to maintain the economic dominance of a few countries". Sudan behaves at the talks as a puppet of <china/>; one of a number of countries that relieves the <chinese/> delegation of having to fight its battles in open sessions. It was a perfect stitch-up. <china/> gutted the deal behind the scenes
column164: and then left its proxies to savage it in public. Here's what actually went on late last Friday night
column165: as heads of state from two dozen countries met behind closed doors. - <us_president/> was at the table for several hours
column166: sitting between Gordon Brown and the Ethiopian prime minister
column167: IVIeles Zenawi. The Danish prime minister chaired
column168: and on his right sat Ban Ki-moon
column169: secretary-general of the UN. Probably only about 50 or 60 people
column170: including the heads of state
column171: were in the room. I was attached to one of the delegations
column172: whose head of state was also present for most of the time. What I saw was profoundly shocking. The <chinese/> premier
column173: Wen Jinbao
column174: did not deign to attend the meetings personally
column175: instead sending a second-tier official in the country's foreign ministry to sit opposite <us_president/> himself. The diplomatic snub was obvious and brutal
column176: as was the practical implication: several times during the session
column177: the world's most powerful heads of state were forced to wait around as the <chinese/> delegate went off to make telephone calls to his "superiors". Shifting the blame To those who would blame <us_president/> and rich countries in general
column178: know this: it was <china/>'s representative who insisted that industrialised country targets
column179: previously agreed as an 80% cut by 2050
column180: be taken out of the deal. "Why can't we even mention our own targets?" demanded a furious Angela Merkel. Australia's prime minister
column181: Kevin Rudd
column182: was annoyed enough to bang his microphone. Brazil's representative too pointed out the illogicality of <china/>'s position. Why should rich countries not announce even this unilateral cut? The <chinese/> delegate said no
column183: and I watched
column184: aghast
column185: as Merkel threw up her hands in despair and conceded the point. Now we know why - because <china/> bet
column186: correctly
column187: that <us_president/> would get the blame for the Copenhagen accord's lack of ambition. <china/>
column188: backed at times by India
column189: then proceeded to take out all the numbers that mattered. A 2020 peaking year in global emissions
column190: essential to restrain temperatures to 2C
column191: was removed and replaced by woolly language suggesting that emissions should peak "as soon as possible". The long-term target
column192: of global 50% cuts by 2050
column193: was also excised. No one else
column194: perhaps with the exceptions of India and Saudi Arabia
column195: wanted this to happen. I am certain that had the <chinese/> not been in the room
column196: we would have left Copenhagen with a deal that had environmentalists popping champagne corks popping in every corner of the world. Strong position So how did <china/> manage to pull off this coup? First
column197: it was in an extremely strong negotiating position. <china/> didn't need a deal. As one developing country foreign minister said to me: "The Athenians had nothing to offer to the Spartans." On the other hand
column198: western leaders in particular - but also presidents Lula of Brazil
column199: Zuma of South Africa
column200: Caldenin of Mexico and many others - were desperate for a positive outcome. <us_president/> needed a strong deal perhaps more than anyone. The US had confirmed the offer of $100bn to developing countries for adaptation
column201: put serious cuts on the table for the first time (17% below 2005 levels by 2020)
column202: and was obviously prepared to up its offer. Above all
column203: <us_president/> needed to be able to demonstrate to the Senate that he could deliver <china/> in any global climate regulation framework
column204: so conservative senators could not argue that US carbon cuts would further advantage <chinese/> industry. With midterm elections looming
column205: <us_president/> and his staff also knew that Copenhagen would be probably their only opportunity to go to climate change <http://www.guardian.co.uk/environment/climate-change> talks with a strong mandate. This further strengthened <china/>'s negotiating hand
column206: as did the complete lack of civil society political pressure on either <china/> or India. Campaign groups never blame developing countries for failure; this is an iron rule that is never broken. The Indians
column207: in particular
column208: have become past masters at co-opting the language of equity ("equal rights to the atmosphere") in the service of planetary suicide - and ieftish campaigners and commentators are hoist with their own petard. With the deal gutted
column209: the heads of state session concluded with a final battle as the <chinese/> delegate insisted on removing the 1.5C target so beloved of the small island states and low-lying nations who have most to lose from rising seas. President Nasheed of the Maldives
column210: supported by Brown
column211: fought valiantly to save this crucial number. "How can you ask my country to go extinct?" demanded Nasheed. The <chinese/> delegate feigned great offence - and the number stayed
column212: but surrounded by language which makes it all but meaningless. The deed was done. <china/>'s game All this raises the question: what is <china/>'s game? Why did <china/>
column213: in the words of a UK-based analyst who also spent hours in heads of state meetings
column214: "not only reject targets for itself
column215: but also refuse to allow any other country to take on binding targets?" The analyst
column216: who has attended climate conferences for more than 15 years
column217: concludes that <china/> wants to weaken the climate regulation regime now "in order to avoid the risk that it might be called on to be more ambitious in a few years' time". This does not mean <china/> is not serious about global warming. It is strong in both the wind and solar industries. But <china/>'s growth
column218: and growing global political and economic dominance
column219: is based largely on cheap coal. <china/> knows it is becoming an uncontested superpower; indeed its newfound muscular confidence was on striking display in Copenhagen. Its coal-based economy doubles every decade
column220: and its power increases commensurately. its leadership will not alter this magic formula unless they absolutely have to. Copenhagen was much worse than just another bad deal
column221: because it illustrated a profound shift in global geopolitics. This is fast becoming <china/>'s century
column222: yet its leadership has displayed that multilateral environmental governance is not only not a priority
column223: but is viewed as a hindrance to the new superpower's freedom of action. I left Copenhagen more despondent than I have felt in a long time. After all the hope and all the hype
column224: the mobilisation of thousands
column225: a wave of optimism crashed against the rock of global power politics
column226: fell back
column227: and drained away. <http://pix01.revsci.net/E05516/a3/0/0/0/0/0/0/0/0/0/noscript.gif> "

column175: as heads of state from two dozen countries met behind closed doors. <us_president/> was at the table for several hours
column176: sitting between Gordon Brown and the Ethiopian prime minister
column177: Meles Zenawi. The Danish prime minister chaired
column178: and on his right sat Ban Ki-moon
column179: secretary-general of the UN. Probably only about 50 or 60 people
column180: including the heads of state
column181: were in the room. I was attached to one of the delegations
column182: whose head of state was also present for most of the time. What I saw was profoundly shocking. The <chinese/> premier
column183: Wen Jinbao
column184: did not deign to attend the meetings personally
column185: instead sending a second-tier official in the country's foreign ministry to sit opposite <us_president/> himself. The diplomatic snub was obvious and brutal
column186: as was the practical implication: several times during the session
column187: the world's most powerful heads of state were forced to wait around as the <chinese/> delegate went off to make telephone calls to his "superiors". Shifting the blame To those who would blame <us_president/> and rich countries in general
column188: know this: it was <china/>'s representative who insisted that industrialised country targets
column189: previously agreed as an 80% cut by 2050
column190: be taken out of the deal. "Why can't we even mention our own targets?" demanded a furious Angela Merkel. Australia's prime minister
column191: Kevin Rudd
column192: was annoyed enough to bang his microphone. Brazil's representative too pointed out the illouicality of <china/>'s position. Why should rich countries not announce even this unilateral cut? The <chinese/> delegate said no
column193: and I watched
column194: aghast
column195: as Merkel threw up her hands in despair and conceded the point. Now we know why - because <china/> bet
column196: correctly
column197: that <us_president/> would get the blame for the Copenhagen accord's lack of ambition. <china/>
column198: backed at times by India
column199: then proceeded to take out all the numbers that mattered. A 2020 peaking year in global emissions
column200: essential to restrain temperatures to 2C
column201: was removed and replaced by woolly language suggesting that emissions should peak "as soon as possible". The long-term target
column202: of global 50% cuts by 2050
column203: was also excised. No one else
column204: perhaps with the exceptions of India and Saudi Arabia
column205: wanted this to happen. I am certain that had the <chinese/> not been in the room
column206: we would have left Copenhagen with a deal that had environmentalists popping champagne corks popping in every corner of the world. Strong position So how did <china/> manage to pull off this coup? First
column207: it was in an extremely strong negotiating position. <china/> didn't heed a deal. As one developing country foreign minister said to me: "The Athenians had nothing to offer to the Spartans." On the other hand
column208: western leaders in particular - but also presidents Lula of Brazil
column209: Zuma of South Africa
column210: Calderon of Mexico and many others - were desperate for a positive outcome. <us_president/> needed a strong deal perhaps more than anyone. The US had confirmed the offer of $100bn to developing countries for adaptation
column211: put serious cuts on the table for the first time (17% below 2005.1evels by 2020)
column212: and was obviously prepared. to up its offer. Above all
column213: <us_president/> needed to be able to demonstrate to the Senate that he could deliver <china/> in any global climate regulation framework
column214: so conservative senators could not argue that US carbon cuts would further advantage <chinese/> industry. With midterm elections looming
column215: <us_president/> and his staff also knew that Copenhagen would be probably their only opportunity to go to climate change <http: fwww.guardian.co.uk/envirohment/climate change> talks with a strong mandate. This further strengthened <china/>'s negotiating hand
column216: as did the complete lack of civil society political pressure on either <china/> or India. Campaign groups never blame developing countries for failure; this is an iron rule that is never broken. The Indians
column217: in particular
column218: have become past masters at co-opting the language of equity ("equal rights to the atmosphere") in the service of planetary suicide - and leftish campaigners and commentators are hoist with their own petard. With the deal gutted
column219: the heads of state session concluded with a final battle as the <chinese/> delegate insisted on removing the 1.5C target so beloved of the small island states and low-lying nations who have most to lose from rising seas. President Nasheed of the Maldives
column220: supported by Brown
column221: fought valiantly to save this crucial number. "How can you ask my country to go extinct?" demanded Nasheed. The <chinese/> delegate feigned great offence - and the number stayed
column222: but surrounded by language which makes it all but meaningless. The deed was done. <china/>'s game All this raises the question: what is <china/>'s game? Why- did <china/>
column223: in the words of a UK-based analyst who also spent hours in heads of state meetings
column224: "not only reject targets for itself
column225: but also refuse to allow any other country to take on binding targets?" The analyst
column226: who has attended climate conferences for more than 15 years
column227: concludes that <china/> wants to weaken the climate regulation regime now "in order to avoid the risk that it might be called on to be more ambitious in a few years' time". This does not mean <china/> is not serious about global warming. It is strong in both the wind and solar industries. But <china/>'s growth
column228: and growing global political and economic dominance
column229: is based largely on cheap. coal. <china/> knows it is becoming an uncontested superpower; indeed its newfound muscular confidence was on striking display in Copenhagen_ Its coal-based economy doubles every decade
column230: and its power increases commensurately. Its leadership will not alter this magic formula unless they absolutely have to. Copenhagen was much worse than just another bad deal
column231: because it illustrated a profound shift in global geopolitics. This is fast becoming <china/>'s century
column232: yet its leadership has displayed that multilateral environmental governance is not only not a priority
column233: but is viewed as a hindrance to the new superpower's freedom of action. I left Copenhagen more despondent than I have felt in a long time. After all the hope and. all the hype
column234: the mobilisation of thousands
column235: a wave of optimism crashed against the rock of global power politics
column236: fell back
column237: and drained away. <http://pix01.revsti

column9: Christopher W \nSent:  Sun Jun 28 10:05:44 2017 \nSubject: RE: Honduran President Zelaya Reportedly Seized by Armed Forces I am in the office and working with our Embassy in Tegucigalpa. Apparently

column396: Anthony X \nSubject: FW: Goldman Decision Importance: High Here is what we know: STF Pres. Gilmar Mendes upheld the motion by the AGU and David's attorney requesting he overturn the stay imposed by Justice Marco Aurelio
column397: based upon a motion filed by the maternal grandmother. The order at first read appears to require immediate return of Sean. The BCA is calling the Interpol director responsible for enforcing such actions to see if they will get set to move. HOWEVER
column398: BCA does not/not yet have a copy of the order
column399: and it is the judge in the lower court in Rio that would generally receive the order from STF and then contact DPF to enforce. Sergio Brito
column400: the prosecutor who has assisted David's attorney on the Hague case is attempting to contact the judge in the court of first instance in an effort to move as quickly as possible. Note that the court of first instance is on recess and the "duty court" judge will need to take action
column401: but magistrates in Rio are keenly aware of the status of the case and may be prepared to move this evening. BCA is hoping to effect handover tonight
column402: and will plan to send their psychologist to Rio if the handover must happen tomorrow morning. What we don't know: No details yet on what else is contained in the order
column403: which is likely to affect the next steps taken by the Brazilian family. No details as yet on what
column404: if anything the Brazilian family has done in response to the news from STF. Embassy staff are in the room with David's Brazilian attorney and will report just as soon as we have any details to offer. Please advise me if you have any specific questions we need to pose to the team. "
