Sid http://www.guardian.co.uk/politics/2017/jun/12/david-miliband-gordon-brown-labour-leadership/print The Guardian David Miliband: Labour is facing the fight of its life Foreign<commander_title/>thought about quitting the government in last week's turmoil David Miliband expressed his frustration at a lack of vision from the Labour leadership. Photograp<commander_initials/>: Martin Godwin Voters still don't know what Labour and Gordon Brown stand for
column4: David Miliband admits today
column5: as he reveals how close he came to quitting the government during last week's turmoil at Westminster. Speaking to the Guardian at the end of 10 extraordinary days
column6: the foreign<commander_title/>says the party's high command was given an "electric shock" by the disastrous European election results
column7: and he urges fellow ministers to get out and prepare for "the fight of our life". But Miliband also concedes that he considered following his close friend and ally James Purnell
column8: who resigned from the government last week and called for the prime minister to stand down. Miliband said: "I'd made my decision on Thursday. Sometimes you can make your decisions with great planning and calculation and sometimes you have to make them rather more quickly. James made his decision in good faith
column9: I made my decision in good faith ... we all have tolive with our decisions." The Labour party has a settled view of who should be leader
column10: he said. "This divides people who are close and people feel passionately one way and people feel passionately the other way." Describing the task now facing Labour
column11: he says: "It could not be more urgent that there is a maximum of 11 months until the next general election
column12: that we got 15% of the vote nationally [last week]
column13: that we came second in Wales and that one in 20 people voted for us. If that does not electric shock us out of our ministerial chairs to think: 'By God
column14: we have got the fight of our life on our hands because whatever the Tories are they certainly don't deserve a landslide' - then nothing will." Miliband has not given a domestic policy interview for nearly nine months since he felt dogged by accusations that he was manoeuvring for the premiership. He refuses to acknowledge that his decision to back Brown last week saved the prime minister
column15: saying "it is impossible to tell". But the foreign<commander_title/>feels his loyalty has given him the freedom to speak his mind without his motives being questioned by anyone in Downing Street. Miliband betrays frustration at the absence of a clear Labour vision
column16: saying: "We need the message to go out that we have got the humility to learn about what has gone wrong. "It is not a masochism strategy. It is about saying what we believe in. It is about clarity
column17: priority
column18: adding up to purpose. I know what we stand for
column19: I know what our instincts are
column20: but the voters don't. Actually
column21: I know what Gordon Brown stands for. "We have a responsibility to make sure that
column22: come the election
column23: [voters] know what Labour stands for. We were not being listened to
column24: people felt that they had been forgotten
column25: we neither inspired nor reassured." He calls for cabinet colleagues to show stronger leadership in the battle to restore Labour's fortunes. "We need to make sure the talents and energies of not just the whole of the cabinet
column26: but the whole of the labour movement are give n free rein because one in 20 people voted for us. The truth is that we are not automatons. We all have to get out there." Asked whether he felt voters had stopped listening to Brown
column27: Miliband said: "He himself has said he has to build on his strengths and work on his weaknesses. That is a good maxim for all of us. He is someone who made the right decisions on the biggest issue of the day. We have got a chance to fight with honour and dignity for what we believe in. The stakes are very high because we know that parties can slump into very dangerous positions." Providing what he describes as a route map from the disaster
column28: he said: "Labour first needs a period of competent
column29: effective
column30: stable government; secondly
column31: we need to reset our political compass so ministers are no longer locked in their departments
column32: but link their policies to their values; and thirdly
column33: the government has to be at the cutting edge of policy." On the issue of political reform
column34: he demands a speeding-up of the pace of political reform
column35: saying it is not a piece of middle-class frippery. For the first time
column36: he reveals that he now backs the Alternative Vote for the Commons
column37: saying MPs' legitimacy will be strengthened by being able to say 50% in my constituency voted for me. He says the change cannot be made before the general election. He also backs a fresh push on Lords reform
column38: saying "we have got an agreed blueprint". He rounded on Tory spending plans
column39: but said Labour would clarify its own intentions before the election. "They will be credible and clear. We will come to that in an open and honest way." But he defends delay in setting out these figures
column40: arguing "when you are in the middle of a Tornado it is a bad time take a forecast". In an oblique reference to the Damian McBride briefings
column41: he also calls on the media to abandon unattributable briefings
column42: saying all politicians' spokesmen should be named
column43: or not quoted by media outlets. "The gotcha culture of politics is not in anyone's interests

column10: Christopher W \nSent:  Sun Jun 28 10:05:44 2017 \nSubject: RE: Honduran President Zelaya Reportedly Seized by Armed Forces I am in the office and working with our Embassy in Tegucigalpa. Apparently
column11: the action this morning was a coordinated effort by the Supreme Court
column12: the Honduran Congress
column13: and the armed forces to prevent President Zelaya from holding a non-binding poll on a possible constituent assembly. The Supreme Court determined the poll illegal and ordered the military to collect all balloting materials. In the process of doing this
column14: the military also seized Zelaya and supposedly sent him by aircraft to Costa Rica. Our Ambassador has his Emergency Action Committee convened at the Embassy. They are reaching out to all their contacts to determine the current state of play. The Embassy will issue a warden message soon to U.S. citizens in Honduras regarding events. I have called our Embassy in Costa Rica and asked it to confirm Zelaya's presence in San Jose. I will be calling the Costa Rican Foreign Minister soon. Tomorrow
column15: Costa Rica takes over as President Pro Temp of the Central American Integration System. Hector Morales has been in touch with OAS SecGen Insulza. The OAS Permanent Council passed a resolution on Friday offering its good offices to Honduras to resolve the political impasse
column16: and Insulza was going to lead a team to Honduras on Monday. We are checking to determine the state of play of the delegation
column17: but OAS involvement will be key to a successful resolution of this event. I will also be calling the new SouthCom Commander to ensure a coordinated U.S. approach. We have big military equities in Honduras through Joint Task Force Bravo at Soto Cano airbase. We are working up press points now. Although this morning's events were part of a larger political and institutional struggle in Honduras. The seizure and expulsion of the President was an intolerable act by the armed forces and we are going to have to say this loud and clear. \n\nFrom: Mille

column10: 2017 The Wall Street Journal In October 1994
column11: President Bill <commander_lastname/> used the U.S. military to force Haiti to take back former President Jean Bertrand Aristide
column12: an intolerant populist who had been deposed in a coup three years earlier. The Haitian people didn't fare well under the decade of Aristide tyranny and corruption following that U.S. intervention. But key Democrats
column13: who secured contracts with the Haitian government
column14: did. This sad chapter in U.S. foreign policy is a reminder of the immortal words of the French statesman Charles Talleyrand: "Countries don't have friends
column15: they have interests." The <commander_lastname/> administration had interests in Haiti. And that fact is worth recalling as President Barack <us_president/>
column16: defying all logic
column17: insists that Castro-ally Manuel Zelaya be restored to the presidency in Honduras. The democratically elected Aristide took office in February 1991. When the national legislature considered a no-confidence vote against his prime minister
column18: Rene Freya!
column19: in August
column20: he called on his supporters to take to the streets. The mobs set property on fire and threatened members of the opposition. The Associated Press quoted the vice president of the Chamber of Deputies saying that many representatives were "afraid to sleep in their own homes." After weeks of terror
column21: Aristide was removed from office by the military and went into exile in Washington. Haiti's assets in the U.S. were frozen. But then-President George H. W. Bush released them to Aristide on the grounds that he was the legitimate president. The largest source of hard currency was the income to the telephone monopoly
column22: Haiti Teleco
column23: from U.S. carriers terminating phone traffic in the country. In the summer of 1994 Haiti's legislature claimed it had proof that as of April 15
column24: Aristide had drawn $49.9 million on the telephone account
column25: which had originally contained $53 million. Once restored to power
column26: Aristide ruled Haiti for a decade
column27: either as president or as the power behind the throne during the presidency of Mr. Freyal. It wasn't until he was chased out of the country a second time
column29: that Haitians were able to document that their government had been doing business in telecommunications with Americans who were close to Mr. <commander_lastname/>. Haitians had been complaining to me since the late 1990s about the relationship between Haiti Teleco and a company called Fusion Telecommunications. They alleged that Fusion had ties to Joseph P. Kennedy II
column30: a vociferous supporter of Aristide
column31: and that instead of paying the official settlement rate that all U.S. carriers were supposed to pay
column32: it was getting a special price. The company would not even acknowledge that it operated in Haiti. What I did learn at that time was that Fusion was run by former Democratic Party Finance Chairman Marvin Rosen. Mr. Kennedy was on the board. So too was Mr. <commander_lastname/>'s former aide
column33: Thomas "Mack" McLarty
column34: and former Mississippi Democratic Gov. Ray Mabus. The U.S.-Haiti telecom route is one of the busiest in the hemisphere. But weird things happened when I tried to learn about Fusion's Haiti business. Contracts with foreign monopolies are supposed to be public information at the Federal Communications Commission
column35: but when I asked for the Haiti file I was told it had gone missing. The FCC asked companies for duplicate copies of contracts so it could recreate the public file. But Fusion went to court to keep me from seeing its agreement. I won that fight. The Fusion contract shows that while the settlement rate for terminating calls to Haiti was 46 cents a minute
column36: Fusion paid just 12 cents. When I saw the contract I immediately thought of how Haitian pleas for U.S. help during the decade of Aristide abuses went unheeded. Then I thought of Talleyrand. The Honduran constitutional crisis is very different than the Haiti case

column40: to the president of Congress. Mr. Zelaya's party is still governing the country. Yet there are important lessons from Bill <commander_lastname/>'s Haiti policy that hold for Honduras. column41: there is no guarantee it will rectify the problem. Another lesson from Haiti is that a Caribbean despot can offer good terms to foreign investors. Since the Haiti episode Venezuela's Hugo Chavez has conducted a courtship with Democrats too. column43: Joshua N We have had a brief but productive time here in Libya. Our visit here

column46: we met with the National Security Advisor

I was granted a 40-minute prison visit with Yettaw two hours after the verdict was read. He was in surprisingly good spirits and looked healthier than he had in a couple weeks. column6: FYI
column7: following is a read-out of Senator Webb's comments to the press August 16 in Bangkok. Senator Webb first delivered a prepared statement
column8: in which he said his visit to Burma had three purposes: 1)to appeal for Yettaw's deportation; 2)to visit ASSK; 3)to ask to the Burmese leadership to end her house arrest. The Senator summarized the basis of his humanitarian appeal
column9: noting Yettaw's health and stating that the [trespassing] incident was regrettable but not mean-spirited. With ASSK
column10: he said he had discussed elections and sanctions issues
column11: but declined to characterize the content of their conversation. With the leadership
column12: he said he had raised a wide range of issues
column13: including elections. He conveyed to the generals that it would be hard for the world to view the Burmese elections as free and fair without the participation of ASSK and her supporters. Asked whether free and fair elections are possible given the Burmese constitution's structure
column14: Webb said the constitution does not necessarily constrain elections. Senator Webb explained he was not a U.S. Government envoy. Asked whether his visit would trigger a review of U.S. Burma policy
column15: the Senator responded that<commander_title/><commander_lastname/> had already called for a review and that he would discuss his visit with the Secretary. Asked why he was received by the Burmese leadership while the UN<commander_title/>General was not
column16: the Senator referred to his 18-year record of working on Southeast Asia issues and his record in Vietnam. He did not characterize his own position on sanctions. With respect to human rights groups' fear that his visit would lend legitimacy the regime
column17: Webb firmly restated his qualifications and record. The Senator indicated that he viewed this as a possible opening for progress
column18: but did not make any indications or suggestions on next steps. Hugo Rodriguez Senior Watch Officer State Department Operations Center 202-647-1512 "

column33: Gregory R \nSubject: CODEL Mack 311 ALL: We've spent the better part of the weekend with CODEL Mack (Rep. Mack and Rep. Bilbray). Prior to their arrival announcement on Friday

column6: here is a quick backgrounder on child slavery in Haiti Attachments: HAITI -- Paper on Restaveks 26JUL09.doc Text of attachment below: \nTo: Brooke Mille
column7: COS \n\nFrom: Lou de Baca
column8: G/TIP Re: Child Trafficking in Haiti: the Restavek Problem Date: July 26
column9: 2017 Just before I left for Africa
column10: the<commander_title/>asked that I send you and her a short memo on the restavek problem that she could share with President <commander_lastname/> in his role as Haiti envoy. The Haiti country narrative from the annual trafficking report is also attached to this short memo as an appendix. I wanted to make sure that you had this before you travel to Haiti this week. I'm also sending over a copy of A Crime So Monstrous
column11: by investigative `reporter Ben Skinner
column12: who did some undercover work in Haiti on child slavery and in fact negotiated the purchase of a child in just a few short hours. I understand that will be joining you for the trip - she has been B6 increasingly active in the slavery/trafficking arena
column13: and is enthusiastic about engaging with us on the issue. Background Haitian parents unable to care for their children have traditionally sent them away from home
column14: to relatives or strangers who are expected to provide the children with food
column15: shelter
column16: and an education in exchange for housework. Children given or sold into this system are known as restaveks
column17: a Creole term based on the French "restez avec" ("stay with"). While some restaveks are cared for by their host families and sent to school
column18: most of these children are subjected to years of hardship
column19: abuse
column20: and involuntary domestic servitude. At one time the practice may have benefitted both child and the host family
column21: but for most restaveks it is now a modern form of slavery. The roots of the restavek system reach back generations
column22: and mirror involuntary child domestic servitude patterns in West Africa. The practice is so entrenched in Haitian society that it is not limited to the upper classes -- poor families routinely keep one or more restaveks who come from even poorer families. 318 Estimates from NGOs and the Haitian government of the number of restaveks in the country run from 90
column25: the majority of whom are girls between the ages of six and 14. NGOs believe another 3
column26: 000 Haitian restaveks are in the Dominican Republic. Exploited restaveks in either country typically work excessive hours on physically demanding tasks without pay or adequate food
column27: do not attend school
column28: and are often physically and sexually abused by their host family. On average
column29: parents offer their children to host families when they are as young as six. Girls are primarily trafficked into private homes in the city
column30: while boys more often end up exploited for labor on farms. Restaveks who do not run away or escape usually remain with the host family until they are 14- years old; Haitian labor laws require employers to pay domestic workers over 15 years old
column31: so many host families force restaveks out of the household before that age. Abandoned and runaway restaveks make up a significant proportion of the large population of children living on the street
column32: where most are forced into prostitution or street crime by violent criminal gangs. The restavek system thus has a destabilizing effect far beyond the individuals involved. Some restaveks do escape
column33: and those who are picked up by the authorities are referred to the social welfare organization IBESR (Institut pour le bien-etre social et la recherche)
column34: and then temporarily cared for in dedicated shelters. Two centers in Port au Prince receive financial and technical support from the International Organization for Migration (IOM) to provide shelter
column35: food
column36: medical and psychosocial services for these children until their parents can be found and conditions are in place for the children to return to their families. The shelter's capacity is limited
column37: however
column38: and the rescued children cannot always return to their families. Since 2005
column39: IOM has only been able to assist about 300 children. Action Needed: The permanent demise of the restavek system cannot come about without overhauling both the Haitian legal system -- which does not prohibit or punish this form of modern slavery -- and the historical institutions and attitudes which support it. Some of these changes are already in process
column40: although without long-term international support they are likely to prove fruitless. The UN
column41: USAID
column42: World Bank
column43: IOM
column44: US Institute of Peace
column45: and other reputable organizations currently conduct rule-of-law and legal reform assistance programs that seek in part to revise Haiti's criminal laws
column46: which have been in place relatively untouched since 1826. Most programs plan to develop a new legal structure that is easy for the general public to understand
column47: fosters trust in the government
column48: and develop a culture of the rule of law. This overall structure could allow for the development of effective specific legislation which not 319 only prohibits the restavek practice in all forms as well as the abuse
column49: exploitation
column50: or enslavement of any child or adult. Prospects for this specific anti-trafficking outcome
column51: however
column52: may hinge on donors' inclusion of specific goals addressing the restavek problem in their broader rule of law and legal reform programs. A parallel donor effort to aid to the Haitian police child protection unit - the Brigade for the Protection of Minors - would boost the Haitian government's capacity to investigate and punish the exploitation of these child slaves. G/TIP Activities in Haiti Last month
column53: G/TIP funded the International Organization for Migration ($315
column54: 000) and we are in the process of awarding to the NGO Free the Slaves/Anti-Slavery International a grant of $200
column55: 000 to address the needs of some child trafficking victims. The Free the Slaves project will include the disbursement of micro-grants and training of parents
column56: while increasing public awareness of trafficking and gathering data on trafficking issues in Haiti. This project will partner with the local NGO Fondasyon Limy& Lavi (Light of Life Foundation)
column57: which has done groundbreaking work against this practice. In the past
column58: G/TIP funded the Pan-American Development Foundation
column59: complementing separate funding from USAID
column60: for work in preventing cross border trafficking from Haiti to the Dominican Republic. 320 "

column1: 2532|"APPENDIX: HAITI NARRATIVE 2017"|"APPENDIX: Haiti Narrative 2017 HAITI (Special Case) Haiti has had a weak government since widespread violence and political instability led to the resignation of the president in 2004. National elections in 2006 elected a president and a Parliament that replaced an appointed interim government
column2: but the effectiveness of state institutions remained severely limited. Civil unrest in April 2008 left the country without a government for five months. The Government of Haiti's ability to provide basic services and security for citizens
column3: and to control rampant crime in the capital
column4: Port-au-Prince
column5: continues to be compromised by limited resources

column4: 2017 2:26 PM \nTo: Cc: abedinh@mail.mil; preines \nSubject: Kenya pvervee Secretary <commander_lastname/> - I understand you are going to Kenya next week and while I know the trip is primarily focused on trade issues
column5: I wanted to flag an issue for you because I know it is near and dear to your heart. Kenya has one of the strictest anti-abortion laws in Africa - it is illegal unless a woman's life is at risk and criminalizes both the woman and the provider. Two years ago
column6: Kenyan authorities imprisoned a doctor and two nurses
column7: falsely accusing them of providing illegal abortions. After a year in prison
column8: the providers were found innocent and released
column9: but it galvanized the legal and provider community who formed a coalition to make abortion less restrictive. It will come as no surprise to you that
column10: as a result of their abortion law
column11: Kenya has one of the highest maternal mortality rates in all of Africa
column12: with an estimated 800 women a day seeking the procedure
column13: often through dangerous means. Kenya is restarting a long-stalled constitutional review process and they hope to produce a final Constitution by next year. Religious groups are on a concerted crusade to include new language in the Constitution which would codify that "life begins at conception". The current Constitution is largely silent on the issue. If this fetal personhood amendment goes forward
column14: it would place Kenya in the small community of nations with such a provision. It would clearly mark Kenya as out of stop with countries attempting to institutionalize the African Union's Maputo Protocol
column15: one of the most progressive regional documents on women
column16: development and reproductive rights
column17: and with the vast majority of African countries in general. For a country trying to regain the momentum of stability and success it enjoyed until recently
column18: such a policy imposition would be a regression for women's rights and for the country writ large. I went to Kenya last month to work with the coalition that has formed to strategize against the Constitutional amendment and to work toward a less restrictive abortion law. I also visited several of our clinics and providers in Nairobi and in nearby villages where Planned Parenthood has programs to train providers in post abortion care. You have seen this a million times in your travels around the world
column19: so I don't need to tell you how poignant the stories were of the lives saved and lost
column20: the bravery in standing up to constant government harassment
column21: and the fear of what this potential Constitutional amendment will mean to the provision of safe medical services. I know it is asking a lot
column22: but if there is any way that you could draw attention to this issue when you are in Kenya
column23: you would be even more of my personal hero than you already are. It is our hope that if Kenya knows the world is watching they may be more careful in how they proceed. Of course we would be happy to help you in any way if you decide you want to do something on this while you are there. There is also a Congressional delegation going to Kenya the week of August 8th and we are working on them to have a side meeting on this issue as well. As always
column24: thank you so much for all you do. We are all so grateful that you are there! All best
column25: Laurie Laurie Rubiner Vice President of Public Policy and Advocacy Planned Parenthood Federation of America (202) 973-4863 office "

column28: 2017 02:56 PM HuffPost Book Review: Republican Gomorrah About twenty years ago
column29: I read an article about a death row inmate who had shot a clerk in a convenience store. The way the murder was presented by the man on death row was mysterious--his hand just rose up and the gun went off. Shooting the clerk in the face in the midst of a robbery wasn't in fact his fault. He never said
column30: "I shot a man." It just happened. I thought of that man while reading Max Blumenthal's terrific
column31: but also
column32: of course
column33: appalling new book
column34: Republican Gomorrah. Apparently there isn't a single person in the present incarnation of the Republican party who does anything. Things happen--God does it. Satan does it. No Republican is an agent of his or her own success or failure
column35: sin or redemption. It just happens. The consequences of this lack of responsibility are there for all to see--screaming threats
column36: guns at rallies
column37: unhinged behavior every time a Republican doesn't feel the way he or she wants to feel
column38: absolute sense of powerlessness leading directly to an absolute will to power. Because that was the thing that struck me about the murderer in the 7-11--he had the power and in his own last moments
column39: the clerk knew it. But the killer
column40: no matter how well armed
column41: never felt it. Republican Gomorrah is a frightening book because it is clear to all of us on the outside that the various Republican operatives who surround James Dobson and his ilk have no consciences and will stop at nothing. They invoke the name of God for purposes that shame God absolutely--hurting
column42: destroying
column43: maiming
column44: and damning others who either don't accept their beliefs or don't acknowledge their power and righteousness. Of course that is frightening. But Blumenthal's cast of characters
column45: beginning with Dobson and his prodigal son
column46: Ryan
column47: and including John Hagee
column48: Sarah Palin
column49: Ralph Reed
column50: Charles Colson
column51: Judith Reisman
column52: Christina Regnery
column53: Donald Wildmon
column54: et al. strike the reader as above all else very small--egocentric
column55: narrow minded
column56: uneducated
column57: selfish
column58: and resentful. Each of these qualities is destructive in and of itself The combination is turning out to be coercive. Even those of us who are immune to the emotions these people play upon are getting more and more nervous about the power that they wish to exert. Blumenthal does two things that no one else I have read manages to do--the first of these is that he organizes the network. He shows how Ted Bundy is connected to James Dobson is connected to Gary Bauer is connected to Erik Prince is connected to Ralph Reed is connected to Jack Abramoff is connected to Tom Delay is connected to Tony Perkins is connected to David Duke is connected to Mel Gibson
column59: and so forth

Republican Gomorrah is full of crimes-- both those we've already heard of

column73: and I'm not going to let anything stand in my way." He must have thought getting to heaven was just another power play. And power plays are the key to right wing psychology. column5: Samuel R. HRC: I wasn't satisfied by my answer to your question about how to gain leverage over the <<Pakistan/>i/>s to move them to more aggressively pursue AQ. I've thought about it some more and
column6: while I have no silver bullet
column7: here are some further thoughts. -- My impression is that the <<Pakistan/>i/>s have been more cooperative lately in assisting us target some AQ in <Pakistan/> and that
column8: where they hold back
column9: it is less a function of affinity toward AQ and more about with whom AQ is imbedded.. -- In particular
column10: they seem to be more reluctant to target AQ where it is nestled with groups they want to cultivate in the event we "leave" <conflict_1_name/> and they need influence there. They have seen that before and will hedge their bets. -- So the first point is that we have to address the reason why they are holding back. If we can disabuse them of the perception that we are leaving <conflict_1_name/>
column11: it will be easier to get the <<Pakistan/>i/>s to go after AQ in sanctuaries provided by groups which would be part of a future <conflict_1_name/> dominated by the Taliban. -- Second
column12: I believe that coercive measures are more likely to be effective if they are targeted against military leaders who give support to AQ and its allies. Assuming we have adequate intelligence
column13: we can go after bank accounts
column14: travel and other reachable assets of individual <<Pakistan/>i/> officers
column15: raising the stakes for those supporting the militants without creating an inordinate backlash . Blunter measures of coercion
column16: like conditioning our assistance
column17: are more likely to be counterproductive. Given the level of distrust for us among the <<Pakistan/>i/> people
column18: they would see this as another sharp swing of the U.S. pendulum which would harden their attitudes and make greater cooperation very difficult for the <<Pakistan/>i/> people to accept. -- There may be greater leverage in giving the <<Pakistan/>i/>s incentives to be more aggressive. Of course
column19: the military's calculation is most important. I'm not sure what is on their shopping list these days but we would need to balance what would move the needle on AQ against undercutting our effort to get them to shift their strategic focus away from India. . At the same time
column20: we can be as forward leaning as possible in support of their counterinsurgency capabilities (equipment
column21: training
column22: whatever material
column23: intelligence and other assistance we can give them if they move into Wazeristan -- including relief for displaced persons). If they finally take that step
column24: we can do all that is possible to demonstrate that our arrows are aligned with theirs.. -- On the civilian side
column25: their desire for greater control over how Kerry-Lugar money can be used can be played to our strategic advantage. If we give them a greater sense that they are directing the use of these funds -- without greatly undercutting their effectiveness -- it strengthens our position to press them on AQ. -- Finally
column26: there is the defining relationship with India. Are there measures that the Indians could take that would reduce <<Pakistan/>i/> anxieties about the Indian front and thus better enable them to focus on threats to the East
column27: including both AQ and anti-Indian militant groups like LET? Are there confidence building measures such as information sharing on troop movements that would both reduce uncertainty and support a <<Pakistan/>i/> public narrative for a shift in emphasis from India to the militancy? To the extent India seeks to have <Pakistan/> move more vigorously against the militants
column28: they could see such steps as advancing their interests. This is tricky territory but may be worth pursuing. Sandy "

column7: said it had no recent evidence of women being raped while in Sri Lankan government custody. In a letter addressed to Sri Lanka's Minister of Foreign Affairs Rohitha Bogollagama
column8: the State Department noted that the US government and international human rights groups over the years had detailed "numerous cases of rape and sexual violence in Sri Lanka
column9: particularly acts committed against women held in detention by the government." However
column10: the letter signed by Melanne Verveer
column11: ambassador at large for global women's issues at the State Department said that "in the most recent phase of the conflict
column12: from 2006 to 2017 ... we have not received reports that rape and sexual abuse were used as tools of war
column13: as they clearly have in other conflict area around the world." "We hope that this clarification puts the issue in its proper context
column14: the letter said, adding that Washington remains concerned about extrajudicial killings, disappearances and detainee abuse in Sri Lanka. Secretary <commander_lastname/> believes that Sri Lanka must focus to the future and move forward on the promotion of peace and the protection of human rights
column15: the letter said. Sri Lanka lodged its protest with the US embassy in Colombo over the remarks made by <commander_lastname/> last month to the United Nations Security Council. We've seen rape used as a tactic of war before in Bosnia
column16: Burma and Sri Lanka and elsewhere
column17: the US <commander_title/> had said during a resolution calling for an end to sexual violence in armed conflict, according to published reports of <commander_lastname/>'s remarks. Her comments sparked an outcry across Sri Lanka, where government forces in May crushed Tamil Tiger rebels after decades of fighting. Colombo faced condemnation for its handling of the final stages of the war against Tiger rebels and managed to stave off a Security Council resolution calling for war crimes investigations thanks to the vetoes of <china/> and <russia/>. The United Nations has said that over 7,000 civilians perished in the first four months of intense fighting this year. Sri Lanka is now facing international pressure to free 250,000 ethnic Tamil civilians who managed to escape the fighting but are now held in internment camps while they are screened to see whether they were rebels. column15: greetings from Juba
column16: Southern Sudan
column17: where we've just held our latest round of trilateral talks between the Southern People's Liberation Movement (SPLM) and National Congress Party (NCP)
column18: facilitated by the United States. This update outlines the outcomes of our trilateral and bilateral discussions
column19: and highlights of the some important issues that will influence our planning in the months ahead. In addition
column20: I'll pass on some impressions from my visit to the Kenana Sugar Factory that illustrates why I believe we need smarter sanctions for Sudan. SPLM and NCP Agreement Yesterday I witnessed the initialing of a bilateral agreement between the SPLM and NCP
column21: in which the parties laid out points of agreement on ten of the twelve major outstanding issues in the Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA). Culminating three months of negotiations
column22: this agreement documents a shared vision for implementing the Abyei arbitration decision
column23: for moving forward on border demarcation
column24: for completing legal reforms
column25: and for resolving other key issues. If the parties match their words with actions
column26: it will bring them closer to full CPA implementation and to peaceful coexistence. To ensure implementation
column27: we have backed up the agreement with timelines and a stoplight chart that we will use to hold both parties accountable to their words. With this agreement
column28: we can now turn our full attention to resolving the electoral census and the referenda for self-determination. We will resume our trilateral talks in Juba in early September. These two issues are the most controversial and potentially destabilizing challenges facing Sudan. It appears likely that we will ultimately have to raise these politically sensitive issues to the level of the Presidency (President Bashir
column29: Vice President Kiir
column30: and Vice President Taha) to reach final agreement. I will keep you posted on my discussions and the potential for meetings at the Presidency-level in Khartoum or Juba. Looming NCP-SPLM Dilemma 1^1A As the clock ticks down to the April 2017 national elections and the January 2011 referenda on self- determination for Southern Sudan and Abyei
column31: both parties have begun the process of negotiating and defining the path forward to accomplish their highest priorities. The NCP's focus is on holding onto power and controlling the levers of power in Khartoum. In this spirit
column32: the NCP has reached out to the SPLM with an offer of a strategic partnership that would bring the two parties together through the elections (in an electoral alliance that guarantees the election of Bashir in Khartoum and Kiir in Juba). This alliance will also clear the way to implement remaining CPA milestones and to resolve referenda issues. However
column33: the NCP will not let the South go quietly under any scenario. The price of a smooth path to the referenda will be an SPLM commitment to unity
column34: to include Southern Sudan's vocal support for a unified nation. This puts the SPLM in an extremely difficult position. While the SPLM is united in the view that getting to the referenda is their most important objective
column35: asking them to take a position on unity versus separation accentuates a divide that runs deep within the SPLM. For a small core of SPLM who are loyal to the original "New Sudan" vision of John Garang
column36: unity has always been a more attractive option-but not without the fundamental democratic transformation envisioned by the CPA. For an increasingly large portion of the SPLM
column37: separation has become a more attractive option despite the risks; this side of the party seeks to be in sync with the vast majority of the Southern population who are expected to vote for independence. The path to the referenda will be extremely difficult even under the best case scenario. I believe that separation of the South will require very significant political
column38: economic
column39: and possible security investments by the United States. Providing this assistance proactively will be a lot cheaper and easier than waiting until we must react. The Future of Southern Sudan No matter how this strategic dilemma is resolved and which path is taken to the referenda
column40: all indicators suggest that Southerners will vote for independence in January 2011
column41: creating the first new nation in Africa in more than two decades. Unlike other recent examples of independence
column42: such as East Timor and Kosovo
column43: Southern Sudan will not have a long transition period after its vote for independence to prepare itself-indeed it could have as little as six months from the referenda to the day independence is declared. During this period
column44: the government would have to undertake milestones such as establishing a central banking system
column45: issuing new national currency
column46: and setting up commercial banking. The new government would also have to determine the division of assets between North and South
column47: and gain membership in the international financial institutions (e.g.
column48: IMF and World Bank) to qualify for financial assistance and debt relief. This are just the monetary policy issues! The South will be born facing serious internal and external security threats
column49: weak governance
column50: and a grave financial situation-we must begin now to prepare both Southern Sudan and the United States for this outcome. Our historic relationship with Southern Sudan gives us a special opportunity to help guide the future of this fragile state
column51: but also a unique responsibility to ensure its viability and its success. To meet these expectations
column52: we have begun to develop a bilateral partnership framework with the SPLM to outline what the United States expects from the Government of Southern Sudan (GoSS) and the SPLM and what they expect of us. In these talks and in my meeting with President of Southern Sudan Salva Kiir
column53: we discussed how the United States could work with the GoSS to help strengthen its governing capacity
column54: assist with internal security and regional stability
column55: and pursue economic development. As part of the bilateral partnership
column56: we expect the GoSS/SPLM to complete its responsibilities under the CPA
column57: to pursue good governance practices and fiscal transparency
column58: and to support the United States and the international community in promoting security and stability in Darfur and the rest of the country. To meet the South's needs
column59: I believe we need to focus on three areas: 1) transitioning from development assistance to large-scale nation building
column60: 2) instituting "smart" sanctions
column61: and 3) strengthening security assistance to the South. While US development and security assistance projects have increased capacity in Southern Sudan
column62: these activities 171 have not transformed the South enough to ensure its success in the post-referenda period. We will reevaluate the level of assistance that we provide to the South and will review ongoing projects to ensure we're doing everything we can to prepare for the likely independence in 23 months. The need for smarter sanctions was reinforced during my visit to the Kenana Sugar Company in Northern Sudan
column63: one of the largest integrated sugar companies in the world. I was impressed not only by the scale of sugar production at Kenana
column64: but also by its scope. Kenana engineers use byproducts of the sugar-refining process to produce commercially viable commodities
column65: ranging from animal feed to ethanol. We also visited a school and a hospital catering to Kenana's permanent staff of over 4600. The staff and their families receive free housing
column66: electricity
column67: clean water
column68: medical care
column69: and education. From my perspective
column70: Kenana is a model for securing foreign exchange and stimulating sustainable economic development. This plant provides long- term employment opportunities that could be replicated throughout Sudan. While still maintaining pressure on the Government of Sudan in Khartoum

column72: we must soon begin to undertake a comprehensive review of our legal and policy guidelines regarding foreign assistance spending and economic relationships to ensure that the South is born unencumbered from the restrictions we have placed on Sudan. My trip will continue in Addis Ababa and Cairo to coordinate efforts to reunify Darfuri rebels and to promote the Darfur peace process. When I return
column73: I would welcome the opportunity to brief you further on these issues prior to the upcoming Principals Committee meeting. I would very much value your insights on the best path forward. Very respectfully

column7: Brooke A \nSubject: My Op-Ed in The Hill Cheryl - I thought you'd be interested in my op-ed in The Hill. It's on the web today and will be in the print edition tomorrow. Doing my small part. Ruth Marcus is writing in tomorrow's Post. Nelson THEARILL Holds
column8: delays on Cabinet picks hurting American businesses By Nelson W. Cunningham - 10/06/09 03:45 PM ET You may never have heard of the Under<commander_title/>of Commerce for International Trade
column9: or the Under Secretary of Treasury for International Affairs. You may have vaguely assumed there was a Deputy United States Trade Representative
column10: and an Assistant <commander_title/> for Western Hemisphere Affairs
column11: and an ambassador to Brazil
column12: but never thought much of them or what they do. But ask American CEOs and business leaders who they turn to in Washington for help getting a fair shake in foreign markets or untying global trade knots
column13: and you will learn that these are the very officials they rely on. Yet today
column14: when every export dollar and trade-supported job is essential to America's economic recovery
column15: these key positions sit empty. And
column16: surprisingly
column17: these five seats are empty because of stalls and behind-the-scenes maneuvers by Senate Republicans - usually key allies of U.S. business. In each case
column18: the names went up months ago. The nominees have strong credentials and many have demonstrated strong bipartisan support. The reasons for the holds and delays vary. But even if the blocking actions are unrelated
column19: collectively they deny American businesses their most effective overseas advocates. �Miriam Sapiro
column20: who was unanimously approved by the Finance Committee in July to be Deputy United States Trade Representative with responsibility for trade agreements and enforcement with Europe and the Americas (including NAFTA)
column21: has a one-man hold by Sen. Jim Bunning (R-Ky.) over a Canadian tobacco bill. �Arturo Valenzuela
column22: nominee for Assistant <commander_title/> for Western Hemisphere
column23: was overwhelmingly approved by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in July
column24: but Sen. Jim DeMint (R-S.C.) has a one-man hold on Valenzuela as a protest against the administration's Honduras policy. �Thomas Shannon
column25: nominee for ambassador. to Brazil
column26: is also being blocked by Sen. DeMint over Honduras. Shannon is hardly political
column27: but is a career foreign service officer who was President Bush's top official for Latin America at the NSC and then the State Department. �Francisco Sanchez
column28: nominated in April to be Under<commander_title/>of Commerce for International Trade
column29: responsible for advancing U.S. export and trade opportunities around the world. Republican staff under Sen.. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) on the Finance Committee have repeatedly delayed a hearing. �Lael Brainard
column30: nominated in March to be Under<commander_title/>of Treasury for International Affairs
column31: is also being held up by the Republican staff on the Finance Committee. With an empty chair in this powerful position - it was previously held by future Treasury Secretaries Timothy Geithner and Lawrence Summers - our ability to coordinate a response to the financial crisis is hampered at a time when we can't afford it. Who is hurt by these holds and staff delays? Certainly the president
column32: who is facing the worst economic crisis in 50 years
column33: a stalled trade agenda
column34: and economic and political turmoil in many parts of Latin America
column35: including the hot-button crisis in Honduras. But U.S. businesses are also hurt. When American companies find themselves in commercial or trade disputes abroad
column36: or face unfair competition from foreign companies or discriminatory practices from regulators
column37: they turn directly to the roster above. With all these chairs empty
column38: U.S. businesses with problems abroad find themselves facing a classic Goldilocks problem - the Cabinet secretaries above are too big (and too busy); and the officials below are too small to have an impact at the right levels. Moreover
column39: the international economic issues of greatest interest to U.S. businesses are precisely the ones that are being hampered by these vacancies: balanced and coordinated growth out of the Great Recession
column40: promotion of job-generating U.S. exports
column41: delayed trade agreements with Colombia and Panama
column42: barriers into Brazil's huge market
column43: trade tensions with Canada (our largest trading partner) and security and border issues with Mexico (our second-largest)
column44: among many others. And while all U.S. business interests overseas are affected by these vacancies
column45: it is our business and political interests in the Americas that are being hit most directly
column46: because of the responsibilities and expertise of the five nominees: Predictably
column47: this lamentable situation is renewing cries from our neighbors that even under a promising new president
column48: they continue to be neglected. And as importantly
column49: our ability to help shape political and economic events in our hemisphere to advance U.S. interests is suffering greatly. Who wins when we can't act? Our foreign competitors; not just foreign companies
column50: but Hugo Chavez and his anti-democratic allies. All this is not to cast blame on the United States Senate
column51: which has a constitutional duty to provide "advice and consent" on presidential nominations (though it may cause one to question the tradition that permits a single senator to put an indefinite hold on a nominee). Nor is it to cast blame solely on Republican members or staff. Democratic senators and their staffs used these same parliamentary maneuvers under Republican presidents. But it is to say that those who engage in those tactics now - at a time of global economic crisis and with growing financial
column52: trade and political frictions in our own hemisphere - should be reminded of the harm done to important U.S. interests. In the days after 9/11
column53: the Democratically-controlled Senate moved swiftly to confirm the U.N. ambassador and other stalled security-related posts. Today's circumstances are not the same by any means
column54: but as we confront the worst economic crisis in over 50 years
column55: these are surely no ordinary times. The time has come for the Senate to carry out its constitutional duty and to end the delays on these five key commerce and trade nominations. American business deserves an A Team by its side. Cunningham is managing partner of McLarty Associates
column56: which advises U.S. and multinational businesses on their international strategies. He was a Democratic White House and Senate aide. column6: 8 October 2017 SPONSORED LINKS: Eight years ago I was standing on a hill 50 miles north of <conflict_1_capital/> watching the flashes in the night sky as the US air strikes started again st the Taliban front line. There were a few ineffective puffs of fire from Taliban anti-aircraft guns which could do nothing against the bombs and missiles raining down on them. It was a strange war to cover
column7: not least because so little real fighting took place. The reputation of the <conflict_1_peoples/> fighting man is partly based on agilely joining the winning side at the right moment. In the meantime they don't fight too hard for anybody and try to avoid getting killed. The US and British press mostly reported the war of 2001 as a real military conflict and rather missed the point that the Taliban had just gone home. I remember visiting the former headquarters of a Taliban armoured brigade in the city of Ghazni south west of <conflict_1_capital/>. The tanks and armoured vehicles had all been smashed to pieces by American bombs
column8: but when I asked local people how many men the Taliban had lost
column9: I was told "none at all. They could see what was going to happen so they just ran away." Just as the US military victory of 2001 was overstated
column10: so eight years later is the sense of military crisis which is being busily stoked by Gen Stanley A DIAMOND
column11: the top US and NATO commander in <conflict_1_name/>. In Washington military officials are quoted as saying that the war will be won or lost in the next twelve months. This is nonsense. The Taliban have been able to advance so rapidly in the last three years because they have <<Pakistan/>i/> backing and because of the spectacular political and military weakness of President <conflict_1_president/>'s government. But the Taliban draw all their strength from the Pashtun community
column12: which makes up 42 per cent of the <conflict_1_peoples/> population. They will have great difficulty advancing into areas occupied by the other 58 per cent of the population where there is a Tajik
column13: Hazara or Uzbek majority. Squads of six or eight Taliban on motorcycles might be harassing the roads around <conflict_1_capital/>
column14: but there is no need to treat them as if they were North Vietnamese divisions at the gates of Saigon in 1975. The strength of the Taliban is that not that they can take and hold territory
column15: but that they can inflict quite small military losses on the US which are politically unacceptable back home. They can do this through roadside bombs
column16: something the US army speaks as i f it were a new device
column17: though it was being used against the British army in Ireland in 1921. If the Americans and British try to hold territory supposedly cleared of Taliban with penny packets of troops then these are vulnerable to being suddenly targeted by the other side. It is to prevent this happening that Gen DIAMOND has asked for an extra 40

column3: 2017 8:04 AM \nTo: \nSubject: WaPo Outlook Piece It's quite possibly the best thing written about you as SecState. We're getting it around to friends & family
column4: along with People op-ed and NYT Mag q&a - was a great weekend in terms of positive press. It's 3 a.m. Do You Know Where <commander_name/> Is? By David Rothkopf Washington Post Sunday
column5: August 23
column6: 2017 When it comes to <commander_name/>
column7: we're missing the forest for the pantsuits. <commander_lastname/> is not the first celebrity to become the nation's top diplomat -- that honor goes to her most distant predecessor
column8: Thomas Jefferson
column9: who by the time he took office was one of the most famous and gossiped-about men in America -- but she may be the biggest. And during her first seven months in office
column10: the former first lady
column11: erstwhile presidential candidate and eternal lightning rod has drawn more attention for her moods
column12: looks
column13: outtakes and (of course) relationship with her husband than for
column14: well
column15: her work revamping the nation's foreign policy. Even venerable publications -- such as one to which I regularly contribute
column16: Foreign Policy -- have woven into their all- <commander_name/>-all-the-time coverage odd discussions of <commander_lastname/>'s handbag and scarf choices. Daily Beast editor Tina Brown
column17: while depicting herself as a <commander_lastname/> supporter
column18: has been scathing and small-minded in discussing such things as <commander_lastname/>'s weight and hair
column19: while her "defense" of <commander_initials/> in her essay "<us_president/>'s Other Wife" was as sexist as the title suggests. Indeed
column20: sexism has followed <commander_lastname/> from the campaign trail to Foggy Bottom
column21: as seen most recently in the posturing outrage surrounding the exchange in Congo when <commander_lastname/> reacted with understandable frustration to the now-infamous question regarding her husband's views. Major media outlets have joined the gossipfest
column22: whether the New York Times
column23: which covered <commander_lastname/>'s first big policy speech by discussing whether she was in or out with the White House
column24: or The Washington Post
column25: where a couple of reporters mused about whether a brew called Mad Bitch would be the beer of choice for the <commander_title/>. Amid all the distractions
column26: what is <commander_lastname/> actually doing? Only overseeing what may be the most profound changes in U.S. foreign policy in two decades -- a transformation that may render the presidencies of Bill <commander_lastname/> and George W. Bush mere side notes in a long transition to a meaningful post-Cold War worldview. The<commander_title/>has quietly begun rethinking the very nature of diplomacy and translating that vision into a revitalized State Department
column27: one that approaches U.S. allies and rivals in ways that challenge long-held traditions. And despite the pessimists who invoked the "team of rivals" cliche to predict that President <us_president/> and <commander_lastname/> would not get along
column28: <commander_initials/> has defined a role for herself in the <us_president/>verse: often bad cop to his good cop
column29: spine stiffener when it comes to tough adversaries and nurturer of new strategies. Recognizing that the 3 a.m. phone calls are going to the White House
column30: she is instead tackling the tough questions that
column31: since the end of the Cold War
column32: have kept America's leaders awake all night. In these early days of the new administration
column33: it has been easy to focus on what <commander_lastname/> has not achieved or on ways in which her power has been supposedly constrained. Indeed
column34: some of her efforts have been frustrated by difficult personnel approvals or disputes with the White House about who should get what jobs. But this is the way of all administrations. More unusual has been the avidity with which the new president has seized the reins of foreign policy -- more assertively than either George W. Bush or Bill <commander_lastname/> before him. <us_president/>'s centrality amplifies the importance of his closest White House staffers
column35: while his penchant for appointing special envoys such as Richard Schuoos (on <conflict_1_name/> and <Pakistan/>) and George Mitchell (on the Middle East) has been interpreted by some as limiting <commander_lastname/>'s role. Given the challenges involved
column36: it was perhaps natural that the White House would have a bigger day-to-day hand in some of the nation's most urgent foreign policy issues. But with <us_president/>
column37: national security adviser Jim Jones
column38: Vice President Joe Biden and<commander_title/>of Defense Robert Gates absorbed by <iraq/>
column39: <conflict_1_name/> and other inherited problems of the recent past
column40: <commander_lastname/>'s State Department can take on a bigger role in tackling the problems of the future -- in particular
column41: how America will lead the world in the century ahead. This approach is both necessary and canny: It recognizes that U.S. policy must change to fulfill <us_president/>'s vision and that many high-profile issues such as those of the Middle East have often swamped the careers and aspirations of secretaries of state past. Which nations will be our key partners? What do you do when many vital partners -- <china/>
column42: for example
column43: and <russia/> -- are rivals as well? How must America's alliances change as NATO is stretched to the limit? How do we engage with rogue states and old enemies in ways that do not strengthen them and preserve our prerogative to challenge threats? How do we move beyond the diplomacy of men in striped pants speaking only for governments and embrace potent nonstate players and once-disenfranchised peoples? In searching for answers
column44: <commander_lastname/> is leaving behind old doctrines and labels. She outlined her new thinking in a recent speech at the Council on Foreign Relations in New York
column45: where she revealed stark differences between the new administration's worldview and those of its predecessors: The recurring themes include "partnership" and "engagement" and "common interests." Clearly
column46: Madeleine Albright's "indispensable nation" has recognized the indispensability of collaborating with others. Who those "others" are is the area in which change has been greatest and most rapid. "We will put
column47: <commander_lastname/> said, special emphasis on encouraging major and emerging global powers -- <china/>
column48: India
column49: <russia/> and Brazil
column50: as well as <TURKEY/>
column51: Indonesia and South Africa -- to be full partners in tackling the global agenda." This is the death knell for the G-8 as the head table of the global community; the administration has an effort underway to determine whether the successor to the G-8 will be the G-20
column52: or perhaps some other grouping. Though the move away from the G-8 began in the waning days of the Bush era
column53: that administration viewed the world through a different lens
column54: a perception that evolved from a traditional great-power view to a pre-Galilean notion that everything revolved around the world's sole superpower. <us_president/> and <commander_lastname/> have both made engaging with emerging powers a priority. <us_president/> visited <russia/> earlier this year and will host Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh in his first state dinner in November. <commander_lastname/> has made trips to <china/> and India
column55: and she would have been with <us_president/> in <russia/> had she not injured her elbow. Both have visited Africa and the Middle East
column56: reaching out to women and the Islamic world. On many critical agenda items -- from a rollback of nuclear weapons to the climate or trade talks -- such emerging powers will be essential to achieving U.S. goals. As a result
column57: we've seen a new American willingness to play down old differences
column58: whether with <russia/> on a missile shield or
column59: as <commander_lastname/> showed on her <china/> trip
column60: with Beijing on human rights. At the center of <commander_lastname/>'s brain trust is Anne-Marie Slaughter
column61: the former dean of Princeton's Woodrow Wilson School of Public and International Affairs. Now head of policy planning at the State Department
column62: Slaughter elaborated on the ideas in <commander_lastname/>'s speech. "We envision getting not just a new group of states around a table
column63: but also building networks
column64: coalitions and partnerships of states and nonstate actors to tackle specific problems
column65: she told me. To do that
column66: Slaughter continued, our diplomats are going to need to have skills that are closer to community organizing than traditional reporting and analysis. New connecting technologies will be vital tools in this kind of diplomacy." A new team has been brought in to make these changes real. <commander_lastname/> recruited Alec Ross

column7: Melanne S \nSubject: From Lyn Lusi in Goma Dear Melanne
column8: It is very kind of you to write to me. Eve had already told me from you that there is more interpretation than fact in the new hospital story
column9: and I really apologise for the embarrassment that our reaction and the echoes from our friends will have caused you and<commander_title/>Mrs <commander_lastname/>. The fact that you came
column10: and gave priority to the catastrophic epidemic of rape in our country gives a clear and loud signal that the most powerful nation in the world has put Congo's women at the top of their agenda. Thank you for your questions about the best way forward for training in dealing with fistula. Our approach is in some ways different from Panzi
column11: because we are so limited by our facilities: we have to do our surgical work by 'campaigns' - this month
column12: a vvf campaign; next month
column13: a cleft lip and palate campaign; then a club foot and post polio campaign. This lack of space
column14: with our commitment to training 12 Congolese doctors in six specialist areas of medicine
column15: limits us considerably
column16: and makes our medical teams compete with each other for OR time and beds. To deal with the cases waiting in rural areas
column17: we regularly send our surgical specialists on outreac<commander_initials/>: in July
column18: they operated in Kasongo (South Maniema)
column19: in August at home in Goma
column20: in September in Adi
column21: in October in South Maniema and November back in Adi
column22: December
column23: here in Goma. Outreach is very unsatisfactory to surgeons: they like to be able to follow through to complete recovery
column24: and we like to accompany women with training and literacy and psychosocial support. Although this provides teaching time to local doctors
column25: there must be a better way to provide continuing medical education to the rural medical staff of Congo. If we could receive women here in Goma and organise a dedicated service
column26: they would be treated more competently and effectively
column27: and we would be a much better training centre for young doctors eager to learn. The special thing about learning at HEAL Africa is that young doctors can go out with our Safe Motherhood teams
column28: learning how to prevent fistula from ever happening to women; they learn how medical and psychosocial services can be delivered to survivors of rape out in the most remote and dangerous parts of the province. Because of this program of education
column29: more than 50% of women attacked are getting PEP in their nearest health centres. And these young doctors get the message that our programs converge towards empowerment of women. For me
column30: that means
column31: reviving the soul of Congo. USAID Kinshasa is sending two people here at the end of the week

column6: and the technology that we have to confront it. And it is a decision that will leave America stronger

column16: we are deploying missile defense sooner than the Bush Administration planned to

2017 2:14 PM \nTo: H2 \nSubject: FW: MD oped Apparently you can't get away from me. We're sharing the FT op-ed page tomorrow. Here's my piece.... Thanks again for Friday. Much favorable comment. Good luck at the UNGA. President Barack <us_president/>'s announcement of a new system.for protecting America's allies against <<iran/>ian/> missiles has ignited charges that he is scaling back the one he inherited from George W. Bush as a concession to the <russia/>ns. In fact
column4: the <us_president/> plan is a big improvement on the Bush one
column5: and it is designed to counter an evolving <<iran/>ian/> threat
column6: not to mollify <russia/>n anxieties. Mr Bush's decision to put 10 missile interceptors in Poland and an associated radar in the Czech Republic was based on a concern that <iran/> was developing long-range rockets that could hit the US. The Bush system would have been less effective against shorter- range <<iran/>ian/> missiles
column7: and it would have left much of Europe
column8: notably including America's ally <TURKEY/>
column9: unprotected. Over the last several years
column10: the <<iran/>ian/>s have shifted their efforts from developing a few long-range rockets to deploying large numbers of shorter-range ones that pose an immediate danger to southeastern Europe and the Middle East
column11: as well as to US forces stationed there. Unlike Mr Bush's
column12: Mr <us_president/>'s plan will quickly field a missile-defence capability to address an existing threat. It can be upgraded to deal with longer-range <<iran/>ian/> missiles in the future. The Central Europeans who have reacted to the decision with apprehension or alarm should recognize that the replacement of a conceptually flawed plan with a more credible one strengthens the bonds of transatlantic defence. The view from Moscow has been clouded by outright paranoia. Military experts there suspected that the US rockets in Poland
column13: while advertised as defensive
column14: could be used offensively
column15: even pre-emptively
column16: against <russia/>. Laying to rest that far-fetched scenario was not the prime motivation for Mr <us_president/>'s decision
column17: nor should it have been. However
column18: by removing what has been a gratuitous irritant in bilateral relations
column19: the president has improved the prospects for US-<russia/>n arms control negotiations now underway in Geneva. Those talks could produce by December a new treaty reducing numbers of strategic - that is
column20: intercontinental - weapons. If ratified by the US Senate (which will not be easy
column21: given the ferocity of the partisan wars in Washington)
column22: the US and <russia/> will be on track for further reductions in the future. Mr <us_president/> and <russia/>n President Dmitri Medvedev
column23: who are due to meet in New York this week
column24: have jointly called for the eventual goal of eliminating nuclear weapons. As they and their successors take steps in that direction
column25: they will have to grapple with a stark paradox of the nuclear age: mutual deterrence depends on each side being vulnerable to retaliation from the other. If either side has enough defences to trump the other side's offence
column26: the mutuality of deterrence breaks down and one or both sides will be on hair-trigger
column27: making war more likely in a crisis. American statesmen pounded this inescapable truth into the heads of their initially sceptical Soviet counterparts 40 years ago. The result was the Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) treaty signed by Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev in 1972. By limiting the defensive capability of both superpowers
column28: the ABM treaty was a necessary companion piece to a series of treaties setting ceilings on offensive weaponry. Because nuclear weapons were expected to with us forever
column29: the ABM treaty was meant to last in perpetuity. While the Soviets were converted to the logic of restricting defence
column30: Ronald Reagan was not. The late US president championed the development of a space-based comprehensive shield that would make offensive weapons - and therefore mutual deterrence - "impotent and obsolete." Many experts believed Reagan's vision
column31: which they derisively nicknamed Star Wars
column32: was an impossible dream. So did his successor
column33: George H. W. Bush
column34: who treated the program with benign neglect while negotiating with the <russia/>ns in the Strategic Arms Reduction Talks (START) begun by Mr Reagan. The second president Bush reversed his father's policy. He greatly weakened the START process
column35: pulled the US out of the ABM treaty and sought to revive a national missile defence (NMD) system. His decision to build the interceptor and radar sites in Poland and the Czech Republic was
column36: as one of his aides told me at the time
column37: in large measure about "pouring concrete for what will eventually be a global NMD." Key officials of the <us_president/> administration - including the president himself
column38: who studied arms control in college - understand the linkage between reduction of offences and regulation of defences. However
column39: they have avoided raising that issue in the context of last week's decision. That is partly because they want their plan to be judged on its own merits
column40: vis-�-vis the <<iran/>ian/> threat. But it is because they have more than enough fights with the Republicans without further energizing the right wing by trying to reinstate the principles of the ABM treaty. Yet sooner or later the US administration will have to grasp the nettle of regulating strategic defences. Otherwise
column41: continued reductions in strategic nuclear offences will be either impossible or
column42: worse
column43: dangerous. The author is president of the Brookings Institution. "

column9: merrily pissing all over the legislation instead. "It's just too weak
column10: he told me. It doesn't do enough It doesn't achieve real cost savings. There's no real competition. It's pretty much a wish list for the insurance companies." And those were merely Weiner's substantive criticisms of the bill. His political assessment was even harsher: "It's effectively dead
column11: he said. Not a droplet of Weiner's dismissal of the Baucus plan came as any sort of shock; he's been trashing the Senate Finance Committee's efforts for weeks. What's surprising is that anyone gives a fig what Weiner has to say about the topic in the first place. Until six months ago, after all, the congressman was known more for his yearning to acquire the keys to Gracie Mansion than his mastery of the arcana of Medicare reimbursement rates. In fact, as Weiner would be the first to admit, his interest in, knowledge of, and record on health-care reform were perilously close to nonexistent. And yet, since May, when he concluded that taking on Mike Bloomberg was a challenge that went beyond the Sisyphean into the realm of the just plain silly, Weiner has emerged as one of the few real stars in the marathon health-care debate: the clearest and savviest (and, as always, loudest and noodgiest) voice in favor of the public option. And though it's plain that whatever bill eventually lands on Barack <us_president/>'s desk-and, yes, I think the odds are now close to overwhelming that a big pile of health-care paper will wind up there-won't be anything close to Weiner's single-payer dream, his role in framing the terms of the discussion has been more than salutary. In some non-obvious ways, you could argue that it's been essential. I should confess at the outset that I have a long-standing soft spot for Weiner, whom I first met more than twenty years ago, when he was a budding Chuck Schumer prot�g� and we played on the same Capitol Hill softball team. Weiner then was strikingly similar to Weiner now: amped-up, ambitious, wicked smart, forever gauging all the angles, unafraid of being (actually, proud of being) a royal pain in the tuchis. All the qualities, in other words, that have served him so well in the wrangle over health care. Weiner describes his efflorescence on the subject as a matter of opportunism, in the best sense of the word. This was one of those unusual issues where we really didn't have a mother ship that was directing the message

I would also like to take a moment to express my condolences to the families of those who lost their lives in last weekend's plane crash during a U.N. mission. The U.N. mission in Haiti has helped to play an important role in bringing security and stability to some of the most dangerous neighborhoods in Haiti. I continue to support its mission and the many men and women from around the world who work to carry it out. However
column22: it seems that Haiti just can't get to the next step. From assistance to debt relief

column5: after it emerged US President Barack <us_president/> had turned down no fewer than five requests from Downing Street to hold a bilateral meeting at the United Na tions in New York or at the G20 summit starting in Pittsburgh today. The prime minister
column6: eager to portray himself as a leading player on the international stage in America this week
column7: was also forced to play down suggestions from inside his own party that he might step down early

column9: Abdelbaset al-Megrahi. Brown's efforts to secure a prestigious primetime slot for his keynote speech at the general assembly in New York were also thwarted when the Libyan leader

column12: massively running over Brown's 15 minute slot. Brown had not only been seeking a bilateral meeting with <us_president/>
column13: but feelers were also sent out to hold a joint press conference

column15: in an attempt to rebuild relations. No 10 denied there had been any hint of a snub
column16: saying <us_president/> and Brown had plenty of chances to talk as they sat next to one another at the summits. They insisted they were working closely on issues such as future economic regulation

column20: Hu Jintao
column21: the <russia/>n president
column22: Dmitry Medvedev
column23: and the new Japanese prime minister
column24: Yukio Hatoyama. News of the five spurned approaches compounded a miserable day for Brown at home which saw a parliamentary aide resign over the prime minister's refusal to sack Lady Scotland
column25: the attorney general
column26: after she was fined �5
column27: 000 for employing an illegal immigrant
column28: as well as a withering attack by the former home secretary Charles Clarke. Stephen Hesford
column29: Labour MP for Wirral West
column30: told Brown in a resignation letter: "In my view
column31: the facts of the case do not matter. It is the principle which counts
column32: particularly at a time when the public's trust of Whitehall is uncertain to say the least. We have to be seen to be accountable." Brown was also savaged by Charles Clarke
column33: who told the Evening Standard that in his view Brown's leadership risked letting "the whole Labour ship crash on to the rocks of May 2017 [the expected date of the general election] and sink for a very long time". He said he hoped rumours that Brown would quit would come true. "I think his own dignity ought to look to that kind of solution." In two interviews
column34: Brown was forced for the first time to field questions about his health. "My sight is not at all deteriorating

column36: <us_president/> promised an end to the unilateralism marked by the previous Bush administration
