column5: 2017 Op-Ed Columnist <us_president/> Backs Down on Sudan By NICHOLAS D. KRISTOF JUBA
column6: Sudan Until he reached the White House
column7: Barack <us_president/> repeatedly insisted that the United States apply more pressure on Sudan so as to avoid a humanitarian catastrophe in Darfur and elsewhere. Yet
column8: as president
column9: Mr. <us_president/> and his aides have caved
column10: leaving Sudan gloating at American weakness. Western monitors
column11: Sudanese journalists and local civil society groups have all found this month's Sudanese elections to be deeply flawed - yet Mr. <us_president/>'s special envoy for Sudan
column12: Maj. Gen. Scott Gration
column13: pre-emptively defended the elections
column14: saying they would be "as free and as fair as possible." The White House showed only a hint more backbone with a hurried reference this week to "an essential step" with "serious irregularities." President Omar Hassan al-Bashir of Sudan - the man wanted by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity in Darfur - has been celebrating. His regime calls itself the National Congress Party
column15: or N.C.P.
column16: and he was quoted in Sudan as telling a rally in the Blue Nile region: "Even America is becoming an N.C.P. member. No one is against our will." Memo to Mr. <us_president/>: When a man who has been charged with crimes against humanity tells the world that America is in his pocket
column17: it's time to review your policy. Perhaps the <us_president/> administration caved because it considers a flawed election better than no election. That's a reasonable view
column18: one I share. It's conceivable that Mr. Bashir could have won a quasi-fair election - oil revenues have manifestly raised the standard of living in parts of Sudan - and the campaigning did create space for sharp criticism of the government. It's also true that Sudan has been behaving better in some respects. The death toll in Darfur is hugely reduced
column19: and the government is negotiating with rebel groups there. The Sudanese government gave me a visa and travel permits to Darfur
column20: allowing me to travel legally and freely. The real game isn't
column21: in fact
column22: Darfur or the elections but the maneuvering for a possible new civil war. The last north-south civil war in Sudan ended with a fragile peace in 2005
column23: after some two million deaths. The peace agreement provided for a referendum
column24: scheduled to take place in January
column25: in which southern Sudanese will decide whether to secede. They are expected to vote overwhelmingly to form a separate country. Then the question becomes: will the north allow South Sudan to separate? The south holds the great majority of the country's oil
column26: and it's difficult to see President Bashir allowing oil fields to walk away. "If the result of the referendum is independence
column27: there is going to be war - complete war
column28: predicts Mudawi Ibrahim Adam, one of Sudan's most outspoken human rights advocates. He cautions that America's willingness to turn a blind eye to election-rigging here increases the risk that Mr. Bashir will feel that he can get away with war. They're very na�ve in Washington
column29: Mr. Mudawi said. They don't understand what is going on." On the other hand
column30: a senior Sudanese government official
column31: Ghazi Salahuddin
column32: told me unequivocally in Khartoum
column33: the nation's capital
column34: that Sudan will honor the referendum results. And it's certainly plausible that north and south will muddle through and avoid war
column35: for both sides are exhausted by years of fighting. Here in Juba
column36: the South Sudan capital
column37: I met Winnie Wol
column39: who fled the civil war in 1994 after a militia from the north attacked her village to kill
column40: loot
column41: rape and burn. Her father and many relatives were killed
column42: but she escaped and made her way to Kenya - and eventually resettled as a refugee in California. She now lives in Olathe
column43: Kan.
column44: and she had returned for the first time to Sudan to visit a mother and sisters she had last seen when she was a little girl. Ms. Wol
column45: every bit the well-dressed American
column46: let me tag along for her journey back to her village of Nyamlell
column47: 400 miles northwest of Juba. The trip ended by a thatch-roof hut that belonged to her mother
column48: who didn't know she was coming - so no one was home. Ms. Wol was crushed. Then there was a scream and a woman came running. It was Ms. Wol's mother
column49: somehow recognizing her
column50: and they flew into each other's arms. To me
column51: it felt like a peace dividend. Yet that peace is fragile
column52: and Ms. Wol knows that the northern forces may come back to pillage again. "I don't want war
column53: she said, but I don't think they will allow us to separate." My own hunch is that the north hasn't entirely decided what to do
column54: and that strong international pressure can reduce the risk of another savage war. If President <us_president/> is ever going to find his voice on Sudan
column55: it had better be soon. "

column9: a lot of the violence in Cuidad Juarez has historically been targeted against women. In 2002

column12: winning the Annenberg Online Journalism Award
column13: the equivalent of the Pulitzer Prize. &It:script language="JavaScript" type="text/javascript"> document.write('&Ita href="http://clk.atdmt.com/CNT/go/197071989/directwi.728;hi.90/01/" target=" blank"&gtAltimg src="http://view.atdmt.com/CNT/view/197071989/direct;wi.728;hi.90/01/"/>&it ;/a>'); &It:/script><noscript>&Ita href="http://clk.atdmt.com/CNT/go/197071989/direct;wi.728;hi.90/01/" target=" blank"&gtAltimg border="0" src="http://view.atdmt.com/CNTIview/197071989/direct;wi.728;hi.90/01/" />El tia>&lt:/noscript> http://www.salon.com/news/feature/2002/12/04/juarez/print.html Day of the dead More than 325 women have been murdered in the free-trade boomtown of Ciudad Juarez in the past decade. Faced with government incompetence and corruption
column14: people are rebelling. By Max Blumenthal Dec 4
column15: 2002 I The body of another murdered woman was found late last month in the Mexican industrial hub of Ciudad Juarez
column16: dumped behind some shrubs in the squalor of the Anapra neighborhood
column17: a ramshackle hodgepodge of corrugated tin and cardboard shacks on the sludge-washed banks of the Rio Grande. Her hands had been tied
column18: and the evidence suggested she had been raped. The body was so badly decomposed that investigators calculated that she'd been dead for seven months. However horrific the details
column19: they were numbing in their familiarity. The body of a woman who had died in similar circumstances was found in the same dusty lot a couple of months earlier. The bodies of eight women were found in a lot not far away a little more than a year ago. So many women have been murdered here in the past 10 years that there is no reliable count. Most experts place it close to 325
column20: an average of 32 a year
column21: nearly three every month. At least 90 of the deaths are believed to be the work of one or more serial killers. Hundreds more women have simply vanished. Like so many of the others
column22: the woman whose body was found in late October had probably come to Juarez from the poverty of southern Mexico to work for about $10 a day in one of the many foreign-owned assembly plants known as maquiladoras that sprouted up in Juarez after the North American Free Trade Agreement was signed in 1994. And like them
column23: too
column24: her body was unclaimed in death and buried alone and anonymous. Such death has become a way of life here. So
column25: too
column26: with the fear and paranoia that rise in such a climate. Nobody knows who is doing the killings
column27: and the mystery only seems to deepen. Arrests made by local authorities have produced allegations of torture
column28: witness tampering and frame-ups -- but no convictions. Most here believe that the killer or killers must have enormous clout. Perhaps
column29: some say
column30: the killers are narcotrafficantes disposing of witnesses. Perhaps they are the sons of the wealthy and powerful indulging in sick sex. Perhaps they are cultists whose members come from the highest levels of government and finance. The theories differ
column31: but a common assumption is that arrests made thus far are only a smokescreen for an historically opaque and corrupt government that will protect its dark secrets at any cost. One thing seems clear: The murders arise from a social landscape that has been transformed by global economic forces. Where Ciudad Juarez was once a small
column32: sleepy desert outpost just across the border from El Paso
column33: Texas
column34: the population in the past decade has exploded to 1.2 million people
column35: many of them drawn by the lure of the maquiladoras. The tides of people have overwhelmed the ability of the city to absorb them
column36: overwhelmed health services
column37: social services and law enforcement. Free-trade advocates once promised that NAFTA would transform Juarez into the City of the Future -- and they have been proven right in a way they never could have imagined. Today
column38: Juarez still has the feel of the lawless Old West
column39: but with a grim 21st century edge. Despite promises of swift justice from Mexican President Vicente Fox and Chihuahua Gov. Patricio Martinez
column40: they have yet to take up offers of assistance from the FBI; bureau agents in Texas have suggested that official corruption is hindering efforts to stop the murders. Chihuahua state investigators have seemingly adopted a "don't ask
column41: don't tell" policy towards Juarez's homicides
column42: fostering an atmosphere of impunity and pervasive fear. Foreign corporations operating in Juarez that have employed many of the murdered women largely deny that such an atmosphere exists. But in this postmodern urban culture
column43: where the very concept of community has broken down

column53: the mother says in Spanish, her face flaring with anger. They promised me prompt action but when I checked back a week later
column54: the Missing persons report was never filed and the investigation had not even begun. When they finally got witnesses together
column55: none of them would talk because they were too afraid." Even as Mexico continues to make strides toward becoming an open and democratic society
column56: the epidemic of rape and murder here has exposed the heavy residue of its corrupt and authoritarian political legacy as well as the contradictions of its efforts at economic expansion. To understand the magnitude of the breakdown

Imagine that Montgomery County Police Chief Charles Moose held a press conference and asked local citizens to catch the sniper themselves because local police were not up to the task and the federal government was not being helpful; imagine that the federal government charged that local officials in Montgomery County were complicit in the killings and impeding the investigation. Chaos would ensue

column62: or more. That's Juarez today. The jumbled

column66: to 2 million people. Many of them directly or indirectly rely on the 300 or so maquiladoras for their livelihoods. To accommodate the new army of workers
column67: the city has given birth to entirely new sectors. The Campestre Juarez is a luxurious conglomerate of gated communities

column79: the lot bustles as customers scurry back and forth
column80: hauling their purchases to their cars -- a sight similar to any mall in the suburban United States. By night
column81: however

column100: sometimes arriving alone and with little means of contacting their families back home. The maquiladoras

column102: prefer to hire young women for assembly-line jobs. An entry-level assembly-line worker makes minimum wage
column103: about $2 an hour. With experience

column108: the wages that seem so high to new maquiladora workers actually ensure poverty. The workers can be hired and fired on the spot
column109: with little pretext and no legal protection. And union activities are prohibited. Even for those who accept the conditions
column110: security is elusive. More often now
column111: the global companies that own maquiladoras are closing up shop and transferring operations to <china/> to take advantage of lower taxes

column114: at a cost of 900 jobs. On July 1

column119: too. The city's health system
column120: Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social

column122: 000 people falling from its list of insured after losing their company policies

The combination of poverty and a lack of social connections renders women on the assembly line powerless and virtually invisible. And that has made them easy prey. According to the El Paso Times
column127: about a third of the approximately 325 slain women were employed by maquiladoras at the time of their murder. Given that few of the maquiladoras provide shuttle service to and from the colonies
column128: the female workers often are preyed upon while walking through perilous places like Sitio Colosio Valle in the darkness of the early morning. At such an hour
column129: the only nearby activity is that of bars and nightclubs closing up as male patrons filter into the street after a long night of drinking. Besides <china/>'s attractive economic climate
column130: an intangible cause of maquiladora flight is Juarez's chronic violence. The effect is difficult to measure. Two companies in the city's industrial sector -- including TDK
column131: the audio tape maker -- have posted banners on their factories reading: "STOP THE VIOLENCE. To Better Our City

column134: by the dictates of efficiency. They have maintained a stunning silence even as their female workers are slaughtered. Consider the case of 17-year-old Claudia !vette Gonzalez. Her body was found in November 2001 along with seven others in an overgrown cotton field on Avenida Technologico
column135: just blocks from Sitio Colosio Valle mall and across the street from the offices of the Association of Maquiladoras. She had worked on the assembly line for the Lear Corp.
column136: a Detroit-based auto-interior supplier. Lear has declined to publicly address Gonzalez's murder. Greg Bloom
column137: editor of the Frontera Norte Sur -- an Internet news service that focuses on the U.S.-Mexico border -- recalled a conversation with Gonzalez's mother
column138: Josefina
column139: in which she recounted her daughter's last day. In the darkness of the early morning

column142: Claudia lvette was promptly sent away under a policy barring tardy assembly-line workers from their shifts. A half-hour past when she usually would have returned home
column143: her mother knew something was gravely wrong. Her worst fear -- the same nagging fear shared by so many Juarez mothers -- would soon be realized. Andrea Puchalsky
column144: Lear's director of communications
column145: acknowledged that the company has not made any public statements regarding Gonzalez's murder
column146: nor has it enacted any proactive measures to protect employees from another wave of violence. "Adding security is not a question that relates to Lear
column147: she said. [Gonzalez's murder] did not happen on Lear property." When questioned about the murder and Lear policies
column148: Puchalsky mentioned that a company memo was prepared for her with responses to possible questions. As to Lear's worker-lockout policy
column149: which apparently put Gonzalez in a precarious situation the day of her abduction
column150: Puchalsky declined to comment on whether Gonzalez was locked out or sent home from Lear's plant on her last day. "We have a policy for tardiness and she was tardy many times
column151: Puchalsky said. When she had arrived late to work her shift
column152: she was not there in time to work her shift." When asked whether Lear's offices in the U.S. have a similar policy in which late employees are barred from working their shifts
column153: Puchalsky reversed her earlier statement
column154: vehemently denying that such a policy existed anywhere within Lear's operations. "There is not a policy to send a worker home after X number of tardy arrivals
column155: she said. Typically what we do is if there is someone arriving late on kind of a warning system
column156: there might be a notification that 'the next time you arrive late
column157: you have to take a day off ...' It's not a policy
column158: though. There is no written policy like that throughout Lear Corp." The body of 17-year-old Lilia Alejandra Garcia was found mutilated just 300 feet from her maquiladora in February 2001
column159: and since then her case has come to embody the incompetence and corruption of police and prosecutors from Ciudad Juarez to the state capital in Chihuahua City and south all the way to Mexico City. Garcia
column160: the mother of a 5-month-old baby and a 2-year-old child
column161: apparently was kidnapped just after she left work. She was held in captivity for a week
column162: repeatedly beaten and raped
column163: and then strangled. Then-prosecutor Suly Ponce told the Juarez newspaper El Diario that Garcia was the first woman of the year to be murdered and raped in this area of the city - - even though two days before
column164: the body of an unidentified woman was found naked just blocks away. When an FBI leak revealed witness testimony linking Lilia Garcia's killers to drug dealers
column165: Suly Ponce dismissed it
column166: calling it erroneous. She instead blamed workers in a circus across the street from the strip mall where Garcia was last seen. When circus managers claimed that Ponce offered them money to blame co-workers
column167: she dropped the investigation. According to a July article in the El Paso Times
column168: former Chihuahua state forensic chief Oscar Maynez Grijalva said Garcia was killed in a similar manner as three of the eight women found in the cotton field with Claudia 'vette Gonzalez in November 2001. Curiously
column169: local authorities behaved just as evasively in that investigation as in Garcia's. When Gonzalez and the seven other women's bodies were found in November 2001
column170: ex-Chihuahua Attorney General Arturo Gonzalez Rascon immediately fingered two local bus drivers as the culprits. Yet doubts about their guilt arose
column171: especially after Grijalva -- who was Rascon's evidence expert at the time -- resigned from his post
column172: citing pressure to fabricate evidence against them. And the head of a local prison was forced from office when he documented signs of torture on the accused men after they had returned from Rascon's office. Four months later
column173: in February 2002
column174: a search-and-rescue team combing the cotton field found Claudia lvette Gonzalez's overalls in a plastic bag
column175: along with strands of hair and other crucial pieces of evidence that Rascon's investigators had failed to discover. In response
column176: Rascon offered his opinion to the El Paso Times: "The state police have done a thoroughly professional job. I have no doubt about that." But on Oct. 28
column177: DNA results revealed that Rascon's investigators had properly identified only one of the eight dead women -- Gonzalez. Stuck with a far more dubious task than catching one madman or replacing one feeble leader
column178: Juarez's fractured civil society has been paralyzed. A cynical mood is palpable just by speaking to citizens on the street
column179: who unanimously express fear and distrust of law-enforcement and government officials. Some local cops are just as cynical. "We can't just sit around in deserted places waiting for someone to drive up and dump bodies off
column180: said one municipal police officer seated in an idling paddy wagon who refused to give his name for security reasons. There are too few of us and the city's too big ... We don't get much support from the federal government. Judicially
column181: we are not protected like cops in the U.S. Plus
column182: the arms they give us are weak and the bulletproof vests don't really stop bullets. It's not just that
column183: though. I have a young woman in my home so I can put myself in the place of the parents who have lost their daughters. But it's a question of society. We need their support and they need them to be more conscious if it is going to get any better here." The scope of the crime is so enormous
column184: and there has been so little success in stopping it
column185: that suspicion breeds on itself. The litany of theories as to who the killers are and what their motive might be suggests that Juarez has become a breeding ground for every imaginable predator. And yet
column186: nobody knows. Nothing is certain. And that feeds the climate of paranoia. Garcia and Gonzalez's murders are rumored to be the work of a serial killer with possible ties to drug dealers. Yet Garcia was found with marks on her wrists that
column187: according to local forensics experts
column188: were identical to those made by police handcuffs. And upon the discovery of her daughter's overalls
column189: Josefina Gonzalez told the El Paso Times that someone powerful was undoubtedly responsible for the murder. Many in Mexico's law enforcement community agree that a ring of rich men are behind some of the killings
column190: but they have no evidence to support the theory. Some suggest that some young men from the local aristocracy are responsible
column191: but are being protected by their parents. A persistent theory holds that the murders -- or a significant subset of them -- are linked to powerful narcotraficantes who have co-opted segments of the local ruling class. And the cynicism has been exacerbated by the fact that of the 17 men and one woman accused as serial killer masterminds of the murders

column209: Ponce said she hadn't known this. Angela Paiaveras

column212: says Miguel Angel Jaramillo, a mid-level manager for the Lear Corp. It's obvious that they're just scapegoats." Yet Ponce remains ardent in her belief that Sharif is at the center of the murders. "Today the killings continue because there are many imitators

column215: the year immediately after Sharif was jailed -- a period spanning from October 1995 to October 1996 -- 28 young women were found murdered. Meanwhile

column219: powerful men. Another theory posits a financial motive for murder. "We're finding a lot of girls that are mutilated in the same way
column220: says a young municipal police officer who declined to give his name. Someone's probably killing them to take their organs to sell them for a lot of money in the U.S." When asked if there was any evidence to support the theory
column221: the officer replied that it was only a hunch. Such a climate sends a message to the killers every day: You can get away with anything
column222: even a crime on this scale. But where such a climate breeds cynicism and hopelessness among people who live and work here
column223: it has also provoked an incipient revolt. On her radio show "Grueso Calibre" ("Large Caliber")
column224: popular host Samira lzaguirre frequently aired the views of guests who were critical of how authorities handled the murders. When Attorney General Rascon accused the two bus drivers of the cotton field murders in November 2001
column225: lzaguirre hosted the drivers' wives on her show. After that interview
column226: advertisements began appearing in local newspapers smearing lzaguirre with claims that she frequented strip clubs and was romantically involved with one of the bus drivers. News media on both sides of the border have reported that the receipt for the ad was signed by government officials who paid for it. Then

She claims she was threatened by ex-Chihuahua District Attorney Arturo Gonzalez Rascon. "Rascon came all the way to Juarez [from Chihuahua City] to tell me not to involve myself in all the cases
column241: she tells Salon. Then I got a message on my phone saying: 'You have daughters that are alive. Take care of them." Rascon
column242: in an earlier story by the Associated Press

column251: who was two months old. By now their granddaughter would be 7
column252: and Lopez and Aguilar's own investigation has led them to believe that she is alive and living in the custody of a well-connected local family. To an outsider it is a desperate story

Lopez recalls an incident in which he had gone to Juarez's judicial building to press his granddaughter's case and did not exactly find the kind of support Ponce mentioned. While leaving the court
column258: he was confronted by a high- ranking minister who warned that if he didn't drop the investigation

column260: Lopez adds with a wistful smile. Despite the campaign against lzaguirre, or perhaps because of it, the vigil took place as scheduled in March. It was an unprecedented show of solidarity, with thousands of people gathered in the cotton field where Gonzalez and the seven others were found in an irrigation ditch. There are still tatters of yellow police tape there, and candleholders left from the vigil are strewn over the site. Eight red crosses mark the spot where the bodies were found. However, city officials have no plans to memorialize the site as Juarez's residents have. Near downtown Juarez there is a monument to Abraham Lincoln, honoring him for establishing North American industries
column261: today the most important in the world." Not far away is a simple gallery where the Collective Antigone [Antigone Collective]

column263: has organized a series of public performances
column264: installations and conferences focused on Juarez's crisis of violence. Each week
column265: the artists gather to collaborate and discuss strategy. At a table with 12 other artists and writers
column266: in an expansive room filled with cubist-inspired paintings
column267: Antonio Munoz Ortega
column268: a 51-year-old writer
column269: describes the Collective's goals and the problems confronting the group. "Our government is authoritarian
column270: and authoritarian governments are principally concerned with the manipulation of life

He describes the building of an impromptu church in front of the Association of Maquiladoras office as an effort to "communicate through a different language

The Collectiva also has begun to establish a visual presence around central Juarez, most noticeably by painting a wall spanning an entire block with poetry written by participants in a recent writer's conference on violence against women. An estimated 1,500 people viewed the exhibit. It is absolutely necessary to affect civil society with the intention of shaking the indolence and to provoke some sort of reaction from the people

column287: serves as president of one of Banda Civil's six divisions. Guerra tells of how it began as a search-and-rescue group in 1985 to assist during a massive earthquake in Mexico City and evolved to respond to Juarez's crisis. She herself found the first slain women's bodies in 1989

column297: some view it with suspicion. Yet they have had success where most other activist groups have failed. It was Banda Civil members who made the crucial discovery of Claudia lvette Gonzalez's overalls in February

column302: the searches are a family activity. On one recent Saturday
column303: the search was joined by about 60 participants of all ages and from all sectors of Juarez society
column304: including a middle manager from the Lear Corp. There were no terrible discoveries that day
column305: and yet afterward

column5: 2017 I.H.T. Op-Ed Contributor Germany in Need of a Dream By JOHN KORNBLUM Has Germany abandoned Europe? Do Angela Merkel's tough conditions for aid to Greece mean that Germany is no longer the motor of European integration? Has Frau Merkel in fact morphed from the Miss Europa of 2007 to the Fraulein Germania of 2010
column6: as Germany's own former foreign minister Joschka Fischer has suggested? As a former American ambassador who has lived arid worked the better part of four decades around Germany
column7: my Blackberry often glows red hot with messages from persons asking these questions. My response is always the same: Germany has changed very little
column8: but Europe and the world have changed a lot. Therein lies the dilemma. Germany has worked hard to dig its way out of the disaster of 1945
column9: but trauma remains a defining issue for German society. Sixty five years later
column10: Germany is still focused on the three essentials of its recovery: stability
column11: respectability and peace. Keep this triangle in mind and lots of things quickly come into focus. From the first days of the Federal Republic. Germany's leaders emphasized the importance of defining interests solely within a common European and Atlantic vocation. But they also understood that renouncing national ambitions did not remove the responsibility to pursue specific German goals through the common institutions. Many important postwar accomplishments were conceived and pushed by Germany
column12: sometimes over the opposition of others - including the United States. Ostpolitik was controversial for years
column13: as was NATO enlargement. Germany pushed them with determination. Helmut Kohl did not consult before promulgating his 10 points on reunification. He agreed to French desires for a common currency
column14: but only if it could be a mirror of the Deutsche mark
column15: for decades the European monetary standard. The euro stability pact
column16: now the object of so much controversy with Greece
column17: was the result. After 1990
column18: the E.U.'s eastward expansion was Germany's way of firming up its Eastern flank. Slowly and without fanfare
column19: Germany has been remaking the European Union in its image. At each step of the way
column20: Germany made its wishes more palatable by paying more than its share. Part of today's misunderstanding is caused by Germany's success in using its contributions to build an image of selflessness. Germany has been as single-minded in pursuit of its goals as Charles de Gaulle ever was for his
column21: but it almost always left leadership to others. A new consciousness grew after the costs of reunification began to mount. "Europe" in the institutional sense has become increasingly unpopular. German courts have begun to define German European issues in the context of the German Constitution rather than on the basis of E.U. law. At least some of Ms. Merkel's refusal to allow immediate assistance to Greece was based on her fears that it would fan anti-E.U. sentiment at home. Are these the first signs of a German Tea Party? Here we find the source of most of the hand wringing about Germany's role as the "motor of Europe." Ms. Merkel's unwillingness to sweeten the financial pot echoed throughout Brussels. To many
column22: it signified the decline of German willingness to "salute the French flag three times before raising the German flag
column23: as Konrad Adenauer used to put it. Germans are not alone in objecting to throwing more money into the E.U. pot, but they happen to be the only ones who can do something about it. Many fear that without German complaisance, the E.U. will stutter to a stop. But such self- denial could never offer a viable foundation for a new Europe. Neither could the inefficiency and even corruption that characterizes many E.U. programs. Most maddening for most thinking Europeans is the knowledge that the Germans are right. But to them, the question is whether Germany is remaking the E.U. in a fashion palatable to the majority of other member states. They are not so sure that its focus on stability and accountability is the right way to help such a diverse collection of peoples adjust to a globalized world. And so when Angela Merkel raps Greek knuckles, she is sending a message most Europeans don't want to hear. Not that Germany is dangerous; even worse, that it is unrelenting. The Neue aricher Zeitung probably spoke for many others when it once accused Germany of wanting Europe to become a large Switzerland. The growing gap between Germany's aspirations and the perceived needs of other members of the E.U. is beginning to burden both sides. Most Europeans are simply not ready to live up to German standards. Without a more flexible sense of common purpose, the project to build a democratic Europe could stop dead in the water. But as Germans will themselves often tell you: They have forgotten how to dream. Younger Germans feel this lack of inspiration as well. Dreams were what 200,000 of them were waiting to hear when they rallied to hear Barack <us_president/> in Berlin two summers ago. They wanted more than to Dare to Hope
column24: which is the characteristically timid German translation of the title of the president's best seller. And they are still waiting. America seems busy elsewhere. The main conclusion I draw from the debate about Germany is that it is not about Germany at all. The task of building a democratic Europe is far from complete. Most of the foundations have been laid and now the residents are starting to haggle over the design. Weaving today's 27 states into a true trans-Atlantic partnership is a task that is too big for Germany or even Europe to accomplish alone. They desperately need some skilled architectural assistance. Uniting Europe and North America is the most audacious project ever conceived. If it works, the United States will be joined by nearly 500 million Europeans to form a democratic space, within which modern democratic values will harness more energy than in any single nation on earth. Democracy's future as the operating system for a globalized world will be assured. European fecklessness seems to worry Washington officials these days. But if Germany has forgotten how to dream and the United States is too busy to try, we will both be guilty of perpetuating the aimlessness we so criticize. To hold up its side of the bargain, Europe needs exactly what Barack <us_president/> originally promised - the audacity of hope. John Kornblum, senior counselor with the international law firm Noerr LLP in Berlin, served as the U.S. ambassador to Germany from 1997 to 2001.

column13: said a senior U.S. official involved in the nuclear diplomacy. The official highlighted the importance of raising Mideast nuclear-free zone issues. column3: 20106:23 PM \nTo: Subject FW: fyi FYI http://thecable.foreignpolicy.com/posts/2010/03/10/lugar no more money for development banks until reform Lugar: No more money for development banks until reform Posted By Josh Rogin Wednesday
column4: March 10
column5: 2017 In the wake of the global financial crisis
column6: a slew of multinational development banks are asking for large amounts of new capital to both replenish and in some cases expand their resource pools
column7: and much of the burden will fall on the United States. This creates a unique opportunity for the <us_president/> administration to press these organizations to implement long-awaited reforms
column8: according to the Senate's top Republican on foreign relations
column9: who has a big say in whether and how the Congress doles out the funds. "As the world struggles to emerge from the worst economic crisis since World War II
column10: it is an appropriate time to ask whether the [International Financial Institutions] are performing optimally and doing the jobs they should be doing
column11: reads a newly released report by the staff of Sen. Richard Lugar, R-IN, The crisis should not be used as an excuse to win increases that could not otherwise be justified. As the requests for capital are negotiated with the international donor community
column12: there is a window of opportunity for significant reform." The report
column13: which is the culmination of six years of research
column14: including half a dozen hearings when Lugar was committee chairman
column15: outlines several dozen recommendations for what the <us_president/> administration
column16: Congress
column17: and the banks can do to update their relevance. "Does the world really need the IMF
column18: World Bank
column19: African Development Bank
column20: Asian Development Bank
column21: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
column22: and Inter-American Development Bank today? Can they be changed to better address our needs? How should we re-design them?" the report asks. "Such questions are particularly timely because nearly all the IFIs have sought
column23: or will soon seek
column24: major new infusions of money from their donors
column25: including the taxpayers of the United States." The Asian Development Bank has already asked the <us_president/> administration for new funds
column26: and the administration has requested in its new budget $533 million in direct money and $12.8 billion in borrowing authority for the ADB. A committee staffer told The Cable that Lugar wants to see progress on reform before he would support authorizing the money. "We want to make sure that before the American taxpayer puts more money in there that things are fixed
column27: the staffer said. It's not possible for them to do everything
column28: but they could certainly make progress." The reforms the administration could press for in the short term include pressing the banks to focus more on development goals rather than the structure and size of loans and "work with the other donor countries to step back and slow down the process
column29: the staffer said. Congress is also concerned that the <us_president/> administration might not be interested in pressing for these reforms, considering that <us_president/> issued a signing statement in June indicating he did not feel bound to follow congressional direction on such international negotiations. Negotiations between several banks and the Treasury Department are ongoing. The U.S. side is led by Scott Morris, deputy assistant<commander_title/>of the Treasury's Office of International Development Finance and Debt. The issue will next surface at the end of March when the Inter-American Development Bank convenes its annual meeting in Cancun. Michael H. Fuchs U.S. Department of State (202) 647-1709

column3: 2017 10:16 AM <commander_initials/>: Haaretz chief columnist on Bibi's visit. Sid htto://www. haaretz.com/hasers/spagesil 158992. html Aluf Benn / <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> leaves U.S. disgraced
column4: isolated and weaker By Ake Berm Details emerging from <friendly_nation_leader_name/>'s visit to Washington remain incomplete
column5: but the conclusion may nonetheless be drawn that the prime minister erred in choosing to fly to the United States this week. The visit - touted as a fence- mending effort
column6: a bid to strengthen the tenuous ties between <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> and U.S. President Barack <us_president/> - only highlighted the deep rift between the American and <friendly_nation_peoples/> administrations. The prime minister leaves America disgraced
column7: isolated
column8: and altogether weaker than when he came. Instead of setting the diplomatic agenda
column9: <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> surrendered control over it. Instead of leaving the <Palestinian/> issue aside and focusing on <iran/>
column10: as he would like
column11: <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> now finds himself fighting for the legitimacy of <friendly_nation_peoples/> control over East Jerusalem. Advertisement The most sensitive and insoluble core issues - those which when raised a decade ago led to the dissolution of the peace process and explosion of the second intifada - are now being served as a mere appetizer. At the start of his visit
column12: <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> was tempted to bask in the warm welcome he received at the AIPAC conference
column13: at which he gave his emotional address on Jerusalem. Taking a page from Menachem Begin
column14: he spoke not on behalf of the State of <friendly_nation_name/>
column15: but in the name of the Jewish people itself and its millennia of history. His speech was not radical rightist rhetoric. Reading between the lines
column16: one could spot a certain willingness to relinquish West Bank settlements as long as <friendly_nation_name/> maintains a security buffer in the Jordan Valley. But at the White House
column17: the prime minister's speech to thousands of pro-<friendly_nation_name/> activists and hundreds of cheering congressmen looked like an obvious attempt to raise political capital against the American president. Knowing <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> would be reenergized by his speech at the lobby
column18: <us_president/> and his staff set him a honey trap. Over the weekend they sought to quell the row that flared up during U.S. Vice President Joe Biden's trip here two weeks ago
column19: and U.S. <commander_title/> <commander_name/> described <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/>'s response to the ultimatums Washington presented to him as "useful." Special envoy George Mitchell made a televised visit to the prime minister's bureau Sunday to invite <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> to the White House. Washington
column20: it seemed
column21: was trying to make nice. Far from it. Just when <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> thought he had resolved the crisis by apologizing to Biden
column22: <commander_lastname/> called him up for a dressing down. This time as well
column23: <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> almost believed the crisis had passed
column24: that he had survived by offering partial. noncommittal answers to the Americans' questions. Shortly before meeting with <us_president/>
column25: <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> even warned the <Palestinian/>s that should they continue to demand a freeze on construction
column26: he would postpone peace talks by a year. His arrogant tone underscored the fact that <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> believed that on the strength of his AIPAC speech
column27: he could call the next few steps of the diplomatic dance. But then calamity struck. At their White House meeting
column28: <us_president/> made clear to his guest that the letter <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> had sent was insufficient and returned it for further corrections. Instead of a reception as a guest of honor
column29: <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> was treated as a problem child
column30: an army private ordered to do laps around the base for slipping up at roll call. The revolution in the Americans' behavior is clear to all. On Sunday morning <us_president/> was still anxiously looking ahead to the House of Representatives vote on health care - the last thing he wanted was a last-minute disagreement with congressmen over ties with <friendly_nation_name/>. The moment the bill was passed
column31: however
column32: a victorious <us_president/> was free to deal with his unruly guest. The Americans made every effort to downplay the visit. As during his last visit in November
column33: <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> was invited to the White House at a late hour
column34: without media coverage or a press conference. If that were not enough
column35: the White House spokesman challenged <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/>'s observation at AIPAC that "Jerusalem is not a settlement." The Americans didn't even wait for him to leave Washington to make their disagreement known. It was not the behavior Washington shows an ally
column36: but the kind it shows an annoyance. The approval of construction at the Shepherd Hotel in Sheikh Jarrah
column37: announced before his meeting with <us_president/>
column38: again caught <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> unawares. Apparently the special panel appointed after the Ramat Shlomo debacle to prevent such surprises failed its first test. <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> is having his most difficult week since returning to office
column39: beginning with the unfortunate decision to relocate the planned emergency room at Ashkelon's Barzilai Medical Center and lasting through his humiliating jaunt through Washington. Returning to <friendly_nation_name/> today
column40: <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> will need to work hard to rehabilitate his image
column41: knowing full well that <us_president/> will not relent
column42: but instead demand that he stop zigzagging and decide
column43: once and for all
column44: whether he stands with America or with the settlers. "

column9: 2017 Haiti recovery blueprint includes foreign donors BY JACQUELINE CHARLES jcharles@MiamiHerald.corn Call it the $100 million club. That's the amount each donor nation will have to ante up for a say in Haiti's early recovery under a plan Haitian President Rene Preval plans to present at an international donors conference in New York at month's end. While Haitian and foreign disaster experts were tallying the cost to rebuild after the Jan. 12
column10: 7.0-magnitude earthquake -- $11.5 billion -- Preval and his advisors have been quietly negotiating the blueprint of the development plan that will shape Haiti's reconstruction over the next decade. "It moves it in the right direction
column11: Mark Schneider, senior vice president of the Washington D.C.-based International Crisis Group, said of the plan, which he has seen. I've said
column12: the first phase of reconstruction is a decade. The real test is a generation and hopefully with partnerships both inside and outside of Haiti
column13: it will continue for that time period." The plan includes creation of an Interim Haitian Recovery Commission that will -- for the first time -- seek to guide how and where aid is spent by giving both Haitians and foreigners a vote in reconstruction priorities and projects over the next 18 months. Haiti's president will retain veto power and there's a starring role for former U.S. President Bill <commander_lastname/> if he wants it. The blueprint is certain to come under plenty of scrutiny in Haiti
column14: a country plagued and in-fighting among donors. Over the years
column15: billions of dollars in aid -- often delivered after hurricanes or political coups -- has failed to produce any signs of lasting progress in a country that remains the poorest in the Western Hemisphere. <commander_lastname/>
column16: who is to visit Haiti Monday along with former President George W. Bush
column17: will be asked to help lead Haiti's reconstruction planning over the short-term as co-chair -- along with the Haitian prime minister - - of the commission
column18: several sources confirmed to The Miami Herald. <commander_lastname/>
column19: who is already in charge of the international relief effort for the United Nations
column20: has not said whether he'll accept the job as Haiti's reconstruction czar but he has championed the strategy
column21: saying the goal is to provide to Haitians the success that has long eluded them.He and Bush are visiting Haiti
column22: where more than 200
column23: 000 people were killed in the quake
column24: in their roles as co-chairs of the <commander_lastname/> Bush Haiti Fund. The private U.S. fundraising effort
column25: initiated by President <us_president/>
column26: has raised more than $36 million. The commission's goal will be to plan and coordinate reconstruction priorities and projects over the next 18 months with recommendations from a 20-member board made up of Haitians and foreign donors. Eventually
column27: the commission would morph into the Haiti Development Authority (HDA)
column28: a central planning agency tasked with approving all reconstruction projects in Haiti regardless of which country or aid agency is funding it. The authority's executive director
column29: like that of the commission
column30: likely would be a well-respected Haitian. "Haitians must have the chance to lead the rebuilding of Haiti
column31: said U.S. <commander_title/> <commander_initials/> <commander_lastname/>'s chief of staff Brooke Mille, a key person in talks. Development authorities have helped other countries that have large donor communities to accomplish their visions -- we want no less for Haiti and its citizens." The original plan
column32: first reported by The Herald last month
column33: was modeled on the successful reconstruction authority created in Indonesia after the 2004 tsunami and presented by Mills to Preval and top Haitian officials last month. Other countries and multilateral institutions also presented plans to the Haitian government. The U.S. plan has since undergone several revisions at Preyal's urging. Among them: offering a voting seat on the commission's board to each donor pledging $100 million or more over the next two years and donors who provide $200 million in debt cancellation. As a result
column34: Venezuela is among the likely donors to help review and approve projects. Initially 16 members
column35: the board was expanded to give a say-so to Haiti's private sector and labor unions and the 15-nation sub-regional Caribbean Community (CARCIOM). The plan also establishes a Multi-donor Trust Fund
column36: administered by the World Bank
column37: to possibly pool donors' dollars for reconstruction projects. For decades
column38: Haiti has been plagued by a lack of planning and coordination among donor nations and aid groups as they battled among each other in the poverty-stricken country. Using the Indonesian model employed in Indonesia after the Asian tsunami
column39: plan supporters say the reconstruction commission offers Haiti the best chance to lead its own redevelopment and to change the way donors do business
column40: ending an era where aid groups spend budgets larger than Haitian ministries without any accountability to the Haitian people. But that can only be achieved in Haiti
column41: say supporters
column42: if donors and their projects are coordinated
column43: and in line with Haiti's vision and post-disaster reconstruction needs
column44: which will be presented at the March 31 New York conference and remains a work in progress while the government seeks input from various Haitian groups
column45: including the Diaspora. Also Haiti's parliament must vote on the creation of the Interim Haitian Recovery Commission. Still
column46: the idea of putting Haiti's reconstruction into the hands of one central authority -- or having some donors channel their money into a trust fund -- is not without detractors. Some argue that the authority could render government ministries obsolete because projects would now bypass them
column47: while others point out that a similar World Bank fund in the Sudan has been troubled by rules leaving schools and healthcare facilities undone as hundreds of millions of dollars remain unspent. Meanwhile
column48: Haitian government officials worry that donors may not want to change the way they do business with Haiti
column49: rendering the reconstruction a failure before it gets started. "The creation of the [trust fund] or the [Haiti Development Authority] are improvements to changing the paradigm if and only if everybody plays the game -- putting most of their money in the fund -- and access to the funds is more flexible than the usual process of disbursing from the international donors
column50: Haitian Prime Minister Jean-Max Bellerive told The Herald. In the past, donors have pledged hundreds of millions of dollars to assist Haiti but have fallen short in disbursing those dollars -- or at times spent the money on projects without consulting the Haitian government about whether the projects were needed. Last week, as representatives of the Haitian government and others met to prepare for the New York conference, Bellerive warned that New York could be a failure if we don't reach an agreement on the structure for the coordination and the organization of the trust fund. ..(and) don't manage to establish together the priorities for immediate investments

column4: 2017 10:46 AM \nTo: Subject message from Jerry Hauer re Haiti coordindation Jerry
column5: as you may recall
column6: was Guiliani's homeland security guy in NYC and became B6 one of the world's experts. He also worked for <commander_lastname/> Admn and helped with disaster relief (including earthquakes) around the world. He called me today with some suggestions (some of which may be moot)
column7: so I asked him to put them into a memo. Here it is
column8: for what it's wort<commander_initials/>: I think the fundamental issue is that no one seems to be in charge and no one person has been tasked with trying to pull all of the pieces together into a short term and long term plan. Obviously in the short term
column9: search and rescue and food and water are the main priorities. There seems to be little communication between the various areas where people have congregated and a central command post where agencies can call or radio for additional supplies including food
column10: water and medical. I don't recommend DoD be put in charge of this. They rarely have the kind of touch that brings together all the necessary agencies under one roof. I would set up a central command that has representatives from all federal agencies in one place. There is no reason things should be this disorganized. I would break the island into grids and assign one person to be the coordinator for each of the grids. That person will be responsible for all activities within their grid and will report activities to the island on-scene coordinator. We should get a radio company like Motorola to set up temporary towers and give the State Department several hundred radios so everyone involved in the response is able to communicate with the command post and with each other. I think one of the most important roles for DoD is to provide security for the rescue teams and medical teams. They also should be responsible for the operation of the airport
column11: for off loading planes and for scheduling all incoming flights so there is no lost time waiting for planes to land. I also think DoD should be responsible for airlifting supplies that are requested by each one of the grid coordinators. Additionally
column12: the helicopters should be used to move critical patients to the hospital ship on the way and to the aircraft carrier currently on station. At least once a day
column13: the coordinator assigned by the President and the <commander_title/> should be responsible for getting situation reports from all agencies on site
column14: particularly regarding food and water
column15: security
column16: medical and search and rescue. The lack of command and control is allowing the situation to become more chaotic rather than more coordinated. I believe that if the<commander_title/>were to talk to the other nations involved through the UN
column17: they would be supportive of better coordination. Bottom line is that there is no order to the operation and you need strong people in there who can speak on behalf of the President and the Secretary and get things under control quickly. I hope this is helpful. If you or the<commander_title/>have any questions please feel free to call me on my cell We leave for Tokyo at 7:15 am tomorrow and transfer to a United flight due back in DC at 2:30 pm tomorrow. Please give the<commander_title/>my best regards. I hope to see you soon. B6 "

column17: but both are also resistant to key elements of <us_president/>'s policies. Handling them well requires skillful and subtle diplomacy by the U.S. president and by those who carry out his policies. And <us_president/> has not done well. In fact
column18: his treatment of the <friendly_nation_peoples/> and <conflict_1_peoples/> leaders during one week in late March -- immediately after his victory on health care -- marked a low point of his performance as president. First
column19: <us_president/> seized on an errant <friendly_nation_peoples/> announcement about housing construction in East Jerusalem to reopen a pointless battle with <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/>. During a disastrous March 23 meeting at the White House
column20: <us_president/> demanded - - in vain -- that <friendly_nation_name/> stop all building in Jerusalem; and at one point he left <friendly_nation_leader_lastname/> and his delegation to stew in the Roosevelt room while he retired to the second-floor residence for dinner. Five days later
column21: <us_president/> flew to <conflict_1_capital/> for another cold meeting
column22: this time with <conflict_1_president/>. In a briefing for reporters on the plane
column23: national security adviser James Jones made it clear that <us_president/> was displeased with <conflict_1_president/>'s lack of progress since beginning a new term as president last fall. In case there was any doubt

column27: after a couple of weeks of sulking
column28: he defiantly announced that settlement construction in Jerusalem would continue. <conflict_1_president/> summoned <<iran/>ian/> President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad to <conflict_1_capital/>

column40: even if he wanted to. <us_president/> has to find a way to coax each of them toward a change of course. Public bullying won't do it. Assurances of U.S. support and stroking by special envoys go only so far. What's missing is personal chemistry and confidence

column24: Just to put this into perspective....yes
column25: the UN Flash Appeal for Haiti is only funded at 48% ($718 million). Just for comparison
column26: here are figures for other UN humanitarian appeals: DRC is funded at 5%
column27: Sudan at 23%
column28: <conflict_1_name/> at 31%
column29: Kenya at 18%
column30: Chad at 4%. Clearly
column31: not all disasters/responses are the same. Perhaps the scenario that most closely approximates the needs generated by the Haiti earthquake is that of the Indian Ocean tsunami (2004/2005). Oddly enough
column32: the UN Flash Appeal for the Indian Ocean Tsunami ran to $1.4 billion (the exact same figure as for the Haiti Flash Appeal). In the end
column33: the UN humanitarian appeal for the Indian Ocean tsunami stood at $1.2 billion (a coverage rate of 85%). In the worst of disasters
column34: the funding for UN humanitarian appeals never reaches 100%. We should not forget that there is an enormous amount of money being funneled through channels outside the UN appeal system. For example
column35: the Red Cross movement (including IFRC
column36: ICRC and the national societies) has raised between $700 and $800 million for Haiti. The American Red Cross alone raised $400 million (they project that it will take them five years to spend this money on relief and recovery activities in Haiti). InterAction
column37: the consortium of US- based NGOs has announced that its members have raised nearly $700 million for relief and early recovery activities in Haiti. I met with two NGOs today: OXFAM has raised over $100 million. World Vision has raised $250 million specifically for its earthquake response in Haiti (on top of its regular budget of $50 million for Haiti). We haven't been able to get reliable figures on what non-US NGOs have raised
column38: but I would imagine it to be considerable (at least over $500 million as a conservative estimate). Clearly
column39: there is an enormous amount of money raised for Haiti relief and recovery efforts through the UN system and outside the UN system. The challenge is to get an accurate tally of the funding available from UN agencies
column40: lOs and NGOs (perhaps a tasking for the OSE and/or OCHA) and maximize coordination among the various agencies holding this money to improve allocation of resources. There very well may be underfunded sectors and overfunded sectors in terms of the humanitarian response. Information sharing among donors and aid agencies sitting on funding is critical to avoid spending too much money in some sectors/geographic areas and spending too little in others. column3: RECENTLY TRAVELED TO MALI AND THROUGHT COTE D'IVOIRE"|"June 30
column4: 2017 Dear Mr. John Olver: We thought you would be interested to know that three members of Kaleidoscope Trio
column5: located in your district
column6: recently traveled to Mali and throughout Cote d'Ivoire as part of the Performing Arts Initiative
column7: a cultural exchange program supported by the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs. This program is an important way to engage foreign audiences by providing U.S. embassies financial support for presentations of American performing arts and artists. We received excellent feedback on the Kaleidoscope Trio. This outstanding jazz ensemble delighted hundreds of people in Mali through concerts and many thousands more through feature programming on nationwide radio and TV outlets. During stops in Yamoussoukro
column8: Tiassele
column9: and Abidjan
column10: the group conducted participatory workshops and discussions for nearly 475 students. The ensemble's packed schedule included workshops at the Bamako School for the Blind as well as music and high schools throughout the capital; an outdoor concert for 500 in a town in southwest Mali; and
column11: a joint performance with Grammy-nominated Malian artist Bassekou Kouyate. The Trio members' willingness to provide free music lessons during their downtime deeply impressed Malian audiences. Perhaps the greatest cultural exchange occurred in Abidjan when group member
column12: Gilad Dobrecky
column13: was presented with an "ahoko
column14: an African percussion instrument, and to the surprise and enjoyment of the audience seamlessly incorporated it into the trio's repertoire. We are thrilled to have the opportunity to showcase America's accomplished and talented artists through our cultural projects. Your constituents' willingness to undertake the rigors of international travel to engage foreign audiences, foster goodwill and provide insight into our culture and values makes them true citizen diplomats. We are grateful to them for helping us accomplish our country's foreign policy objectives. Sincerely, Maura M. Pally Deputy Assistant<commander_title/>for Professional and Cultural Exchanges The Honorable John Olver, House of Representatives.

column25: Reconstruction is to rebuild the region: rebuilding the economy (production
column26: trade and banking); the transportation
column27: telecommunications
column28: and social and cultural systems; improving institutional capacity; and housing. 4. The Government set up a ministerial-level agency to manage the MPRR program from Aceh itself
column29: the Rehabilitation and Reconstruction Agency for Aceh and Nias. The BRR was formally established end April 2005 and became operational early May. The World Bank Board on 30 March 2005 formally established the Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDF) with a Steering Committee comprised of BRR
column30: GOI
column31: donors and civil society. Having a credible local coordinators was key to success. 5. The EC channels nearly 93% of its funds through the MDF

column33: disbursements out of it were to begin with even slower. By October 2005
column34: project agreements for about USD 200 million had been signed
column35: but only USD 3 million had actually been disbursed. Disbursements picked up the pace thereafter. The delay was caused by two principal impediments: first
column36: donors were quick to pledge funds
column37: but getting all the exact written agreements in place took time. This points to the need for donors to be flexible regarding formal agreements
column38: and accept simple
column39: generic paragraphs that can contribute to speedy resolution of slightly differing phrasings and concerns. Second
column40: the processing time for project approval and implementation was a concern. Since the MDF was to have funded projects on-budget
column41: they had to be implemented by government institutions. This crated bottlenecks. 6. Smaller donors joined because they wished to support the reconstruction efforts in Aceh but do not have own capacity and often not strong views on how best to pursue this. They want the Bank to assume fiduciary responsibilities for the funds in a high-risk environment
column42: and also to take a lead in ensuring that the funds go to prioritized activities. The MDF is thus seen a well-managed bank account with some paid- for administrative services. However
column43: the all-inclusive Steering Committee made membership large and to some extent unwieldy
column44: and forced it to discuss both policy and operational issues. 7. The Multi Donor Fund Secretariat has developed an Outreach Strategy that includes regular radio talk shows
column45: field visits to meet and discuss with beneficiaries and communication through advertisements as well as a telephone hotline. 8. column46: relevance and impact. 9. Because the MDF does not accept strict ear marking of donor contributions - though it does allow for preference indications - it means that the funds are freely available for programming according to the criteria and priorities that the MDF agrees to. Given strong GOI participation
column47: the MDF is seen as the most successful instrument for harmonization and coordination in an environment that has been criticized for a lack of coordination. column2: 20-22 November 2017 Council Report - Issue Overview (page 1) Council Name: GAC on Fragile States States suffering fragility are those states where the national public authority is not providing the basic public goods that allow their societies to live in peace and improve their prospects for the future. These are states that do not provide (1) accountable and effective security and social protection; (2) predictable and enforced laws that are generally accepted as legitimate; (3) revenue collection and management of external aid to ensure the delivery of basic social and economic services to society; (4) mechanisms of accountability of state authorities to society. These states are vulnerable to both internal and external shocks and thus their populations are likely to suffer the most from the vagaries of climate change and the impact of droughts and flooding
column3: regional insecurity
column4: and regional and international economic crises. They are marked by low food security
column5: high crime rates and high youth unemployment and are susceptible to the mobilisation efforts of entrepreneurs of violence of all sorts. In all these respects they represent the weakest links in the global community. The causes of state fragility are varied and historically and context specific
column6: so action by the international community needs to be based on an understanding of the particularities of each fragile situation. While not all states marked by poverty and underdevelopment are fragile
column7: almost all fragile states are poor and underdeveloped
column8: so international action needs to be concerned with the reduction of poverty and the creation of wealth in these societies. The past half century of experience underscores that reforming the institutions and organisations of the state in fragile states is a decadal
column9: possibly even generational challenge. The international community must consider what needs to be done today or tomorrow to create the stability and breathing space that will allow these longer term efforts to take root and flourish In recent years the international community has increasingly recognised that to ensure a prosperous and secure global community there is a need to increase foreign assistance to fragile states and to support processes of state-building. We follow the OECD in recognizing that state-building is "an endogenous process to enhance capacity
column10: institutions and legitimacy of the state driven by state-society relations". Important analytical work on understanding the conditions of fragility and the requirements of external assistance to state-building has been undertaken by the OECD
column11: the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund and by individual bilateral development agencies. The Council wishes to build on these initiatives
column12: avoid duplication and draw attention to areas that have not received enough attention. Council Report - Summarized Proposal(s) (page 2) Council Name: GAC on Fragile States Innovating in Governance in fragile states: A New System of Mutual Responsibility in Delivering Basic Economic and Social Services In fragile states
column13: there is a challenge to meet the urgent needs of the population through the delivery of essential social and economic services
column14: while building sustainable and accountable systems of public authority. Often states are heavily dependent on external resources to finance such services and the challenge is to put these to good use without undermining incentives to raise domestic revenue that can eventually replace external assistance. Donors in a hurry to see that funds are spent effectively often channel them outside state systems
column15: which can undermine or pre-empt the consolidation of viable and accountable state organisations. At the same time
column16: for understandable reasons
column17: donors are cautious about budget support
column18: where blank cheques are written to governments without assurances that accountability standards will be met. The existing tools of development assistance
column19: however appropriate for delivering aid to poor but stable and relatively well functioning states
column20: are not adequate for confronting the conditions of state fragility: where people have a deep distrust of states where states are often weak and repressive where societies nonetheless have considerable resilience The costs of donor mistakes in delivering aid are high everywhere
column21: but in fragile states the costs can be catastrophic
column22: leading to state collapse
column23: violence and in the worst cases regional instability and war. The existence of fragile states compels us to look for imaginative solutions. An innovative approach will ensure: Mutual responsibility between donors and states in spending public resources Accountability to local communities in how public resources are spent Building upon existing local capacities and drawing on capacities at the regional and national levels Delivering resources in ways perceived as equitable and iust Long term commitment by donors that matches the long term task of overcoming fragility Objectives: A New Aid Delivery Mechanism would: 1. Allow for domestic resources to be collected and donor moneys channelled according to a set of accountability mechanisms that would be transparently measured and reported upon; and 2. Key policies and services to be implemented through "National Programs" that would implement specific functions at the appropriate level of governance
column24: through a system of implementation within state systems
column25: thereby avoiding the creation of parallel organisations outside the state and instead contributing to developing state systems that can eventually replace external aid with domestic revenue; 3. Ensure that representative organisations in society have the opportunity and means to participate in
column26: monitor and supervise the exercise of power and dispensation of public resources. Means: 1. A set of Accountability Standards across the key state functions should be agreed

column29: asset disposal and acquisition
column30: budgets
column31: expenditures
